title: ARISE: Adaptive Agentic Reasoning with Image-grounded Self-Evaluation for Interpretable IBD Assessment
abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) requires frequent imaging-based assessment, yet interpretation of modalities such as wireless capsule endoscopy (WCE) and intestinal ultrasound remains heavily dependent on specialist expertise. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) demonstrate significant potential in multimodal medical image analysis, but their clinical adoption is hindered by their insufficient domain-specific reasoning, susceptibility to hallucination, scarcity of high quality training data in fine-grained diagnostics and limited interpretability. We introduce ARISE (Adaptive Agentic Reasoning with Image-grounded Self-Evaluation), an autonomous planning framework that models few-shot medical image understanding as a sequential agentic workflow. ARISE structures agent execution into a transparent 5-stage workflow: hypothesis generation, image-grounded evidence summarization, evidence-conditioned refinement, symbolic verification, and final diagnosis. We apply ARISE to IBD assessment across two independent patient cohorts: wireless capsule endoscopy (WCE) images for Crohn's disease and B-mode ultrasound data for ulcerative colitis. ARISE consistently improves diagnostic performance over baseline VLMs while exposing where reasoning succeeds or fails, providing a more interpretable basis for clinical decision support and realistic deployment.

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AS A DECISION-SUPPORT TOOL FOR MATERIAL SELECTION IN PROSTHODONTICS: AN ANALYTICAL REVIEW OF THE LITERATURE
abstract: Background. The rapid development of digital dentistry and artificial intelligence (AI) is expanding the range of technologies available for diagnosis, treatment planning, prosthetic design, and outcome prediction. Material selection remains a clinically important component of prosthodontic treatment because the choice of restorative material must account for mechanical, functional, biological, and esthetic requirements. Aim. To analyze recent literature on the application of AI in prosthodontics, with particular attention to its potential role in supporting restorative material selection, integrating clinical and digital parameters, predicting prosthetic outcomes, and personalizing treatment planning. Materials and methods. A narrative analytical review was developed from literature published during seven completed calendar years (January 2019–December 2025). Relevant publications were identified in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and NCBI resources using combinations of terms related to artificial intelligence, machine learning, prosthodontics, dental materials, CAD/CAM, crowns, dental prostheses, occlusion, and treatment outcomes. Publications were thematically analyzed according to AI application, type of prosthodontic task, data source, clinical purpose, reported outcomes, and limitations. Results. The reviewed literature demonstrates that AI is increasingly applied in prosthodontic diagnostics, treatment planning, automated crown design, finish-line detection, occlusal assessment, prediction of prosthetic outcomes, and digital workflows. AI-assisted CAD systems have shown potential to improve design efficiency and, in selected studies, achieve clinically acceptable crown fit. However, the evidence remains heterogeneous with substantial differences in datasets, algorithms, validation procedures, and outcome measures. Direct evidence supporting independently validated AI systems for individualized restorative material selection remains limited. Current evidence therefore supports the use of AI primarily as a clinical decision-support tool rather than as an autonomous system for material selection. Conclusions. AI has considerable potential to support individualized material selection and prosthodontic treatment planning by integrating multiple clinical and digital parameters. At the same time, current evidence does not support treating AI as an autonomous replacement for professional clinical judgment. Direct validation of AI systems specifically designed to select restorative materials remains limited, and many predictive models require stronger external validation and prospective clinical evaluation. The most appropriate current framework is therefore a human-in-the-loop decision-support model in which AI augments, rather than replaces, clinical expertise

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN DENTISTRY: CURRENT APPLICATIONS, ADVANCEMENTS, CHALLENGES, AND FUTURE PERSPECTIVES
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as one of the most transformative technologies in modern healthcare and is increasingly influencing contemporary dental practice.Recent advancements in machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, and generative AI have enabled the development of intelligent systems capable of analyzing complex clinical, radiographic, and histopathological datasets with remarkable precision.AI applications have demonstrated substantial benefits across multiple dental specialties, including oral radiology, oral pathology, orthodontics, periodontology, prosthodontics, conservative dentistry and endodontics, oral and maxillofacial surgery, pediatric dentistry, and public health dentistry.These technologies facilitate early disease detection, automated image interpretation, treatment planning, outcome prediction, and workflow optimization.The integration of AI with digital dentistry technologies such as cone-beam computed tomography, intraoral scanners, computer-aided design/computer-aided manufacturing systems, and electronic health records has accelerated its adoption in clinical settings.Despite these advantages, challenges such as data privacy concerns, algorithmic bias, transparency issues, implementation costs, and regulatory uncertainties continue to limit widespread clinical implementation.Furthermore, ethical considerations regarding patient confidentiality and professional accountability remain important concerns.This review provides a comprehensive overview of current AI applications in dentistry, recent technological advancements, existing limitations, and future opportunities for integrating AI into routine dental practice.

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN DIABETES MANAGEMENT: EMERGING APPLICATIONS, CLINICAL OPPORTUNITIES AND CHALLENGES
abstract: Diabetes mellitus is a serious chronic metabolic disease marked by continuous problems in the regulation of glucose and is linked to a wide range of cardiovascular, renal, neurological, ophthalmic and other complications. Because of the growing number of people with diabetes, the difficulty of providing individualized treatment and the large amount of health data that is produced as part of routine care, there is a growing need for more intelligent methods of managing the disease. Artificial intelligence (AI), which encompasses machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing and predictive analytics, is becoming increasingly the subject of investigation as a means of improving diabetes prevention, screening, diagnosis, monitoring, treatment selection and the management of complications. These AI systems are able to combine data fromcontinuous glucose monitors, electronic health records, laboratory tests, medication records, dietary information, physical activity, wearable sensors and medical images in order to detect patterns that are hard to spot using traditional methods. The applications involve the prediction of diabetes risk, forecasting glucose levels, the detection of both hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia, automated insulin delivery, the giving of individualized treatment recommendations, screening for diabetic retinopathy, the identification of the risk of diabetic kidney disease and digital assistance in making lifestyle changes. AI can also help healthcare professionals by decreasing the amount of information they have to deal with and allowing for more personalized decisions. Yet problems relating to data quality, algorithmic bias, explainability, privacy, cybersecurity, interoperability, regulatory supervision, cost and unequal access still constitute significant obstacles. AI should thus be seen as a decision-support tool and not as a substitute that can operate autonomously for healthcare professionals. This review looks at the principles, major applications, benefits, limitations, ethical issues and future possibilities of the use of AI in the management of diabetes, with a special focus on its potential role in achieving precision and patient-centred diabetes care.

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-ASSISTED EARLY DETECTION OF OCCLUSAL AND PERIODONTAL CHANGES FOR PERSONALIZED PREVENTIVE DENTAL CARE
abstract: Disorders of occlusion and periodontal diseases are among the most prevalent oral health disorders and remain one of the primary reasons for functional impairments, tooth loss, and low quality of life. In order to prevent further development of such disorders and to ensure good oral health status in the future, it is vital to identify pathological changes at an early stage. With the advancements in artificial intelligence (AI), there are new opportunities for enhancing diagnostic precision, monitoring, and individual preventive treatment in dentistry. This review paper is aimed at discussing the biological association between modification of occlusion and periodontal diseases, as well as current state of applying AI technologies in the early diagnosis and management of periodontal diseases. Machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, and predictive analytics in the analysis of radiographic images, intraoral scans, clinical histories, biomarker profiles, and other functional data are emphasized in the current review paper. It is possible to highlight the ability of AI assisted systems to diagnose teeth wear, monitor orthodontic movement, assess periodontal bone loss, evaluate TMD, and predict the course of the disease. Moreover, multimodal AI approaches, incorporating clinical, imaging, behavioral, and biological information, contribute to the transition to precision dentistry and tailored preventive approaches. Although considerable achievements have been made, there are still some issues affecting the application of the models clinically, namely, low interpretability, validation of the model and quality of the data, privacy concerns, and ethics of governance. Innovations like digital twins, federated learning, and intelligent decision support systems are likely to improve predictive power and personalized approach of providers. In summary, AI can bring about a revolution in preventive dental care, allowing for intervention at an early stage and management of risks.

title: Acoustically driven micro/nanobubbles: from fundamental mechanisms to biomedical applications
abstract: Acoustically driven micro/nanobubbles, as a bridge between macroscopic acoustic fields and microscopic biological machinery, have shown considerable promise due to their non-contact actuation, tunable mechanical responses, and favorable biocompatibility. Recent advances in bubble formulation and acoustic control have further expanded their capabilities, enabling targeted membrane permeabilization, enhanced molecular transport, and precise manipulation at the microscale. In this review, we summarize the fundamental mechanisms linking bubble dynamics to biologically relevant effects under ultrasound and establish quantitative design criteria that govern the coupling between acoustic parameters, bubble behavior, and therapeutic performance. We then organize biomedical applications across scales, spanning single-cell manipulation, tissue-level barrier modulation, and organ-scale imaging and therapeutic interventions. Particular attention is given to how acoustic modes and bubble configurations translate into measurable performance metrics, as well as the limitations that constrain reproducibility and safety in complex biological environments. Finally, we discuss key challenges for practical translation from an engineering perspective and propose strategies for improving controllability, standardization, and system integration. By providing a framework to overcome the inherent randomness of bubble-acoustic interactions in clinical translation, this review outlines a roadmap toward reliable and programmable mechano-bio platforms for closed-loop, patient-adaptive interventions.

title: Active sensing explains cortical variability and improves visual information
abstract: Abstract Active vision is often considered at the scale of saccades, with each fixation treated as a static visual sample. Yet the eyes continue to move during fixation, continually transforming the retinal input. Here we measured these movements at high precision while recording neuronal populations in the foveal primary visual cortex of awake marmosets viewing repeated flashed natural images. Fixational eye movements accounted for most conditional firing-rate variability and nearly all shared variability not explained by the trial-averaged response. An image-computable model captured this modulation largely from gaze-dependent retinal input; explicit eye-position and eye-velocity signals added little predictive power. Under natural viewing, retinal motion redistributed image power across temporal frequencies, and motion effects grew when this power engaged spatiotemporal tuning. In model-derived populations, fixational motion increased the spatial information carried per spike relative to stabilized input, with sharpening growing across successive nonlinear stages. Thus, activity commonly assigned to cortical noise is not just structured visual reafference generated by the movement of the observer, but is beneficial signal which sharpens spatial representations.

title: Adult Meckel’s Diverticulum Presenting with Massive Lower Gastrointestinal Bleeding and Hemorrhagic Shock: A Case Report
abstract: Meckel’s diverticulum (MD) is a congenital ileal outpouching that may contain ectopic gastric mucosa. Although typically asymptomatic, it may cause significant lower gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding in adults and, rarely, hemorrhagic shock.We report a case of a 31-year-old man who presented with sudden-onset painless hematochezia, syncope, and eventual hemorrhagic shock. Despite negative CT angiography and upper endoscopy, colonoscopy revealed active bleeding originating in the terminal ileum and entering the cecum, suggesting a small-bowel source and providing partial localization. The patient required substantial blood transfusion support, including 3 units of packed red blood cells, 2 units of platelets, and 2 units of cryoprecipitate. Ongoing hemorrhage and hemodynamic instability prompted emergent laparotomy, which identified and allowed for resection of an MD. Histopathologic examination confirmed MD containing ectopic gastric mucosa with an ulcerated bleeding focus.This case highlights the clinical challenges of MD in adults. It demonstrates that it may present with life-threatening lower gastrointestinal bleeding despite initially non-diagnostic imaging and the absence of definitive endoscopic identification of the lesion. Although uncommon, this case supports maintaining clinical suspicion for MD in adults with unexplained severe gastrointestinal hemorrhage and further characterizes its potential presentation in the adult population.

title: Advanced Medical Optics & Surgical Robotics: Applications of Jana's Invariant Lens Equations in Orthopedics, Neurosurgery, Ophthalmology, and Dentistry
abstract: This paper establishes a high-precision computational paradigm for biomedical optics, robotic surgery, and advanced diagnostic imaging by extending Jana’s Invariant Lens Governing Equations—specifically the dif- ferential velocity profile (dv/du + (v/u) 2 = 0), the cubic spatial matrix (Equation C), and the radical symmetry boundary (Equation K). Traditional surgical microscopes, intra-oral scanners, and autonomous robotic cutting arrays experience processing latencies when adapting to micro-scale tissue variations and localized movement-driven focal shifts. By hardcoding Jana’s non-linear spatial transformations directly into optical tracking firmware, this model eliminates computational tracking lag by roughly 65%. We de- tail direct engineering frameworks to achieve absolute focus stabilization in orthopedic bone cutting, deep micro-vascular neurosurgery, LASIK ophthalmic tracking, and intra-oral 3D dental mapping.

title: Advances in Dental Imaging and the Integration of Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Diagnostic imaging of the oral and maxillofacial region is of paramount importance in clinical diagnosis, treatment planning, and follow-up procedures in dentistry. Periapical radiographic examinations and various panoramic imaging systems are routinely employed in clinical dental practice. Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) has become a widely used and currently preferred imaging modality in dental implantology, endodontics, maxillofacial surgery, periodontology, temporomandibular joint disorders, orthodontics, airway assessment, sleep disorders, and forensic dentistry. However, relatively high radiation doses, prolonged scanning times, and high costs limit its routine clinical use. Ultrasound imaging is also among the recommended techniques in dental practice, as it provides real-time imaging using an ionizing radiation-free, cost-effective, rapid, and user-friendly technique. Ultrasonography can be utilized in the dentomaxillofacial region for various diagnostic purposes, including the examination of the salivary glands and superficial tissues. More recently, dedicated dental magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has been introduced, incorporating specialized software, hardware, imaging sequences, and fields of view tailored to the anatomical characteristics of the dentomaxillofacial region. Another important topic in dental and maxillofacial radiology is artificial intelligence (AI). Artificial intelligence is a field of computer science dedicated to developing systems or machines capable of performing tasks that have traditionally been associated with human intelligence. Further research and investigation in the field of dental and maxillofacial radiology are expected to make substantial contributions to diagnostic imaging across various dental specialties. This article provides insights into current applications and emerging trends in the field of diagnostic imaging in dentistry.
authors: Nebiha Hilal Bilge

title: Advances in integrated diagnostics: Innovation and translation of laboratory diagnostic technologies
abstract: Integrated diagnostics is reshaping modern laboratory medicine by shifting diagnostic practice from fragmented test utilization toward a clinically oriented, data-driven, and patient-centered model. In this review, we summarize the conceptual foundations, technological advances, and translational challenges of integrated laboratory diagnostics. We propose a five-dimensional framework—intelligence, timeliness, accuracy, standardization, and interdisciplinary integration—to describe the core attributes of this emerging paradigm. Within this framework, diagnostic innovation is driven by the convergence of multiple enabling technologies, including liquid biopsy, mass spectrometry, high-throughput and single-cell sequencing, spatial multi-omics, digital pathology, point-of-care testing, organoid models, microfluidics, and interoperable digital infrastructure. Together, these advances support a transition from isolated result generation to dynamic, contextualized, and actionable diagnostic insights, thereby promoting earlier detection, more precise risk stratification, individualized therapeutic guidance, and longitudinal health monitoring. We further discuss the major barriers to clinical translation, including technical and data complexity, limited evidence for clinical utility, workflow integration challenges, and the need for systemic transformation in workforce training, governance, and equitable implementation. Overall, integrated laboratory diagnostics represents a transformative direction for laboratory medicine and precision healthcare. Its successful adoption will depend on coordinated progress in evidence generation, interoperability, and multidisciplinary collaboration, ultimately enabling a more predictive, preventive, personalized, and participatory diagnostic future.
authors: Sergio Bernardini; Jun Zhang

title: Adversarial domain adaptation for false-positive reduction in hospital-to-robotic echocardiographic screening under limited target-domain data
abstract: Hospital-trained deep learning models for echocardiographic wall motion abnormality detection achieve strong performance under standard clinical acquisition conditions but often degrade substantially when deployed on autonomous robotic acquisition systems. Most existing models are developed and validated under controlled clinical acquisition conditions, limiting their robustness when deployed in emerging autonomous imaging systems. A hospital-trained wall motion abnormality detection model trained on 10,000 hospital echocardiograms achieved 92.3% accuracy (94.0% sensitivity, 90.6% specificity) when applied to an independent hospital test data set of 500 studies. However, direct deployment on 150 robotic echocardiograms from 15 healthy subjects reduced the normal-case specificity to 65.7%, representing a 24.9 percentage-point drop compared to the performance when applied to the hospital-acquired data. No statistically significant difference in SNR was observed between domains (p = 0.31; d = 0.12), with similarly small standardized differences in contrast and sharpness, although formal equivalence was not established. Acquisition-geometry measures differed descriptively between domains, suggesting that geometry-associated factors may contribute to the observed domain shift. We propose an adversarial domain adaptation framework built upon a 3D ResNet-18 backbone with a gradient-reversal domain discriminator for aligning hospital and robotic feature representations while retaining the hospital-trained classification objective. This design enables adaptation to the robotic domain without requiring labeled robot-acquired pathological cases, which are particularly difficult to obtain during early-stage robotic system development. Under leave-one-subject-out validation across robotic subjects, Mixed-DANN improved specificity to 86.1% ± 4.3%, while Normal-only DANN improved specificity to 89.3% ± 4.8% (p < 0.001 versus direct transfer), recovering 94.8% of the hospital-to-robot specificity gap. Because the robotic cohort comprises only healthy subjects, evaluation is appropriately restricted to specificity and false-positive rate; sensitivity evaluation requires future acquisition of robot-acquired pathological cases. These findings suggest that acquisition-associated domain shift substantially impacts cross-platform deployment. The proposed adversarial domain adaptation framework provides a potential pathway for adapting hospital-trained cardiac AI models to autonomous robotic ultrasound under conditions of limited target-domain data, although validation using robot-acquired pathological cases remains necessary before clinical translation.
authors: Hsu Thiri Soe; Yamauchi Yuki; Hiroyasu Iwata

title: Agreement and reproducibility of intraoral scan- versus CBCT-based three-dimensional implant position assessment in the posterior mandible — a paired in vitro method-comparison study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Three-dimensional postoperative implant assessment is increasingly performed using intraoral scan (IOS) superimposition as a radiation-free alternative to cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT). However, it remains unclear to what extent IOS- and CBCT-based measurements agree and how reproducibility changes across posterior mandibular configurations. METHODS: In this paired in vitro method-comparison study, based on the experimental platform of a previous study, 60 implants placed at Fédération Dentaire Internationale (FDI) positions 35, 36, 45, 46 and 47 in bounded edentulous spaces (BES) and distal extension situations (DE) underwent three IOS-based and three CBCT-based postoperative assessments relative to the virtual plan using the Treatment Evaluation Tool of the planning software. Angular, mesiodistal, buccolingual, apico-coronal, and three-dimensional (3D) deviations at implant base and apex were recorded, resulting in 180 paired measurements. Agreement was assessed by Bland-Altman analysis, and within-method reproducibility by the within-implant standard deviation (Sw). IOS variability was additionally separated into within-scan and between-scan components. Non-parametric analyses were used for comparisons by indication and FDI position. RESULTS: Mean absolute IOS-CBCT differences were 0.73° ± 0.55° for angular deviation, 0.22 ± 0.20 mm for the 3D base offset and 0.26 ± 0.22 mm for the 3D apical offset. Bland-Altman bias (CBCT - IOS) was small (- 0.35°; -0.05 mm; -0.07 mm) with 95% limits of agreement of [- 2.01°; +1.31°], [- 0.62; +0.53] mm and [- 0.73; +0.58] mm. Within-method reproducibility was superior for IOS in 8 of 9 parameters (e.g., Sw 0.20° vs. 0.55° for the angle), and IOS variability was dominated by scan-to-scan rather than within-scan re-evaluation. Discrepancies were larger in DE than in BES sites in 7 of 9 parameters (all p < 0.001 for the principal apical and buccolingual components) and were larger at position 47 than at position 35 (3D base p = 0.004; 3D apex p = 0.011). CONCLUSIONS: In this in vitro setting, IOS- and CBCT-based implant assessment in the posterior mandible showed good agreement with small overall differences, and IOS demonstrated lower within-method variability than CBCT. IOS-based superimposition may therefore serve as a radiation-free complement to CBCT for the postoperative evaluation of single implants in bounded posterior sites. Agreement decreased in distal extension situations and at more distal positions; in these configurations, and whenever clinical decisions depend on sub-millimeter or sub-degree precision, CBCT remains the reference technique. Confirmation in vivo is required before routine clinical use.

title: An Accurate and Efficient 3D Reconstruction Method for Wireless Capsule Endoscopy Based on Harris Corner Detection and Fixed Template Matching
abstract: To overcome the limitation of wireless capsule endoscopy (WCE) in providing only two‑dimensional intestinal images—which constrains accurate diagnosis of intestinal lesions—this study proposes an accurate and efficient three‑dimensional detection method. The approach applies 3D reconstruction to WCE images by computing corresponding points across successive frames and estimating the capsule’s position and orientation. A critical step involves the selection of highly specific feature points and the determination of their correspondences. Accordingly, this paper combines a Harris corner‑based feature extraction algorithm with a fixed matching template algorithm to achieve robust feature point matching in WCE intestinal images, substantially improving both matching efficiency and robustness. Using the obtained feature matching points, an intestinal model is reconstructed via 3D reconstruction. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method offers advantages in efficiency and reconstruction quality compared with conventional 3D reconstruction approaches, indicating its potential to enhance WCE‑based lesion localization and diagnostic accuracy.

title: An Adaptive Bayesian Active Learning Framework for Automated Subjective Refraction in Digital Phoropters
abstract: Abstract Subjective refraction is the clinical gold standard for determining corrective ophthalmic prescriptions. While modern computerized phoropters—such as the [NIDEK RT-6100](https://www.nidek-intl.com/items/intelligent-refractor-rt-6100/?utm_source=gemini)—have automated lens rotation and enabled remote examination, the sequential logic of lens selection remains bound to fixed, deterministic heuristic trees (such as Jackson Cross Cylinder [JCC] bracketing and manual fogging). These rigid protocols lead to prolonged examination times, patient fatigue, and susceptibility to erroneous responses. In this paper, we formulate an autonomous Bayesian Active Learning Framework for Subjective Refraction. We map traditional spherocylindrical parameters $(S, C, A)$ into an orthogonal 3D Euclidean space via Thibos Power Vectors$\mathbf{x} = (M, J_0, J_{45})$. The patient is modeled as a probabilistic psychophysical observer with a three-alternative response likelihood (Lens 1 clearer, Lens 2 clearer, or Unsure/Same), incorporating sensory discrimination threshold $\alpha$, lapse rate $\lambda$, and blur indifference deadbands. At each examination step, the agent calculates the Expected Information Gain (Mutual Information) across candidate lens pairs and selects the query that maximizes Shannon entropy reduction, while enforcing an ophthalmologically grounded Fogging Safety Constraint to suppress accommodation spasm. In Monte Carlo simulations across $N = 300$ virtual patients with representative refractive distributions, our Bayesian active learning agent converged to clinical accuracy ($\le 0.25\text{ D}$) in an average of 5.4 steps, compared to 8.9 steps for the conventional rule-based clinical protocol—achieving a 39.4% reduction in testing steps. Furthermore, at 20 steps, the residual dioptric vector error was reduced by 43.6%($0.165\text{ D}$ vs. $0.293\text{ D}$, $p < 0.001$). This framework provides a verifiable theoretical foundation and software architecture for embedding autonomous AI decision-making into next-generation digital phoropters.

title: An Adaptive Inhibitory WSe 2 Transistor for Retinomorphic In‐Sensor Image Processing
abstract: ABSTRACT Retinomorphic vision systems have emerged as a promising approach for low‐power in‐sensor image processing by mimicking the human retina. Retinal contrast enhancement amplifies local visual features at the sensor level, eliminating the need for computationally intensive external processing. However, most conventional retinomorphic devices require illumination‐dependent bias adjustments, which introduce decision‐making overhead and limit scalable array integration. Here, we report an adaptive inhibitory WSe 2 transistor that performs decision‐free, intensity‐adaptive image processing within a single pixel. The current inhibition ratio decreases monotonically from ∼16.2 to ∼1.2 as the back‐gate voltage increases from 3 to 13 V, reflecting regime‐dependent carrier transport. When integrated with photodiodes, the transistor switches between subthreshold and accumulation regimes depending on local illumination. Under a common top‐gate pulse, dim pixels are strongly suppressed while bright pixels largely retain their current. We then processed gradient and noisy “G” patterns on the 5 × 5 photodiode array, achieving contrast enhancement and noise filtering. Furthermore, simulations of license‐plate recognition under rain and fog show that processing restores character morphology, improving classification accuracy from 47.7% to 97.3%. These results show that adaptive inhibition offers a scalable, energy‐efficient route to adaptive in‐sensor processing for edge‐vision hardware in low‐visibility environments.
authors: Juhwan Baek; J.-E. Oh; Hyeonjung Kim; 박민식; Haein Cho; Jin Young Park; Hyeonchang Son; Taeyun Kim; Sung‐Un An; Yamin Zhang; Hyeon‐Jin Shin; Seyong Oh; Dong‐Ho Kang

title: An Expertise Transfer Framework For Autonomous Surgical Assistance
abstract: Autonomous surgery holds the potential to transform operative practice by enhancing procedural safety and consistency. While substantial progress has been made on episodic sub-tasks, achieving autonomy for long-horizon tasks that span the entire procedure remains challenging. Current logic-based heuristics and end-to-end learning approaches, though effective for short-term actions, struggle to adapt to the evolving dynamics of complete surgical workflows. To address this gap, an expertise transfer framework is introduced to achieve procedure-spanning autonomous view assistance by emulating expert logic. Specifically, the framework instantiates situational awareness via a novel hierarchical granularity perception network that jointly captures surgical workflow and fine-grained instrument-tissue interactions; models attention allocation for inferring assistance needs by systematically characterizing surgeon visual attention patterns; and encodes decision-making logic for actionable behaviors by formalizing expert assistance policies as a heterogeneous knowledge graph. Equipped with this architecture, the proposed framework successfully enables autonomous view assistance in vivo animal trials throughout complete nephrectomy procedures, while demonstrating improved visualization quality compared to human assistance. This expertise transfer paradigm provides a promising pathway toward trustworthy autonomy in clinical applications, advancing the shift toward procedure-spanning autonomous workflows.
authors: Yuan Gao; Guangdi Chu; Wei Jiao; Yuchuan Zhong; Hang Yuan; Chengjun Li; Jinhua Li; Jinhua Li; Shuxin Wang; Bo Guan; Jianchang Zhao; Lizhi Pan; Pengfei Zhang; Jianmin Li; Jianmin Li

title: An Intelligent Hybrid Deep Learning Framework for Automated Dental Caries Detection, Segmentation, Multi-Class Classification, Severity Assessment, and Treatment Recommendation Using Dental Radiographic Images
abstract: Dental caries stays one of the most widely wide-spread oral health disorders worldwide, affecting people throughout all age businesses and causing widespread healthcare burdens. accurate and early prognosis of dental lesions is essential for stopping sickness progression and improving treatment results. but, conventional diagnostic strategies often suffer from subjective interpretation, low sensitivity to subtle lesion boundaries, and restrained functionality in severity assessment. This study proposes an advanced synthetic Intelligence pushed framework named automatic Dental Caries Detection using Synaptic Intelligent Convolutional Neural network (ADCD-SICNN) for automatic dental radiographic evaluation. initially, dental X-ray photos are obtained from the Dental Analyze and diagnosis of radiography data (DRAD). Bayesian Boundary fashion Filtering is employed for image enhancement and noise discount even as keeping essential anatomical systems. eventually, a Dense Channel Spatial Semantic steerage interest UNet (DCSSGA-UNet) is utilized for unique lesion segmentation. neighborhood texture and side statistics are extracted thru Residual Neural Networks (ResNet), while structural lesion traits are captured using Multi-hypothesis Fuzzy Matching Radon transform (MHFMRT). title: Application of Artificial Intelligence in Diagnostic Medical Imaging and Radiotherapy
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming healthcare, particularly in diagnostic imaging and radiotherapy. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in the field of diagnostic medical imaging and radiotherapy has witnessed significant advancements, revolutionizing the healthcare landscape. This review delves into its diverse applications, exploring its potential to boost accuracy, streamline workflows, and improve patient outcomes. A systematic literature search identified relevant studies on AI's role in these domains. Articles covered topics like image analysis, pattern recognition, decision support, and treatment planning. AI algorithms, performance, and integration into clinical practice were critically evaluated. In diagnostic imaging, AI shines in modalities like MRI, CT, and PET. AI algorithms excel in image interpretation, aiding early detection, characterization, and staging of various diseases. Additionally, these tools show promise in predicting treatment response and personalizing treatment plans. Within radiotherapy, AI automates and improves treatment steps. Machine learning algorithms efficiently contour target volumes and organs at risk, facilitating optimal treatment planning. Real-time image guidance and AI-driven adaptive radiotherapy techniques enhance precision and safety during treatment delivery. Moreover, AI-based predictive models assist in assessing outcomes and optimizing therapeutic strategies, ultimately improving patient care. Despite the advancements, challenges like data privacy, standardization, and ethical considerations persist. This review paints a comprehensive picture of AI's current applications in diagnostic imaging and radiotherapy, highlighting its transformative impact on disease diagnosis and treatment planning. As AI evolves, its integration into clinical practice holds immense potential to revolutionize patient care, ushering in a new era of precision medicine.
authors: Buhari Samaila

title: Artificial Intelligence Approaches for Gastrointestinal Bleeding Detection in Capsule Endoscopy: A Systematic Review and Critical Analysis
abstract: Background/Objectives: Gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding is a common, potentially life-threatening condition, and capsule endoscopy (CE) is the principal investigation for suspected small-bowel bleeding after non-diagnostic upper endoscopy and colonoscopy. Because manual review of thousands of CE frames is labor-intensive, artificial intelligence (AI) has been proposed to automate bleeding detection. Methods: Following PRISMA 2020, this systematic review synthesizes 15 peer-reviewed journal studies (2020–2025) applying traditional machine learning, convolutional neural networks, transfer learning, attention-based or hybrid architectures, segmentation, or object detection to GI bleeding detection in CE. Methodological quality was appraised with an AI-adapted risk-of-bias framework informed by QUADAS-2 and PROBAST. Results: Frame-level classification accuracy ranged from 90.6% to 99.9% (median 98.5%; 13 studies), with the lowest values from evaluations closest to clinical practice; the segmentation and detection studies reported a mean intersection-over-union of 86.9% and an mAP@0.5 of 79.0%. Only two studies (13%) were at low risk of bias for validation strategy, none reported patient-level separation of training and test data, only four (27%) used clinical patient data, and none compared AI with conventional endoscopy or clinical outcomes. Conclusions: Current evidence demonstrates high performance on curated datasets but not yet generalizability or clinical readiness; patient-level, external, and prospective multicentre validation is required.
authors: Nasima Mohammad Helal; Jon Zaccary Regala; K. K. Mujeeb Rahman

title: Artificial Intelligence and Imaging Technologies in Orthodontic Assessment, Referral and Care Pathways: A Scoping Review
abstract: Abstract* Background Artificial intelligence (AI), integrated with imaging technologies, is increasingly applied across orthodontic assessment and care pathways. However, the evidence remains scattered across imaging modalities, clinical applications, AI methodologies, and stages of clinical translation. Methods A scoping review was conducted in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and reported in line with the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. PubMed, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore were searched for studies published between January 2016 and June 2026, with searches supplemented by Google Scholar, OpenAlex, grey literature sources, and citation searching. Eligible studies were mapped descriptively and synthesised thematically using Braun and Clarke’s framework. Results Fifty-four studies were included. AI applications used intraoral and facial photographs, cephalometric radiographs, CBCT, intraoral scans, three-dimensional dental models, and multimodal imaging. Applications ranged from landmark localisation, segmentation, and malocclusion classification to treatment-need assessment, screening, referral support, treatment planning, and remote monitoring. Evidence was strongest for bounded, anatomically verifiable image-analysis tasks, whereas applications involving referral, triage, treatment-need decisions, longitudinal prediction, and workflow integration were less mature. Common limitations included retrospective, single-centre designs; heterogeneous reference standards; limited external validation; inconsistent reporting of calibration and uncertainty; and insufficient evaluation of patient-centred, equity, and service-level outcomes. Conclusions Imaging-based AI in orthodontics has evolved from automated image interpretation to clinician-assisted decision support across the care pathway. Current evidence most strongly supports AI for structured image-analysis tasks, but does not yet support autonomous referral, triage, or treatment-planning decisions. Future research should prioritise prospective multicentre validation, transparent reporting, explainability, fairness, uncertainty handling, and workflow-integrated evaluation to enable safe and clinically useful implementation.
authors: Kayali S, Bernabe E, Golkari A.

title: Artificial Intelligence as a Catalyst for Cell-Based Therapies in Retinal Disease
abstract: Retinal degenerative diseases, including age-related macular degeneration (AMD), retinitis pigmentosa (RP), and Stargardt disease, represent leading causes of irreversible vision loss worldwide, collectively affecting hundreds of millions of people. Cell-based therapies, particularly those leveraging induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) transplantation, and CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, have emerged as promising treatment modalities that may preserve, replace, or partially restore retinal function. However, these approaches face significant challenges in patient stratification, manufacturing consistency, surgical precision, and long-term outcome monitoring. Artificial intelligence (AI), encompassing machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and computer vision, is increasingly being integrated across the cell therapy pipeline to address these limitations. This review comprehensively explores the role of AI in enhancing cell-based retinal therapies, spanning disease diagnosis and patient selection, stem cell quality control and differentiation optimization, CRISPR off-target detection, retinal organoid characterization, scalable manufacturing, and post-transplantation monitoring through multimodal retinal imaging. Throughout, we distinguish direct retinal cell-therapy evidence from retinal-adjacent, cross-domain, and conceptual evidence. We also propose an AI-powered end-to-end pipeline that connects patient profiling through gene editing, cell production, and transplantation to longitudinal outcomes tracking (a forward-looking framework that needs to be clinically validated in future). While AI offers powerful tools to enhance efficacy, reproducibility, and personalization, it does not replace the clinical and biological foundations of cell therapy. Critical challenges remain, including data scarcity, algorithmic interpretability, regulatory compliance, and clinical validation. This review concludes that the strategic integration of AI has plausible potential to become supportive infrastructure for scalable and reproducible cell-based treatments for retinal diseases, although its necessity has not been demonstrated and prospective clinical validation is still required, and biological insight and rigorous empirical verification remain fundamental.
authors: Girish Kumar Srivastava; Priyank Shukla; Sara Crespo Millas; Yogeswaran Lokanathan

title: Artificial Intelligence for Benign Esophageal Stricture Dilation: An Evidence‐Transferability Framework and Safety‐First Roadmap
abstract: ABSTRACT Background Endoscopic dilation is first‐line therapy for symptomatic benign esophageal strictures but remains operator‐dependent. Artificial intelligence (AI) could support assessment, risk stratification, and documentation; however, evidence from adjacent tasks is often mistaken for procedure‐specific validation. Aim To map the evidence for AI in benign esophageal stricture dilation, assess transferability and methodological quality, and propose a translational pathway. Methods We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Europe PMC from inception through June 28, 2026, using prespecified searches in adults and children. Studies were classified by evidence provenance and appraised using design‐adapted domain considerations. Results Within the search date and eligibility criteria, no AI system was identified that guided, monitored, or assessed dilation itself; two retrospective single‐center studies applied machine learning in the target population for other tasks. Adjacent neoplasia and engineering studies support component feasibility, while clinical cohorts identify candidate predictors. Functional lumen imaging probe technology provides non‐AI measurement and potential reference labels. Recurrent concerns included selected or retrospective samples, limited external validation, and high concern about applicability to dilation. Performance cannot be transferred across mismatched target tasks, acquisition physics, reference standards, populations or operating contexts, or consequences of error. Conclusion Adjacent evidence can justify candidate components. Procedure‐specific calibration and validation remain necessary. Priorities are calibrated morphometric variables with prespecified reference standards and reproducible documentation using synchronized multimodal and outcome data. External validation should be followed by human‐controlled advisory testing before intraprocedural automation.
authors: Ahmed Salman; Mohamed Abdalla Salman

title: Artificial Intelligence in CBCT for Dental Implantology: Current Applications, Limitations, and Future Perspectives - A Literature Review
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT)-based workflows in dental implantology.This structured narrative literature review evaluated current AI applications in implant dentistry, critically assessed their technical and clinical limitations, and discussed future perspectives for integration into implant planning and treatment workflows.A literature search was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Embase.Evidence was synthesized according to clinically relevant domains, including anatomical segmentation, identification of edentulous regions and implant sites, bone assessment, virtual implant planning, comparison with expert planning, workflow optimization, and outcome prediction.AI demonstrated encouraging performance in CBCT segmentation, anatomical and bone assessment, and selected components of virtual implant planning.Automated systems showed substantial agreement with expert-generated plans in selected clinical settings and consistently reduced planning time while providing high repeatability.However, performance varied according to anatomical complexity, imaging conditions, software environment, and the specific task evaluated.Limited external validation, heterogeneous datasets and evaluation methods, and the gap between technical performance and demonstrated clinical benefit remain important barriers to generalizability.Current evidence supports AI primarily as a decision-support tool that complements professional judgment.Future research should prioritize multicenter prospective validation, standardized evaluation frameworks, multimodal data integration, explainable and uncertainty-aware models, and clinically meaningful outcomes.
authors: Nabil EL SAHILI
venue: Online Journal of Dentistry & Oral Health

title: Artificial Intelligence in Contemporary Dentistry: Applications Across Dental Specialties and Future Challenges
abstract: Modern artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping contemporary dental practice through efficient diagnosis, improved treatment planning, and patient personalization across various settings.By leveraging innovations in computer vision, deep learning, and multimodal pattern recognition, computational models are being applied across the major fields of dentistry today.These AI-based approaches are used for automated lesion detection in diagnostic imaging, precision alignment in orthodontics, root canal mapping in endodontics, and robotic assistance in surgical procedures.Despite the substantial improvements in diagnostic accuracy, objectivity, and efficiency, there are several major challenges with implementing these technologies into clinical practice.These challenges include algorithm bias, data privacy concerns, the absence of regulatory guidelines for the development of such tools, and cost.This review aims to provide an overview of the applications of artificial intelligence in the different fields of dentistry, to highlight the current challenges and directions for future research and development, and to discuss the potential of generative language models, real-time augmented reality (AR), and the prediction of dental healthcare outcomes.
authors: Sumit Bhatt; Prantika Mandal; Shweta Vijaykumar Sagare; Sanjay J Gawali; Kunal Nischal; Sai Chandan Das; Pratik Surana

title: Artificial Intelligence in Dental Implant Treatment Planning: A Systematic Review
abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into digital dentistry and dental implantology, particularly for three-dimensional image analysis, anatomical segmentation, implant-site identification, bone assessment, and computer-assisted treatment planning. Because implant placement is prosthetically and anatomically driven, reliable interpretation of cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) data is central to reducing surgical and prosthetic complications. Objective: To systematically synthesize current evidence regarding AI applications in dental implant treatment planning, with emphasis on CBCT-based anatomical identification and segmentation, edentulous-site detection, bone-dimension assessment, technical assistance in planning, and emerging outcome prediction. Methods: Evidence was synthesized from recent systematic reviews, meta-analyses, scoping reviews, and representative primary studies addressing AI-assisted implant planning. The review framework follows PRISMA 2020 principles and organizes evidence according to population, intervention, comparison, outcomes, AI architecture, imaging modality, and clinical application. Because substantial heterogeneity exists in algorithms, datasets, reference standards, and reported endpoints, quantitative pooling was restricted to outcomes already meta-analyzed in the literature. Results: Published reviews consistently show high technical performance for several CBCT-based tasks. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis reported pooled accuracy of 96% for mandibular and 83% for maxillary edentulous-site identification. A 2026 systematic review of 28 implant-planning studies reported anatomical-segmentation accuracy ranging from 66.4% to 99.1%, with 18 studies addressing segmentation and eight examining technical assistance. A 2026 meta-analysis of U-Net-based mandibular-canal segmentation reported pooled Dice similarity coefficient of 0.84 and substantial heterogeneity. AI-assisted systems can markedly reduce segmentation and planning time, but evidence remains dominated by retrospective, single-centre, and technically focused studies. Conclusion: AI has substantial potential to improve the speed, consistency, and anatomical precision of dental implant treatment planning, particularly when applied to CBCT segmentation and risk-structure identification. Current evidence does not justify autonomous implant planning. External validation, multicentre prospective studies, standardized reporting, explainability, regulatory oversight, and clinician-in-the-loop workflows are required before routine autonomous use.
authors: Dr. Sowmiya. T; Mihir Joshi; Mohammad Jalaluddin; Pawan Dawane; Jyotsna Seth; Neha Liya

title: Artificial Intelligence in Gastroenterology: Towards Explainable, Generalisable and Clinically Actionable Decision Support
abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used in gastroenterology for endoscopic detection and characterisation, disease-activity assessment, risk prediction, treatment-response estimation and workflow support. However, high retrospective accuracy does not necessarily translate into reliable or beneficial clinical decision support. This structured narrative review examines the clinical development of artificial intelligence across gastrointestinal endoscopy, inflammatory bowel disease, hepatology and pancreaticobiliary diseases through three translational dimensions: explainability, generalisability and clinical actionability. Communication, human oversight and lifecycle governance are considered cross-cutting determinants of implementation. The evidence is most mature in gastrointestinal endoscopy, particularly for computer-aided polyp detection, although benefits vary across operators, indications and practice settings. Applications in inflammatory bowel disease, hepatology and pancreaticobiliary care remain predominantly retrospective, with limited prospective evidence that model outputs alter management or improve patient outcomes. Explainability is commonly represented by heatmaps or feature-attribution methods, but rarely evaluated in terms of clinician understanding, calibrated trust or patient communication. External validation is becoming more frequent, yet geographic and technological transportability, calibration and performance under dataset shift remain insufficiently assessed. Prospective implementation and health-economic studies are uncommon, and available economic evidence is largely model-based. Clinical artificial intelligence should therefore be evaluated as a sociotechnical intervention comprising the model, interface, users, workflow, communication process and associated care pathway. Translation requires clinically defined use cases, representative multicentre validation, human-centred evaluation, prospective assessment of benefits and harms, and continuous post-deployment surveillance. Clinical AI in gastroenterology should complement clinical expertise through transparent, contestable and continuously monitored decision support that preserves clinician accountability and supports informed, patient-centred decisions.
authors: Ismail BAYDİLİ; Burak Taşçı; Şengül Doğan; Türker Tuncer

title: Artificial Intelligence in Invisible Orthodontics: From Digital Impressions to Adaptive Treatment Management
abstract: ABSTRACT Digital transformation in orthodontics has significantly revolutionized clinical practices over recent decades. Advancements such as intraoral scanners, 3D imaging (including cone‐beam computed tomography, CBCT), and advanced treatment planning software have increased diagnostic accuracy and the ability to design personalized treatments. These technologies have primarily focused on static aspects and still require continuous human oversight. Machine learning algorithms, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and artificial neural networks (ANNs), offer superior performance in tasks such as identifying anatomical landmarks on radiographic images, assessing skeletal maturity, and predicting treatment outcomes. Research has shown that AI in static diagnosis and planning has achieved an accuracy greater than 90%, outperforming traditional methods. Moreover, AI reduces processing time, minimizes operator performance variability, and serves as a supportive tool in digital orthodontic workflows. Despite these advancements, there remains a significant gap in research regarding adaptive AI for treatments involving clear aligners. Most studies focus on static planning, while dynamic aspects, such as real‐time treatment adjustments based on the patient's biological responses or deviations in tooth movement, are less explored. This research gap may arise from factors such as patient biological diversity, a lack of real clinical data, and the need for multi‐center validation. Adaptive AI, based on reinforcement learning and digital twin modeling, has the potential to reduce the average treatment duration by approximately 3 to 4 months and increase patient satisfaction. The aim of this review is to provide a comprehensive examination of AI's role in real‐time management of invisible orthodontic treatments, focusing on clear aligner‐based treatments. This study analyzes AI applications going from digital data processing to integration with supervisory platforms, discussing challenges, limitations, and future perspectives. This review not only summarizes current achievements but also proposes practical solutions to overcome existing barriers and presents adaptive AI as a pivotal tool for the future of orthodontics.
authors: Soodeh Hosseini; Hossein Seilani; At‐har Nasari

title: Artificial Intelligence in Ophthalmic Surgery: Applications Across the Perioperative Pathway
abstract: This narrative review examines how artificial intelligence is being applied across the ophthalmic surgical pathway, spanning preoperative planning, intraoperative guidance and training, and postoperative prediction, and it identifies the priorities required for responsible clinical adoption. Recent studies show that preoperative biometric planning in cataract surgery and surgical video analysis are currently the most mature applications, while image-based risk stratification in corneal and retinal surgery and prediction of postoperative visual or refractive outcomes are advancing steadily. By contrast, real-time intraoperative guidance and autonomous robotic support remain earlier in development and are still limited by data heterogeneity, workflow-integration challenges, and sparse prospective validation. Artificial intelligence is unlikely to replace ophthalmic surgeons in the near term, but it can augment clinical judgment, standardize workflows, and improve efficiency and safety across the perioperative pathway. Wider clinical adoption will depend on stronger external validation, better interpretability, integration into real-world surgical workflows, and prospective studies demonstrating meaningful patient benefit.
authors: Andrzej E. Grzybowski; Kai Jin

title: Artificial Intelligence in Ophthalmology: From Methodological Advances to Clinical Translation and Future Directions
abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping ophthalmology from task‐specific image analysis toward multimodal, longitudinal, and clinically integrated decision support. This narrative review summarizes the methodological evolution of ophthalmic AI, including traditional machine learning, task‐specific deep learning, self‐supervised learning, foundation models, multimodal AI, and generative AI, and examines their applications across major ophthalmic diseases. Current evidence is strongest for autonomous diabetic retinopathy screening, whereas AI applications in glaucoma, age‐related macular degeneration, anterior segment disease, ocular surface disorders, and ocular tumors are primarily positioned as decision‐support tools for screening, diagnosis, risk stratification, progression prediction, treatment monitoring, and quantitative imaging analysis. Recent advances in ophthalmic foundation models, multimodal learning, three‐dimensional optical coherence tomography analysis, and generative AI have expanded the scope of AI beyond single‐modality classification, but improved benchmark performance does not necessarily indicate clinical readiness. Successful translation requires robust external and prospective validation, reliable uncertainty estimation, cross‐device and cross‐population generalizability, fairness, interpretability, privacy protection, safety, and effective human–AI collaboration. Emerging directions include AI‐generated virtual patients and digital twins, home and portable imaging for decentralized monitoring, AI‐driven imaging biomarker discovery, oculomics for systemic health assessment, and interactive clinical copilots. Overall, the future value of ophthalmic AI will depend not only on increasingly powerful models but also on their ability to provide reproducible, clinically actionable, and trustworthy benefits within real‐world clinical workflows.
authors: Yuxin Liu; Hanruo Liu

title: Artificial Intelligence in Optical Coherence Tomography‐Based Ophthalmic Imaging: From Automated Diagnosis to Personalized Disease Monitoring
abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to optical coherence tomography (OCT) in ophthalmology, but evidence for automated diagnosis is stronger than evidence for longitudinal monitoring. This narrative review evaluates OCT‐based AI with emphasis on disease monitoring and progression, particularly in retinal disease and glaucoma. Literature from 2016 to 2026 was screened across major biomedical databases, and 45 verifiable sources were included. Retinal OCT models support referral triage, fluid segmentation, and treatment‐response prediction, whereas glaucoma applications face specific challenges: retinal nerve fiber layer floor effects, inconsistent progression definitions, reference‐standard circularity, spectrum bias, high myopia, anomalous discs, and device‐related domain shift. Recent meta‐analyses show high diagnostic performance for glaucoma detection, but progression prediction remains less externally validated. Clinically useful OCT‐based AI should therefore be implemented as clinician‐led decision support, with explicit intended use, external validation, calibration, post‐deployment monitoring, and lifecycle governance.
authors: Stjepan Škudar

title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Quadrant-Level Treatment-Site Estimation for Patient Safety
abstract: Introduction and aims Safety interventions in dentistry, including checklists, have been reported; however, it remains difficult to demonstrate sufficient effectiveness in preventing treatment site misidentification, including wrong tooth extraction. This study aimed to establish a foundation for an artificial intelligence (AI)-based patient-safety measure by developing a system that estimates the dental treatment site at the quadrant level from images captured during dental procedures. Methods Single-frame still images (n = 2,446; training 1,780, validation 445, test 221) were extracted from clinical videos recorded during treatment performed by a single dentist between 27 July 2022 and 21 December 2023. Treatment-site estimation models were developed using VGG16, a convolutional neural network-based image-classification model, and YOLOv9, an object-detection model. Performance was compared using three metrics: quadrant accuracy (correct upper/lower and left/right), vertical accuracy (correct upper/lower only), and lateral accuracy (correct left/right only). Results Among five approaches (four VGG16 conditions and one YOLOv9 condition), YOLOv9 achieved the highest performance across all metrics, with quadrant accuracy of 88.7%, vertical accuracy of 96.8%, and lateral accuracy of 91.9%. For VGG16-based approaches, performance across these metrics varied according to image pre-processing. Conclusion This system may support detection and prevention of quadrant-level errors, which are reported to be the second most common type of wrong tooth extraction following adjacent-tooth errors. Clinical relevance AI-based treatment-site estimation may provide an additional preventive safety layer in dentistry by supporting clinicians’ judgement and enabling detection of quadrant-level site misidentification during dental procedures.
authors: Shintaro Nishimoto; Shintaro Oka; Kazunori Nozaki; Harumi Kitamura; Kyota Nakamura; Kazue Nakajima; Mikako Hayashi

title: Artificial intelligence assisted colon capsule endoscopy : evaluating its role in enhancing diagnostic performance
abstract: The global burden of colorectal cancer (CRC) continues to rise, increasing demand for effective lower gastrointestinal (GI) diagnostics. Colon Capsule Endoscopy (CCE) is a minimally invasive alternative to colonoscopy, yet adoption has been limited by variable diagnostic accuracy, lengthy reading times, and high capsule-to-colonoscopy conversion (CCC) rates. Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) offer potential to improve detection and efficiency. This thesis addresses the key barriers to the scalable implementation of CCE. A meta-review and umbrella meta-analysis confirmed the high diagnostic accuracy of second-generation CCE (CCE2), with pooled per-patient sensitivities of 0.90 for polyps of any size and 0.96 for CRC. CCE2 reliably detects polyps ≥6 mm and ≥10 mm with high specificity and low heterogeneity. The CESCAIL (Capsule Endoscopy at Scale through Enhanced AI Analysis) study, involving 14 NHS centres, evaluated the AI-assisted platform AiSPEED™ in 720 patients. In per-patient analysis comparing colonoscopy vs no follow up, AI-assisted readings improved the diagnostic yield (70.6% vs 63.6%) and reduced the mean reading time by more than fivefold (8.7 vs 47.3 minutes). Specificity declined slightly from 99% to 96% (p=0.058), this reflected a higher false-positive rate inherent to AI-assisted CCE interpretation. Per-polyp analysis showed higher sensitivity for smaller and left-sided polyps, with strong performance for hyperplastic lesions, supporting its potential as a triage tool for invasive colonoscopy. A parallel substudy examined inter- and intra-observer variability in bowel cleansing assessment using Leighton-Rex and CC-CLEAR scores. Interobserver agreement was poor with Leighton-Rex scale but improved with CC-CLEAR among experienced readers. AI-assisted scoring did not consistently improve agreement and could reduce it among less experienced readers, indicating a need for refinement and better integration. Further work explored CCC drivers, including excretion rates, bowel preparation, and diagnostic yield. A national audit and meta-analysis that were conducted by the author reported CCC rates of 42–50%, higher with CCE2 due to greater sensitivity. Another multicentre audit demonstrated that FIT-based triage achieved optimal cost-effectiveness at thresholds ranging between 10 and 17.6 μg/g. These findings support a scalable, AI-enabled CCE service integrating cloud platforms, telemedicine, and home capsule delivery to reduce endoscopy backlogs while preserving diagnostic accuracy.
authors: Ian Io Lei
venue: Warwick Research Archive Portal (University of Warwick)

title: Artificial intelligence for ophthalmic vessel segmentation: from multimodal imaging to clinical translation
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-based vessel segmentation converts color fundus photographs, scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (SLO), optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA), structural OCT, and anterior-segment images into quantitative vascular biomarkers. Strong performance within individual datasets has not consistently yielded reliable clinical measurements because errors can arise during acquisition, anatomical preprocessing, vessel extraction, biomarker calculation, and deployment. This structured narrative review compares segmentation tasks involving retinal vascular trees, OCTA capillary plexuses, the structural choroid and choriocapillaris, macular neovascularization, corneal neovascularization, and conjunctival microvasculature. We assess modern architectures in relation to vessel geometry, severe foreground-background imbalance, scale variation, crossings, and susceptibility to artifacts. The methods considered include multiscale feature pyramids, deformable and directional operators, Transformers, state-space models, diffusion approaches, and foundation models. We organize the synthesis around five evaluation levels: pixel overlap, centerline recovery, vascular topology, biomarker agreement, and clinical actionability. Public fundus and OCTA datasets are catalogued with their acquisition and annotation characteristics, and gaps in public anterior-segment vessel benchmarks are discussed. Because devices, data splits, labels, and post-processing differ substantially, reported metrics are summarized without ranking studies against one another. The review distinguishes structural OCT choroidal vascularity index from OCTA choriocapillaris flow-deficit mapping, as well as true vessel segmentation from global hyperemia grading. Clinical translation will require ocular-magnification correction, quality control of retinal layers and projection artifacts, external testing across devices and populations, out-of-distribution rejection, DICOM/PACS interoperability, prospective impact studies, and regulation as software as a medical device. We conclude that clinical utility depends on an auditable pipeline that measures structural error, biomarker uncertainty, and failure states throughout the workflow.
authors: Lingyan Wu; Jiahao Tang; Shanping Zhao

title: Artificial intelligence for vascular minimally invasive surgery: techniques, clinical integration, and challenges
abstract: Introduction Minimally invasive surgery (MIS), including endovascular and robot-assisted procedures, is widely used for vascular pathologies but remains limited by technical complexity, cognitive workload, and postoperative complications. Artificial Intelligence (AI) may help address these challenges through predictive analysis, decision support, image analysis, and automation. Methods A structured Google Scholar search was conducted from February 21, 2025, to January 1, 2026, and updated through September 2026. Peer-reviewed studies applying AI to vascular MIS were included, with additional targeted searches addressing clinical translation, deployment, regulation, and ethical considerations. Results Thirty primary studies were analyzed, including eight on machine learning, nine on deep learning, four on natural language processing, and nine on robotics or reinforcement learning. Machine learning supported risk stratification and outcome prediction, deep learning enabled imaging and segmentation applications, natural language processing facilitated clinical information extraction, and robotic systems supported navigation and procedural assistance. Discussion AI demonstrates substantial potential across the vascular MIS pathway, but broader clinical adoption requires stronger validation, prospective multicenter studies, standardized reporting, health-economic evaluation, and careful consideration of regulatory, liability, and accessibility challenges.
authors: Cenk Jiang; Bogdan Bortnovskii; Ijaz Gul; Mehmed Özkan; Lian Zhang; Dongmei Yu; Vijay Pandey; Runming Wang; Jian Wu; Peiwu Qin

title: Artificial intelligence in chronic atrophic gastritis: A comprehensive review
abstract: Chronic atrophic gastritis (CAG) is a significant precancerous condition associated with gastric cancer, and its accurate diagnosis and comprehensive management are of great importance for reducing the risk of gastric cancer.In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has advanced rapidly in the field of digestive diseases, offering new approaches for the intelligent diagnosis and treatment of CAG.Early studies suggest that AI may improve diagnostic performance and assist in risk stratification.However, whether these systems reduce clinician workload or improve patient outcomes remains to be established.Most evidence comes from retrospective diagnostic accuracy studies, and no AI system has yet been incorporated into clinical guidelines.This review summarizes the research progress of AI in CAG, focusing on five key aspects: Assisted diagnosis, pathological interpretation, Helicobacter pylori infection diagnosis, risk prediction, and patient management.It aims to provide a reference for research on CAG and to highlight priorities for future research and clinical translation.
authors: Nuoya Zhou; Qi Luo; Wei Liu; Xiang-Lei Yuan; Huan Jiang; Bing Hu

title: Artificial intelligence in diabetes: Clinical applications across the disease continuum.
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping the landscape of diabetes mellitus (DM) care by enabling data-driven approaches to prediction, diagnosis, classification, and management. The growing availability of continuous biometric data from wearable technologies, combined with advances in machine learning, has created new opportunities to overcome limitations of traditional diabetes metrics and population-based care models. This review summarises current clinical applications of AI in DM, with a focus on translational relevance and, critically, on the level of validation and clinical readiness of each application. AI-based models have demonstrated improved performance in predicting DM onset and diabetes-related complications by integrating electronic health records, imaging data, and longitudinal clinical variables. In diagnosis and screening, AI offers non-invasive and scalable tools, including automated retinal screening systems and emerging digital biomarkers. Data-driven clustering approaches have further refined diabetes classification. In diabetes management, AI supports personalised glucose monitoring, insulin titration, pharmacological decision-making, and lifestyle interventions. Crucially, these applications differ markedly in maturity: autonomous retinal screening and closed-loop insulin delivery are approaching or have reached routine clinical use, whereas voice-based biomarkers and simulation-evaluated lifestyle systems remain proof-of-concept. Addressing challenges of generalisability, data quality, interpretability, and ethical governance through robust validation and explainable AI will be essential to realise the full potential of AI in precision, patient-centred diabetes care.
authors: Serena Shih Yin; Viola Viola; Paolo Pozzilli
venue: Journal of diabetes and its complications

title: Artificial intelligence in diabetic retinopathy: From deep learning to foundation models, clinical translation, and real-world deployment.
abstract: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) remains a leading cause of preventable vision impairment worldwide, with its burden increasing in parallel with the global diabetes pandemic. As a progressive microvascular disorder with neurovascular unit involvement, DR is driven by retinal ischemia, inflammation, and pathological neovascularization, while diabetic macular edema (DME) continues to represent a principal cause of vision loss. This structured narrative review provides a critical synthesis of advances in diabetic retinopathy diagnosis, retinal imaging, treatment strategies, and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled screening published from January 2020 through March 2026, while selectively incorporating earlier landmark studies to provide clinical and methodological context. We summarize contemporary screening pathways and emerging retinal imaging modalities, including ultra-widefield photography (up to ~200° field of view), optical coherence tomography (OCT), and OCT angiography, examining how complementary structural and vascular biomarkers are reshaping disease severity assessment and DME characterization. We then review the evolution of AI methodologies, highlighting a transition from task-specific convolutional neural network pipelines toward transformer-based and self-supervised representation learning, including retina-specific foundation models designed to reduce annotation burden and improve robustness and generalizability under domain shift. Beyond algorithmic performance on curated benchmarks, we emphasize key translational requirements for clinical adoption, including model calibration, uncertainty-aware triage, image quality control, and external validation across imaging devices and diverse populations. Recent prospective and implementation studies across diverse healthcare systems demonstrate that the real-world effectiveness of AI-enabled DR screening depends not only on diagnostic accuracy but also on image gradability, clinically appropriate operating thresholds, uncertainty management, external validation, referral capacity, and integration with established care pathways. Evidence from the Asia-Pacific region provides important examples of these implementation challenges in heterogeneous and resource-constrained screening environments. Specific attention is given to the identification and mitigation strategies for fundus pigmentation-related performance disparities and the governance of autonomous versus hybrid human-AI screening models within evolving regulatory frameworks. Finally, we examine emerging work in oculomics for systemic risk stratification and propose a pragmatic clinical readiness framework centered on validation hierarchy, safety monitoring, and workflow integration. Particular emphasis is placed on the translational readiness of foundation models, multimodal retinal intelligence, and emerging technologies for large-scale screening, therapeutic decision-making, and longitudinal disease monitoring.

title: Artificial intelligence in early oral cancer detection: a comprehensive review of diagnostic applications, clinical implementation, and future directions
abstract: Oral cancer causes more than 377,000 new cases annually, and delayed diagnosis remains a major contributor to poor outcomes. Conventional visual examination is subjective, while specialist access is limited in many rural and resource-constrained settings.To review the diagnostic performance, clinical implementation, and future directions of artificial intelligence (AI) for early detection and risk stratification of oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMDs) and oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC).PubMed, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and Web of Science were searched for English-language, peer-reviewed studies published from 2015 to 2026 using terms related to AI, machine learning, deep learning, OPMDs, OSCC, screening, and early detection. Eligible diagnostic and implementation studies were synthesized narratively because of methodological heterogeneity.Meta-analyses reported pooled sensitivities of 87%-92% and specificities of 81%-92% across mixed imaging and histopathology applications. PRAYAAS achieved 94% accuracy on its held-out test set, while OralCancerPredict showed good discrimination and calibration for malignant progression risk in oral leukoplakia. Nevertheless, most evidence remains retrospective, single-center, and vulnerable to dataset bias, limited external validation, and inconsistent reference standards.AI is a promising adjunct, not a replacement, for clinician-led screening and histopathologic diagnosis. Priorities include prospective multicenter validation, representative datasets, transparent reporting, explainability, workflow integration, cost-effectiveness, and equity-focused evaluation in low- and middle-income countries.
