title: Endoscopic Endonasal Approaches to Anterior Cranial Base Meningiomas: Indications, Limitations, and Surgical Decision-Making
abstract: Endoscopic endonasal surgery (EES) has fundamentally changed the management of anterior skull base meningiomas by enabling access to many lesions through a direct minimally invasive corridor that avoids traditional transcranial exposure. Improvements in endoscopic optical technology, surgical instrumentation, and skull base reconstruction have steadily expanded the range of tumors that can be treated through an endonasal approach. Even so, EES is not appropriate for every lesion, making thoughtful patient selection and surgical team experience the most important determinants of surgical success. This review explores where EES fits in the contemporary management of anterior skull base meningiomas, including olfactory groove, tuberculum sellae, and planum sphenoidale meningiomas, with particular attention to its indications, limitations, and situations in which EES may not be appropriate. Evidence comparing endoscopic endonasal and transcranial approaches for anterior skull base meningiomas is reviewed, with attention to how tumor anatomy, oncologic objectives, and individual patient characteristics influence the choice of approach. A major consideration is how surgical morbidity can be minimized without compromising oncologic and safety outcomes. Current strategies to protect critical neurovascular structures, reduce the risk of cerebrospinal fluid leakage, and improve skull base durability, including advances in vascularized reconstruction techniques, are discussed. Emerging outcome data and the evolving learning curve associated with EES are also reviewed. Rather than presenting EES as a universal solution, the evidence points toward a patient-centered approach in which operative strategy and clinical decision making is guided by tumor characteristics, anatomy, and surgical goals.
authors: Manat Chopra; David John; David J. Coté; Gabriel Zada

title: Endoscopic and Robotic Minimally Invasive Breast Surgery (MIBS) for Benign Breast Lesions: Our Experience of 80 Cases and Descriptive Comparison
abstract: Objective: Minimally invasive breast surgery (MIBS) via an extramammary approach offers an alternative to conventional open lumpectomy, eliminating breast scarring and improving psychological outcomes in patients with benign breast lesions.While endoscopic MIBS (EMIBS) has been described, data on robotic MIBS (RMIBS) are sparse.We analyzed the clinical and cosmetic outcomes of EMIBS and RMIBS.Materials and Methods: Eighty patients undergoing MIBS for benign breast lumps were divided into endoscopic (n = 40) and robotic (n = 40) groups.Primary endpoints included cosmetic outcomes [evaluated via Patient and Observer Scar Assessment Scale (POSAS) and BREAST-Q], total operative and docking times, and complications, which were statistically analysed (IBM SPSS Statistics version 30).Results: Groups were comparable in age (p = 0.325), lesion size (median 2.0 vs. 2.75 cm; p = 0.247), and number of lumps (median 1 in both groups; p = 0.165).Operative time analysis showed that operative time was significantly longer in the robotic group (median 150 vs. 95 minutes; p<0.001).Complications were minor, self-resolving, and comparable across both groups (Fisher's exact p = 0.647).Cosmetic outcomes (at 1 month) were comparable between the two groups: median POSAS score 2 and median BREAST-Q score 88 (breast-conserving therapy module, satisfaction with breasts subscale).A subjective reduction in physical strain on the surgeon was noted in the robotic group; no objective ergonomic measurements were performed. Conclusion:We demonstrate the feasibility and safety of both approaches for benign breast lesions, with comparable and favorable cosmetic outcomes, and with the robotic platform offering subjective improvement in ergonomic strain, especially in difficult-to-access medial quadrants.These findings are hypothesis-generating and require validation using instruments such as NASA-TLX or the Borg CR-10 scale in larger studies.
authors: Rakesh S. Ramesh; Nikhil Dehankar; Guruvasanth Saravanan; Medha Sugara; Vijaya Lakshmi Vemula Venkata; Sujeeth Aroumougame; Neelesh Kanderi

title: Evaluating an AI-assisted triage workflow for retinal diseases
abstract: The clinical value of artificial intelligence (AI) in fundus photography depends on workflow efficiency as well as diagnostic performance. We evaluated an AI-assisted negative-screening workflow for diabetic retinopathy (DR), retinal vein occlusion (RVO), and age-related macular degeneration (AMD) using 6,904 color fundus photographs independently graded by three retina specialists. In this workflow, AI-negative images were classified as negative without ophthalmologist review, whereas AI-positive images were referred for human interpretation. For each reader-disease pair, the reference standard was agreement between the other two readers; discordant cases were excluded (DR, 1.2%-2.3%; RVO, 0.3%-0.6%; AMD, 6.1%-11.6%). The workflow reduced direct ophthalmologist review to 7.3%-8.0% of images for DR, 11.7%-11.9% for RVO, and 13.5%-16.8% for AMD. For DR, sensitivity decreased significantly (0.9168 to 0.8838; difference, -0.0330; 95% confidence interval [CI], -0.0495 to -0.0165; p < 0.001), whereas specificity did not change significantly (0.9961 to 0.9983; p = 0.183). For RVO, sensitivity was unchanged (0.9807) and specificity did not change significantly (0.9985 to 0.9988; p = 0.320). For AMD, sensitivity decreased significantly (0.8570 to 0.8445; difference, -0.0124; 95% CI, -0.0215 to -0.0033; p = 0.008), whereas specificity did not change significantly (0.9685 to 0.9843; p = 0.324). In an exploratory image-level analysis for at least one target disease, review decreased to 27.7%-30.1%; sensitivity changed from 0.9122 to 0.9039 (difference, -0.0083; 95% CI, -0.0131 to -0.0035; p < 0.001) and specificity from 0.9659 to 0.9804 (p = 0.334). AI-assisted negative-screening can reduce ophthalmologist workload across multiple retinal diseases, but with disease-specific safety trade-offs: because AI-negative images are not reviewed, reduced sensitivity for DR and AMD means a small proportion of true-positive cases would go undetected, potentially delaying diagnosis and treatment for sight-threatening disease. These results support disease-specific implementation strategies that balance workload reduction against missed positive cases.
authors: Doohyun Park; Richul Oh; Jihyeon Baek; Kunho Bae

title: Explainability-informed patient-disjoint evaluation of deep learning for plus disease in retinopathy of prematurity with an ophthalmologist reader study
abstract: Background: Plus disease is a treatment-relevant sign of retinopathy of prematurity, but fundus images from the same infant may differ in image quality, posterior-pole coverage, and visible vascular severity. We evaluated deep-learning classification using a patient-disjoint design, within-infant variability, and an ophthalmologist reader study. Methods: The primary analysis included 732 Phoenix ICON fundus images from 38 infants, assigned exclusively to a 634-image development pool or a 98-image hold-out set from eight previously unseen infants. Five pretrained convolutional neural networks were evaluated at the image level. Hold-out predictions were grouped by infant and laterality to characterize descriptive within-infant variation. A historical secondary analysis used a random image-level partition without enforced patient separation and was considered exploratory. Two ophthalmologists independently graded 30 unique isolated images for inter-observer analysis; 10 were presented twice, resulting in 40 presentations for intra-observer repeatability. Results: DenseNet121 achieved an image-level ROC-AUC of 0.929; however, infant-equal-weighted image-level ROC-AUC was 0.905 and leave-one-infant-out ROC-AUC ranged from 0.838 to 0.989, demonstrating sensitivity to the small clustered hold-out cohort. At a development-defined threshold of 0.0184, sensitivity increased to 98.0%, while specificity decreased to 46.8%. Within-infant probability variability was observed across all five CNN architectures. Ophthalmologists 1 and 2 assessed 14/18 and 17/18 plus-reference images, respectively, as Healthy. Exact three-category inter-observer agreement was 26/30 (86.7%), and both reproduced the same severity grade for all 10 repeated images. Conclusions: Patient-disjoint evaluation revealed substantial uncertainty in image-level performance and variability among images from the same infant. Cluster-aware analyses showed dependence on the small hold-out cohort, while the development-defined operating point demonstrated a marked sensitivity-specificity trade-off. The reader study showed that an examination-derived reference label and the diagnostic evidence visible in an isolated image are not equivalent, despite high inter-observer agreement and complete categorical repeatability. Because examination identifiers were unavailable, within-infant analyses were interpreted descriptively and not as infant or examination-level diagnostic performance. Clinically useful systems should assess image quality, select informative views, and integrate evidence across multiple images and both eyes. External prospective multicentre validation is required before clinical implementation.

title: F2D-RetinaNet: a feature-to-decision dual-path network with fractional operators for retinal disease detection and grading
abstract: Visible pathological abnormalities and vascular integrity help diagnose retinal diseases. This paper introduces a unified feature-to-decision framework that first extracts vasculature and enhances lesions. First, this study proposes the fractional anisotropic diffusion–based hybrid enhancement (FADHE) method that selectively amplifies lesion contrast and vessel visibility in the green channel using long-memory fractional diffusion dynamics. Second, this study introduces a fractional Hessian-based attention U-Net (FHAU-Net), a multi-scale vessel segmentation model that leverages fractional Hessian responses across eight fractional orders and attention-guided skip connections to capture fine vessel structures. Finally, this work designs a dual-branch disease grading model, F2D-RetinaNet, which jointly processes the enhanced image and vessel map to learn lesion-related and vascular feature representations for the recognition and grading of retinal diseases. The FHAU-Net model achieved a Dice coefficient of 0.8987, a sensitivity of 0.9084, an accuracy of 0.9804, and a specificity of 0.9876 across the unified test set, which contains variations in resolution, acquisition site, camera type, and imaging conditions. The F2D-RetinaNet is evaluated for Diabetic retinopathy (DR) detection, DR grading, and multiclass retinal disease classification tasks. Extensive testing and comparisons to the baseline procedures support the reliability of the proposed methodology on the datasets evaluated here.
authors: Mukesh Delu; Priyanka Harjule; Rajesh Kumar; Kushal Gajjar; Pilani Nkomozepi

title: FAR-POLYP-SEG: A Prospective Single-Center Colonoscopy Dataset for Colorectal Polyp Segmentation with Patient-Level Metadata and Baseline Cross-Dataset Evaluation
abstract: Reliable computer-aided colonoscopy depends on well-organized imaging data, transparent benchmarking, and validation of artificial intelligence (AI) tools on independent data. Many public colonoscopy datasets are limited in size, omit normal-mucosa frames, or lack linked patient-level clinical context, which constrains their use as imaging informatics benchmarks. We present FAR-POLYP-SEG, a prospective single-center colonoscopy dataset for colorectal polyp segmentation, developed as an imaging informatics resource for the validation of segmentation algorithms. The dataset was acquired at Farhikhtegan Hospital, Islamic Azad University, Tehran, Iran, between February and December 2025 during routine colonoscopy, without modification of the standard diagnostic workflow. It contains 8181 frames from 455 patients: 432 polyp-positive frames with expert pixel-level segmentation masks and 7749 normal-mucosa frames. Patient-level clinical and procedural metadata (age, sex, colonoscopy indication, Boston Bowel Preparation Scale (BBPS) score, and procedure duration) are linked to every case. Six segmentation architectures (UNet, UNet++, UNet (MiT-B0), nnU-Net 2D, PraNet, and YOLOv11m-seg) were trained and evaluated under one standardized protocol using patient-grouped five-fold cross-validation, so that no patient contributed frames to both the training and the test set of any fold. PraNet reached the highest internal segmentation performance (Dice 0.755), while nnU-Net reached the highest internal IoU (0.665) and pixel accuracy. A complementary evaluation on the dataset's 7749 normal-mucosa frames shows that the models most sensitive to real polyps are not the most specific: gated false-positive rates on normal mucosa ranged from 24.9% (YOLOv11m-seg) to 59.5% (nnU-Net), an almost complete inversion of the internal Dice ranking. All models were then evaluated on the public Kvasir-SEG dataset as an unseen external test set; Dice ranged from 0.756 to 0.829 across models, and the relative ordering was largely preserved, although nnU-Net's internal advantage on accuracy and IoU did not carry over to external Dice. The dataset, structured metadata, and evaluation code are publicly released to support reproducible imaging informatics research.

title: Fed-ADApt: Federated Anytime Depth Adaptation for Resource-Aware Medical Image Segmentation
abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative training of medical image segmentation models without sharing raw patient data, yet existing approaches assume a homogeneous compute budget across institutions, limiting participation of low-resource sites. We propose Fed-ADApt, a depth-adaptive federated framework for UNet-based segmentation that jointly addresses low-compute training and inference. Fed-ADApt integrates multi-depth supervision with hierarchical depth-wise aggregation, allowing each site to train according to its local compute budget while contributing to a global model that supports dynamic depth selection at deployment. We evaluated Fed-ADApt on multi-site 2D retinal fundus disc segmentation and 3D brain tumor segmentation. Across both tasks, federated collaboration substantially improves robustness under domain shift. Fed-ADApt matched the full-resource FedAvg performance in 3D and achieved competitive 2D performance with a 4.7% average Dice reduction, while reducing average inference cost by 19.5% in 3D and 34.5% in 2D and substantially reducing training cost by 98% at the most constrained sites. Importantly, Fed-ADApt enables low-resource institutions that cannot train full-capacity models to participate in federations while maintaining competitive global performance under a favorable accuracy to efficiency trade-off. By considering training and inference compute budgets, Fed-ADApt provides a practical and equitable solution for federated medical image segmentation across heterogeneous clinical and edge-enabled imaging environments.

title: FedFound: Federated Foundation Model for GI endoscopy imaging
abstract: Gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy is essential for identifying abnormalities and enabling early diagnosis, thereby improving diagnostic accuracy and facilitating timely clinical intervention. While deep learning has shown promise in supporting GI diagnostics, most models require carefully labeled datasets that are costly to acquire and limited in scope. Foundation models offer a paradigm shift by learning general-purpose representations that can be adapted for diverse tasks, addressing data scarcity and variability. However, training such models on medical imaging data remains challenging due to privacy regulations, security concerns, and fragmented digital infrastructures that prevent centralized data aggregation, even as hospitals collectively generate vast amounts of endoscopic data. To overcome these barriers, we propose a federated learning (FL) framework for GI foundation models, allowing data to remain local while collaboratively training a shared model. We extensively evaluate multiple FL algorithms under both homogeneous and heterogeneous settings across three clinically relevant downstream tasks-classification, detection, and segmentation. We further evaluate our framework with a larger number of clients and across diverse pretraining strategies to assess its scalability and robustness. Our results demonstrate consistent performance gains, underscoring the potential of Federated Foundation Models to enable clinically validated AI applications and support secure, regulation-compliant deployment in real-world gastroendoscopy practice.
authors: Alina Devkota; Annahita Amireskandari; Joel R. Palko; Soban A. Maan; Shyam J Thakkar; Tapan Khan; Xiajun Jiang; Donald Adjeroh; Binod Bhattarai; Prashnna Gyawali

title: Ferroptosis in retinal neurodegeneration: mechanistic vulnerability, therapeutic targeting, and translational barriers
abstract: Progressive retinal neurodegeneration remains a major therapeutic challenge in ophthalmology because structural and functional loss may continue despite control of the primary insult, including intraocular pressure reduction in glaucoma, metabolic management in diabetic retinopathy, or suppression of acute inflammatory activity. Ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of regulated cell death driven by phospholipid peroxidation and insufficient antioxidant buffering, has emerged as a potential mechanism linking metabolic stress, ischemic injury, excitotoxicity, and neuroinflammatory signaling to sustained retinal neurovascular unit damage. In this review, we synthesize current evidence supporting ferroptosis-related vulnerability in retinal neurodegenerative diseases. Particular emphasis is placed on expansion of the labile iron pool, PUFA-phospholipid remodeling, dysfunction of the System Xc⁻/glutathione (GSH)/glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) axis, and multicellular amplification within the neuro-glial-microvascular unit. We further compare disease-specific evidence in glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy, and selected optic nerve injury contexts, emphasizing that causal validation remains uneven across models, cell types, and disease stages. From a translational perspective, we discuss why anti-ferroptotic strategies face distinct ophthalmic barriers, including limited retinal access, insufficient local exposure, short intraocular residence, and safety constraints associated with chronic modulation of iron and redox metabolism. Finally, we evaluate emerging enabling strategies, including nanocarrier-based delivery, long-acting gene modulation, and biomarker frameworks integrating ocular fluids, imaging, multi-omics, and artificial intelligence. Ferroptosis-targeted neuroprotection is therefore best viewed as a disease- and stage-dependent translational framework rather than a universal therapeutic solution.
authors: Guangguang Wu; Suyu Wang; Ziyi Chen; Jiajun Li; Keran Li

title: FoViTA: A Transformer-Based Multimodal Framework for Diabetic Retinopathy Detection Using Fundus and OCT Images
abstract: Diabetic Retinopathy (DR) is one of the most prevalent causes of avoidable blindness for diabetics across the world. In this paper, a transformer-based multimodal interaction module for feature interaction is proposed to allow better cross-modal focus to learn strong dependencies between fundus image surface-level characteristics and depth-wise representations of OCT images. Extensive validation of the developed methodology is carried out on the benchmark multimodal retinal image datasets, and the efficacy of the developed non-invasive multimodal retinal image analysis and classification system is ensured as the developed system is able to achieve the classification accuracy of 98.25%, thereby showing better performance compared to the recent state-of-the-art techniques, namely, transformer-based classifiers, Vision Transformer-Capsule Network-based techniques, and multimodal fusion techniques. This is due to the fact that the developed methodology is able to show the improvement of approximately 1.9-4.8% compared to the recent techniques, which show the accuracy of 95-97% while diagnosing the early stages of diabetic retinopahty.
authors: Ojas Shrivastava; Manoj Diwakar; Neeraj Kumar Pandey; prabhishek singh; Anchit Bijalwan; Sanjay Roka

title: Force-Torque Classification of Reference-Profile-Defined Drilling States During Robot-Assisted Dental Implant Osteotomy
abstract: PURPOSE: To evaluate whether force-torque features can classify three predefined, reference-profile-defined operational drilling states during robot-assisted implant osteotomy under specimen-level separation. Materials and Methods: Thirty porcine hemimandibular specimens underwent 180 robot-controlled osteotomies under three drilling conditions. Axial force (Fz) and drilling torque (Mz) were sampled at 1000 Hz, segmented into 100-ms windows with a 50-ms step, and represented by 42 time-, frequency-, and wavelet-domain features; 23 features were selected using training-only ANOVA ranking and correlation pruning. Specimens were separated into training, validation, and held-out test sets (18/6/6). Linear support vector machine (SVM), random forest (RF), and XGBoost were evaluated against predefined depth-indexed operational reference profiles; a same-acquisition CBCT rule served as an imaging comparator. Results: The dataset contained 92,675 overlapping windows. On six held-out specimens (36 osteotomies; 18,496 windows), XGBoost achieved 93.0% accuracy (specimen-clustered 95% CI, 92.0-94.0%), 82.9% balanced accuracy, and 85.6% macro-F1. RF and SVM accuracies were 90.5% and 88.8%, respectively. The CBCT rule achieved 92.3% accuracy but lower balanced accuracy (80.1%) and transitional recall (51.1%). XGBoost transitional recall was 59.6%, increasing to 73.0% in a weighted sensitivity configuration at the cost of lower overall accuracy. Accuracy decreased from 94.1% away from class boundaries to 75.6% in boundary-adjacent windows. Conclusion: Force-torque features differentiated the three predefined reference-profile-defined drilling states under specimen-separated evaluation. XGBoost achieved the highest classification performance, with errors concentrated primarily in transitional and boundary-adjacent windows. Keywords: robot-assisted implant osteotomy; force-torque sensing; reference-profile classification; drilling-state classification; XGBoost; specimen-level validation .
authors: Jiaqiang Li; Yangdong Wu; Yao Wang; Min Shao

title: From Accuracy to Reliability: What Prevents Artificial Intelligence from Being Clinically Reliable for Periapical Lesion Detection? A Review
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning, has shown potential in detecting periapical radiolucencies on dental radiographs. However, accuracy on a retrospective research dataset does not guarantee clinical performance. This narrative review explores the discrepancy between algorithmic accuracy and real-world clinical reliability, including dataset representativeness, spectrum and selection bias, cropped-image evaluation, lesion size and anatomical complexity, reference-standard uncertainty, domain shift in imaging systems, external validation, explainability of AI, and the limited integration of radiographic AI with clinical information. Recent systematic reviews report high pooled diagnostic performance, but consistently cite substantial heterogeneity, risk of bias, limited prospective evidence, and insufficient external validation. The argument for this review is that the next phase of research should change the question from 'Can AI detect a periapical lesion?' to 'Can AI reliably detect an unexpected lesion in an unselected clinical image and improve the clinician's decision?' Clinical reliability should therefore be viewed as a multidimensional concept incorporating technical performance, generalizability, calibration, interpretability, workflow compatibility, and impact on clinician and patient outcomes. A staged framework of internal validation, external validation, prospective clinical validation, human-AI evaluation and post-deployment monitoring is proposed. AI should be regarded as an adjunctive second reader and decision-support tool rather than an autonomous diagnostic replacement.
authors: Priyanka Sharma

title: From Freehand Demonstrations to Autonomous Robotic Ultrasound: An Anatomy-Anchored Learning Framework
abstract: Ultrasound imaging is highly operator-dependent, motivating robotic systems that reproduce expert scanning skills consistently. These skills involve coordinated interpretation of anatomical landmarks, ultrasound images, and probe-tissue interactions that are difficult to encode in hand-designed control strategies. Imitation learning offers an alternative, but its observation and action representations should reflect the anatomically structured nature of scanning. We propose an anatomy-anchored imitation-learning framework that combines anatomy-guided probe placement with learned ultrasound navigation. The placement module identifies a task-specific anatomical starting point from external visual observations and establishes the initial probe pose as the reference frame for scanning. A flow-based policy then generates scanning motions from anchor-relative probe poses, ultrasound images, probe-mounted camera views, and contact forces, while a termination head predicts task completion. This avoids continuous reliance on third-person vision and reduces dependence on the robot-patient configuration. A handheld acquisition platform enables multimodal demonstrations to be collected during natural freehand scanning without a robot. On 16 unseen participants, task success reaches 96%, 94%, 88%, and 94% for kidney, gallbladder, and liver standard-plane acquisition and radial artery sweeping, respectively. Compared with a fine-tuned pi_0 model, success on the abdominal tasks improves by 10-42 percentage points, with lower time-to-target, peak contact force, and trajectory jerk. Ablations support the complementary roles of anatomical anchoring, egocentric vision, and force feedback. End-to-end trials with automatic placement achieve 90-100% success, and the policies transfer without retraining to a second robot with 83-100% success.

title: From Image-Guided Surgery to Autonomous Decision-Making: Artificial Intelligence, Computational Anatomy and Intelligent Surgical Ecosystems in Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery: A Narrative Review
abstract: Oral and maxillofacial surgery has moved from two-dimensional planning toward computational, patient-specific workflows and artificial intelligence now extends beyond image interpretation into diagnosis, navigation, robotics and postoperative monitoring, raising unresolved questions about autonomy, accountability and surgical oversight. This narrative review examines the role of computational anatomy, artificial intelligence and digital biomarkers in improving diagnosis, personalized planning, intraoperative guidance and prediction of surgical outcomes, tracing the evolution of virtual surgical planning into artificial intelligence-assisted and robotic surgery. Computational modeling augmented and mixed reality, robotics and digital biomarkers improved planning accuracy, spatial orientation and postoperative monitoring while reducing cognitive workload, although registration accuracy, latency, dataset quality and the scarcity of prospective multicenter validation remain important limitations. Artificial intelligence is advancing the specialty within an emerging intelligent surgical ecosystem, yet broader adoption requires robust validation, ethical governance, multicenter studies and continued surgeon oversight.

title: From Prompts To Masks: Assessing Gemini Image Models for Tooth Segmentation on Panoramic Radiographs
abstract: Introduction and aims Tooth-region segmentation on panoramic radiographs supports annotation, region-of-interest extraction, and dataset triage, but conventional approaches require task-specific training labels. Although vendor-hosted multimodal models can follow natural-language prompts, their pixel-level reliability in dental radiographs remains unclear. This study assessed the accuracy, false-positive behavior, and run-to-run stability of two Gemini Image models for prompt-based tooth-region masking. Methods Ninety-six panoramic radiographs from the Tufts Dental Database (32 permanent dentition, 32 mixed dentition, 32 edentulous) were standardized to 2880 × 1472 pixels. Each image was submitted five times to Gemini 3 Pro Image and Gemini 3.1 Flash Image using a fixed text-to-mask prompt. Permanent- and mixed-dentition outputs were evaluated using mean Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) and intersection over union (IoU); edentulous outputs were evaluated using specificity, false-positive (FP) area ratio, and no-mask rate. Bootstrap 95% confidence intervals and Holm-corrected paired permutation tests were used for inference. Results In the pooled permanent- and mixed-dentition group, both models achieved a mean DSC of 0.883; mean IoU was 0.794 and 0.795 for Gemini 3 Pro Image and Gemini 3.1 Flash Image, respectively. Permanent dentition favored Gemini 3 Pro Image numerically (DSC 0.905 vs 0.896), whereas mixed dentition favored Gemini 3.1 Flash Image (DSC 0.871 vs 0.861). For edentulous radiographs, specificity and FP area ratio were comparable between models, and the no-mask rate was numerically higher for Gemini 3 Pro Image (76.3% vs 63.8%). No comparison remained significant after Holm correction, and k-of-5 analysis revealed variable run-to-run stability. Conclusion Prompt-based tooth-region segmentation yielded clinically plausible outputs without task-specific training, but dentition-dependent performance, target-absent false positives, and limited reproducibility support expert-supervised rather than autonomous use. Clinical relevance Expert-reviewed annotation support, dataset triage, and human-in-the-loop preprocessing are more appropriate than stand-alone clinical segmentation.

title: From Repetition to Reform: Confronting Academic Redundancy in Dental Education
abstract: Introduction: Why This Conversation Matters NowModern dental education was built on a vision of continual improvement.Nearly over a century ago the great visionary William J. Gies said, What we want is a better class of better dentists, because the world is, I believe, suffering from a lack of good dental service more than from any bodily ailment of which we have any knowledge .This insightful vision has helped shape the foundations of modern dental education; the profession faces a different but related challenge: How to preserve educational rigor and institutional memory while ensuring that accumulated curricular and organizational structures remain responsive to contemporary learners and professional needs.Calls for transformation in dental education are not new.The American Dental Education Association (ADEA) Commission on Change and Innovation in Dental Education identified the need to reconsider traditional educational approaches and promote deliberate change in response to evolving societal, professional, and educational demands [ 1,2 ].The Commission's work also highlighted concerns about curricular complexity and educational environments that may be expensive and dissatisfying for learners [ 2 ].Yet curricular renewal remains challenging.New knowledge, technologies, expectations, and educational priorities are often added to existing structures, while fewer mechanisms exist for systematically determining what should be integrated, reduced, or retired.

title: From algorithm performance to clinical value in AI-assisted skin cancer diagnostics
abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) has demonstrated high diagnostic performance in skin cancer detection and is increasingly being integrated into clinical workflows. However, whether these advances translate into meaningful patient-relevant and healthcare system outcomes remains unclear. Evidence on value-oriented outcomes has not been systematically synthesized. Methods We conducted a PRISMA-ScR–guided scoping review of studies published between January 2015 and October 2025 identified through PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science. Studies evaluating AI-based technologies for skin cancer diagnosis, triage, risk stratification, or management were included if they reported outcomes beyond technical performance metrics. Reported outcomes were mapped to three value-oriented domains: clinical and prognostic, process and experiential, and system-level and economic outcomes. Results Of 4,021 records identified, 33 studies met the inclusion criteria, whereas 389 publications were excluded because they reported only technical performance metrics without value-oriented outcomes. Reported outcomes were predominantly process and experiential (28/33 studies), including diagnostic confidence, workflow efficiency, and user acceptance. Clinical and prognostic outcomes were reported in only five studies, with four studies focussing on prognostic utility and one study focussing on patient management, while system-level and economic outcomes were identified in three studies. Most evaluations were conducted in controlled experimental settings, whereas prospective real-world implementation studies were less common. Overall, the available evidence predominantly focused on process-level benefits, with limited evidence for clinical and prognostic or system-level and economic outcomes. Discussion Current evaluation strategies for AI-based skin cancer diagnostics remain predominantly performance-oriented and are largely focused on process and experiential outcomes. From a value-based healthcare perspective, current evidence remains largely confined to intermediate stages of the diagnostic value chain: although AI-assisted systems may improve diagnostic workflows, clinician confidence, and clinical decision making, few studies have evaluated their impact on downstream patient-relevant clinical and prognostic, or system-level and economic outcomes. Future research should prioritize prospective real-world studies, outcome-driven evaluation frameworks, and economic assessments that examine the impact of AI-supported decision-making on clinical outcomes and healthcare systems. Conclusion Despite promising effects on diagnostic processes, evidence for the clinical and system-level value of AI-based skin cancer diagnostics remains limited. Outcome-driven evaluation frameworks are needed to bridge the gap between algorithmic performance and meaningful healthcare impact.

title: From pain relief to mucosal grief: A comprehensive review of NSAID enteropathy.
abstract: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are essential for their analgesic, anti-inflammatory and anti-pyretic properties. However, their extended use can lead to NSAID enteropathy, a frequently underdiagnosed condition of the small intestine. This pathology manifests as mucosal damage, ulcerations, strictures and increased intestinal permeability, potentially resulting in complications such as bleeding, protein loss and nutrient malabsorption. Modern diagnostic technologies, particularly capsule endoscopy, have revealed that small-bowel injury affects up to 70% of chronic NSAID users, although many patients remain asymptomatic. This comprehensive review explores the epidemiology, underlying mechanisms, clinical manifestations, diagnostic approaches and treatment strategies for NSAID enteropathy, while emphasizing the growing importance of increased clinical awareness and continued research into preventive and therapeutic interventions, especially as long-term NSAID use becomes more prevalent in our aging global population.

title: From validation to public health impact: implementing equitable AI-enabled diabetic retinopathy screening
abstract: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) remains a preventable cause of vision loss as diabetes prevalence rises worldwide. Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled retinal screening has progressed from retrospective validation to prospective and real-world deployment, with recent reviews showing high diagnostic performance across fundus photography, smartphone-based systems, and autonomous platforms. Yet diagnostic accuracy alone does not ensure public health benefit. Population impact can be lost when eligible people are not reached, images are ungradable, results are delayed, referrals are incomplete, treatment capacity is insufficient, or disadvantaged groups face financial, geographic, or digital barriers. Unlike reviews centered mainly on diagnostic accuracy or economic performance, this Mini Review reframes AI-enabled DR screening as a population-health intervention spanning detection through completion of effective eye care. We synthesize evidence on diagnostic validity, implementation, economics, referral completion, care cascades, patient-centered outcomes, equity, and governance. We argue that effectiveness and cost-effectiveness are properties of the complete screening-to-treatment pathway, not the algorithm alone, and propose a four-domain framework encompassing technical validity, service integration, population impact, and equity and sustainability. Future research should prioritize comparative implementation studies and outcome sets that capture screening reach, gradability, referral completion, treatment initiation, time to treatment, avoidable vision loss, vision-related quality of life, acceptability, costs, and subgroup equity. The policy question is no longer whether AI can detect DR, but whether health systems can translate automated detection into equitable completion of effective eye care at scale.

title: Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumor of the Jejunum with Recurrent Bleeding: A Case Report and a Brief Literature Review
abstract: Bleeding from gastrointestinal (GI) stromal tumour (GIST) of the jejunum is rare and is reported in the literature as isolated clinical observations or small series.In the present study, we report a case of a 64-year-old woman who presented with recurrent GI bleeding.Upper endoscopy revealed no signs of bleeding.A contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) scan was performed, and a predominantly intraluminal, heterogeneous, tumour-like mass in the proximal jejunum was visualised, with dimensions 4.6x4.4x6.1 cm.A midline laparotomy was performed, and exploration of the abdominal cavity revealed a tumour in the lumen of the jejunum located 30 cm from the ligament of Treitz.Segmental resection of the jejunum with tumour, followed by anastomosis, was performed.On pathologic examination and immunohistochemistry, a spindle cell variant of GIST (c-KIT/CD117 +++) with negative resection margins (R0) was recognised.GIST of the jejunum is a relatively rare cause of gastrointestinal bleeding.The main diagnostic method is contrast-enhanced CT.The treatment of choice for bleeding jejunal GIST is segmental resection with a negative surgical margin (R0 resection), without compromising tumor integrity.

title: Genetic Algorithm-Based Weighted Ensemble of Deep CNN Models for Dental Disease Detection
abstract: Accurate categorization of dental imagery is crucial to facilitate early identification and efficient treatment strategizing in dental healthcare. This investigation aspires to establish a multiclass dental pathology classification framework employing a Genetic Algorithm (GA)-based weighted ensemble of deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architectures. The resources used in this scholarly inquiry comprise a publicly accessible dental image repository encompassing four categories: caries, calculus, discoloration, and hypodontia, sourced from diverse clinical and web-based sources. The proposed methodology implements transfer learning by fine-tuning three pre-trained CNN frameworks, specifically ResNet50V2, EfficientNetB4, and EfficientNetB5. Each foundational model is trained autonomously, and their predictive probabilities are amalgamated via a weighted ensemble approach. A Genetic Algorithm is utilized to autonomously ascertain the optimal ensemble weights by maximizing the macro F1-score, thereby ensuring equitable performance across all pathological categories. Experiments were executed utilizing varying training epochs to assess model convergence and generalizability. The experimental findings reveal that the GA-based ensemble attained optimal efficacy at a configuration with a maximum of 300 training epochs, with an accuracy of 98.71%, a precision of 98.62%, a recall of 97.66%, and an F1-score of 98.12. A minor reduction in performance at elevated epochs indicates the emergence of overfitting. Compared with individual CNN models and non-optimized ensemble methods, the proposed framework exhibits enhanced robustness and more consistent class-wise classification. These results underscore the efficacy of metaheuristic optimization in advancing ensemble deep learning for dental disease classification. Prospective research should concentrate on validation utilizing larger multicenter clinical datasets, exploration of alternative optimization algorithms, and real-time clinical implementation.

title: GeoCM-Pose: geometry-aware monocular dental 2D/3D registration benchmarked against reference-assisted methods
abstract: Abstract Objective. To develop GeoCM-Pose, a geometry-aware monocular dental 2D/3D registration method that predicts metric model-to-camera 6DoF pose from one image under weak texture, repetitive anatomy and partial visibility. Approach. GeoCM-Pose comprises cross-modal adaptation (CMA) and geometry-aware pose regression (GAPR). CMA uses fixed-Gaussian frequency separation and a high-frequency structure-preservation module with multi-scale edge extraction, spatial–channel gating and cross-resolution refinement. GAPR uses a ResNet-50/U-Net to predict dense object-coordinate maps; hierarchical geometric feature aggregation and geometry-aware channel refinement feed decoupled unit-quaternion and translation heads. Joint 20-point pose-matching and dense-coordinate losses train the network. The study comprised 30 in vitro training cases, five in vivo validation cases, five in vivo internal-test cases, 10 fully held-out Teeth3DS+ dental surface models and a 200-frame benchmark generated from a single three-dimensional dental model. Main Results. GAPR/V0 generated pose estimates for all 200 query frames, with median reprojection, rotation and translation-vector errors of 2.156 px, 1.252° and 0.653 mm, respectively, and a <5 px pass rate of 91.5% across all attempts. It used no inference-time reference-image bank. At R01, scale-invariant feature transform and ORB generated 85/200 and 89/200 valid estimates, with <5 px all-attempt pass rates of 40.5% and 40.0%; at R20, each generated 197/200 valid estimates, with pass rates of 98.0% and 95.5%. Thus, conventional performance increased with the available reference bank, whereas GAPR/V0 provided complete query coverage from a single image without inference-time reference images. Median GAPR/V0 inference latency, including image I/O, was 11.459 ms. Significance. GeoCM-Pose integrates CMA, dense object-coordinate supervision and metric pose regression for monocular dental 2D/3D registration. Further case-level evaluation using intraoral endoscopic images acquired from independent patient cases and additional image domains, together with robot-integrated experiments, is required to assess generalisation and system-level performance.

title: Giant Cavernous Hemangioma in the Mesentery of the Descending Colon: A Case Report
abstract: Gastrointestinal hemangiomas are rare, and those involving the mesentery are even more infrequent. The majority of cases reported in the literature had mesenteric cavernous hemangioma of the small intestine. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first documented case of a hemangioma originating from the mesentery of the descending colon. Preoperative diagnosis is exceedingly difficult, and various imaging modalities may be inconclusive. The patient was a 71-year-old Asian male presenting with recurrent dizziness and fatigue over several months. Physical examination revealed a mass that was palpable in the left mid-abdominal region. Laboratory examinations suggested gastrointestinal bleeding and anemia. Abdominal CT scans revealed a large mesenteric mass in the descending colon. The mass was surgically resected, and histopathological examination confirmed mesenteric cavernous hemangioma. The patient showed no signs of recurrence in 1 year of postoperative follow-up.
authors: Dong xie; Jinna Yu; Dan Shi; Yaqi Jiang

title: Global research trends in interventional bronchoscopy: a bibliometric analysis of publications from 2005 to 2025
abstract: Abstract Background The field of interventional bronchoscopy (IB) has experienced rapid advancements over the past two decades, evolving from a predominantly diagnostic modality into a highly technological specialty encompassing use of endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS), electromagnetic navigation bronchoscopy (ENB), robotic-assisted bronchoscopy (RAB), transbronchial cryobiopsy, airway stenting, and image-guided interventions. Although there have been emerging advancements in the practice of IB, no global research studies have comprehensively evaluated trends in the field. Objective To analyze the global scientific output, collaboration patterns, influential contributors, and thematic evolution of IB research from 2005 to 2025. Methods The bibliometric analysis was performed using Scopus database. Studies related to IB published from January 2005 to December 2025 were identified using predefined search strategy. Records were identified using the predefined search terms. The dataset was then cleaned by removing similar but non-relevant terms, and eligibility was restricted to research articles and conference papers, with review articles, book chapters, and other document types excluded. No language restriction was applied. Data were analyzed using the Bibliometrix and Biblioshiny packages in R. Results A total of 18,019 records were identified, of which 652 eligible publications were included, comprising 609 original research articles and 43 conference papers, with no language restriction. Publication output increased markedly after 2020. Zaroulidis P was the most productive author, while the United States, China, Japan, Germany, and the United Kingdom were among the leading contributing countries, with Nagoya University as the most productive institution. Highly cited studies mainly focused on airway stents and tracheal prostheses, bronchoscopic lung volume reduction, diagnostic and image-guided bronchoscopy, and procedural sedation and safety. More recent highly cited studies increasingly addressed robotic, computational, and artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted bronchoscopy. Randomized and comparative clinical trials are relatively limited but included EBUS-TBNA and ENB for diagnostic strategies, bronchoscopic lung volume reduction, airway stenting, hybrid EBUS, radial EBUS, and AI-assisted bronchoscopy. Research themes progressively shifted from diagnostic and imaging applications toward therapeutic, navigational, robotic, bioengineering, and AI-enabled approaches. Conclusions In conclusion, IB research has transitioned from predominantly diagnostic and imaging-based techniques (EBUS-TBNA and navigational bronchoscopy), toward therapeutic, robotic, image-guided, bioengineering, and AI-assisted interventions. Emerging bioengineering, and AI-assisted technologies hold promise for IB but require clinical validation.

title: Global trends and hotspots in robot-assisted gastrointestinal endoscopy: a bibliometric and visualization analysis.
abstract: Robot-assisted gastrointestinal endoscopy represents an emerging frontier that extends robotic assistance from the abdominal cavity to the organ lumen; however, this field lacks comprehensive bibliometric mapping at a global level. We analyzed 886 articles published between 1999 and 2026 (2026 data are partial) and indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection using established bibliometric and visualization tools, and assessed author impact using composite bibliometric indices. Research activity progressed through three distinct phases: germination (1999-2010), growth (2011-2018), and rapid development (2019-2025). China led global output, whereas Italy achieved the highest per-article citation impact. The therapeutic share increased to 40.6% in the latest phase, yielding a therapeutic-to-diagnostic ratio of 1.19 and indicating a shift in research activity toward therapeutic interventions. Co-citation analysis revealed a maturing intellectual structure shifting from diagnostic platforms to therapeutic endoscopy and the integration of artificial intelligence, with permanent-magnet-driven systems, robot-assisted endoscopic submucosal dissection, and emerging endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography and endoscopic ultrasound platforms representing the current frontiers. A dual-hub pattern emerged, with Italian engineering centers producing high-impact foundational work and a broad group of Chinese institutions driving high-volume clinical validation. The 2024-2026 interval suggested accelerated clinical translation, including first-in-human robotic procedures and regulatory milestones. This study provides a comprehensive bibliometric overview of robot-assisted gastrointestinal endoscopy, highlighting the importance of multicenter randomized trials, prospective health economic evaluations, and strengthened cross-institutional engineering-clinical collaboration.
authors: Xianglong Meng; Yifang Li; Xiaoping Han; Ge Liu; Ying Geng; Jian Jiao

title: Grounded ophthalmic AI beyond the electronic health record trap: a critical narrative review
abstract: Electronic health records (EHRs) show that health information technology can digitise clinical work while increasing documentation burden, workflow rigidity and professional burnout. Artificial intelligence (AI) may enter a deeper layer of medicine than the EHR because it can draft summaries, interpret images, recommend follow-up and influence decisions. This critical narrative review uses ophthalmic vision-language models as a concrete case study. Diabetic retinopathy screening AI and lesion-level deep learning have achieved important successes in defined tasks, but clinical interpretation is not classification. A sentence such as ‘hard exudates have increased in the macula’ requires localisation of the fovea and macula, lesion segmentation, longitudinal registration, change quantification and faithful language generation. We argue that the unresolved informatics challenge is grounded in clinical interpretation: the auditable translation of images into finding-location-change triples that remain inspectable by clinicians. The article proposes a three-layer architecture: globally standardised objective observation, explicit local policy and workflow adaptation and clinician-authored AI operations governed by safety gates. Customisation should not be monetised as bespoke vendor work; it should be a safety function built into procurement, audit and lifecycle regulation. The three-layer architecture is a conceptual governance framework derived from published evidence rather than a prospectively validated implementation, and we specify the observable failure modes and metrics that would refute it. Ophthalmology illustrates the broader design principle for medical AI: automation should make evidence more visible, not convert care into another opaque information-processing layer.
authors: Hitoshi Tabuchi; Mao Tanabe; Keita Kihara; Takaaki Moriguchi; Fumi Gomi

title: Health and Well-being
abstract: From smart wearables, implants, and ingestible electronics to remote physiological monitoring and public health, wireless technology has numerous applications in healthcare.It has the potential to create a pervasive environment for monitoring people's health and well-being while improving how physicians deliver care.It can also boost patient engagement and satisfaction by allowing them to spend more time in the comfort of their homes and interacting with their care centres whenever needed.The End-to-End (E2E) health data connectivity involves the development of technologies that enable reliable and location-agnostic communication between patients and healthcare service providers.The increasing penetration of connected devices in healthcare is a significant driver towards creating an intelligent network that enhances people's quality of life.In recent years, wearable biomedical sensors have experienced remarkable growth; however, there are still many societal challenges, including safety, security, interoperability, and integration with existing wireless infrastructure that need to be addressed.This chapter addresses various cutting-edge scientific problems dealing with communications inside or around the human body, novel antenna designs for wearables and implants, propagation channel characterisation, remote health monitoring, and innovative public health and safety applications.
authors: Sławomir J. Ambroziak; Kamran Sayrafian

title: Herbal and Natural Products for NSAID-Induced Small Intestinal Injury: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
abstract: Objectives: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), including aspirin, are widely used medications that frequently cause small intestinal injury (enteropathy). Conventional proton pump inhibitors do not prevent this injury and may exacerbate it through dysbiosis. Herbal medicines and natural products offer potential therapeutic benefits, but synthesized clinical evidence remains limited. Thus, this study will systematically evaluate the efficacy and safety of herbal medicines and natural products for preventing NSAID-induced small intestinal injury. Methods: MEDLINE, Embase, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and the China National Knowledge Infrastructure will be searched to identify articles published since inception, without restrictions on publication date or language. Randomized controlled trials involving adults aged ≥ 18 years receiving NSAIDs will be included. Two reviewers will independently perform study selection, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment using the RoB 2 tool. If appropriate, a meta-analysis will be conducted. The primary outcome will be mucosal injury, objectively assessed using video capsule endoscopy or measures of intestinal permeability. Secondary outcomes will include symptoms and adverse events. Results: This study will synthesize the current clinical evidence on natural interventions for NSAID-induced enteropathy. Conclusion: The findings will inform the management of small intestinal injury and guide future research.
authors: Ji Hye Hwang; You-Kyung Choi

title: HiRNet: A Hierarchical-Refinement-Guided Hybrid Retinal Vessel Segmentation Network for Smartphone-Based Fundus Images
abstract: Smartphone-based fundus photography provides a low-cost and convenient approach to retinal screening and follow-up examinations. As a fundamental step in fundus image analysis, retinal vessel segmentation plays an important role in the diagnosis and monitoring of retinal diseases. However, existing methods often exhibit limited performance on smartphone-based fundus images. This limitation mainly arises from the significantly lower image quality that affects the clarity and detail of the retinal vessels, making accurate segmentation more difficult. To address these challenges, we propose a hierarchical-refinement-guided hybrid network (HiRNet), which incorporates a hybrid CNN-Transformer feature extractor to jointly model local vascular structures and global contextual information. Specifically, consecutive asymmetric dilated convolutions capture multi-scale local features, while multi-path dilated attention enhances contextual representations across different receptive fields. In addition, a hierarchical context information transmission module is introduced to progressively integrate features from different resolutions during multistage upsampling, thereby improving vessel continuity and boundary delineation. Experiments on RVD, DRIVE, and CHASE_DB1 demonstrate the effectiveness of HiRNet. On the smartphone-based RVD dataset, HiRNet obtains the highest mean sensitivity (58.36%), specificity (97.81%), accuracy (95.83%), F1-score (58.39%), and AUC (95.16%). The improvements in sensitivity, accuracy, F1, and AUC over the strongest competing methods are statistically significant. HiRNet also obtains sensitivity values of 82.73% and 82.13%, accuracy values of 95.59% and 95.98%, F1-scores of 82.76% and 80.37%, and AUC values of 98.83% and 97.90% on DRIVE and CHASE_DB1, respectively. These results indicate that HiRNet provides a relative improvement on the challenging domain of smartphone-based fundus images while maintaining strong performance on conventional fundus datasets.

title: High-Precision RCM Motion for Ophthalmic Robotics via Hierarchical QP Control and Authority-Guided Recovery Planning
abstract: General-purpose manipulators can position ophthalmic instruments under a software Remote Centre of Motion (RCM). However, at some reachable configurations that are nonsingular for the tip task alone, the RCM and tip-tracking objectives conflict and the servo oscillates. We formalise this failure as a constraint-induced task singularity: the RCM-projected tip Jacobian loses rank while the unprojected tip Jacobian stays well conditioned. Thus, the effective tip authority collapses although the target remains reachable. We present a high-precision RCM servo architecture with built-in singularity recovery: for each commanded target, an authority-guided planner selects a well-conditioned arm configuration that reaches it and plans an RCM-consistent route, executed by a fixed hierarchical-QP controller. On a 200-scenario kinematic benchmark, the complete nominal-and-recovery protocol reaches 128/128 near-singular targets and 71/72 near-joint-limit targets (100% and 99%, respectively), with the software-RCM residual below 0.142 mm. On a physical 6-DOF arm it executes across four RCM entry points, with a worst-case kinematically reconstructed RCM residual of 178 μm and a median tip-regulation error of 32μm, within the 200μm control requirement adopted for the ophthalmic task.
authors: Huanyu Tian; Adriana Namour; Lingyun Zeng; Zicong Wu; Sebastien Ourselin A; Lyndon da Cruz; Christos Bergeles

title: How does hard magnetic soft matter deform?
abstract: Abstract Hard Magnetic Soft Materials, i.e., elastomers seeded with hard magnetic particles, convert magnetic energy into complex motion and have become central to the design of untethered soft robots, biomedical devices, and, in general, for enabling fast, wireless actuation. Their behavior depends critically on how the surrounding soft matrix deforms and transmits torque to each magnetized inclusion, yet there is no consensus on the correct mapping between macroscopic strain and microscopic motion. Competing models predict conflicting particle rotations and magnetic responses under identical loads. Here, we construct counterexamples that show the key shortcomings in these models, and then establish a first-principles framework that leads to an optimal deformation mapping. The resulting closed-form law unifies conflicting models and shows that they are, in fact, simply different limits of our general approach. Our work permits the rational design of magnetically actuated soft devices and a unified view of deformation in magnetic soft matter, and broadly, in similar architectured materials.
authors: Daniel Katusele; Carmel Majidi; Liping Liu; Pradeep Sharma; Kaushik Dayal

title: Human-Centered Robotics for Surgery
abstract: Surgical ergonomics is influenced by many aspects associated with posture, vision, hand motion, and haptic feedback. Specific ergonomics aspects can induce long-term effects in the surgeon directly affecting the performance. One of the major disadvantages of Minimally Invasive Surgery (MIS) remains the non-ergonomic design of the entire surgical environment. This condition results in a significant reduction in the quality of interventions and discomfort for the medical operator. Modern teleoperated surgical robots offer an optimized console, in which the surgeon can operate in a seated position with specific arm support and a 3D view of the operating site. The da Vinci surgical console offers ergonomic improvements over standard endoscopic surgery. Modern robotic platforms stand beyond the da Vinci System, offering more advanced ergonomic solutions in terms of haptic feedback and visual perception. Due to the introduction of more advanced technology, surgery has changed, resulting in increased system complexity at the technical, human and organizational levels, which may lead to higher variability of patient outcomes due to new error pathways. Adopting a proactive approach enables the prior identification of critical factors and the design of safer socio-technical systems, thanks to a multi-level perspective. This chapter addresses the fundamental elements of surgical ergonomics, considering the factors that affect performance and healthiness during traditional procedures, with specific reference to MIS and microsurgery. This baseline is then compared to the use of surgical robots by evaluating the effect of design decisions on operator ergonomics. In addition, studies propose proactive methodologies that assess the personal and organizational factors of surgical performance in this complex socio-technical system.
authors: Rocco Moccia; Raffaella Mancino; Emanuele Ruffaldi; Massimiliano Simi; Rossella Onofrio; Fanny Ficuciello

title: Humanoids for Robot-Assisted Surgery: Bimanual Base Placement and Tool-Mount Optimization via Capability Maps
abstract: Rapid advances in humanoid robotics have motivated growing interest in the application of humanoids for healthcare and clinical tasks. However, it remains unclear how close contemporary humanoids are to meeting the kinematic demands of robot-assisted laparoscopic surgery. In this work, we address the question of optimal robot positioning through a quantitative analysis of workspace and robot setup configurations. We present a capability-map-based robot setup framework that optimizes humanoid base placement and tool mounting orientation to maximize bimanual humanoid reachability while accounting for tool-tip kinematics and remote-center-of-motion (RCM) constraints. We evaluate three humanoid platforms spanning different body dimensions and kinematic redundancy on workspace reachability for three representative general surgery procedures: cholecystectomy, inguinal hernia repair, and sleeve gastrectomy. The proposed joint optimization of base placement and tool mounting consistently outperforms base-only optimization and heuristic baselines. For cholecystectomy and inguinal hernia repair, which are characterized by relatively small and minimally overlapping workspaces, humanoid reachability approached 90%. For the larger, overlapping multi-port arm workspace of sleeve gastrectomy, humanoids yield substantially lower coverage. These results quantify the near-term promise of humanoids for selected laparoscopic procedures and clarify key limitations that must be addressed for broader deployment.

title: Image-based classification of bolus phases in robotic mastication using hybrid machine learning analysis
abstract: Non-invasive, continuous monitoring of food bolus transformation during robotic mastication remains a significant challenge, as existing methods rely on physical extraction of the bolus or single-modality image features that lack robustness across the continuous and non-linear nature of food breakdown. This paper investigates whether hybrid machine-extracted image features can reliably classify chewing phases during in vitro robotic mastication without physical intervention. A hybrid feature-extraction framework is proposed that integrates deep convolutional features from VGG16 with classical texture descriptors, Grey-Level Co-occurrence Matrix (GLCM), image lightness, and variance, applied to a dataset of 1024 segmented chewed biscuit bolus images captured across two chewing trajectories: vertical motion (T1) and combined vertical and lateral motion (T13). Supervised classifiers, Support Vector Machines, Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), and Random Forests were evaluated using trial-level grouped cross-validation. Using a 3-phase schema conceptually aligned with the Hutchings and Lillford Mouth Process Model, LDA achieved accuracies of 75.9% for T1 and 82.3% (T13), with the hybrid feature set outperforming the ablation study. Improved separability with T13 demonstrates that shear effect produces more distinctive bolus image features. The unchewed class was consistently well separated, while structured misclassification patterns occur mainly between adjacent phases highlight the challenging nature of the study. These results establish a non-contact, vision-based measurement framework for classifying bolus evolution as a proof-of-concept foundation for robotic chewing systems.
authors: Isurie Akarawita; Bangxiang Chen; Jaspreet Singh Dhupia; Martin Stommel; Weiliang Xu

title: Image-enhanced autonomous navigation in intestinal robotics: a threshold-triggered approach combining dark-area localization and morphological contour guidance short title: enhancing visibility and navigation precision in confined spaces.
abstract: Robotic endoscopy offers a potential route to autonomous gastrointestinal navigation. However, autonomous intestinal navigation is hindered by non-rigid lumen deformation and visual degradation from specular reflections, which compromise accurate perception and stable control. We propose a threshold-triggered, vision-driven framework incorporating Navier-Stokes-based highlight suppression. Algorithmically, the system is governed by a threshold-triggered mechanism that acts as a conditional perception gate, dynamically alternating between a lightweight 'dark-area guidance' algorithm for approximately centered navigation and a more detailed 'contour-based guidance' pipeline for corrective steering. The switching policy avoids executing highlight suppression and morphological contour processing in every frame. In phantom-based trials, the system achieved an average speed of 3.10 cm s<sup>-1</sup>on the triangular path. Highlight suppression increased the proportion of frames with normalized center error below 0.1 from 65% to 71%, below 0.2 from 95% to 97%, and below 0.3 from 98% to 100%. The adaptive mechanism decreased runtime by approximately 2% compared to continuous contour processing. Although this absolute reduction was modest, it recovered approximately 89% of the runtime difference between the contour-only and dark-area-only baselines. These phantom-based results support conditional perception allocation while keeping average processing time close to that of lightweight navigation.
authors: Wang S, Yuan J, Deng H, Deng H, Yue X, Zhang T, Chen S, Chen H.

title: Imaging biological tissue at extended depth using swept-source visible-light OCT
abstract: Abstract We present a swept-source visible-light optical coherence tomography (SS-vis-OCT) system with twice the imaging depth of prior SS-vis-OCT and improved sensitivity for imaging biological samples, achieving shot-noise-limited operation. Because second-harmonic generation is limited by the booster optical amplifier’s output power, the visible-light SS power is capped at 450 µW. Increasing it further would require a more powerful, but costlier, amplifier. Instead, we reduce the receiver noise floor by selecting a balanced detector with NEP approaching the thermal (Johnson–Nyquist) limit. Real-time numerical k-linearization increases the effective number of linear-in-wavenumber samples per sweep, further improving SNR and extending the imaging range. Together, these improvements yield a sensitivity of 89 dB and an imaging depth of 9 mm in air or 6.5 mm in tissue, enabling full anterior-segment imaging of ex vivo porcine eyes.
authors: Weijia Fan; Roman V. Kuranov; Menglin Shi; Fengyuanshan Xu; Junfang Zhang; Hao F. Zhang

title: Impact of AI‐Assisted Endoscopy on Secondary Review and Referral Decisions in Gastric Cancer Screening: A Multicenter Real‐World Study
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted endoscopy may support gastric cancer screening, but its impact on structured secondary human review remains unclear. We evaluated secondary review modifications and referral decisions before and after AI implementation. METHODS: This retrospective multicenter study included 5013 screening esophagogastroduodenoscopy examinations performed before (n = 2021) and after (n = 2992) AI implementation. The primary outcome was secondary review modifications. Secondary outcomes included referral for further diagnostic evaluation. Multivariable logistic regression analyses adjusted for age, sex, Helicobacter pylori eradication status, prior-year endoscopy, and endoscopist experience were performed. Interaction analyses according to endoscopist experience and inverse probability of treatment weighting analyses were conducted. No external reference standard was available to verify secondary-review modifications or referral decisions. RESULTS: Secondary review modifications increased from 1.2% in the pre-AI period to 3.7% in the AI period (p < 0.01). A significant interaction was observed between AI implementation and endoscopist experience (p for interaction < 0.01), with increased modifications primarily among nonexpert endoscopists. Cancer-related modifications remained uncommon but increased after AI implementation (0.6% vs. 0.2%, p = 0.04). Referral rates decreased from 4.9% to 2.8% (p < 0.01), and AI implementation was independently associated with lower odds of referral (adjusted OR = 0.53; 95% confidence interval = 0.36-0.77). CONCLUSIONS: AI-assisted endoscopy was associated with lower referral rates; however, secondary review modifications persisted after AI implementation, particularly among nonexpert endoscopists. These findings describe workflow changes and do not establish the clinical validity of the modifications or the appropriateness of referral decisions.
authors: Sachiyo Onishi; Seiji Adachi; Masahito Shimizu

title: Impact of Data Augmentation on Confidence Calibration in Melanoma Classification
abstract: Accurately quantifying the predictive uncertainty or improving model calibration plays an important role in medical image classification, in particular in melanoma diagnosis, where accurate uncertainty quantification can have significant implications for patient care. One of the methods for calibration improvement is data augmentation. In addition, data augmentation as a method for synthetically increasing the size of the dataset has been proven to improve the performance of models trained on imbalanced datasets. However, the impact of data augmentation, as a transformation of a part of the original data, on calibration of models trained on imbalanced datasets, in particular in melanoma classification is under-explored. We train neural networks on SIIM-ISIC 2020 melanoma classification dataset under two conditions: with and without data augmentation, and compare the differences in AUC and expected calibration error (ECE) in both scenarios. Our results shows improvements in uncertainty calibration using different augmentation methods.
authors: Morgan May; Simon J. Caton; Pierpaolo Dondio

title: Implementing AI-supported Screening for Retinopathy of Prematurity in Low-resource setting on a Relatively Small Set of Data: A Retrospective Cohort Study
abstract: Background: Context-adapted screening programs supported by AI-enabled teleretinopathy of prematurity (ROP) systems are essential to improve access, efficiency, and early diagnosis in underserved settings, particularly for often overlooked diseases such as ROP. This study aims to evaluate the diagnostic performance of an AI-based model for detecting and classifying ROP using wide-field retinal images and assess its relevance for neonatal screening systems in limited and middle-income countries (LMIC). Methods: This retrospective cohort study analyzed 5531 RetCam II images from 950 preemies (2018–2023) at Eye World Hospital, Giza, Egypt. Images were graded using international classification of ROP (ICROP) 3rd edition by a trainee and confirmed by a vitreoretinal consultant. A CNN-based model was developed to classify ROP stage, zone, and severity after augmentation up to 8500 images. Performance was assessed using standard metrics. Results: A total of 5531 RetCam II images from 950 preemies were analyzed. The AI model demonstrated good performance in detecting advanced ROP, particularly treatment-requiring stages (stages 4 and 5 and type 1 ROP), with high precision and recall. Overall classification accuracy was 66%. Performance was lower in early-stage disease and in differentiating closely related subtypes, particularly aggressive type ROP (A-ROP) and early stages. Conclusion: The CNN model based on 5531 RetCam II images, augmented up to 8500 images, shows good performance in detecting advanced ROP but limited sensitivity for early stages. Constraints include small, imbalanced data and reduced generalization. The system is intended for triage and decision support in tele-ROP screening, not autonomous diagnosis. Future improvements require larger multicenter datasets, better class balance, and advanced architectures with transfer learning to enhance early detection accuracy and clinical reliability.

title: Improved diagnostic model for gastrointestinal disorders through novel masking and semantic segmentation
abstract: The integration of advanced computing techniques, such as computational intelligence, in disease classification and prediction through medical imaging has become a prominent practice within the field of computer vision. A critical aspect of this process is precise image segmentation, which helps identify and isolate relevant areas in medical images, thereby streamlining the analysis and enhancing the accuracy of predictions. Among various segmentation methods, semantic segmentation, which assigns class labels to each pixel, has proven particularly effective. In this study, we introduce the U+EfficientB0 Net model, specifically designed to segment gastro-intestinal images, including dyed-lifted polyps, polyps, and ulcerative colitis. The proposed work is different from traditional EffeicientNetB0 encoder as it utilizes Decoder-guided Adaptive Skip Refinement (DASR) module for feature refinement before combining the features obtained from encoder with the features obtained through decoder. Utilizing advanced computing techniques like computational intelligence for disease classification and prediction through medical imaging is a prominent practice in computer vision. Precise image segmentation is crucial as it identifies relevant areas, streamlining analysis, and bolstering prediction accuracy. Semantic segmentation, assigning class labels to each pixel, proves especially effective. This study introduces the (U+EfficientB0) Net model specialized in segmenting gastro-intestinal images, notably dyed-lifted-polyps, polyps and ulcerative colitis leveraging the Kvasir-Seg dataset for polyps and while corresponding masks for dyed-lifted polyps and ulcerative colitis are generated using pixel-based annotation approach. Trained on a thousand images supervised by medical experts, proposed model achieved remarkable accuracy (92.89%) and dice coefficient (80%). Additionally, the study presents a classification approach using DenseNet-121 that uses the predicted segmented images as input and its performance is compared with similar model’s using non-segmented image and achieved better results (Accuracy 99.63) over segmented images in earlier epochs.

title: Information-based Unified Design Framework for NMR Magnetic Tracking System
abstract: Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) magnetic tracking offers a promising alternative to magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based localization for medical robotic guidance. However, scalar field measurements and field-aligned marker moments constrain position and orientation tracking, requiring careful configuration design. We present a unified information-based framework that uses local covariance analysis to evaluate receiver geometry, marker separation, and external source configuration in on/off-board NMR tracking. Numerical evaluation shows that planar-array precision depends jointly on receiver count and geometry, with triangular lattice arrays achieving the lowest best-case position uncertainty among the evaluated layouts for 9--20 receivers. Two spatially separated, field-aligned markers enable device-axis tracking, with predicted angular uncertainty below $2^\circ$ at the evaluated workspace center for suitable marker separations. We further establish point-dipole source--receiver duality, unifying the analysis of on/off-board NMR tracking. These
