title: The future of surgery
abstract: Abstract Surgery is entering a period of accelerated transformation driven by artificial intelligence, robotics, and emerging postmodern medical technologies. Unlike prior technological shifts, innovation cycles are compressing into years, challenging established models of evidence generation, regulation, training, and professional identity. This Perspective examines plausible trajectories for digital surgery, emphasizing ethical, educational, and institutional adaptation under conditions of continuous technological acceleration rather than offering definitive predictions.
authors: Donald W. Weaver; J. Edson Pontes; David S. Edelman; S. Kiran Koya; David Ellis

title: The key mechanisms and intervention strategies of cell-type-specific mitochondrial metabolism in ophthalmic diseases
abstract: The eye is one of the most metabolically active organs, and mitochondria serve as the central hub for cellular energy metabolism by providing adenosine triphosphate through oxidative phosphorylation. Disruption of mitochondrial metabolism-including insufficient adenosine triphosphate synthesis, excessive production of reactive oxygen species, and dysregulated quality control-can trigger various ocular diseases. Common blinding diseases such as myopia, diabetic retinopathy, and glaucoma are closely associated with mitochondrial dysfunction in specific cell types. This review delineates the mechanisms by which metabolic adaptations in scleral fibroblasts induce myopia and the synergistic action of lipofuscin, the high-glucose-triggered mitochondrial reactive oxygen species bursts and metabolic memory in diabetic retinopathy, and the roles of mitochondrial dynamics imbalance and energy exhaustion in trabecular meshwork cells in glaucoma. Based on these mechanisms, the article proposes intervention strategies targeting mitochondrial antioxidant defense, enhancing mitochondrial biogenesis, regulating mitochondrial dynamics, and restoring mitophagy, aiming for precise prevention and treatment of ocular diseases at the mitochondrial level.
authors: Shouyao Zhang; Xiaochun Yang; Chenggui Xu; Shuang Wang; Xiantao Tai

title: The perceived facilitators and barriers to the potential adoption of teledentistry among dental care providers in Saudi Arabia: A systematic review
abstract: Teledentistry has emerged as a tool that holds great potential to enhance access, efficiency, and continuity of oral healthcare delivery. In Saudi Arabia, its adoption is important in the context of the health transformation programme and Vision 2030, particularly given the high prevalence of dental caries among schoolchildren. Despite this potential, actual implementation is still limited. In this context, there is a need to systematically assess the factors influencing its potential adoption from the care providers' perspectives. This review aimed to systematically identify how dental care providers perceive the facilitators and barriers to the adoption of teledentistry in Saudi Arabia, with a focus on the perception of dental care providers, including dental students. Following PRISMA 2020 and SWiM guidelines, PubMed, Scopus, Medline, Embase, and CINAHL databases were searched, covering publications up to 4 July 2025. The PICO framework was used to define the inclusion and exclusion criteria, and the CASP checklist was used to assess study quality. Data were synthesised using vote counting by direction of effect, categorising findings into facilitators and barriers. Out of 156 records, 11 studies met the inclusion criteria. Study quality ranged from 7 to11 out of 11 based on the CASP checklist for cross-sectional studies. Key findings included potential facilitators such as improved access, efficiency and cost-effectiveness, communication and referral enhancements, educational benefits, and positive perception of technology. The key reported barriers were limited awareness and training, infrastructure and equipment reliability, privacy and data security, cost and financial issues, diagnostic accuracy, and the preference for in-person meetings. While teledentistry holds great potential, its integration in Saudi Arabia could be hindered by educational and technical challenges. Addressing them through improved infrastructure, enhanced training and integration into dental curricula, and strengthened regulatory frameworks may facilitate and support equitable adoption.
authors: Amjad Hakami; Sarika Mohan

title: The rise of agentic AI in drug discovery from static tools to autonomous virtual scientists
abstract: Driven by large language models, AI agents are transforming drug discovery, enabling AI to break free from task-specific tools and advance toward the vision of autonomous virtual scientists. This perspective reviews applications across the R&D lifecycle. To evaluate system maturity, we introduce a 6-level "Spectrum of Agentic Autonomy." We advocate for novel evaluation paradigms centered on full-chain traceability and outline adoption barriers, positioning AI agents as pragmatic scientist-in-the-loop co-pilots.

title: The role of 11C-Choline PET/CT scanning of the bladder in the diagnosis of late radiation cystitis (pilot study)
abstract: The aim of the study was to consider the possibilities of using 11 C-choline PET/CT for visual and ultrastructural assessment of bladder wall barrier functions in women with late radiation cystitis. Materials and methods. A comprehensive examination of four women with varying visual manifestations of late radiation cystitis was conducted. The affinity of the bladder wall for 11 С-choline was studied using PET/CT as the standardized uptake level of labeled molecules (SUV max ) coming from urine in combination with the results of scanning electron microscopy of all bladder wall elements in a single block. Results. It was found that the affinity of the bladder wall for labeled 11 С-choline molecules in late radiation cystitis correlates with the severity of ultrastructural changes in its wall, which can be used as an additional marker of bladder barrier function integrity. Conclusion. The clinical application of our developed computer program allows urologists to obtain a probable visual and ultrastructural 3D reconstruction of all elements of the bladder wall using the digital value (SUV max ) of 11 С choline PET/CT.

title: The role of digital twin technology in transforming medical education: a scoping review
abstract: This scoping review mapped the current landscape of digital twin applications in health professions education and identified gaps in the evidence. The review followed Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines. Six bibliographic databases (MEDLINE via PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL, and IEEE Xplore) were searched from inception to March 10, 2026, supplemented by a register search (ClinicalTrials.gov) and a search of Google Scholar as an additional source. Studies describing the development, implementation, or evaluation of digital twins in health professions education were included. Data were extracted using a standardized charting form, and methodological quality was assessed with appropriate JBI critical appraisal tools. Findings were subsequently reviewed in a one-round modified Delphi consultation with stakeholders. Seventeen studies published between 2022 and 2025 met the inclusion criteria. Because three publications report the same critical care platform, these 17 reports describe 15 distinct systems. Digital twins were applied at patient-, organ-, device-, and environment- or institutional-levels across surgery, critical care, anatomy, radiology, and dentistry. Each included system was verified against three defining characteristics of digital twins: personalization, a counterpart-derived data pathway, and generative or predictive capability. Four studies satisfied all three, eight satisfied two, four satisfied one, and one proposed all three without implementing any; only a single study reported continuous closed-loop bidirectional synchronization between a physical and a virtual counterpart. Most studies were technical reports or proof-of-concept demonstrations, and no controlled educational trials were identified. Evaluations focused primarily on learner perceptions and satisfaction, whereas only one study reported quantitative learning outcomes. No study assessed behavioral transfer to clinical practice or patient-level outcomes. Digital twin technology in health professions education is, therefore, best characterized as an active area of technical development that remains educationally unvalidated. The principal contribution of this review is a structured map of what has been built, how it has been verified against the digital twin construct, and precisely where educational evidence is absent. Future research should emphasize theory-informed development, rigorous experimental designs, and validated educational outcomes to determine the educational value of these approaches.
authors: Sogand Sarmadi; Akbar Zare‐Kaseb; Neda Sanaie; Shabnam Shariatpanahi; Mahsa Boozari Pour

title: Therapeutic Balloon‐Assisted Enteroscopy: Recent Advances in the Management of Small Bowel Diseases
abstract: Balloon-assisted enteroscopy (BAE) has substantially advanced small bowel disease management. This review summarizes recent therapeutic BAE advances, focusing on three major indications: small bowel vascular lesions, hereditary polyposis syndromes, and Crohn's disease (CD). For suspected small bowel bleeding from vascular lesions, morphological classification guides lesion-specific hemostasis-primarily using argon plasma coagulation and clipping-while gel immersion endoscopy helps secure the visual field. In hereditary polyposis syndromes (e.g., Peutz-Jeghers syndrome and familial adenomatous polyposis), endoscopic ischemic and cold snare polypectomy prevent intussusception and reduce cancer risk, decreasing surgical needs. Additionally, endoscopic balloon dilation is an established bowel-preserving treatment for fibrotic CD strictures, reducing surgical resection and short bowel syndrome risk. Driven by evolving imaging and devices, BAE remains central to small bowel management, improving patient outcomes and quality of life.

title: Thirty years of paediatric colonic motility assessment modalities: a systematic review
abstract: Introduction: Disorders of paediatric colonic motility may arise following operative repair of congenital colorectal conditions, as well as spontaneously. This may lead to symptoms of faecal incontinence, in addition to constipation. Management of such typically requires several investigations, clinic appointments and treatment strategies. Different investigation modalities are available to objectively and accurately describe gastrointestinal transit time. In the paediatric setting, most of these investigations are invasive, involve radiation, or require patient hospital admission. This systematic review summarises paediatric colonic motility investigations by compiling an assessment of modalities available over the last 31 years, their uses, advantages, and limitations. Methods: The following databases (Cochrane, EMBASE, MEDLINE) were interrogated. The keywords used were "paediatric", "pediatric", "colonic motility", and "investigation", searched as keywords and Medical Subject Heading/Emtree subject heading. Studies that were included were case reports, prospective and retrospective cohort studies, case series, and reviews discussing and comparing modalities to investigate paediatric (< 18 years old) colonic motility. Inclusion criteria included papers published in the last 31 years, including data about paediatric colonic motility investigations indications, rationale for investigation of choice, advantages and limitations. The protocol was registered with PROSPERO (ID 1034832). Study selection was conducted according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) protocol. Results: The initial search yielded 1061 papers. After removing duplicates and screening abstracts and full texts, 122 papers were included for analysis. The most widely-used motility investigation types were radiopaque marker studies, scintigraphy and colonic manometry. However, these had limitations, including radiation exposure, the need for an experienced-centre, and invasiveness. Hydrocolonic ultrasonography was radiation-free, not expensive, and safely repeatable for serial monitoring or assessment, but results were operator-dependent. Newer non-invasive tests that aim to limit radiation exposure have been emerging, such as cine-MRI, wireless capsule and the electromagnetic capsule tracking system. Assessment of anorectal function was often combined with colonic motility assessment to provide a full assessment, depending upon the clinical picture and diagnostic objectives. Discussion: Over the last 31 years numerous investigations have been utilised to study bowel anatomy, function, and neuromuscular ability. Each of these modalities have advantages, but also limitations. It is crucial to know the intrinsic characteristics of each modality to help decide which is most appropriate for the clinical indication in question. Radiopaque marker studies, scintigraphy and colonic manometry were the three most widely reported colonic motility studies methods. Evidence regarding colonic motility modalities in paediatrics was limited compared with the adult population. This lack of evidence is likely due to the invasive nature of some of these investigations, costs, radiation exposure, and limited availability at specific centres. It is crucial for clinicians involved in paediatric patient care to be familiar with available tests, their properties, availabilities, and to use the most appropriate investigation to answer each specific clinical question. Conclusions: This systematic review has shown that, to date, there are several colonic motility assessment modalities that all have their advantages, limitations and different indications. It is imperative for clinicians to base their investigative plan on the specific patient, clinical/centre expertise and clinical question. In the future, there is a need to develop a non-invasive, objective, world-wide reproducible and ambulatory method that may provide information on actual day-to-day physiological colonic motility. Systematic Review Registration: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251034832, PROSPERO CRD420251034832.

title: Toward Governance-Aware Autonomous GIS: A Narrative Review of Ethical and Privacy Risks in LLM-Enabled GeoAI
abstract: Geospatial artificial intelligence (GeoAI) powered by large language models (LLMs) is expanding the capacity to query, generate, and interpret spatial information through natural-language interfaces and agentic autonomous GIS workflows. This capability creates governance challenges that general AI ethics discussions do not fully capture, including passive location inference from mobility traces, spatially structured bias amplification driven by spatial autocorrelation and scale effects, hallucinated spatial facts, and uncertainty compounding across multimodal geospatial inputs. This narrative review identifies eight recurring issues in LLM-enabled GeoAI: data provenance and consent, spatial privacy and inference risk, algorithmic bias and spatial inequity, spatial mechanisms as structural risk (spatial autocorrelation, the modifiable areal unit problem, and scale effects), LLM-specific technical risks, explainability, policy and regulatory gaps, and public enablement and workforce development. For each issue, we characterize the underlying mechanism, ground it in an illustrative example from the literature, and assess the current state of technical or institutional responses, ranging from largely unaddressed to actively debated or subject to emerging policy. Building on this synthesis, we propose a governance-aware architecture for LLM-enabled autonomous GIS that maps each issue to enforceable controls and auditable artifacts across the geospatial data lifecycle, illustrated through a worked flood-response routing scenario. The review highlights a persistent evidence gap: proposed responses remain largely conceptual, and field-tested evaluations of governance controls for LLM-enabled GeoAI remain limited. We close by outlining a research agenda emphasizing empirical validation, spatially specific interpretability tools, and workforce training aligned with these emerging risks.
authors: Maya Subramanian; Devika Jain

title: Towards Automated Pars Plana Vitrectomy and Epiretinal Membrane Peeling
abstract: Vitreoretinal surgery treats diseases of the posterior segment of the eye and demands some of the most delicate and precise manipulations in surgery. This dissertation presents an image-guided robotic system that combines optical coherence tomography (OCT) with a high-precision robotic manipulator to address two challenging vitreoretinal procedures: pars plana vitrectomy and epiretinal membrane (ERM) peeling. Pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) is the surgical removal of the vitreous humor, the gel-like substance that fills the posterior segment of the eye. The procedure requires precise manipulation within the confined intraocular workspace while operating with limited visualization. We present a semi-automated strategy for vitreous removal using OCT-based eye modeling, anatomy-aware trajectory planning, and real-time intraocular distance sensing with feedback control to maintain a safe distance from the retina. The approach was evaluated on ex vivo porcine eyes, demonstrating successful core vitreous removal without lens or retinal injury, as well as safe regulation of the retina-tool distance during the delicate peripheral shave step. An epiretinal membrane (ERM) is a thin, semitransparent membrane that forms on the retinal surface and is surgically removed through delicate peeling with micro-forceps, requiring exceptional precision to avoid retinal damage. We present an OCT-guided robotic membrane peeling strategy that integrates membrane modeling, safe targeting and approach, iterative grasping, feedback-controlled peeling, and automated regrasping following membrane release. The strategy was evaluated on Parafilm membrane phantoms and demonstrated successful membrane targeting, grasping, and peeling with real-time regulation of the peel angle. In summary, this dissertation combines OCT-based perception, anatomy-aware planning, and real-time feedback control to automate key steps of vitreoretinal surgery. Together, these contributions establish a foundation for increased autonomy in robot-assisted eye surgery.
authors: Mia Reyes

title: Towards Robust Prehensile Manipulation in Open-Ended Environments
abstract: We propose to use Quality-Diversity (QD) algorithms to solve robotic prehensile manipulation tasks in open-ended environments. Our approach enables the efficient discovery of a wide range robust grasp configurations, which serve as reliable starting points for generating diverse prehensile manipulation trajectories on articulated objects. The resulting diversity in manipulation behaviors enhances generalization and adaptability, enabling effective deployment continuously evolving open-world settings.
authors: Mathilde Kappel; Mahdi Khoramshahi; Louis Annabi; Faïz Ben Amar; Stéphane Doncieux

title: Tracker-Free Robotic Ultrasound Calibration with a Spherical-Marker Phantom and Threshold-Free Center Localization
abstract: Robotic ultrasound (US) calibration is essential for accurately relating US images to the robot coordinate system, but accurate and automated calibration remains challenging because existing methods often require complex phantoms or external 3D trackers. In this work, we develop a tracker-free robotic US calibration framework using a spherical-marker phantom and a highly automated perception pipeline for sphere-center localization. The proposed threshold-free image-processing method localizes the spherical feature based on each US image's intensity distribution, eliminating hand-tuned intensity thresholds and improving robustness across imaging settings without per-system retuning. Multi-pose observations of the spherical fiducial are then used to estimate the US-to-EE transformation without external tracking or prior localization of the sphere center in the robot base frame. We validate the proposed framework on a robotic US platform through repeated sphere scans and further assess the calibrated system using geometrically distinct phantoms with known CAD models. Across 12 cross-validation folds, single-marker calibration achieved sphere-center accuracy and precision of $1.75\pm0.51$ mm and $0.85\pm0.11$ mm, respectively, compared with $1.72\pm0.51$ mm and $0.84\pm0.12$ mm for three-marker calibration. Across the three reconstruction sets, the single-marker calibration yielded pooled post-registration point-to-surface MAE$\pm$SD values of $0.41\pm0.35$ mm for the cone and $0.50\pm0.41$ mm for the triangular prism, closely matching the three-marker results of $0.40\pm0.35$ mm and $0.48\pm0.40$ mm, respectively.

title: Transoral Robotic Surgery in the Treatment of Head and Neck Cancer: Application and Prospect
abstract: Transoral robotic surgery (TORS) has reshaped the surgical management of head and neck neoplasms since its introduction in the mid-2000s, offering a minimally invasive transoral route to lesions of the oropharynx, larynx, hypopharynx, and nasopharynx. This narrative review synthesizes the technical foundations, current clinical evidence, and emerging directions of TORS, with explicit attention to study rigor and evidentiary hierarchy. Powered by the da Vinci platform, TORS provides magnified three-dimensional visualization and wristed instrumentation that enable en bloc resection with reduced external morbidity, shorter hospitalization, and the potential to spare or de-intensify adjuvant radiotherapy in selected human papillomavirus (HPV)-driven oropharyngeal cancers. For early-stage oropharyngeal disease, local control rates of 90–95% and disease-specific survival above 90% are consistently reported, and recent systematic reviews and large multicenter cohorts, including the international Recurrent Tumors of the Upper Aerodigestive Tract (RECUT) experience, confirm durable oncologic and functional outcomes in both primary and salvage settings, although randomized trials have yielded nuanced, sometimes divergent quality-of-life results. We appraise outcomes by anatomical subsite, the de-escalation trial landscape, complications and their mitigation, learning-curve dynamics, health economics, and the rapidly evolving integration of artificial intelligence in segmentation, augmented-reality navigation, intraoperative margin assessment, and outcome prediction. Recent evidence confirms that TORS is a valuable but expertise-dependent option whose benefit is greatest in carefully selected patients managed within multidisciplinary, high-volume pathways. We conclude by defining the principal unresolved questions and the evidence required to position TORS appropriately within contemporary multidisciplinary care.

title: Transoral robotic reconstruction of a posterior palatal defect using an upper arm flap following polymorphous adenocarcinoma resection: a novel minimally invasive approach
abstract: Abstract Background Surgical management of malignant tumors in the orofacial region frequently necessitates extensive resection, resulting in significant functional and aesthetic morbidity. In younger patients, these sequelae carry a substantial psychosocial burden, emphasizing the need for minimally invasive reconstructive strategies that preserve quality of life while maintaining oncological safety. Case presentation A 36-year-old female patient presented with a small 1 × 1 cm swelling at the junction of the hard and soft palate on the left side. Incisional biopsy confirmed a malignant minor salivary gland tumor but did not permit definitive subtyping. The final diagnosis of a polymorphous adenocarcinoma (PAC), conventional subtype, was established only on the complete resection specimen. Following oncologically adequate resection, including partial hard palate and tuberosity removal, a 3 × 4 cm defect was reconstructed with a free upper arm flap. Supermicrovascular anastomoses to the superior labial and facial arteries (vessel diameter ~ 0.2 mm) were performed via a transoral approach using the Symani ® robotic surgical system with 20× motion scaling. Venous anastomoses to the facial vein were completed end-to-end and end-to-side via the same intraoral access. Selective lymph node sampling of the four radiologically prominent ipsilateral level II lymph nodes through a minimal cervical incision showed no metastases, both on frozen section and on final histopathology (0/4). Final histopathology demonstrated a 15 mm low-grade PAC resected in sano, without lymphovascular invasion, without unequivocal perineural infiltration and without bone invasion, classified as pT1 pN0 (0/4) cM0, R0. Postoperative course was uneventful; functional rehabilitation including speech and swallowing therapy is ongoing. Conclusions Robotic-assisted supermicrosurgery using the Symani ® system enabled safe transoral free flap reconstruction of a posterior palatal defect with anastomoses at the sub 0.2 mm scale. This approach minimizes donor-site morbidity and demonstrates the feasibility of intraoral robotic supermicrosurgery as a novel reconstructive modality in head and neck oncology.

title: Transoral robotic surgery in otorhinolaryngology: patient perspectives and determinants of outcomes
abstract: A retrospective study in the North of the Netherlands Simple SummaryTransoral Robotic Surgery (TORS) is increasingly used for various conditions, yet its success and failure remain underexplored.In this multicenter study, we assessed 220 TORS interventions across 211 patients.Success criteria differed by condition, including tumor identification for CUP, resection margins for malignancies, and symptom improvement for benign cases like OSA and chronic lingual tonsillitis.Predictors of success varied, with factors such as patient comorbidity, tumor characteristics, and demographics playing roles.Conversely, failure predictors encompassed postoperative complications and pain, linked to patient health and demographics.These insights into TORS outcomes may aid in patient selection and counseling across different conditions, informing clinical practice and enhancing patient care.

title: Trends and safety of small bowel endoscopy in Crohn’s disease in Japan: a large-scale claims database analysis
abstract: Background/Aims: Evidence on the population-level utilization and safety of balloon-assisted endoscopy (BAE) and small bowel capsule endoscopy (SBCE) for Crohn's disease in Japan is limited. We aimed to characterize trends in BAE, SBCE, and patency capsule examination, as well as adverse events (AEs). Methods: We analyzed the Medical Data Vision claims database. Annual utilization was assessed per patient-year for the complete calendar years 2009-2021. AEs were defined by claimsbased therapeutic interventions after procedures. The association between patency capsule examination and SBCE-related AEs was assessed using generalized estimating equations (GEE) adjusted for age, sex, and calendar year. Results: Among 19,881 eligible patients with Crohn's disease, 4,657 BAE and 2,679 SBCE procedures were identified. Modality switching was uncommon, with 83.9% of patients with ≥2 examinations (n =1,683) undergoing the same modality at the second examination. Utilization of both modalities increased over time, and patency capsule examination before SBCE increased from 2013 to 2021. SBCE-related AEs were rare in patients with patency capsule examination compared to those without patency capsule examination (0.88% vs. 1.47%). In the main GEE analysis, patency capsule examination was not independently associated with lower odds of SBCE-related AEs (adjusted odds ratio, 0.62; 95% confidence interval, 0.28-1.37; P= 0.235), with a similar result in sensitivity analyses. Conclusions: The use of BAE and SBCE has increased in Japan alongside the spread of patency capsule examination. SBCE-related AEs were uncommon overall and numerically less frequent when preceded by patency assessment.

title: Tribology of dental materials: from laboratory metrics to clinical durability: review and translational roadmap
abstract: The functional integrity of dental restorations is known by their resilience within the dynamic and hostile tribological ecosystem of the oral cavity. Despite significant advancements in material science, the premature failure of restorations due to wear remains a critical clinical challenge, rooted in a persistent disconnect between controlled laboratory metrics and unpredictable clinical realities. This review provides a comprehensive critical appraisal of dental tribology, delineating the complex interplay of wear mechanisms, attrition, abrasion, erosion, and abfraction, and evaluating the spectrum of current assessment methodologies, from fundamental in vitro simulations to advanced clinical quantification. We identified the primary limitations hindering accurate material prediction, specifically the lack of protocol standardization, the inability to replicate synergistic degradation processes such as tribo-corrosion, and the exclusion of patient-specific variables. To bridge this translational gap, we proposed a strategic roadmap integrating multi-tiered testing standardization, finite element analysis, and machine learning to enhance predictive capabilities. Furthermore, we advocated for the development of clinically relevant in vitro models that incorporate patient-specific parameters, such as occlusal loading profiles and salivary properties. By shifting the paradigm from descriptive testing to predictive, patient-centric material science, this review outlined a transformative pathway for the development of next-generation restorative materials, ultimately optimizing clinical longevity and treatment outcomes.
authors: Naif H. Al-Qahtani; Shahad Alqahtani; Shorooq K. Almajhad; Amjaad M. Almarzoogi; Noha Taymour

title: UltraDiff: Differentiable Ray Tracing in Ultrasound for Shape Optimization
abstract: Physically-based differentiable rendering enables gradient-based optimization of scene parameters by matching rendered images to measurements, but has so far mainly focused on light transport. We extend this paradigm to medical ultrasound, where image formation resembles transient rendering: echoes are binned by time-of-flight rather than projected onto an image plane. We present UltraDiff, a modular framework for differentiable ultrasound ray tracing. UltraDiff formulates ultrasound image formation as a path-space integral, gated by travel time between the transducer and tissue interfaces, and derives a Monte Carlo estimator of both the forward model and its gradients with respect to scene parameters. We demonstrate this on an inverse geometry estimation: starting from a sphere, an SDF is optimized until simulated echoes match measured ones, recovering vertebral surfaces from simulated B-mode sweeps and from a real robotic acquisition of a spine phantom. Unlike state-of-the-art ultrasound shape reconstruction methods, which rely on pre-segmented images, our approach operates unsupervised on B-mode images through analysis-by-synthesis, while achieving competitive geometric accuracy. Implemented on top of Mitsuba 3, UltraDiff brings differentiable path tracing to a new sensing modality and provides a foundation for inverse problems in acoustic imaging.

title: UltraWorld: Learning Interactive Ultrasound World Models from Untracked Clinical Videos with Acoustic Sampling Map
abstract: World models can enable autonomous ultrasound scanning by predicting the outcomes of probe motions from local observations. Learning this action--observation relationship typically relies on synchronized video--pose pairs, which are costly to collect at scale and largely unavailable in routine clinical recordings. Reliable action following further requires modeling ultrasound's cross-sectional sampling geometry. We present UltraWorld, a self-distillation recipe that transfers priors from clinical ultrasound videos into interactive world models without real action annotations. Starting from clinical videos, we adapt a video foundation model into an ultrasound generator conditioned on reference images and anatomical masks. Anatomical masks sampled along programmable trajectories through 3D anatomy provide spatial guidance for synthesizing action--video pairs. We then use these synthetic pairs to self-distill the generator into a world model that predicts future observations from local observations and actions, without requiring anatomical masks or other 3D assets at inference time. To further improve action following, we introduce the Acoustic Sampling Map (AsMap), which represents probe poses and imaging settings as pixel-wise 3D sampling positions, beam directions, and depths. Experiments demonstrate improved prediction fidelity and action following. Across nine simulated closed-loop local planning episodes, UltraWorld reduces the mean final distance to the goal and orientation error by 29\% and 38\%, respectively, compared with visual servoing. title: Ultrasonography in disaster medicine: a narrative review
abstract: This narrative review aimed to critically appraise the diagnostic accuracy, clinical impact, and operational feasibility of ultraportable point-of-care ultrasonography (POCUS) across the four domains of disaster medicine. A literature search was conducted following the SANRA and PRISMA-trAIce guidelines. Records were identified through an AI-assisted literature-discovery tool (the Undermind Deep-Search platform, interrogating the Semantic Scholar corpus) run on 15 June 2025, rather than through an independent structured multi-database search. Candidate references were screened manually against pre-specified eligibility criteria by a single reviewer, with the search parameters independently verified by the senior author. Of 71 records identified, 63 met the inclusion criteria. The included studies comprised 32 original studies, 10 systematic or scoping reviews, 20 narrative or operational papers, and one guideline. In CBRN scenarios, lung ultrasound demonstrated sensitivities of 90-97% for COVID-19 pneumonia versus 60-69% for chest radiography while minimizing healthcare worker exposure. For blast and ballistic injuries, FAST showed a pooled sensitivity of 92.1% (95% CI: 87.8-95.6) and specificity of 98.7% (95% CI: 96.0-99.9) for intra-abdominal hemorrhage. In natural disasters, ultrasound altered management in up to 44% of patients. Post-disaster applications included vascular access, tube confirmation, and complication monitoring. Ultraportable POCUS demonstrates diagnostic utility and operational feasibility across multiple disaster domains. However, evidence quality varies significantly, and standardized protocols remain lacking. Prospective studies linking ultrasound deployment to improved patient outcomes are needed. KEY POINTS: Question When disasters disable conventional imaging, how does ultraportable point-of-care ultrasonography perform for diagnosis, triage, and procedural guidance across the four domains of disaster medicine? Findings Across 63 studies, FAST reached 92.1% pooled sensitivity for hemoperitoneum, lung ultrasound 90-97% versus 60-69% for radiography; management changed in up to 44%. Critical relevance statement This review critically appraises ultraportable ultrasound across all four disaster domains, showing that radiation-free bedside imaging accelerates triage, conserves scarce CT capacity, and extends radiological expertise through tele-guidance, while exposing an evidence base still lacking prospective outcome data.
authors: F. Amiot; Karim Tazarourte; G. Gorincour; Axel Benhamed

title: Ultrasound Operator Guidance Using World Modeling and Retrieval Based Action Planning
abstract: Ultrasound is widely used, but acquisition quality is heavily dependent on the operator's knowledge and expertise. With demand for examinations outpacing the supply of trained sonographers, operator-guidance systems aim to close this gap by instructing a less trained user how to move the probe toward a target view. In this paper, we propose a retrieval-induced latent transition model for ultrasound acquisition dynamics, formulating ultrasound operator guidance as multi-step planning and retrieval in a world model. Using a V-JEPA 2.1 backbone, observations are first encoded into a latent space where anatomically related views lie close together. We then retrieve similar views from a reference database containing encoded latent states and corresponding probe positions and orientations. Rather than learning a parametric transition function, we directly use physically executed transitions from the database to establish our nonparametric, retrieval-induced transition model that supports receding-horizon planning. At deployment, guidance is generated from the live ultrasound image feed alone, without any probe tracking hardware. Applied to carotid ultrasound, the proposed planner reaches the target view in 86% of retrospective closed-loop episodes, versus 52% and 43% for representative baselines, outperforming both on every target view, including the challenging longitudinal internal and external carotid artery views. A prospective feasibility study on unseen volunteers, run in real time on a CPU using distillation, reaches 83% target-view reachability. Because planning is driven by proximity to any encodable goal latent, the same world model can navigate back to any previously acquired, patient-specific frame, supporting reproducible longitudinal imaging for e.g. perioperative or follow-up monitoring.

title: Ultrasound Robot Motion Perception and Control Based on Multimodal Sensing
abstract: This project develops multimodal perception and control methods for robotic ultrasound imaging. By integrating ultrasound images with robot motion, probe pose, and force information, the study aims to improve anatomical perception, probe navigation, and autonomous ultrasound acquisition. The project will generate synchronized imaging and sensor data for model development and evaluation, supporting more accurate and reproducible robotic ultrasound scanning.

title: Unsuspected intestinal taeniasis discovered on capsule endoscopy: A case report
abstract: Intestinal taeniasis is a tapeworm infection commonly encountered in endemic regions, including Asia, Africa, and Latin America. Diagnosis is often delayed due to nonspecific gastrointestinal symptoms and limited sensitivity of stool ova and parasite testing. We present a 57-year-old Nepali man undergoing capsule endoscopy for persistent microcytic anemia and abdominal pain, in whom capsule endoscopy revealed unsuspected diffuse small bowel tapeworms. He was treated with praziquantel, but his anemia was unchanged on follow-up, suggesting an alternate etiology. This case highlights capsule endoscopy's ability to visualize helminths in situ and cautions against attributing anemia to incidental findings.

title: Unveiling Glial Heterogeneity in the Inner Retina: Non-Visual Photic Spectrum Responses and Calcium Dynamics in Müller Glial Cells vs. Neurons
abstract: Traditional calcium (Ca2+) imaging analysis often overlooks the non-stationary temporal complexity inherent in retinal circuits, reducing dynamic signaling traces to static summary descriptors. To resolve these dynamic signatures, we implemented a reproducible analytical framework combining Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT) time-frequency decomposition with Sinc baseline filtering and Ward’s agglomerative hierarchical clustering, applied directly to standardized high-dimensional feature spaces, reserving Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) strictly for low-dimensional visualization. This pipeline was deployed across three independent experimental models under blue light stimulation: mixed primary embryonic chicken retinal neurons, primary chicken Müller glial cells (MGCs), and the human MIO-M1 Müller cell line. Functional clustering resolved retinal neurons into three distinct kinetic subpopulations (k = 3), characterized by a kinetically stable core maintaining mid-frequency oscillations (Cluster 0), a cohort undergoing sharp post-stimulus period contraction with late amplitude surges (Cluster 1), and a low-frequency cohort with persistent period elongation (Cluster 2). Chicken MGCs partitioned into two operational clusters (k = 2), contrasting a period-stable, amplitude-decaying subpopulation (Cluster 0) with a dynamic subpopulation exhibiting light-evoked kinetic acceleration (Cluster 1). Similarly, human MIO-M1 glia separated into two major kinetic clusters (k = 2), distinguishing a low-amplitude, longer-period cohort from a high-amplitude, sustained subpopulation operating within an 8–80 s dynamic period band. Restricting phase-coupling and circular statistical analyses strictly to simultaneous Field-of-View (FOV) recordings revealed distinct stimulus-entrained network behaviors: primary avian MGCs maintain a decentralized, weakly coupled regime (“mosaic of autonomy”) that processes light across independent temporal windows, whereas human MIO-M1 glia and embryonic neuronal assemblies exhibit significant stimulus-evoked phase realignment and relative response latency sequencing. These findings demonstrate that inner retinal functional identity is fundamentally rhythmic and cluster-dependent, establishing a quantitative benchmark for decoding multi-scale Ca2+ signaling in healthy retinal preparations.

title: VLM-Based Mesh Segmentation Framework for DDH Robotic Ultrasound
abstract: For robotic ultrasound targeting developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH), reconstructed infant body-surface meshes should preserve the target surface while excluding bed, support, and background geometry. This study proposes a structured vision–language model (VLM)-based multi-view segmentation method for infant phantom mesh cleanup. Text-guided 2D masks provide foreground and background evidence; mask-quality statistics and structured VLM assessments generate view-specific foreground-support weights that undergo deterministic risk suppression before target/non-target classification of 3D vertices. Hard voting and Rule-weighted voting were baselines under identical projection and post-processing settings. We evaluated one physical infant phantom across 150 separate acquisition–reconstruction trials under controlled conditions, each comprising 40 voting views and 10 held-out evaluation views, yielding 1500 manually annotated reference masks. Structured VLM voting achieved a Balanced score (intersection over union minus the 2-pixel tolerant leakage rate) of 0.804 ± 0.085, versus 0.801 ± 0.084 and 0.793 ± 0.086 for Rule-weighted and Hard voting. This leakage rate was 0.087 ± 0.043, versus 0.089 ± 0.042 and 0.092 ± 0.043; mean Coverage remained similar (0.992–0.993). The Balanced-score gain and leakage-rate reduction relative to Rule-weighted voting remained significant after Holm correction (adjusted p = 0.029 and p = 0.033, respectively). Validation using real-infant data, 3D reference standards, and closed-loop robotic scanning is still required.

title: Virtual Chromoendoscopy Enhancing Visualization of Parasite Anatomical Landmarks: A Case Report
abstract: Cestodes are parasitic flatworms transmitted through fecal-oral transmission. Some patients may present with nonspecific gastrointestinal symptoms. Endoscopic identification of intestinal helminths is uncommon and may pose a diagnostic challenge. We describe the endoscopic findings of intestinal cestodiasis and highlight the role of advanced endoscopic imaging techniques in its in vivo recognition. We report the case of a patient with no significant medical history who presented with recent-onset intermittent gastrointestinal symptoms, including abdominal distension and bloating. Laboratory tests and computed tomography enterography showed no abnormalities. Using magnification and virtual chromoendoscopy, detailed visualization of a parasite attached to the terminal ileal mucosa was achieved. Colonoscopy revealed a thin helminth adherent to the terminal ileal mucosa. Virtual chromoendoscopy enhanced visualization of characteristic anatomical structures. This case highlights the diagnostic value of advanced endoscopic imaging techniques and underscores their usefulness for recognizing uncommon intestinal infections during routine colonoscopy.

title: Visual Characteristic Classification of Peritoneal Carcinomatosis Tumors in Laparoscopic Images Using Chained Convolutional Neural Networks and Region of Interest Extraction
abstract: Peritoneal tumor characterization during laparoscopy relies on surgeon-assigned visual characteristics that vary between observers. Automated methods have not addressed these five individual characteristics. A chained Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) was developed to classify Color, Adherant, Mucinex, Nodulaire, and Retractile from tumor Regions of Interest (ROIs). Cramér's V, mutual information, and Random Forest (RF) predictability were used to determine which labels provided context, and later classifiers received soft probabilities from earlier classifiers. The method was evaluated on a private dataset of 3,432 tumor instances using three ROI methods (Box-ROI, Black-Fill-ROI, and Mean-Fill-ROI) with ResNet50 and VGG19-BN backbones. Macro F1 was the primary metric, supported by the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUROC) and the Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (AUCPRC). The best aggregate configuration combined Black-Fill-ROI with chained classification, achieving a mean Macro F1 of 0.7347 and a mean AUROC of 0.8611. Mucinex achieved the highest single-target Macro F1 of 0.8332. For Color, Mean-Fill-ROI achieved the highest independent Macro F1 of 0.7408, whereas Box-ROI achieved the highest chained Macro F1 of 0.7992. Adherant remained difficult despite class weighting. Its independent AUCPRC was higher with Mean-Fill-ROI than with Black-Fill-ROI (0.242 compared with 0.094). Chaining improved Macro F1 in 7 of 15 target-ROI comparisons. The variation across targets shows that ROI design and chaining require target-specific validation. The classifier is intended to support consistent surgical documentation and review rather than autonomous diagnosis.
authors: Hilmi Zharfan Rachmadi; Agus Budi Raharjo; Diana Purwitasari; Frédéric Dumont; Emilie Thibaudeau; Cédric Dumas

title: Visual inspection : image sampling, algorithms and architectures
abstract: The thesis concerns the hexagonal sampling of images, the processing of industrially derived images, and the design of a novel processor element that can be assembled into pipelines to effect fast, economic and reliable processing. A hexagonally sampled two dimensional image can require 13.4% fewer sampling points than a square sampled equivalent. The grid symmetry results in simpler processing operators that compute more efficiently than square grid operators. Computation savings approaching 44% arc demonstrated. New hexagonal operators arc reported including a Gaussian smoothing filter, a binary thinner, and an edge detector with comparable accuracy to that of the Sobel detector. The design of hexagonal arrays of sensors is considered. Operators requiring small local areas of support are shown to be sufficient for processing controlled lighting and industrial images. Case studies show that small features in hexagonally processed images maintain their shape better, and that processes can tolerate a lower signal to noise ratio, than that for equivalent square processed images. The modelling of small defects in surfaces has been studied in depth. The flexible programmable processor element can perform the low level local operators required for industrial image processing on both square and hexagonal grids. The element has been specified and simulated by a high level computer program. A fast communication channel allows for dynamic reprogramming by a control computer, and the video rate element can be assembled into various pipeline architectures, that may eventually be adaptively controlled.
authors: Richard C. Staunton
venue: Warwick Research Archive Portal (University of Warwick)

title: WCE-SECUREAI: A LIGHTWEIGHT HYBRID CRYPTOGRAPHIC FRAMEWORK FOR SECURE DATA TRANSMISSION IN IOMT USING WIRELESS CAPSULE ENDOSCOPY
abstract: Wireless Capsule Endoscopy (WCE) is a diagnostic tool used for the detection of gastrointestinal (GI) diseases due to its non-invasive approach to visualizing the digestive tract. Nonetheless, the application of DPA in Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) is limited due to twofold difficulties, including secure medical data transmission and high computational complexity, as well as the poor applicability of current cryptographic schemes to resource-constrained devices. Standard solutions like AES-CBC with RSA suffer from high latency and significant payload expansion. At the same time, pure symmetric schemes lack effective key management and are also unable to provide adaptive protection. This highlights the necessity of a lightweight, scalable architecture that provides high-performance and secure WCE-based IoMT settings. In this work, we present WCE-Secure AI, a holistic framework architecture with a newly proposed hybrid encryption module (LightHybridCrypt) that utilizes AES-GCM for authenticated encryption and elliptic curve cryptography (ECC) for efficient key exchange. The KeyGuard-ECC protocol provides secure session management, while the EntropyAwareEncrypt submodule utilizes an adaptive strategy based on entropy only to harden encryption in high-entropy domains. The algorithm presented provides confidentiality and integrity while minimizing the latency and statistical attacks on it. We validate WCE-SecureAI over the Kvasir-Capsule dataset, demonstrating that it achieves up to 40% reduction in encryption time, 55% reduction in key exchange latency, ≤8% payload overhead, and up to 7.99/8 bits of entropy, with 99.1% integrity verification accuracy. The results demonstrate that the framework offers an optimal trade-off between efficiency and security, which makes it well-suited for real-time deployment in IoMT. Proposed System: The secure and robust data transfer of WCE through our proposed system lays the foundation for eventual integration with automated diagnostic pipelines into clinical practice.
authors: P.ANITHA SHRAVANI AMAR
venue: Journal of Theoretical and Applied Information Technology

title: Wearable 3D Transmitter for Omnidirectional Wireless Energy Delivery for Microrobot.
abstract: Capsule robot has emerged as a non-invasive and painless diagnostic tool for gastrointestinal examination. However, the growing demand for high-definition video and advanced functionalities significantly increases power consumption, while the capsule's compact size imposes stringent battery constraints. Wireless power transfer (WPT) offers a promising solution to overcome this energy bottleneck. This paper presents a wearable three-dimensional transmitting coil (3DTC) and a one dimensional receiving coil (1DRC) to enable omnidirectional and uninterrupted wireless charging for capsule robots. By acquiring attitude data from the capsule, the magnetic field of the wearable 3DTC is adaptively controlled to maximise receiving efficiency despite changes in the capsule's position and orientation. The capsule's built-in thermal and charging management circuits monitor the device's temperature, battery voltage, and stop charging when necessary to ensure safety. Beyond demonstrating a maximum received power of 1690 mW and a peak efficiency of 16.09%, this work further examines a range of practical challenges including, the effects upon the flexible coil bending in garment, charging robustness under various capsule motions, and thermal safety. These evaluations contribute to safer, more efficient, and more sustainable ingestible biomedical devices.
authors: Heng Zhang; Chi-Kwan Lee
venue: IEEE transactions on biomedical circuits and systems

title: Wearable Sensors for Monitoring Haemodynamics, Tissue Perfusion, and Motion in Microgravity: Systematic Review
abstract: This systematic review protocol outlines the methodology for identifying and synthesising studies that measure haemodynamics, tissue perfusion, or motion in microgravity environments. The data will evaluate the clinical feasibility and baseline metrics for an Autonomous Ultrasound & NIRS Rig designed for orbital redistribution assessment (Headward Fluid Shift Monitor) (AURORA-HFSM). The search strategy targets database literature from 2015 to 2026 across PubMed and the Cochrane Library. Screening, data extraction, and quality assessment (utilising QUADAS-2 and WEAR-BOT tools) will be conducted independently by a four-reviewer team using Rayyan.
authors: Sakina Hassan

title: When Every Test Fails: Multifocal Grade 1 Ileal Neuroendocrine Tumors Causing Transfusion-Dependent Obscure Overt Gastrointestinal Bleeding.
abstract: Small bowel neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) rarely present as obscure overt gastrointestinal bleeding (OGIB), causing significant diagnostic challenges. We report a 56-year-old man who presented with OGIB that required approximately 50 units of packed red blood cells during a 6-week hospitalization. Multimodal evaluation, including computed tomography angiography, tagged red blood cell scan, video capsule endoscopy, computed tomography enterography, provocative mesenteric angiography, balloon enteroscopy, and octreotide scan, failed to identify a source. Exploratory laparotomy identified 3 mid-ileal nodules with histopathology revealing well-differentiated grade 1 neuroendocrine tumors. Bleeding resolved following resection. This case highlights the diagnostic and therapeutic role of surgical exploration in refractory OGIB.
authors: James Mo; Suraj Suresh

title: When Imaging is Negative: Endoscopic Diagnosis of a Secondary Aortoduodenal Fistula
abstract: Aortoenteric fistula is a life-threatening aortic graft complication with a narrow opportunity for treatment. We present a patient with aortobifemoral bypass who developed recurrent anemia and melena. Despite previous upper endoscopy and colonoscopy, computed tomography angiogram, and tagged red blood cell scan, his symptoms were persistent. Capsule endoscopy showed blood in the duodenum. Push enteroscopy revealed graft erosion in the duodenum, confirming aortoduodenal fistula. He underwent aortobifemoral graft excision, and resection of the third portion of the duodenum with end-to-side duodenojejunostomy, highlighting the importance of endoscopy in timely diagnosis of aortoenteric fistulae.
authors: Avneet Kaur; Ayushi Shah; Anand Gupta; Muhammad Nauman Jhandier

title: Zero-shot classification of bleeding, angiectasia, and normal mucosa in video capsule endoscopy by general-purpose multimodal models
abstract: A diagnostic accuracy study measuring how well current general-purpose multimodal models, given no task-specific training and no worked examples, assign video capsule endoscopy frames to one of three categories: fresh blood, angiectasia, and normal clean mucosa. Frames are drawn from the publicly available Kvasir-Capsule dataset by two-stage stratified sampling at the level of the source recording. The primary outcome is macro-averaged F1. Predictive values are recalculated across the range of frame-level lesion prevalence met in clinical reading; calibration of stated confidence and the rate of declining to answer are treated as outcomes; and a prespecified probe tests whether the models recognize the provenance of the images they are shown. This project holds the protocol and the analysis code, registered before any model was queried.
authors: Ahmed Salman

title: Zero-shot performance of a general-purpose vision-language model for pediatric appendicitis diagnosis.
abstract: General-purpose vision-language models can analyze medical images without task-specific training, but their value for pediatric abdominal ultrasound is unknown. To investigate the zero-shot performance of a general-purpose vision-language model to diagnose pediatric appendicitis using multimodal inputs, including images, report text, and clinical information. In this retrospective study, diagnostic capabilities of Llama 4 Maverick were evaluated on the Regensburg Pediatric Appendicitis Dataset. Five experiments were conducted using the following inputs as well as input combinations: images only, ultrasound report text only, images and ultrasound text, images and clinical data, entire multimodal input. Reference standard of appendicitis was defined based on histopathology in patients who underwent surgical resection and on clinical follow-up in patients managed conservatively. Performance was assessed at the patient level using accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, and F1-score. Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was evaluated secondarily as a measure of discrimination. Of 782 patients, 294 met inclusion criteria; based on data availability, four experiments are conducted using 293 patients and in the fifth experiment, 284. Images-only experiment showed very low specificity (13.5%) and had the poorest discrimination (AUROC, 0.567). Ultrasound report text improved classification performance, with specificity increasing to 63.5% while maintaining high sensitivity; discrimination was also strong (AUROC, 0.883). Adding images to ultrasound text or combining all available inputs did not yield further meaningful improvement. Differences between images-only experiment and text-containing experiments were statistically significant (P≤0.002). Zero-shot visual interpretation of pediatric abdominal ultrasound by a general-purpose vision-language model is inadequate for safe appendicitis diagnosis. Performance is driven primarily by a structured sonographic imaging report, supporting a role for such models as text-based decision support tools rather than autonomous ultrasound image interpreters.
authors: Ceren Altintas Mese; Ismail Mese; Tugba Akinci D'Antonoli

title: [Point of care ultrasound: terminology, professional roles and protocols].
abstract: Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) is an imaging modality performed and interpreted by the treating physician at the bedside, with immediate integration of findings into clinical decision-making. Its rapid expansion in emergency medicine, critical care, and resource-limited settings has significantly improved diagnostic and therapeutic timeliness. However, this growth has highlighted the need to clearly define its scope of practice, standardize protocols, and distinguish POCUS from comprehensive consultative echocardiography. This review outlines the historical evolution of POCUS, from early trauma applications to structured protocols for shock, dyspnea, and cardiac arrest, and its current role in cardiopulmonary and hemodynamic monitoring of critically ill patients. Recent international guidelines are summarized, emphasizing POCUS as a distinct and complementary clinical tool rather than a replacement for formal imaging. Finally, future perspectives involving artificial intelligence and robotic ultrasound technologies are discussed, addressing their potential benefits and associated educational, organizational, and ethical challenges.
authors: Simona Giubilato; Francesca Musella; Carlotta Sorini Dini; Francesco Piroli; Nicola Gasparetto; Serena Guasti; Roberta Della Bona; Daniela Zabbia; Francesca Campanella; Salvatore Petrina; Roberta Rossini; Paolo Trambaiolo; Fabrizio Oliva; Federico Nardi; Massimo Grimaldi; Benedetta De Chiara

title: iPSC-derived RPE as a context-of-use defined NAM framework for RPE-centered drug-induced retinal toxicity assessment
abstract: The retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is essential for outer retinal homeostasis and a key target for drug-induced retinal toxicity. However, conventional preclinical models, including immortalized cell lines and animal systems, may incompletely recapitulate human RPE biology because of limited representation of specialized RPE functions and species-specific differences in retinal physiology. Induced pluripotent stem cell-derived RPE (iPSC-RPE) has emerged as a candidate human-relevant platform for New Approach Methodology (NAM) development, with the potential to improve mechanistic relevance by reproducing key structural and functional features of native human RPE. Its translational utility depends on a clearly defined context of use (COU), reproducible differentiation and functional characterization, and benchmark-based frameworks for future assay qualification and validation. This review evaluates the potential of iPSC-RPE as a COU-defined NAM framework for RPE-centered drug-induced retinal toxicity, with particular emphasis on toxicities in which RPE dysfunction represents a primary or mechanistically important component. We summarize differentiation strategies and critical quality attributes that may inform future assay qualification, evaluate disease-modeling evidence supporting physiological relevance, and discuss applications in ocular safety assessment, including chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine-, MEK inhibitor-, and anti-VEGF-associated retinal effects. We further discuss limitations, including cellular immaturity, donor-to-donor variability, incomplete microenvironmental modeling, and the limited validation of long-term exposure paradigms. Current evidence supports mechanistic concordance for selected RPE-centered toxicities, whereas prospective predictive performance across diverse compounds and clinically relevant exposure conditions remains to be established. Further COU-specific qualification and prospective validation will be required to establish the reliability and decision relevance of iPSC-RPE for defined ocular toxicology applications.
authors: Weixiao Ding; Longjun Gu; 董田甜; Minjun Xiong; Chen Wang; Chunlei Ji; Juan Lv; Xuefeng Zhang; Xinjiang Gong

title: “Integration of Embedded AI and Medical Heat Pipes in Robotic Neurosurgery: A Novel Framework Based on Elmas’s Thermodynamic Theory”
abstract: Objective: This study presents an interdisciplinary framework that autonomizes the thermal management of high-temperature laser ablation and ultra-low-temperature cryoprobe applications, which represent opposing thermal poles in robotic neurosurgery operations. The thermal sensitivity of neural tissues and the risk of permanent neuron damage developing at temperatures above 43°C necessitate a micron-level stable thermal control. Accordingly, the study aims to optimize surgical robots both in terms of hardware and software. Method: The theoretical foundation of the study is based on the principles of “ELMAS’s Thermodynamic Theory”, the “5th Law of Thermodynamics”, and “Bio-Robotic Resonance” developed by Asst. Prof. Dr. Emin Taner Elmas. In the hardware layer, dual-phase medical heat pipes integrated into the tip of the robotic arm (end-effector), having a diameter of 0.8 mm, flexible, and containing sintered copper powder micro-capillaries with water-graphene nano-fluid, were utilized. In the software layer, an embedded artificial intelligence (AI) engine supported by machine learning models was developed, capable of real-time data processing from micro-sensors on the heat pipe and performing digital twin-based live thermal mapping (HUD). The validation of the system was designed with a 5-step validation protocol encompassing computerized thermal modeling, synthetic gel tests, ex-vivo organ tests, in-vivo animal experiments, and preclinical human simulation. Findings: The integration of the micro-heat pipe provided passive cooling without requiring an external energy source, thereby suppressing peripheral heat dissipation (thermal dissipation) during laser operations and maintaining healthy neural tissues within a stable range of 37°C - 38°C. In cryoprobe applications, it acted as a passive heat barrier, creating reverse thermal gradients along the probe shaft, protecting healthy tissues along the entry path while performing instantaneous shock freezing cycles (freeze-thaw) at the target tumor site. The predictive algorithms of the AI engine predicted the thermal saturation at the tissue border milliseconds in advance and successfully activated the haptic lock (fail-safe) mechanism that applies resistance to the surgeon’s master control arms at critical thresholds. Conclusion: The developed autonomous thermal management architecture elevates surgical robots beyond being merely devices that produce mechanical motion into intelligent protective shields that thermally sense the tissue. The integration of Dr. Elmas’s medical thermodynamics equations into robotic software demonstrates at a preclinical level that a micron-level precise, autonomous, and thermally safe hybrid surgical platform can be established for brain tumor resections. [1-111]
authors: Emin Taner ELMAS
venue: Biomedical Journal of Scientific & Technical Research

title: 3D-printed microneedles in biomedical applications: Versatile approaches and clinical potential
abstract: Microneedles (MNs) are micron-scale structures that can painlessly penetrate the skin barrier to facilitate drug delivery, biomarker sampling, and biosensing. During MN fabrication, although conventional molding techniques allow for large-scale production, they exhibit inherent limitations in the rapid and personalized customization of geometric structures—parameters that are critical determinants of the biomedical functionality and performance of MNs. As a next-generation manufacturing paradigm, 3D printing offers novel opportunities for the development of personalized and intelligent MNs, leveraging its high precision, design flexibility, and integrated fabrication capabilities. This article reviews the different types of MNs and their geometric characteristics, systematically summarizes the applications, advantages, and limitations of mainstream 3D printing technologies in MN fabrication, and focuses on recent research advances in 3D-printed MNs for drug delivery, biomarker extraction, and biosensor construction. Furthermore, it provides an in-depth overview of the application potential of 3D-printed MNs in the treatment of various diseases. The article also discusses the emerging integration of 4D printing and artificial intelligence (AI) within this domain. Finally, we conclude with a summary and propose potential directions for future research.
authors: Ziqing Su; Sheng Cheng; Weiwei Chen; Menghui Liu; Peng Gao; Liang Xu; Xingliang Dai

title: A COMPLEX MÜLLERIAN ANOMALY MISDIAGNOSED AS FIBROID UTERUS: A CASE REPORT
abstract: We report a 47-year-old woman who had never been pregnant and had suffered from primary infertility. She also had chronic pelvic pain and irregular menstrual periods. She had several uterine abnormalities, including a complete septate uterus, a duplicated cervix, and a longitudinal vaginal septum, with primary infertility. Her diagnosis included a large endometrial polyp and submucosal fibroids in the uterine cavity. This has been reported in only a few cases. The ultrasound diagnosis revealed a single uterine body with a single endometrial cavity and uterine fibroids but missed other diagnoses of two separate cervical canals, a double cervix, or separate vaginal canals, and a large endometrial polyp. The patient opted for definitive treatment and declined fertility preservation, leading to a total abdominal hysterectomy and removal of the uterine corpus, both cervices, and the vaginal septum. She was discharged five days after surgery and recovered. There are three clinical aspects to this case. First, imaging techniques (ultrasonography and MRI) should be used to diagnose and classify atypical Müllerian duct anomalies (MDAs) before applying a classification system. Second, in hysteroscopic septal resection, treatment should be individualized based on age, disease severity, and reproductive status. For younger women who wish to conceive, hysteroscopic septal resection is generally the most appropriate option, and hysterectomy is usually the last resort for suitable candidates. Finally, a multidisciplinary approach is necessary to deal with congenital anomalies that are complicated by acquired uterine pathologies. The diagnostic and surgical plan is required for such a patient to achieve optimal outcomes.
authors: Dil Sahi Roka; Priyanka Gharti Magar; Krishna Kumar Sah; Sandeep Shrestha; Lijing Liu
venue: World Journal of Biology Pharmacy and Health Sciences

title: A European algorithm and strategy for management of chronic postoperative inguinal pain (EurA-CPIP)
abstract: Background Chronic postoperative inguinal pain (CPIP) is a disabling complication affecting 8%–17% of all patients after inguinal hernia repair. It is a complex pain condition with several pathophysiological mechanisms involved, including neuropathic pain, inflammation, and mechanical effects (e.g., mesh or scar tissue). Management remains inconsistent, probably due to limited high-quality evidence, heterogeneous approach, and insufficient standardisation of outcomes. This study aimed to develop EurA-CPIP, a multidisciplinary treatment algorithm and prospective data-collection platform designed to support consistent phenotyping, step-up management, and standardised outcomes across centres, creating an iterative platform for future hypothesis-driven research and multicentre trials. Methods An international multidisciplinary working group from European tertiary referral centres developed the European Algorithm and Strategy for Management of Chronic Postoperative Inguinal Pain (EurA-CPIP). Development was informed by the evidence synthesis underpinning the updated international HerniaSurge guidelines and a critical appraisal of previously published CPIP algorithms. A pragmatic step-up algorithm was designed, integrating pharmacological, interventional, surgical and supportive treatments, with prospective outcome registration and planned data-driven revision on a regular basis. Results EurA-CPIP provides a multidisciplinary algorithm with entry at multiple levels depending on prior treatment attempts. The concept is to begin and, if needed, advance from conservative measures such as systemic medication and topical therapy, to more invasive treatments such as trigger point injections, and ultrasound-guided nerve blocks; predefined investigational add-ons (radiofrequency, cryoneurolysis, botulinum toxin A) are embedded after documented block response. Multidisciplinary team review precedes escalation to more invasive interventions such as surgery. A supportive and rehabilitative coping trajectory is integrated early on. Standardised outcomes include patient-reported pain outcomes, functional impairment, psychological factors, analgesic use, and patient global impression of improvement. Conclusion EurA-CPIP is a pragmatic consensus-based strategy intended to harmonise and improve specialised CPIP care while utilising existing and developing emerging therapies. Future research should investigate pathophysiology and intervention effects within this step-up algorithm.
authors: K. G. Andersen; T. W. K. van der Meer; Nadine van Veenendaal; N. B. Foss; M. J. A. Loos; M. Miserez; M. Pawlak; R. M. H. Roumen; T. Naddaf; M. Togsverd-Bo; M. W. Stadeager; E. K. Aasvang; Willem A. R. Zwaans

title: A Multi‐Axis Plantar Load Measurement Platform for the Assessment of Foot Disorders: Comparison of Patients With Psoriatic Arthritis to a Healthy Control Cohort
abstract: BACKGROUND: Accurate assessment of plantar loading, including shear forces, is crucial for understanding foot pathologies such as dactylitis in psoriatic arthritis (PsA). Existing devices predominantly measure plantar pressures, neglecting important shear stresses which may initiate dactylitis. This study presents a novel multi-axis plantar load measurement platform to address this gap. METHODS: The study utilised a newly developed plantar load measurement system, comprising a Hall-effect-based magnetic sensing array, custom data logging electronics, and tailored data processing software. The system's efficacy was evaluated in a pilot feasibility study involving patients with PsA with no, current, or previous dactylitis, and healthy controls. Participants walked barefoot on the platform, capturing plantar shear and pressure data. FINDINGS: Shear stresses were notably higher in the second to fourth rays compared to other regions, particularly in the left foot, aligning with the hypothesis that repetitive local trauma might initiate dactylitis in PsA. However, no consistent differences in stresses were observed between diagnostic groups, likely due to small sample sizes and gait alterations associated with pain. A marked asymmetry was observed between the right and left feet, suggesting dominant-foot placement effects. INTERPRETATION: The new platform demonstrates potential clinical utility in capturing comprehensive foot-loading profiles, including critical shear stresses previously under-assessed. Although the current pilot study was limited in number, the results support the theory that local mechanical stresses may contribute to PsA-related dactylitis. Future larger-scale studies are needed to clarify these findings and overcome limitations related to altered gait patterns due to foot pain.
authors: D. A. Jones; Lefan Wang; Max Houghton; Jennifer Jones; Richard A. Wilkins; Heidi J. Siddle; Graham Chapman; Ali Alazmani; Peter Culmer; Philip Helliwell
venue: Journal of Foot and Ankle Research

title: A Narrative Review of Early Pregnancy Diagnosis Technologies for Livestock: From Conventional to Intelligent Systems
abstract: Accurate and efficient early pregnancy diagnosis (EPD) in livestock is crucial for optimizing breeding management and enhancing productivity in modern animal husbandry. Over the past century, EPD technology has evolved from empirical methods to sophisticated techniques, encompassing biochemical marker detection, ultrasonic imaging, and further extending to emerging non-invasive approaches such as infrared thermography (IRT) and spectroscopic analysis. These advancements have not only improved diagnostic accuracy but also broadened the research scope to include small livestock and multiple species. This review critically examines the historical evolution, current methodologies, and applications of EPD technology, with a focus on analyzing the advantages and limitations of both traditional and emerging techniques. Additionally, it explores the potential of multimodal fusion strategies and artificial intelligence (AI) in EPD. At present, machine vision, wearable monitoring, and several AI applications remain prospective approaches rather than validated tools for routine EPD. The conclusion highlights that, despite significant progress, current technologies still face limitations in achieving in situ, non-contact, and high-throughput detection. Looking ahead, the integration of cutting-edge technologies, such as AI, small wearable sensors, and physiological time-series data analysis, holds promise for overcoming these bottlenecks, enabling more intelligent and efficient pregnancy diagnosis, and providing scientific support for modern animal husbandry.
authors: Yang Shen; Yujie Zhang; Junyi Meng; Yutong Han; Jitong Xu; Hongying Wang; Liangju Wang

title: A PROSPECTIVE OBSERVATIONAL STUDY ON MANAGEMENT OF ESOPHAGEAL CARCINOMA WITH MINIMALLY INVASIVE IVOR-LEWIS ESOPHAGECTOMY AND ITS OUTCOMES IN A TERTIARY CARE CENTRE IN CENTRAL INDIA
abstract: Introduction: Esophageal cancer is a life threatening malignancy with abysmal survival, even for subjects under therapeutic care.Minimally invasive surgery like minimally invasive Ivor Lewis esophagectomy, which is commonly performed for treating esophageal cancer, has a favourable impact in perioperative morbidity and enhances short term recovery compared to traditional open surgery through thoracotomy.The present study was performed to evaluate the outcomes and complications of minimally invasive Ivor-Lewis esophagectomy (MILE) for esophageal cancer. Methods and Materials:A prospective observational study of 20 patients, with histologically proven adenocarcinoma of lower esophagus and posted for minimally invasive Ivor-Lewis esophagectomy, was performed in Department of General Surgery of Government Medical College and Hospital, Nagpur for a period of 18 months (From August 2022 to January 2024).Results: In this study, predominantly patients were females (60%) in the age group of 61 -70 years, with a mean age of 64.04 ± 5.15 years.All patients experienced dysphagia (100%), and more than half also reported weight loss, odynophagia, and retrosternal pain.Approximately 40 % of patients were diabetic.Additionally, 60% of patients had hypertension, with 20% of those also having diabetes.Around half of patients were smokers (50%).Patients predominantly classified as ASA status II (60%), while the remaining 40% were classified as ASA status III.Predominantly, 60% of patients were classified under the T3 category, while the majority were classified under the N1 category (80%).Majority of patients had duration of surgery 4-5 hours (40%) with mean duration was 4.5 ± 1.72 hours.Among all patients, 40% experienced bleeding in the range of 151 to 200 mL, with a mean blood loss of 176.8 ± 40.07 mL.Among patients with complications, 10% experienced early postoperative bleeding, chyle leak, anastomotic leak, or conduit necrosis, while 60% had no complications.The most common length of stay was 6 days, experienced by 40% of patients, with a mean duration of 6.6 ± 0.97 days.Around 30% patients did not survive, while the remaining 70% survived.
authors: Dr. Kartik Sharma
venue: Indian Journal of Health Care Medical & Pharmacy Practice

title: A Standardized Chewable Conductive Hydrogel Sensor for Direct Monitoring of Masticatory Dynamics
abstract: ABSTRACT Chewing is a fundamental orofacial function closely related to nutrition, digestion, and quality of life, yet current assessment methods generally rely on indirect signals or endpoint measurements and provide limited process‐level information. Here, a hydroxypropyl cellulose (HPC)/polyacrylamide (PAM) conductive hydrogel is developed as a standardized chewable sensor that integrates the test substrate with force‐to‐electrical signal transduction, enabling direct monitoring of masticatory dynamics. The sensor captures chewing frequency, relative force response, chewing duration, relative force response variability, and rhythm variability during standardized tests. Using predefined chewing‐state labels, these features were integrated into a classification framework, with KNN achieving 98.0% accuracy in recording‐level cross‐validation and 76.7% in nested leave‐one‐participant‐out validation, providing an initial assessment of generalizability to unseen participants. The hydrogel exhibits a compressive strength of 2.3 MPa, toughness of 287 kJ m − 3 , a response time of 150 ms, recovery within 173 ms, and less than 3% signal attenuation over 150 cycles. Polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) encapsulation supports stable intraoral operation and biocompatibility.
