title: MoS2 Biosensing: Technologies Insight into Photo and Electrical Detection
abstract: The semiconductor industry has foreseen a replacement for the old-fashioned Si-based technology. For quite some time, since the International Technology Roadmap for Semiconductors (ITRS) predicted it back in 2007, the floating-gate MOS structure cannot be scaled-down due to the tunneling layer reaching an impasse point where the leaking current is a major issue. The ITRS directives focused on the search for a replacement for Si. In 2007, graphene appeared to be the holy-grail material to replace it and to develop the whole brand new electronic-devices for the semiconductor market. Sadly, it did not deliver but shed some light on which sort of material might be the right one. The transition metal dichalcogenides feature key characteristics that might work as the replacement for Si and push forward the semiconductor industry. From those materials, there are a few that can be used in a straight forward manner, such as MoS2 that shows elemental characteristics to be implemented by continuing with the path started by graphene to be the key material for the up-coming semiconductor devices. In this chapter, we show how MoS2 can be the backbone for the semiconductor industry, that is, photo/electrical biosensors.
authors: Andrea Carolina Villalvazo-Hidalgo; Orfil González‐Reynoso; Martha Angélica Hidalgo-Ríos; Gregorio Guadalupe Carbajal Carbajal Arízaga; María Esther Macías-Rodríguez; Everardo Vargas-Rodríguez; ANA DINORA GUZMAN CHAVEZ; Mario Alberto García Ramírez

title: Modeling human skin aging with artificial intelligence: from multi-layer structure to personalized intervention
abstract: Abstract Skin aging is driven by progressive alterations across cutaneous structures and systemic biological processes, yet current assessment and intervention strategies remain largely population based and lack precision. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) enable integrated modeling of skin aging phenotypes, structural dynamics, and individualized rejuvenation responses through multimodal analysis and predictive simulation. Here, we summarize emerging AI-driven approaches in skin aging research, focusing on multi-structure modeling, multimodal data integration, interpretable prediction, and clinically closed-loop optimization. We further discuss current challenges in data heterogeneity, generalizability, fairness, and clinical translation, and outline future directions toward personalized rejuvenation medicine.
authors: Wenyue Zheng; Yantong Cai; Yiwen Xu; Ke Hu; Haoran Zhang; Songshan Li; Zhaowen Wang; Yuanqiu Zhong; Liying Xu; Donghua Chen; Shuya Ren; Ougen Liu; Chao Yuan; Bin Yang

title: Multi-Agent Deferred-Decision Trajectory Optimization with Anytime-Valid Target Retention for Moving Candidates
abstract: We study multi-agent terminal interception when one of several moving candidates is the unknown target and both target identity and candidate terminal locations are uncertain. We develop a receding-horizon deferred-decision trajectory optimization (DDTO) controller that combines conformal terminal-location prediction, sequential candidate rejection, capacity-constrained assignment, and candidate-contingent planning. Under exchangeability conditions for terminal and identity residuals, with predictable querying, we establish fixed-time terminal-location coverage and anytime-valid target retention. At the final replan, when one control step remains, we bound the joint probability that a tightened-set DDTO plan passes nonlinear rollout verification but capture fails. The closed-loop controller applies fallback guidance to any agent without a verified DDTO plan and, across 100 paired scenarios, captures 79% of targets under the strict control-effort budget and 85% when that budget is relaxed.
authors: Farbod Siahkali; Mengxue Hou; Vijay Kumar Gupta

title: Multi-channel shielding induced trap robust plasma wave rectification in AlGaN/GaN HEMT THz detectors
abstract: Abstract This work investigates trap-induced degradation in multi-channel (MC) GaN high electron mobility transistor (HEMT) terahertz (THz) detectors operating in the non-resonant plasma-wave rectification regime. The THz detection characteristics of MC-HEMTs are systematically compared with conventional single-channel (SC) architectures to evaluate responsivity, transient response, and stability under surface and buffer trap conditions. The results demonstrate that the MC-HEMT achieves enhanced responsivity of 12 500 V W −1 compared with 10 000 V W −1 for the SC-HEMT under trap-free conditions due to improved carrier transport and stronger nonlinear rectification behavior. Systematic trap analysis further reveals that surface donor traps have minimal influence on the THz response after saturation of the two-dimensional electron gas density, whereas buffer acceptor traps strongly suppress plasma-wave rectification in SC devices. In contrast, the MC-HEMT exhibits significantly improved robustness against buffer-trap-induced degradation even at high trap densities ranging from 5× 10 16 to 1× 10 19 cm −3 . Numerical physics-based simulations further shows that trap activation is primarily confined to the lower channel while the upper conducting channel remains electrostatically shielded from trap-induced carrier modulation. The results identify a channel-shielding mechanism intrinsic to MC configurations that preserves stable plasma-wave rectification under trap-loaded operating conditions.
authors: Shivansh Awasthi; Vikas Kumar; Ankur Gupta

title: Needles in a Raystack: Ultra-Sparse LiDAR Occupancy Detection for Bat Tracks
abstract: Monitoring flying animals is important for understanding and protecting biodiversity, but nocturnal species such as bats are difficult to observe in the field. Using LiDAR, bat movements at night result in ultra-sparse 3D spatio-temporal data in which standard reconstruction losses tend to predict only background and miss real flight paths. We study this problem as voxel-wise occupancy detection in sensor-centric LiDAR raystacks. A lightweight 3D U-Net is proposed that preserves temporal resolution, uses skip connections for spatial detail, and combines weighted binary cross-entropy with Dice loss to handle the strong class imbalance. In real LiDAR recordings of bats over open fields, cross-checked with acoustic monitoring, a reconstruction-based 3D convolutional autoencoder baseline fails to recover foreground trajectories. In contrast, the proposed U-Net recovers sparse foreground occupancy in diagnostic experiments and produces coherent occupancy patterns along bat flight trajectories, providing a practical basis for validation-scale experiments, later clustering of flight tracks, and future integration of bat activity information into biodiversity-aware turbine curtailment strategies.
authors: Nico Klar; Pankaj Rana; Nizam Gifary; Jakob Traub; Aamir Ahmad

title: Neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome: a review of diagnostic and therapeutic strategies
abstract: The diagnosis and treatment of neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome (nTOS) remain challenging. Although consensus-based clinical frameworks exist, they lack robust externa validation. This study conducts a review of nTOS publications in the PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science databases, with a search cutoff date of December 2025. Current evidence suggests that the incidence of nTOS may be underestimated. Diagnosis should be based on a comprehensive evaluation, including medical history, systematic physical examination, ancillary examinations, diagnostic muscle block, and exclusion of other possible diseases. Treatment should be carried out in a phased manner. For mild cases, nonsurgical treatment is preferred. For patients who experience progressive neurological dysfunction, muscle atrophy, or failure of conservative treatment, timely surgery should be considered. Surgical decompression mainly involves the supraclavicular or axillary approaches. Surgical techniques include first rib resection, rib-sparing scalenectomy, pectoralis minor release, cervical rib resection. However, the optimal treatment remains controversial due to the limited availability of high-quality evidence. Future research should focus on elucidating the pathophysiology of nTOS, improving diagnostic accuracy through technological innovation, and optimizing treatment protocols through prospective multicenter studies.
authors: Guang-Yao Li; Mingqiang Xue; Jing-Wei Wang; Ke Sha

title: Neuroimaging access in Chad: Infrastructure barriers and opportunities for accessible magnetic resonance imaging
abstract: Limited access to neuroimaging remains a major constraint on neurological care in many low-resource areas. We conducted a descriptive landscape analysis of neuroimaging access in Chad using hospital-reported data, publicly available healthcare and infrastructure data, and contextual information from clinicians and radiology personnel at major hospitals in N'Djamena. This analysis characterizes key constraints on neuroimaging access in Chad and highlights practical considerations for expanding imaging capacity in resource-limited settings. Chad has only one magnetic resonance imaging scanner for a population of approximately twenty-one million. The country's major hospitals and imaging workforce are concentrated in the capital, and the sole MRI system is an older 0.35 T scanner located at a private hospital. Access is further limited by scan cost, geographic centralization, unreliable electricity, limited technical support, and shortages of trained imaging personnel. Hospital data indicate a substantial burden of neurological conditions, particularly stroke and neurological infections, for which imaging can be important for diagnosis and management. We place these findings in the context of emerging lower-cost, compact, and mobile magnetic resonance imaging technologies. Such systems may reduce some infrastructure and siting requirements, but limitations related to image quality, maintenance, workforce capacity, and long-term sustainability remain important considerations.
authors: Israa Hissein; Jingting Yao; Foksouna Sakadi; Esias Ka Nanbe Bedingar; Ming Zhao; Andre J. W. van der Kouwe; Jerome L. Ackerman

title: Nociplastic Pain: A Contemporary Narrative Review of Mechanisms, Clinical Assessment, Controversies, and Management
abstract: Background: Nociplastic pain was introduced by the International Association for the Study of Pain (IASP) in 2017 as a third mechanistic descriptor alongside nociceptive and neuropathic pain, denoting pain from altered nociception without unambiguous tissue damage or somatosensory lesion. Fibromyalgia is its prototypical example; nociplastic mechanisms have also been proposed to contribute, often alongside nociceptive or neuropathic components, to irritable bowel syndrome, temporomandibular disorders, chronic primary headache, and much chronic musculoskeletal and visceral pain. Objective and Methods: This narrative review synthesizes evidence published between January 2016 and June 2026 on the mechanisms, clinical assessment, controversies, and management of nociplastic pain, integrating recent (2024-2026) conceptual debates with mechanistic and clinical data. We aimed to clarify the distinctions among central sensitization (a mechanism), nociplastic pain (a clinical-mechanistic descriptor), and chronic primary pain (a diagnosis) in a clinically usable form, to appraise the recent validation evidence for the 2021 IASP clinical criteria, and to identify research priorities for the domains in which those criteria remain unvalidated. Key Findings: The descriptor reflects central sensitization, deficient descending modulation, neuroimmune/glial activation, and maladaptive plasticity, plus increasingly recognized peripheral contributions. The 2021 IASP criteria show acceptable reliability in trained raters but uncertain performance in primary care and non-musculoskeletal domains. Management prioritizes, as first line, exercise, psychological therapy, pain neuroscience education, and multidisciplinary rehabilitation, together with centrally acting agents, although the pharmacological evidence derives largely from fibromyalgia trials; opioids and anti-inflammatory drugs are largely ineffective in predominantly nociplastic pain. Controversies concern the mechanism-versus-diagnosis distinction and the risk that an over-inclusive label obscures occult peripheral pathology. Conclusion: Nociplastic pain is a clinical-mechanistic descriptor, not a diagnosis, and is best applied as a continuous component of complex pain rather than a fixed diagnostic label. Priorities include validation of criteria beyond the musculoskeletal system, objective biomarkers, and phenotype-stratified trials.
authors: Chin‐Chen Chu; Yao-Tsung Lin; Jhi‐Joung Wang

title: Néphrectomies au Centre Hospitalier National de Pikine, Sénégal : indications, techniques chirurgicales et résultats
abstract: Purpose: To describe the indications, surgical approaches, and outcomes of nephrectomies performed at a public urology department in Senegal, in a resource-limited setting. Materials and methods: We conducted a retrospective, descriptive, single-centre study at the Urology Department of Pikine National Hospital Centre (CHNP) in Dakar, Senegal, from January 2013 to December 2023. All adults and children who underwent nephrectomy, regardless of indication or procedure type, were included. Data were collected from medical records and operative logs, including demographics, clinical presentation, imaging, indications, surgical approach and technique, early postoperative course, Clavien- Dindo-graded complications, length of stay, and histopathology. Results: Over 11 years, 36 nephrectomies were performed, representing 2.2% of all urological procedures. We analysed 34 cases. The mean age was 44.7 ± 18 years (range, 12–85), with a female predominance (70.6%, sex ratio 0.4). Flank pain was the main presenting symptom (85.3%). Computed tomography (CT) urography was the key imaging modality in 97.1% of patients. Indications were dominated by solid renal tumours (35.3%) and destroyed nonfunctioning kidneys (35.3%), mostly related to urinary lithiasis. Open surgery via a flank incision was the preferred approach (58.8%). Simple nephrectomy was the most frequent technique (50.0%). The mean hospital stay was 4.7 ± 1.8 days. The overall early complication rate was 11.8% (4/34, 95% confidence interval [CI] ≈ 3 to 28), with one postoperative death (2.9%, 95% CI ≈ 0.07 to 15). Histopathology showed 10 malignant tumours (29.4%), two benign oncocytomas (5.9%), and 13 nontumoural inflammatory lesions (38.2%). Histological results were unavailable in 26.5% of cases due to missing or unretrieved pathology reports. Conclusions: Nephrectomy was performed mainly in young adults for malignant renal tumours and lithiasis-related destroyed kidneys. Open nephrectomy remains the standard approach with seemingly acceptable morbidity and mortality.
authors: JM Randiantsalama; A Sarr; N Bihonda; Babacar Sine; Abdoulaye Ndiath; A Thiam; C Ze Ondo; A K Ndoye

title: Office‐Based Transoral Ultrasonography in the Diagnostic Workup of Oropharyngeal Cancer
abstract: This article demonstrates how to perform and interpret transoral ultrasound of the palatine and lingual tonsils in patients with suspected oropharyngeal cancer. This technique offers a reliable adjunct to conventional assessment but requires substantial operator experience and patient cooperation.
authors: Amalie Hartvig Pall; Martin Garset‐Zamani; Tobias Todsen

title: On Open-Ended Information Seeking for Information Elicitation Agents
abstract: Information elicitation is an open-ended information-seeking problem in which an interaction can unfold in many potentially valuable directions, requiring an elicitor to continually determine which information to pursue as new information emerges. In agentic elicitation, these decisions may be delegated to a foundation model, yet how model choice shapes the resulting information-seeking behavior remains understudied. We study how judgments about information value vary across LLMs and how these differences shape sequential information seeking. We first examine these judgments across 11 LLMs spanning multiple model families and parameter scales, using a shared set of information and elicitation objectives. We then develop a controlled elicitation simulation in which different models encounter the same information space and use the same selection rule, isolating these judgments from question generation and respondent behavior. Using this setting, we characterize the breadth-depth behavior that emerges from model-specific information-seeking preferences over the course of elicitation. We further examine how interaction history changes the evaluation and subsequent selection of prospective information. We test the robustness and boundaries of these findings through sensitivity analyses and ablations over the opportunities available to the elicitor, the response labels used to operationalize information-seeking preferences, the presence of interaction history, and whether redundancy is explicitly relevant to the assessment. The project code, data, and trajectory files are available at https://github.com/infosenselab/open-elicitation.
authors: Victor De Lima; Grace Hui Yang

title: Optimization of Low-Level Laser Therapy via Skin Stiffness Gradient Analysis Using Optical Coherence Tomography
authors: Chien‐Cheng Tai; Gilang Titah Ramadhan; Yih‐Kuen Jan; Ben-Yi Liau; Sheena Christabel Pravin; V. Kiruthika; Winson Chiu-Chun Lee; Congo Tak Shing Ching; Chi-Wen Lung

title: Optimization of copper and tin disulfide based surface plasmon resonance for the detection of brain tumor tissues
abstract: In this study, a surface plasmon resonance (SPR) sensor, including SF5 prism, copper (Cu), Tin Disulfide (SnS2), Molybdenum Ditelluride (MoTe2), and sensing medium (SM) layers, was designed for the detection of brain lesions. With the remarkable sensitivity of 142.15°/RIU found at 33 nm of Cu, 8 nm of SnS2, a monolayer of MoTe2, and refractive index (RI) of SM 1.33–1.50. To obtain the sensitivity of the proposed sensor, different brain lesions, including cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), gray matter, oligodendroglioma, low-grade glioma, lymphoma, and metastasis, were used as SM, while the thickness of the Cu layer was varied from 25 to 60 nm. A sharp SPR dip with a minimum reflectance (Rmin) of 3.9 × 10⁻⁷ a.u. was obtained at a thickness of 33 nm, which also yielded the highest sensitivity (S = 136.47°/RIU) and figure of merit (FoM = 15.01/RIU). The low full width at half maximum (FWHM) at this thickness and the SPR angle shift (Δθres) further confirmed the improved detection capability of the sensor. According to these results, the proposed SPR sensor is very useful for detecting brain abnormalities in real time and without labels.
authors: Rajeev Kumar; Biswajit Brahma; Lalit Garia; Manoj kumar; Akash Kumar Bhoi

title: Order-normalized multi-speed bolt loosening diagnosis under leakage-aware evaluation
abstract: Abstract Discrete multi-speed operation makes bolt-loosening diagnosis difficult because rotation-related spectral components shift with RPM. This study proposes an order-normalized multi-sensor feature representation for 16-case bolt-loosening localization under a leakage-aware temporal evaluation protocol. On a four-bolt vibration dataset measured at 800, 1,000, and 1,200 RPM, the proposed features improve window-level accuracy from 55.3 ± 0.6% to 73.2 ± 0.4%, and record-level aggregation further reaches 87.5%. Feature diagnostics show that order-domain terms provide the main discriminative information, while unseen-speed tests indicate that the method is currently limited to calibrated speed ranges.
authors: Yuqing Liu; Yilong Liu; Huang Huang

title: PASSIVE SMARTPHONE SENSING FOR MENTAL HEALTH MONITORING: A STRUCTURED REVIEW OF BEHAVIORAL BIOMARKERS, PREDICTIVE VALIDITY, AND ETHICAL RISKS
abstract: Methods: This structured review adhered to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) guidelines. Systematic searches were carried out in PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar to identify peer-reviewed articles published between January 2018 and June 2026. Studies met inclusion criteria if they examined passive sensing frameworks (e.g., AWARE, Beiwe, RADAR-Base) collecting GPS, accelerometry, or communication metadata for psychiatric monitoring, resulting in a final sample of 15 core empirical studies. Findings: The evidence shows that changes in spatial mobility, sleep architecture, and communication latency display strong longitudinal correlations with symptom severity scores for major depression (PHQ-9) and generalized anxiety (GAD-7). Machine learning models incorporating multi-modal data streams reached high predictive accuracy (AUC 0.72–0.88) when forecasting depressive shifts and spotting prodromal relapse signatures in bipolar disorder. Even with these advancements, notable translation barriers persist, especially concerning algorithmic generalizability across diverse socioeconomic groups and the ethical threat of "surveillance creep." Conclusion: Passive smartphone sensing offers incredible potential for proactive, continuous psychiatric care. However, actual clinical translation will require strict cross-cultural validation of digital biomarkers alongside the creation of solid data governance frameworks to protect patient autonomy and privacy.
authors: Eliza Zofia Kabat; Krzysztof Konopka; Maciej Kamil Majchrzak; Faustyna Magdalena Kołodziej; Alicja Kwiatkowska; Jakub Juskowiak; Mateusz Lis; Zuzanna Julia Komin; Maryan Liasota; Michalina Justyna Kozłowska
venue: International Journal of Innovative Technologies in Social Science

title: Passive Smartphone-Microphone Phonocardiography for Joint Maternal-Fetal Cardiac Well-Being Monitoring: A Longitudinal Self-Recorded Case Study in Late Pregnancy
abstract: Maternal and perinatal deaths are concentrated in low- and middle-income countries, where routine fetal monitoring is largely inaccessible. With the prevalence of smartphone as personal assistive gadget, we ask whether a phone's built-in microphone, with no extra hardware or emitted signal, can serve as a software-only maternal-fetal cardiac screening aid when moved from the chest to the lower abdomen? We report a longitudinal, self-recorded case study of a single subject (Z) over the last five weeks of a singleton pregnancy, later delivered at term without complications: 28 short, uncontrolled recordings (rest, morning, post-exercise). Lacking maternal/fetal ground truth, we exploit the prior that maternal and fetal heart rates occupy largely disjoint frequency bands, blindly decomposing a Shannon-energy envelope into two candidate-rate bands, and additionally probe a slower breathing-rate band as a rest/exercise discriminator. A fast, regular, fetal-plausible rhythm was recovered from most recordings and remained essentially unchanged across maternal activity states, consistent with normal fetal cardiac autonomy; a slower, noisier maternal-plausible rhythm was recovered less reliably. Beat-to-beat variability proved largely noise-dominated at our short window lengths, and the breathing-rate probe did not significantly separate rest from exercise; both are reported as negative findings. We position the work within AI for global health: a low-cost screening aid for remote and underserved communities, pending reference-validated follow-up, not a replacement for clinical monitoring.
authors: Muhammad Mahboob Ur Rahman

title: Pathwise Information Certificates for Decentralized Adaptive Sensing
abstract: We study decentralized adaptive sensing, where multiple agents choose measurements from evolving local beliefs while exchanging information over a communication graph. We ask whether the measurements actually selected by an adaptive policy have collected enough evidence to distinguish the true target from every plausible alternative. We develop a pathwise certificate based on the Rényi--Chernoff information accumulated along the realized sensing trajectory. It yields nonasymptotic MAP-error bounds and an anytime, network-wide stopping rule for arbitrary history-dependent sensing policies, while separating accumulated statistical information from a bounded network-mixing transient. Linear growth of the information against the least-resolved competitor implies exponential decay of MAP and squared-localization error. A classical pairwise KL converse, specialized to the adaptive decentralized transcript, shows that insufficient information on any pair prevents a positive uniform error exponent, confirming the hardest competitor as a fundamental bottleneck. Across policies, graph topologies, sensor profiles, and seeds, the worst-competitor score correlates more strongly with localization speed than an average-pair proxy in both 1D ($r=0.89$ versus $0.40$) and structured 2D sensing ($r=0.77$ versus $0.48$). Our results provide a practical way to certify and diagnose adaptive multi-agent sensing systems using the evidence they actually collect.
authors: Theodoros Tsiligkaridis

title: Physical-Touch Observability from Wrist Wrench in Granular Scooping
abstract: Mining and earthmoving are important real-world deployment settings for embodied intelligence. Autonomous transport and driving systems have improved substantially, but loading and scooping still often depend on skilled human operators, exposing personnel and equipment to operational risk. For robotic scooping, pre-contact RGB-D sensing reveals surface geometry but not the resistance, compaction, tool engagement, or load transfer that emerge during interaction. We test whether the current scoop's six-axis wrist force/torque (F/T), or wrist wrench, contains information about final collected volume, and whether that information depends on the correctly paired action-terrain interaction. We call this property physical-touch observability. Using 6,700 real-robot scoops across 67 terrains, we evaluate correctly paired current-scoop F/T against pre-contact prediction and correspondence-breaking controls under terrain-held-out testing. At the retrospective 60% sequence boundary, correctly paired F/T reduces mean absolute error by 14.2% relative to Action-only and by 21.9% relative to cross-terrain mismatched F/T. Engineered signal summaries reproduce the result across model architectures. Together, these findings position wrist wrench not merely as a low-level feedback signal, but as a task-level perceptual modality through which embodied robots can infer hidden physical states during interaction, providing a foundation for response-aware autonomy in mining and other contact-rich tasks.
authors: Hongyi Lin; Song Zhang; Xubo Liu; Yang Liu

title: Physiotherapy for Urinary Incontinence After Radical Prostatectomy: Current Evidence and Therapeutic Challenges
abstract: Urinary incontinence remains one of the most frequent and distressing complications after radical prostatectomy and can substantially affect quality of life. Physiotherapy, particularly pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT), is widely used as part of conservative postoperative management; however, substantial variation exists in patient populations, surgical and perioperative factors, intervention protocols, timing of initiation, adjunctive modalities, outcome definitions, and follow-up. This narrative review summarizes current evidence on pelvic floor rehabilitation after radical prostatectomy, focusing on prehabilitation, PFMT, biofeedback, electrical stimulation, neuromodulation, and emerging modalities such as transfer energy capacitive and resistive (TECAR) therapy. PFMT is the most widely studied conservative physiotherapy intervention and may accelerate early recovery of continence in some patients, although its effects on longer-term continence rates are less certain. The role of biofeedback and electrical stimulation remains unclear because of heterogeneous protocols and inconsistent outcome reporting. Evidence for neuromodulation is limited and should be interpreted according to the specific intervention and study population. TECAR therapy currently lacks direct clinical evidence supporting its efficacy in post-prostatectomy urinary incontinence. Across the literature, differences in continence definitions, intervention content and dose, baseline symptom severity, surgical techniques, timing of treatment, and follow-up complicate direct comparison and may confound observed improvements because spontaneous recovery is common after surgery. Current evidence supports PFMT as a reasonable core component of conservative management after radical prostatectomy, particularly for accelerating early continence recovery, whereas long-term superiority and the added value of adjunctive modalities remain uncertain.
authors: Izabela Mastej-Stawarska; Edyta Łuszczki; Maciej Tomasz Kochman

title: Polymer-based biopotential electrode-leadwire prototype for ECG sensing during X-ray and CT examinations
abstract: Introduction: Continuous ECG monitoring during X-ray and CT examinations is crucial for critically ill patients; however, standard Ag/AgCl electrodes and metallic leadwires generate image artifacts that may compromise diagnostic quality. This study aimed to develop and evaluate a non-metallic, radiolucent polymer-based ECG electrode-leadwire system enabling artifact-free ECG sensing during radiological imaging. Materials and Methods: onto cotton and carbon substrates to fabricate dry textile electrodes and carbon-fiber leadwires. The polymer-based electrode-leadwire prototype was compared to standard Ag/AgCl electrodes and metallic leadwires in terms of ECG signal quality and radiolucency. Radiolucency was evaluated using CT and X-ray imaging on phantom models and a veterinary subject, with CT conspicuity quantified by Hounsfield unit attenuation difference |ΔHU|. ECG signal quality was assessed using complementary time-domain metrics, including Pearson correlation, root-mean-square error (RMSE), mean absolute error (MAE), signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and baseline variability, together with the frequency-domain metric magnitude-squared coherence (MSC), under static and simulated CT motion conditions. Results: PPy-coated cotton electrodes demonstrated high agreement with Ag/AgCl references with Pearson correlation coefficients ranging from 0.93 to 0.99 and magnitude-squared coherence values ranging from 0.81 to 0.99 across all tested configurations. Relative R-wave amplitude deviations remained below 13%. PANI-coated carbon-fiber leadwires exhibited low resistance (≈11 Ω/m) and stable signal transmission. CT and X-ray imaging showed complete radiolucency of conductive polymer components, with only faint visibility of auxiliary non-conductive materials under high-contrast CT settings. Simulated CT table motion introduced only minor signal degradation with RMSE values ≤0.05 mV and preserved signal-to-noise ratio and baseline stability within ranges commonly considered acceptable for clinical ECG monitoring. Conclusion: The proposed dry, non-metallic polymer-based ECG prototype provides artifact-free ECG monitoring during X-ray and CT imaging while preserving clinically relevant signal quality. The results demonstrate the feasibility of uninterrupted ECG monitoring during radiological examinations without introducing image artifacts associated with conventional metallic ECG systems.
authors: Marek Penhaker; Jan Polomik; Jan Kijonka; Jaroslav Stejskal; Martin Černý; Dominik Vilímek; Peter Kneppo; Ladislav Janoušek; Ewaryst Tkacz; Jan Kubíček

title: Portable GMR Biosensing with Fe 3 O 4 /PVA-GOx Functionalization and Machine Learning for Quantitative Glucose Detection
abstract: Abstract A portable giant magnetoresistance (GMR) biosensing platform integrating an Fe 3 O 4 /PVA–glucose oxidase (GOx) functional layer, dual-coil magnetic excitation, embedded signal acquisition, and machine-learning-assisted prediction was developed for quantitative glucose sensing. The system exhibited stable concentration-dependent GMR responses over 0.02–0.15 mg mL −1 . Linear Regression (LR) and support vector regression with a radial basis function kernel (SVR-RBF) were evaluated using development-set analysis, leave-one-concentration-out validation, independent external testing, and prepared-saliva samples. On an independent 10-concentration dataset, SVR-RBF achieved R 2 , MAE = 0.0029 mg mL −1 , and RMSE = 0.0040 mg mL −1 , outperforming LR (R 2 , MAE = 0.0048 mg mL −1 , RMSE = 0.0059 mg mL −1 ). In prepared saliva, the fixed SVR-RBF model maintained low prediction errors (MAE = 0.0043 mg mL −1 ; RMSE = 0.0050 mg mL −1 ). These results demonstrate the feasibility of combining magnetic GMR transduction, functional magnetic nanomaterials, and nonlinear regression within a compact platform for quantitative glucose sensing, while further validation in authentic biological samples remains necessary.
authors: W. S. Mada Sanjaya; Hasniah Aliah; Edi Suharyadi; Julia Angel; Vandri Ahmad Isnaini; Dyah Anggraeni; Gilang Pratama Putra Siswanto; Rindra Yusianto; Agung Wijaya Temiesela

title: Posteromedial Knee Capsule Tear Without Concomitant Ligament Rupture or Meniscal Pathology in a Pediatric Athlete
abstract: The posterior knee capsule is a critical structure for tibiofemoral stability, limiting hyperextension, and posterior translation. Injuries to this structure are rare and typically occur alongside anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) or posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) tears. To date, no cases have been reported of a posteromedial capsule tear without concomitant ligamentous rupture or meniscal injury, leaving its clinical significance and optimal management unclear. We report on a 15-year-old male who sustained a hyperextension knee injury while playing basketball, presenting with pain and an abnormal gait. Diagnostic arthroscopy revealed an intact ACL and a full-thickness 3 cm posterior capsule tear, which was repaired arthroscopically. At 6 months postoperative, mild recurvatum persisted. This case parallels ramp lesions, another posteromedial injury with, at times, conflicting management guidelines. This case underscores the need for further research into the diagnosis, management, and long-term outcomes of posterior capsule injuries given that they are poorly understood in isolation due to their frequent association with multi-ligamentous trauma. Future studies should aim to evaluate best practice and determine whether surgical intervention is necessary or if conservative management could yield comparable results.
authors: Arianna Paa; Doyle Ford; Faris Jafri; Kareem Siada; Keith Sims; Micah Lissy

title: Predictive endocrine remodeling and regulatory intelligence: From Nanoremediation to digital–twin toxicology and adaptive environmental governance
abstract: Microplastics and nanoplastics are becoming significant environmental contaminants capable of transporting endocrine–disrupting chemicals, and interact directly with biological systems thereby perturbing hormone receptor signaling and inducing systemic endocrine dysfunction through mechanisms such as oxidative stress, mitochondrial damage, sustained inflammation, and epigenetic modifications. While conventional remediation strategies primarily mitigate environmental contamination and provide limited capacity into how residual particules disrupt endocrine homeostasis across biological systems. Here, we propose an Advanced Predictive Nanotechnological Endocrine Remediation (APN–NER) framework as a conceptual, rather than experimentally validated, paradigm for integrating remediation with predictive endocrine risk assessment. The framework combines 3D–engineered nanomaterials, intelligent remediation platforms, systems endocrinology, multiomics, artificial intelligence, and digital–twin toxicology to connect contaminant capture with mechanistic characterization and endocrine outcome prediction. We critically examine how remediation–generated chemical and biological data could inform computational models of exposure, molecular disruption, and endocrine network responses. APN–NER therefore reframes remediation as both an environmental intervention and a potential source of mechanistic intelligence, providing a proposed pathway toward adaptive, mechanism–informed monitoring and future. However, susbtantial methodological and regulatory validation remains necessary.

title: Preoperative Planning and Risk Stratification
abstract: Complex abdominal wall reconstruction necessitates a meticulous, systematic preoperative evaluation to mitigate high rates of surgical site occurrence and recurrence. This chapter delineates an evidence-based protocol for preoperative optimization, emphasizing that surgical success is predicated on thorough preparation rather than technical prowess alone. Critical components include a comprehensive assessment of patient comorbidities, hernia characteristics, and quantified volumetric analysis via cross-sectional imaging with provocative maneuvers. Formal risk stratification, utilizing validated tools such as the Ventral Hernia Working Group grading scale, is imperative to objectively categorize patient risk and guide therapeutic decisions. A paramount focus is placed on the modification of risk factors—including tobacco use, obesity, hyperglycemia, and malnutrition—through structured interventions. This advocates for a multidisciplinary approach to optimize patient physiology prior to intervention. This rigorous preoperative paradigm enables the surgeon to rationally select the appropriate surgical technique, prosthetic material, and need for adjunct procedures, thereby individualizing care to improve postoperative outcomes.

title: Printable inks for flexible healthcare sensors: From materials to device insights
abstract: Printable inks have been widely used in wearable healthcare sensors, and their functions go beyond simply creating conductive or sensing layers. Ink formulation controls printability, film formation, electrical path creation, adhesion to flexible substrates and stability of the process under mechanical strain such as bending and stretching. This review highlights recent advances in printable inks used in wearable healthcare sensing devices including metal-based, carbon-based, polymeric, and biofunctional ink systems. Their merits as well as limitations including high curing temperature, poor dispersion stability, limited conductivity, poor substrate adhesion, and difficulty of biological functionalization will be discussed. This review focuses mostly on the relationship between ink formulation, rheology, printing, printed microstructure, and sensor performance. The existing research usually studies them separately, therefore, making it difficult for comparison between different ink systems and prediction of the performance of devices in real-life situations. Rheology has been studied usually only as a limitation in printing process although it affects pattern resolution, film homogeneity, formation of conductive paths, and repeatability. The commonly used printing methods, particularly inkjet, screen printing, and flexographic printing, are also compared in terms of resolution, material compatibility, throughput, and scalability. Although wearable healthcare sensors have developed considerably, several challenges still limit their use beyond laboratory demonstrations. These include material-related limitations, poor long-term stability, mechanical degradation, biofouling, and reduction in sensor performance over time. Overall, this review highlights the importance of understanding the process-structure-performance relationships of printable inks for developing reliable, scalable, and real-time wearable sensors.

title: Proton Signaling Biology From Ancient Bioenergetics to Neural Communication: An Exploration of Keratan Sulfate as a Potential Proton-Modulatory Molecule
abstract: This mini review examines the potential roles of proton signaling in the peripheral and central nervous systems and its proposed regulation by keratan sulfate (KS). Protons are central to bioenergetics and rapid chemical signaling, linking metabolism to membrane excitability and receptor activity across tissues. Nanoscale-to-microscale pH transients may add a further layer of intercellular communication in the nervous system through proton-sensitive ion channels and receptors. Extracellular matrix glycosaminoglycans may influence this signaling by buffering and transporting protons. Keratan sulfate has an unusually high capacity to bind and conduct protons. Evidence from electrolocation biology, proton-conductive biomaterials, and brain proton sensors suggests that keratan sulfate may act as a local proton reservoir and shuttle within defined microenvironments, thereby shaping pH-dependent neuromodulatory processes in health and disease. KS-substituted proteoglycans have the potential to act as neuron modulatory molecules mediating effects on cellular metabolism. KS shows considerable promise as a neuromodulatory molecule. Further electrophysiological studies are warranted using KS knockout animal models to test this hypothesis and validate the proposed role of KS as a potential regulatory neural interface molecule.
authors: James Melrose

title: PsyCIDRA: A Dual-Agent Framework for Psychiatric Interviewing and Diagnostic Reasoning
abstract: Large language models show promise in clinical reasoning, but psychiatric interviewing requires guiding an evolving conversation. Their ability to carry out this interactive assessment remains less studied. We present PsyCIDRA, a dual-agent framework linking free-form psychiatric interviewing with diagnostic reasoning for expert review. Its interviewer agent uses tools to maintain working notes, load expert-written skills, and retrieve ICD-11 references to guide inquiry. Its diagnostic reasoning agent then receives the completed interview transcript and reports hypotheses alongside supporting, conflicting, and missing evidence, withholding a final hypothesis when none is sufficiently supported. Using patient profiles generated with PsyCPG, we first evaluate PsyCIDRA in simulation. Across four models on 53 evaluation cases, it achieves higher diagnostic agreement than direct prompting. On 81 held-out simulated cases, rank-1 accuracy is 60.5% versus 51.9%. In a blinded study of 101 human participants in separate arms, PsyCIDRA agrees with psychologists on whether to propose a diagnostic hypothesis in 79.6% of cases, compared with 65.4% for direct prompting. Together, these findings support the potential of LLM agents to assist psychiatric assessment through free-form dialogue. By examining diagnostic reasoning, interview quality, and safety together, this study contributes to understanding the capabilities and limitations of psychiatric interview agents.
authors: Milad Mohammadi; Fatemeh Akrami Shamsabadi; Zahra Mohseni; AmirHossein Safdarian; Malekfarhad Malek; Hadi Moradi; Hesham Faili

title: Pulmonary nodules: classification, biomarkers, signaling pathways, diseases, early diagnosis and management
abstract: Pulmonary nodules are increasingly detected by thoracic imaging and low-dose computed tomography-based lung cancer screening, but most are benign, transient, or indolent. Clinically, the key task is to distinguish nodules that require timely cancer-directed evaluation from those that can be safely observed. This review summarizes the classification, disease spectrum, risk assessment, early diagnosis, biomarkers, signaling mechanisms, translational models, and management of pulmonary nodules. We first distinguish imaging phenotypes and disease entities, then differentiate the individual-level models used to select candidates for lung cancer screening from the nodule-level models and structured reporting systems used after nodule detection. Low-dose computed tomography remains the foundation of screening and surveillance approaches, whereas magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography combined with computed tomography, contrast-enhanced computed tomography, nonsurgical biopsy, surgical diagnosis, and local therapies play more selective roles depending on the probability of malignancy and patient fitness. Noninvasive biomarkers, including circulating cellular, nucleic acid, methylation, protein, autoantibody, extracellular vesicle, and metabolic analytes, are most likely to serve as adjuncts to imaging and clinical risk assessment rather than as stand-alone diagnostic tests. Artificial intelligence may support detection, workflow efficiency, malignancy risk reclassification, invasiveness assessment, and multimodal integration, but its value depends on external validation, calibration, implementation, and prospective evidence of management benefit. Mechanistic studies of adenocarcinoma spectrum subsolid nodules have implicated the involvement of early oncogenic signaling, genomic instability, immune escape, stromal and vascular remodeling, and adaptive survival pathways. Translational models can support mechanistic and procedural research, but do not replicate real-world nodule management in patients. Overall, care for pulmonary nodules should be risk-adapted, longitudinal, multidisciplinary, and patient-centered.

title: Rare Groin Hernias With Unusual Sac Contents: A Systematic Review of Anatomical Variants and Surgical Implications
abstract: Groin hernias are commonly encountered in general surgical practice. Most of these hernias have a typical anatomical structure and contain the usual type of hernia sac content. Still, in some rare cases, a hernia may show abnormal anatomy or contain unexpected material within the sac, which can affect both how it presents clinically and the surgical approach needed for treatment. This systematic review seeks to give an overview of rare groin hernias with unusual sac contents, detail their anatomical variations, describe their clinical features and diagnostic difficulties, and discuss the implications that may come up during surgical management. A systematic review with qualitative synthesis was performed according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. The search was carried out in PubMed/Medical Literature Analysis and Retrieval System Online (MEDLINE) and included studies on rare inguinal and femoral hernias in adult patients. A focused supplementary search was also performed for hernias containing Meckel's diverticulum. Studies were considered eligible when they described unusual hernia sac contents or relevant anatomical variations. Pediatric studies, review articles without original data, retracted publications, studies unrelated to inguinal or femoral hernias, and studies without a clear description of sac contents were excluded. In total, 43 studies were included in the final qualitative synthesis. Several uncommon inguinal and femoral hernias containing unexpected sac contents were found. The documented contents included the vermiform appendix, Meckel's diverticulum, segments of the colon, the urinary bladder, and bowel that became trapped after reduction. The main types described were Amyand hernia, De Garengeot hernia, Littré hernia, sliding inguinal hernia, and reduction en masse. Diagnosing these conditions before surgery was often challenging, since many cases looked like typical incarcerated or strangulated groin hernias. CT scans or ultrasonography were helpful in certain cases, but the diagnosis was usually established during the operation. The surgical approach depended on the sac's contents, the presence of inflammation or contamination, the viability of the bowel, and whether any organs were involved. Inguinal and femoral hernias that contain unusual sac contents are uncommon, but the cases reviewed indicate that they can influence both diagnosis and surgical management. The hernia sac might hold the appendix, Meckel's diverticulum, colon, urinary bladder, or bowel that becomes trapped after what appears to be a reduction. Since the clinical symptoms frequently mimic those of a typical incarcerated or strangulated groin hernia, making a preoperative diagnosis is challenging, and many of these cases are only identified during surgery. The surgical approach should be tailored to the specific sac contents, the presence of inflammation or contamination, the viability of the bowel, whether the bladder or colon is involved, and the overall condition of the patient. As most of the available evidence comes from case reports and small case series, it is not possible to make strong treatment recommendations, and there is a need for more consistent reporting.
authors: Christos-Pavlos Filippou; Dimosthenis Chrysikos; Theodore G. Troupis; Dimitrios K Filippou

title: Real-time environmental understanding through active classification using tactile sensing in robotic disassembly
abstract: This paper proposes a generalized active classification framework designed to classify the environment of a robot through controlled tactile interaction, with direct application to robotic disassembly of Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment (WEEE). In this domain, purely vision-based systems frequently fail due to occlusions, dust, and reflective surfaces, making haptic identification an operational necessity. By formulating environment identification as an active sensing problem, we utilize the entropy of learned interaction models and a receding-horizon optimization to select control inputs that maximize information gain from force–torque feedback. Our approach transitions from a passive classifier to an active framework that dynamically probes the environment to resolve belief uncertainty across six distinct tactile classes, demonstrated through the high-precision detection and unfastening of screws using an industrial 6-DOF robotic arm. Experimental results on a consumer microwave demonstrate that the active framework achieves a 51% reduction in detection latency for screws compared to passive baselines and consistently outperforms expert-designed heuristics. Furthermore, the system exhibits robust zero-shot generalization to novel industrial objects, indicating that learned tactile signatures are invariant to the global object context. These results provide a scalable foundation for autonomous disassembly in high-variance environments like electronic waste recycling, while offering a broader methodology for any robotic classification task where control can be leveraged to accelerate information gain.
authors: Annalena Daniels; Théo Karst; Samuel Tovey; Dirk Wollherr

title: Reframing the lived experience of persistent dizziness: insights from active inference
abstract: We present an active inference account of persistent dizziness predicated on models of enactivism and ecological psychology; including first-hand accounts of the patient’s lived experience. Mechanistically, we consider persistent dizziness to reflect an initial failure of sensory attenuation of vestibular and other sensory prediction errors. This failure becomes self-maintaining if the patient infers—or learns—that unattenuated prediction errors cannot be resolved through action. The ensuing formulation provides an integrative account of the pathophysiology of dizziness and how it underwrites—and is maintained by—affective inference and an altered sense of agency that shapes the experience of the person with dizziness. We foreground the holistic person-centered approach on offer from a clinical perspective, and consider complementary levels of therapeutic intervention under this theoretical framework.
authors: Marc A. Broberg; Mick Thacker; Karl John Friston; Jorge Eduardo Esteves

title: Relationship Quality Among Married Indian Couples: A Narrative Review
abstract: Background: Indian marriages have traditionally been understood as fulfilling religious commitments, forming alliances between families and fostering companionship between spouses. However, relationship quality in such marriages is shaped by structural and cultural factors that Western models of marriage, which consider only the dyadic relationship, do not account for. This narrative review examines relationship quality among married Indian couples across three themes: caste and joint-family structure; communication and conflict; and intimacy, identity and sexual satisfaction, to understand how relationship quality is shaped beyond the couple. Summary: The review draws on attachment theory, social exchange theory and family systems theory, as well as on indigenous Indian thought and the feminist bargaining-power framework of Sen and Agarwal, alongside broader cultural and philosophical perspectives. It considers how structure and individual agency combine in the process of Indian marriage, drawing on narrative, empirical, theoretical, economic and philosophical sources, as well as Indian legal decisions. Caste and kinship structure a wife's bargaining power and household authority before dyadic interactions occur; communication and conflict are shaped by joint-family privacy rather than the dyad alone; and emotional intimacy and identity shape relationship quality, while sexual satisfaction remains comparatively unexplored in the Indian context. The review proposes two original theoretical constructs, active endurance, which extends Das's notion of endurance, and the aspiration-structure gap, to capture patterns evident in the literature but not yet formally theorised. It also notes neurobiological evidence, namely hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis dysregulation in chronic marital distress and oxytocin's modulation of couple conflict, which warrants investigation in Indian samples. Key Message: Therapy and policy addressing relationship quality in Indian marriages need to account for structural barriers, such as caste and household bargaining power, rather than focusing only on communication skills and attitudes, if they are to meaningfully improve relationship quality in this context.
authors: Akanksha Mendiratta; Pankaj Singh; Navin Kumar

title: Remote sensing of hydrothermal alteration in active volcanic environments: A critical review and integrated analysis of Lastarria volcano
abstract: Hydrothermal alteration is a key process in active volcanic systems, influencing edifice stability, fluid circulation, degassing pathways, and volcanic hazards. Remote sensing is widely used to map hydrothermal alteration; however, many approaches treat alteration-related surfaces as static targets, so their reliability, transferability, and process significance in active volcanic environments remain insufficiently evaluated. This study synthesizes commonly used remote sensing approaches and examines the behavior and interpretive implications of representative outputs at Lastarria volcano, which is an arid, high-altitude, vegetation-free system with active fumarolic fields. We compare visual interpretation, VNIR-SWIR reflectance products, pixel-based and sub-pixel mapping outputs, UAV thermal infrared observations, and LiDAR-derived surface-state information. The results show that visual interpretation, reflectance-based products, and pixel-based or sub-pixel outputs delineate broad alteration-related patterns, but their extent, internal structure, and interpretive meaning vary with methodological choices, surface mixing, and environmental surface states. Thermal infrared observations constrain apparent surface-temperature anomalies and fumarole-proximal activity, whereas LiDAR-derived products provide complementary information on surface state, morphology, and roughness. These observations do not converge on a single alteration representation; instead, they capture different aspects of the volcanic-hydrothermal system. Environmental, climatic, and surface controls, including exposure state, moisture, surface reworking, and seasonality, further limit direct transferability among volcanic settings. We suggest that remote sensing of hydrothermal alteration in active volcanic environments should move from deterministic mapping toward process-oriented and uncertainty-aware interpretation, with temporal persistence, spatial coherence, process plausibility, and independent support providing a basis for future multi-temporal analysis and monitoring.
authors: Ge Gao; Thomas R. Walter; Samuel T. Thiele

title: Research on UWB radar human posture recognition in complex disaster environments based on active sensing closed-loop feedback
abstract: Complex disaster rescue scenarios—such as mine accidents, earthquakes, fire sites, and explosion scenes—are often characterized by severe challenges, including multipath reflections, strong background noise, and nonlinear signal interference. These factors significantly compromise the accuracy and stability of traditional Ultra-Wideband (UWB) radar posture recognition systems, making them inadequate for practical rescue requirements. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a UWB radar anti-interference posture recognition method based on active perception theory. We construct a mathematical model for an active perception closed-loop feedback system. By calculating the energy entropy of echo signals and recognition confidence in real time, the system estimates the interference level of the current environment and the uncertainty of posture estimation. Simulation and experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method exhibits significant robustness against interference in complex scenarios involving multipath reflections, noise, and nonlinear disturbances. This study provides effective technical support for the rapid localization and posture determination of trapped victims in disaster rescue operations.

title: Residual governance for responsible embodied AI: authority, contestability, and cognitive sovereignty
abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) ethics increasingly concerns systems that do not merely recommend but intervene: clinical decision support, human–machine teaming, robotics and automated handover protocols can shift timing, attention and authority under uncertainty. This article argues that responsible embodied AI requires residual governance: an explicit account of which approximation errors remain, which are safe to tolerate and who may act on them. The paper develops two linked concepts. A residual ledger records action-relevant remainders across physical, causal, human-state, latency, transfer and energy dimensions. An authority ledger records who converts residual evidence into intervention, on what basis, with what uncertainty and with what opportunity for contestation. This framework extends familiar themes in bounded rationality, active inference and safe reinforcement learning by treating authority, contestability and oversight cost as first-class ethical variables rather than external governance add-ons. It uses physical AI, physiological computing and human-AI handover as pressure cases, and proposes evaluation through action calibration, dual-task interference and auditable authority transitions. The central claim is that cognitive sovereignty is preserved not by eliminating all algorithmic influence, but by making influence accountable, contestable and reversible when AI systems act under approximation.
authors: Chia‐Wei Sun

title: Resistance to technological innovation: the case of teleconsultation before and during COVID-19
abstract: Purpose This study analyzes resistance to technological innovation in the healthcare field, focusing on the formal, long-term adoption of teleconsultation in medical practice, which became established during the COVID-19 pandemic. Different institutional studies on resistance to change were analyzed to evaluate their capacity to explain the phenomenon. Design/methodology/approach Qualitative interpretive research was conducted involving documentary research and interviews with professionals from public and private domains, including health regulation organizations and individual practitioners, to capture their understandings of the issue. Findings The results showed that the primary hindering factors were the need for physical examination, the risk of deteriorating remuneration conditions for doctors, and insufficient undergraduate training in telemedicine. Research limitations/implications Thus, the study infers that institutional logics of the same order can coexist, accommodating contradictions between them. Medical autonomy, a principle of democratic logic upheld by part of the professional community and the imperative of public health emergencies, characteristic of professional logic, provoked a rapid response, constituting the driving pressures for the adoption of teleconsultation. Originality/value Technological innovation tends to face resistance during implementation, but under favorable conditions, it becomes consolidated alongside the previous practice. Traditional professional logic resisted the introduction of the new logic represented by teleconsultation until confronted by the pandemic, when it was compelled to adapt to the circumstances.
authors: Hosana Rodrigues; Arnaldo Luiz Ryngelblum; Ernesto Michelângelo Giglio

title: Robotic Splenectomy for Refractory Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura
abstract: Splenectomy is a well-established surgical option for selected patients with immune thrombocytopenic purpura and persistent thrombocytopenia despite medical therapy. Although laparoscopic splenectomy remains the standard minimally invasive approach, robotic platforms may offer advantages in technically challenging cases. We present a 40-year-old woman with a 4-year history of immune thrombocytopenic purpura, obesity, Hashimoto thyroiditis, and prior sleeve gastrectomy presented with severe thrombocytopenia and abnormal uterine bleeding. After failure of medical therapy, she underwent robotic splenectomy with the da Vinci Xi robotic platform using an anterior approach. Operative time was 240 minutes, and estimated blood loss was 200 mL. The postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient was discharged on postoperative day 3. Pathologic examination findings were compatible with immune thrombocytopenic purpura. Robotic splenectomy is safe and feasible in this selected challenging case and may be considered an alternative minimally invasive approach when enhanced visualization and precise hilar dissection are desirable.

title: STRANGULATED OBTURATOR HERNIA WITH INTESTINAL PERFORATION IN A NONAGENARIAN: A CASE REPORT
abstract: Background: Obturator hernia is a rare pelvic hernia, accounting for less than 1% of abdominal wall hernias, and predominantly affects frail, elderly, multiparous women. Its insidious clinical presentation and high rate of strangulation make imaging, particularly computed tomography (CT) , central to timely diagnosis. Case Presentation: We report the case of a 95-year-old woman with a four-day history of small bowel obstruction and left inner thigh pain, with a positive Howship-Romberg sign. Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis (14,000/mm³) and elevated C-reactive protein (100 mg/L). Imaging Findings: Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated dilated small bowel loops (up to 42 mm) with an abrupt transition point at the left obturator foramen, where a loop of bowel was incarcerated between the pectineus and obturator externus muscles, medial to the femoral vessels, through a narrow neck, findings diagnostic of a strangulated left obturator hernia. No CT sign of bowel ischemia (mural thickening, reduced enhancement, fat stranding, pneumatosis or free fluid) was identified. Management and Outcome: Emergency laparotomy revealed an 8-cm segment of necrotic small bowel with a 1-cm perforation, despite the reassuring CT appearance, illustrating the limits of CT for predicting bowel viability. Segmental resection with primary manual anastomosis and hernia repair using a round ligament flap were performed. The postoperative course was complicated by a superficial surgical site infection and a fixed evisceration, both managed conservatively, with a favorable overall outcome. Conclusion: CT is the imaging modality of choice for suspected obturator hernia, offering excellent sensitivity for hernia detection and anatomical characterization. However, its ability to predict bowel viability remains imperfect, and a reassuring CT should not delay surgical exploration in a symptomatic elderly patient with biological signs of inflammation.

title: Second‐line MRI after expert transvaginal ultrasound in selected patients with suspected complex deep endometriosis: A prospective cohort study
abstract: Abstract Introduction The objective of this study was to evaluate the added diagnostic yield of second‐line magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) after expert transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) for preoperative mapping of deep endometriosis (DE). Material and Methods In this prospective observational cohort study, women with suspected DE scheduled for surgery after expert ultrasound were included. TVS was performed according to the International Deep Endometriosis Analysis (IDEA) protocol. MRI was selectively performed as a second‐line investigation in patients with suspected advanced disease, inconclusive TVS, or advanced symptoms despite negative TVS findings. Surgical visualization served as the primary reference standard, with histopathology used as a secondary reference standard when available. Diagnostic performance (sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, likelihood ratios, and Cohen's κ ) was assessed for TVS, MRI, and their combination, and stratified by prior surgical status. For the combined approach, a positive result was defined as a positive finding on either modality (TVS or MRI), representing a rule‐out strategy. Results Among 221 women with suspected deep endometriosis, 189 underwent surgery, of whom 112 had both TVS and MRI; 55 had previous abdominal surgery. Combined imaging improved sensitivity for rectosigmoid DE (+10.3%; +6 true positives (TP), +3 false positives (FP)) and uterosacral ligament involvement (+29.2%; +14 TP, +12 FP) but reduced specificity for endometriomas (−19.0%; true negatives (TN) 18 to 14), obliteration of the pouch of Douglas (−13.3%; TN 14 to 8), and uterosacral ligaments (−20.3%; TN 35 to 23). Most lesions missed by TVS were in the mid or upper rectum. Accuracy for the urinary bladder and ureters decreased with the addition of MRI (82.2% to 75.7%). Sensitivity for rectosigmoid lesions was higher with the combined method (TVS + MRI) in women with prior surgery. Conclusions Among selected complex patients undergoing second‐line MRI after expert TVS, combined imaging increased detection of rectosigmoid and uterosacral ligament lesions, but at the cost of reduced specificity. The sensitivity for rectosigmoid disease was greatest among patients with prior abdominal surgery, although this subgroup finding should be considered exploratory. These findings are consistent with a selective rather than routine role for MRI after expert TVS.

title: Seeing the patient: professional vision in clinical ward rounds (and beyond)
abstract: Clinical ward rounds are complex, high‑stakes encounters in which physicians must integrate clinical reasoning, team coordination, and patient‑centred communication. While ward rounds are routinely described as occasions on which physicians "see" their patients, ironically, the visual dimension of ward round communication has rarely been examined conceptually. In this paper, we argue that communication during ward rounds and other complex clinical encounters crucially relies on physicians' professional vision: learned, task-specific ways of noticing, interpreting, and using visual information in socially and institutionally structured contexts. Drawing on research from medical education, cognitive psychology, and interaction research, we conceptualize professional vision enacted during ward rounds as encompassing two interrelated aspects: a cognitive aspect (noticing and knowledge‑based reasoning) and an embodied and interactional aspect (the coordination of gaze, body, and talk). We show how these aspects unfold across different phases of ward rounds and enable physicians to align information retrieval, decision‑making, teamwork, and patient engagement. By explicating professional vision as a central yet previously under-theorized resource in clinical practice, exemplified here through ward-round communication, this paper offers a conceptual foundation for future empirical research and suggests new directions for simulation‑based and professional vision‑focused instructional approaches in medical education.

title: Seminal bradykinin, fetuin-a, pentraxin-3, and adipolin levels in infertile men with varicocele and varicocelectomy: a cross-sectional case–control study
abstract: Abstract Varicocele is characterized by abnormal dilatation of the pampiniform plexus accompanied by venous reflux and is one of the leading correctable causes of male infertility. Although several mechanisms have been proposed, the molecular pathways underlying varicocele-induced testicular dysfunction remain incompletely understood. This study aimed to investigate seminal bradykinin, fetuin-A, pentraxin-3, and adipolin levels in infertile men with varicocele and to compare these biomarkers among patients with varicocele, patients who had undergone varicocelectomy, and controls. This cross-sectional case-control study included 90 participants: 30 infertile men with clinical varicocele, 30 patients who had undergone varicocelectomy and 30 healthy controls. Seminal bradykinin, fetuin-A, pentraxin-3, and adipolin concentrations were determined using ELISA. Sperm concentration, rapid progressive, non-progressive, and immotile sperm percentages, together with bradykinin, fetuin-A, and pentraxin-3 levels, differed significantly among the study groups. Fetuin-A and pentraxin-3 levels were significantly elevated in the varicocele group compared with healthy controls. Patients assessed approximately 3 months after varicocelectomy exhibited significantly higher bradykinin, fetuin-A, and pentraxin-3 levels than controls. No significant differences were observed among the groups regarding age, height, body weight, body mass index, abstinence duration, semen volume, slow progressive sperm percentage, or Adipolin levels. Our findings indicate that patients with varicocele and patients assessed after varicocelectomy exhibit differences in inflammatory and cellular stress-related biomarkers compared with healthy controls. The higher levels of bradykinin, fetuin-A, and pentraxin-3 observed in patients assessed after varicocelectomy may reflect differences in inflammatory and cellular stress-related profiles between the study groups; however, the cross-sectional design does not allow these findings to be interpreted as postoperative persistence or treatment-related changes. These biomarkers may provide complementary information regarding inflammatory and cellular stress-related profiles in varicocele; however, their clinical significance and utility for monitoring postoperative changes require confirmation in larger prospective longitudinal studies.

title: Skene’s Gland Malignancy from Imaging Diagnosis to Management: A Narrative Review
abstract: Background/Objectives: Skene’s gland malignancies are extremely rare tumors of the female paraurethral region, known almost exclusively from case reports and small case series. Their diagnosis is often delayed because symptoms are nonspecific and may mimic benign periurethral disorders, urethral diverticula, primary urethral carcinoma or anterior vaginal wall tumors. This narrative review focuses on the role of imaging, particularly pelvic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), in the diagnosis, differential diagnosis, staging and treatment planning of Skene’s gland malignancies, distinguishing evidence from confirmed Skene’s gland cases from evidence extrapolated from female urethral carcinoma. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus and Web of Science were searched on 27 September 2026 (publication years 2015–2026) and supplemented by reference-list screening; an explicit case definition was applied. Results: Of 191 records (93 after de-duplication), 17 reports of Skene’s gland malignancy were included (15 case reports or series and 2 systematic reviews); fewer than thirty cases have been published overall. Patients were mostly postmenopausal (median age about 70 years, range 45–91), presenting with an asymptomatic periurethral nodule, hematuria or vaginal bleeding, or lower urinary tract symptoms; no uniform staging system has been applied. Most tumors were prostatic-type adenocarcinomas treated by local excision alone; radiotherapy, chemotherapy or androgen deprivation were used mainly for nodal, metastatic or recurrent disease. After examination, ultrasonography can detect and characterize a paraurethral mass, whereas MRI best defines tumor epicenter, urethral, periurethral and anterior vaginal wall involvement and regional spread, and should precede cystourethroscopy and biopsy; CT and PET/CT are complementary for systemic staging. No single immunohistochemical marker establishes Skene’s gland origin. Conclusions: MRI is central to localizing and staging suspected Skene’s gland malignancy and thus to guiding biopsy and the choice between local excision and radical surgery, but most imaging recommendations are extrapolated from female urethral carcinoma and require validation in pooled multicenter data.

title: Smooth total variation regularization for interference detection and elimination (STRIDE) for MRI
abstract: Abstract Objective. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is increasingly required to operate near electronic devices that emit dynamic electromagnetic interference (EMI). Existing reference-channel EMI removal methods estimate a transfer function between EMI sensors and imaging coils from the measured data alone, and do not use prior knowledge about the structure of MR images. We develop and validate an EMI removal method that uses the inherent spatial smoothness of MR images as an additional prior, demonstrated on a head-only 0.5 T scanner. Approach. Smooth total variation regularization for interference detection and elimination (STRIDE) operates in the image domain. For each image column, EMI sensor data are combined and subtracted from the imaging coil data such that the L 2 norm of the total variation (TV) along the readout direction is minimized. This exploits the smoothness of MR images, a property well-known in compressed sensing but not previously used in EMI removal. STRIDE was evaluated on phantom and in-vivo brain datasets under EMI scenarios replicating sources encountered at our affiliated hospitals, and compared against two implementations of External Dynamic Interference Estimation and Removal (EDITER). Main results. STRIDE produced visually better EMI removal and generally higher temporal signal-to-noise ratio than both EDITER implementations, with comparable EMI removal percentage. STRIDE also resulted in lower or equal root-mean-square error than both EDITER implementations in all 8 phantom EMI conditions tested. These results held across both phantom and in-vivo datasets. Significance. STRIDE shows that incorporating known properties of MR images into the EMI removal problem provides meaningful improvements over methods that rely on measured data alone. The approach is deterministic, training-free, sequence-independent, and compatible with existing EMI sensor hardware. STRIDE therefore extends reference-channel EMI removal to scenarios where existing methods fail, particularly point-of-care and interventional MRI outside fully shielded environments, providing a deterministic, training-free alternative to machine-learning approaches.

title: Spatially Configurable Conformal Sensor Integration on an Ultra‐Fine Metallic Needle for Minimally Invasive Deep‐Tissue Oxygen Monitoring
abstract: ABSTRACT Precise, real‐time biochemical measurement within deep biological tissue remains limited by the challenge of integrating mechanically robust sensing architectures into minimally invasive needle platforms. Here, we report a multi‐point oxygen‐sensing ultra‐fine clinical needle (MO‐UFN, 30‐gauge, approximately 0.3 mm in diameter), fabricated by conformally integrating a microscale flexible thin‐film electrochemical oxygen sensor array onto a clinical needle. The device provides lithographically defined sensing and insulating regions along the needle surface while preserving the ultra‐small needle diameter. Five‐site oxygen sensing was demonstrated through electrochemical characterization in solution and time‐resolved measurement in a hypoxia‐mimicking hydrogel phantom. Ex vivo insertion testing and short‐term in vitro cytocompatibility assessment further supported the mechanical and biological feasibility of the platform under the tested conditions. This work establishes a spatially configurable needle‐based sensing architecture for minimally invasive biochemical monitoring in heterogeneous deep‐tissue environments.

title: Supraventricular Tachycardia Associated with Cardiac Hemangioma on the Anterior Mitral Valve Leaflet: A Case Report
abstract: Background: Cardiac hemangiomas are exceedingly rare benign vascular tumors, representing <2% of primary cardiac tumors. Case Presentation: A 65-year-old female patient with a history of palpitations, hypothyroidism, and hypoparathyroidism presented with an acute onset of palpitations and dyspnea. On physical examination, the patient had regular tachycardia with clear and equal bilateral air entry. Initial laboratory tests and chest X-ray showed no acute abnormalities. An electrocardiogram (ECG) showed narrow-complex supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) with a heart rate of 170 bpm and a QRS duration of 80 ms, consistent with atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT), which was unresponsive to vagal maneuvers but was successfully converted with 6 mg of intravenous adenosine. Multimodality imaging, including transthoracic echocardiography (TTE), transesophageal echocardiography (TEE), and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR), was performed. TTE showed a fixed, normoechoic mass (1-1.2 cm) at the aortomitral junction involving the A2 segment of the anterior mitral leaflet; TEE described a nonobstructive heterogeneous echodensity (17 × 6 mm) at the leaflet base near the intervalvular fibrosa; CMR showed a 13 × 11 mm arched structure on the anterior mitral leaflet, beneath the aortic valve, with cavity-like perfusion, T2 hyperintensity, and late gadolinium enhancement. Surgical resection was performed 3 weeks after the diagnosis, and histopathology showed a remodeled remnant hemangioma. Postoperatively, continuous telemetry and long-term clinical and serial ECG follow-up confirmed complete resolution of the arrhythmia without tumor recurrence. Conclusion: We report a cardiac hemangioma on the left atrial side of the anterior mitral leaflet, extending slightly into the left atrial cavity without obstructing blood flow, in a patient with episodes of supraventricular tachycardia. She recovered well after tumor resection, with no clinical signs of arrhythmia recurrence.
