title: Factors influencing the intention to use smart wristbands among patients with COPD: an extended UTAUT model
abstract: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) imposes a substantial global health burden. Despite the considerable potential of wearable devices for early detection and disease management, suboptimal engagement limits their clinical utility. This study aims to identify factors associated with the intention to use smart wristbands among patients with COPD. The study extends the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) by incorporating health risk perception and interface presentation. A sequential mixed-methods design was employed, commencing with semi-structured interviews ( n = 28), followed by a questionnaire survey ( n = 233). Structural equation modeling was used to validate the measurement model and examine the hypothesized relationships. All six constructs demonstrated statistically significant positive associations with intention to use ( P < 0.05). Health risk perception (β = 0.272, P < 0.001) and social influence (β = 0.271, P < 0.001) were the primary correlates of intention to use. This study extends UTAUT by identifying factors correlated with COPD patients’ intention to use smart wristbands. The findings offer practical insights for user-oriented device design and intervention strategies, thereby supporting the promotion of digital health monitoring among COPD patients.
authors: Jingyi Ye; Jianhua Chen; Mi Yao; Guanning Jing; Wenping Li; Yujing Su; Hongjing Pei; Jiapei Xu; Chunhua Chi

title: Faradaically Resilient Triphase Wedge‐Shaped Nanowire Arrays for Robust Bioanalysis
abstract: ABSTRACT Gas‐containing triphase interfaces are attractive for oxygen‐mediated electrochemical systems, yet faradaic stress‐induced electrowetting remains unresolved in triphase biointerfaces. This work presents faradaically resilient wedge‐shaped copper nanowire arrays (W‐CuNWAs) that stabilize oxygen‐enriched triphase interfaces during sustained and repeated electrochemical operations. In contrast with conventional passive liquid‐repellent nanostructures, W‐CuNWAs employ co‐programmed structural–wettability anisotropy to reconcile wettable charge‐transfer regions with gas‐retaining regions within a single nanoarchitecture. Compared to cylindrical CuNWAs, W‐CuNWAs introduce shape‐encoded wetting barriers that increase capillary breakthrough pressure by 2.85‐fold and pin the contact line at the upper edge. Across 3 h of continuous bias, 500 potential cycles, repeated impedance perturbations, and cathodic electrodeposition of a high‐surface‐energy co‐catalyst, W‐CuNWAs retain stable wettability and electrochemical responses with only 0.88 kΩ mass‐transport‐resistance drift, whereas cylindrical counterparts undergo electrolyte infiltration and structural failure. The retained atmosphere‐connected gas phase enables Pt/W‐CuNWAs to achieve 1.65‐fold higher oxygen‐reduction current, 8.96‐fold lower oxygen mass‐transfer resistance, and 2.96‐fold faster current stabilization than cylindrical counterparts. Integration with an FeOOH/BiVO 4 photoanode enables near‐drift‐free, unbiased photoelectrochemical operation over 8.42 h of repeated cathodic cycling, and reliable detection of Alzheimer's neurofilament light chain in clinical plasma. This work establishes shape‐encoded faradaic electrowetting resistance as a design principle for operationally stable, oxygen‐mediated triphase nanoarchitectures in bioanalysis.
authors: Hayeon Kim; Hyeok Lim; Sung Hyun Park; Jaejin Kim; Joonseok Lee; Kayoung Kim

title: Fault identification for intelligent real-time monitoring via mobile accessible networks: a critical review of MEMS microphone-based sensing for bearing diagnostics
abstract: The main objective of Condition Monitoring (CM) is to prevent unexpected downtime by monitoring machine conditions and reducing maintenance costs. To prevent failure, particularly in rotating machinery, CM is performed utilizing sensing devices, which have been the focus of extensive research in recent decades. This paper presents a critical review and provides comprehensive coverage of recent advances in CM for rotating machinery that utilize MEMS microphone-based sensing, with particular emphasis on bearing fault diagnosis relevant to the Fault Identification for Intelligent Real-time Monitoring via Mobile Accessible Network research programme. It synthesises recent journal articles focusing on MEMS (Micro-Electro-Mechanical Systems) microphone technologies, signal processing and machine learning techniques, methodological study design and experimental framework, and reported comparative analysis, advantages, limitations, and future research directions. Furthermore, the study reveals a dominant trend toward the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques, resulting in significant advances in CM and an emerging on non-contact-based sensing via mobile accessible system and self-powered sensing. Key gaps identified include the under-representation of MEMS microphone-based sensing, noise robustness and high sensitivity sensors, insufficient edge-deployment validation, the barriers of large datasets processing to achieve effectiveness, and the absence of multi-domain adaptive diagnostic frameworks. As a final point, options for scalable, low-cost, acoustic-based sensing and edge-intelligent computing are proposed, to deliver real-time monitoring across multiple domains.
authors: Firmansyah; Muhammad Khan; Isidro Durazo Cardenas

title: Feasibility of Using a Wearable Device to Identify Loneliness Among Older Adults Living Alone: Mixed Methods Study
abstract: Background: Addressing loneliness is a public health priority, with increasing interest in technological solutions for older adults. However, evidence on real-world feasibility and acceptability of such technologies remains limited. Objective: This study evaluated the feasibility and acceptability of the Conversation as Therapy (CaT) Pin, a wearable device designed to capture time spent in conversation among older adults living alone, following prototype refinement. Specifically, the study assessed whether a sufficient amount of synchronized, device-derived conversation data and self-reported loneliness data could be generated to explore the relationship between conversation time and loneliness. Methods: A 2-phase, mixed methods feasibility study was conducted. In phase 1, a Consumer Advisory Group (CAG) participated in a 1-hour discussion to inform study processes and device design, followed by a 1-week prototype test with older adults (n=3). Prototype usability, device design, and study procedures were explored through interviews and informed iterative refinement. In phase 2, community-dwelling adults aged 65 years or older living alone trialed the device for 2 weeks. Participants completed activity logs capturing loneliness, activity engagement, device wear, and conversations at 6-hour intervals. Device-captured conversation time was compared with self-reported data where available. Qualitative interviews were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis to understand participant experiences of device acceptability and feasibility. Results: In phase 1, 6 CAG participants, including 3 prototype testers, identified usability and design issues that led to modifications before phase 2. Phase 2 involved 23 participants (15 women; mean age 79.4 y, SD 6.7 y), with 7 classified as lonely using the UCLA-3 scale. However, only 8 (34.8%) participants generated sufficient concurrent device and activity log data, preventing meaningful assessment of the relationship between conversation time and loneliness. Feasibility challenges were driven by device acceptability, namely usability, comfort, aesthetics, and integration into daily life, which limited sustained wear and data synchronization. Qualitative findings indicated that participants prioritized quality rather than quantity of social interaction, and many did not perceive personal benefit from device use, citing lack of perceived need or concerns related to functionality and design. Together, methodological and conceptual challenges were identified in using conversation time as a potential indicator of loneliness. Conclusions: This study demonstrated that, in its current form, using a wearable device to capture time spent in conversation and align these data with self-reported loneliness was not feasible among older adults living alone. Feasibility was constrained by device acceptability related to usability, participant adherence, and data synchronization challenges. Findings also suggest that conversation time alone may be insufficient as an indicator of loneliness, given participants' emphasis on the quality and personal meaning of social interaction. These results provide practical lessons for future digital health research with older adults, including the need for early co-design, monitorable data-capture systems, and more nuanced approaches to measuring loneliness.
authors: Rajna Ogrin; Georgina Johnstone; Bradley Crammond; Judy A. Lowthian

title: Financial fraud detection model based on dual-layer knowledge graph
abstract: Corporate financial fraud is becoming increasingly complex and covert, necessitating the development of intelligent identification frameworks that combine accuracy and interpretability. This study proposes a detection method based on a two-layer knowledge graph. A two-layer structure is constructed, combining cross-layer path mining and rule vector discrimination to achieve end-to-end closed-loop detection. Experiments show that the method maintains stable performance as the enterprise scales up. In a sample of 700 enterprises, the method achieves an accuracy of 94.2%, a precision of 92.7%, a recall of 93.5%, an F1 score of 93.1%, an AUC of 0.95, and an MCC of 0.88. In a multi-enterprise scenario in the manufacturing industry, the detection accuracy reaches a maximum of 97%, AUC 0.975, and rule trigger rate 87%. After 100 iterations of rule mining, approximately 390 high-quality rules are retained, with an average support exceeding 0.069. This method demonstrates significant advantages and provides a practical intelligent framework for enterprise auditing and supervision.
authors: Ying Jiang

title: From Measurement Failure to Privacy Infrastructure: Reframing Contact Tracing Governance for the Next Pandemic
abstract: No measurement, no understanding; no understanding, no control: this foundational scientific principle was exposed as a public health dysfunction by the COVID-19 pandemic. Transmission chains spread invisibly, and the contact histories, mobility patterns, and biosignals necessary for control were never systematically collected. Although sensors and digital technologies existed, the fundamental reason measurement failed was the absence of privacy infrastructure that would have enabled people to provide data with confidence. This failure had structural reasons. The object of measurement in infectious disease control is not a physical phenomenon but human beings, and measurement therefore enters the core of privacy: contact histories, social relationships, and bodily states. Because greater precision also deepens privacy intrusion, contact-tracing apps faced 2 failures: privacy-centered designs lost epidemiological utility, while utility-centered designs were rejected through public distrust. Neither achieved sufficient measurement. This Viewpoint reframes the problem. Privacy protection is not a constraint that impedes infectious disease control but the enabling condition upon which effective measurement depends. Existing regulations and technical methods have not been designed from this premise and have therefore failed to break the cycle of structural distrust. As an institutional approach to filling this gap, we present VRAIO (verifiable record of AI output), which integrates democratic rule-setting, metadata declaration, third-party verification, tamper-proof ledgers, and violation-deterrence incentives. Once privacy infrastructure is established, this foundational principle can operate freely in infectious disease control for the first time. It will enable high-resolution epidemiology and precision intervention, opening a new path for public health that reconciles infection control with individual autonomy and social freedom without relying on blanket social shutdowns.
authors: Yusaku Fujii

title: From Promise to Practice A HEALinc Global Summit White Paper
abstract: This paper, developed by HEALinc CEO and Founder Dr. Desirée Cox, translates a day of multidisciplinary discussion at the 2026 HEALinc Global Summit, New York City (NYC) Day Conclave into a coherent systems framework and action agenda. It is not a transcript, clinical guideline, regulatory opinion, or endorsement of every intervention or claim discussed at the Summit. The source material captures perspectives from scientists, physicians, biotechnology leaders, lawyers, investors, former regulators, patient advocates, educators, architects, and other participants. Sponsors, speakers, and key opinion leaders represented at the HEALinc New York City (NYC) Day Conclave are identified in the Appendices. The proceedings ranged from late-stage clinical development and international regulatory pathways to whole-person health, patient experience, digital monitoring, medical education, and the design of healing environments. The purpose of this paper is to identify the recurring system-level insights, clarify where genuine convergence occurred, and convert those insights into a practical architecture for translation. Some interventions and outcomes described during the discussions were preliminary, anecdotal, contested, or outside established standards of evidence. They are treated here as signals of emerging questions and unmet needs – not as validated clinical conclusions. Any therapy must be evaluated according to its own evidence, manufacturing quality, ethical acceptability, regulatory status, and risk profile. Interpretive StanceThe field should neither equate regulatory caution with obstruction nor equate permissive access with progress. The task is to create controlled velocity: faster, more coherent learning and access under stronger evidence, ethics, quality, and accountability.
authors: Desiree C. T. Cox

title: From Speed and Sensitivity to Robust Reliability: Addressing the Detection Bias of Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification (LAMP) in Food Authentication
abstract: Food adulteration poses severe threats to the integrity and safety of global food supply chains. Innovations in analytical techniques, especially the rapid development of LAMP-based detection methods, are indispensable for addressing these risks. However, the dominant research paradigm, which has long prioritized accelerated amplification kinetics and ultralow detection limits, largely obscures a critical limitation: insufficient detection reliability when deployed in complex field environments. This review consolidates state-of-the-art advances targeting reliability optimization and delineates key technical strategies to construct robust, improved-reliability LAMP platforms for real-food testing. Specifically, we summarize critical factors at the reaction and readout levels that compromise the reliability of LAMP under realistic scenarios, such as inexperienced operators, degraded samples, matrices containing inhibitory substances, and uncontrolled environments. We further elaborate on effective solutions to bridge the reliability gap between laboratory validation and on-site deployment, which requires coordinated technical improvements throughout the full LAMP testing pipeline. Ultimately, we propose a forward-looking developmental principle for next-generation LAMP assays: analytical reliability and operational robustness should be elevated to equal priority alongside the traditionally pursued ultra-rapid amplification and high sensitivity. This balanced technical framework may help pave the way toward large-scale standardization of LAMP-enabled food authentication, although its presumptive results must be confirmed by an independent validated method before they can support regulatory enforcement or other formal decisions.
authors: Xiong Xiong; Yahui Zhang; Mengxuan Liu; Yan Guo; Ying Yang

title: From digital phenotype to closed-loop therapy: artificial intelligence–enabled wearable and connected technology for allergic diseases
abstract: Background The prevalence of allergic diseases continues to rise, yet episodic outpatient care remains constrained by delayed symptom recognition, the "black box" of medication adherence, and fragmented management. Wearables, the Internet of Things (IoT), and artificial intelligence (AI) now converge in "digital phenotyping." From a pharmaceutical perspective, this review appraises these AI-enabled technologies for allergic diseases along the thread of "from digital phenotype to closed-loop therapy." Methods A narrative review synthesizing recent literature on the technical framework, real-time monitoring, risk early warning, long-term management, therapeutic wearables, psychological digital phenotypes, and equity and safety. Results These technologies span the "sensing–warning–management–treatment" chain. Adaptive baseline learning, time-aware modeling, and multimodal fusion enable individualized early warning from noisy physiological and environmental signals. The strongest evidence concerns long-term management: digital inhalers and smartwatches, validated in randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses, improve adherence and asthma control and reduce exacerbations, with economic value in averting biologic escalation; devices are extending from passive sensing to active interventions—nasal acoustic therapy, "feedback as therapy," and conceptual closed-loop epinephrine injection. However, most applications remain at small-sample, single-center validation; portable quantitative pollen detection is an empty niche; and drug confounding of digital phenotypes (β 2 -agonist contamination of heart rate variability) and closed-loop amplification of skin-tone–related bias challenge clinical translation. Conclusions AI-enabled wearables are shifting allergy care from intermittent, subjective consultation toward continuous, closed-loop management, with evidence most mature for digital inhalers. Future work should develop multimodal digital phenotypes and allergy-specific foundation models and strengthen medication-covariate modeling, hard-endpoint validation, and whole-lifecycle equity governance.
authors: Yuxiang Pei; Yongxia Wu; Ruoyu Hou; Kun Wan

title: From shōnen to seinen to Studio Ghibli: attraction to anime and manga, and their relation to mental health and social outcomes
abstract: Abstract Aim Interest in anime and manga can be very diverse (from action-packed stories to romantic tales to works by the famous Studio Ghibli). Our aim was to examine the association of interest in manga and anime (and specifically certain genres) with mental health, social disconnectedness, and subjective well-being outcomes. Subject and methods We used data from a sample of the general adult population in Germany ( N = 2591, mean age 47 years, 50.6% female). Outcomes were quantified using psychometrically sound tools (e.g., Patient Health Questionnaire-9 [PHQ-9] or Satisfaction with Life Scale [SWLS]). General interest in manga and anime and also interest in certain genres (among those who were interested) served as key independent variables. Results A general interest in manga and anime was consistently associated with poor mental health and social disconnectedness (compared with the absence of such interest), whereas it was generally not associated with subjective well-being outcomes. Among those who were interested, while most interest in specific manga genres was only partly or not significantly associated with the outcomes, interest in manga from Studio Ghibli was associated with better mental health and less social withdrawal. Moreover, an interest in anime from Studio Ghibli was associated with several favorable outcomes (better mental health, social connectedness, and higher ikigai levels). Conclusion While a general interest in anime and manga was consistently associated with poorer mental health and social disconnectedness, certain genres were associated with favorable outcomes among those who were interested in them. Further differentiated research is needed to better understand the psychosocial outcomes of anime and manga passion.
authors: André Hajek; Hans‐Helmut König

title: Gait Speed in Spinal Muscular Atrophy: A Key Vital Sign Linked to Strength and Fatigability
abstract: ABSTRACT Introduction/Aims Gait Speed (GS), a valid and reliable indicator of function and health in multiple populations, has not been explored in spinal muscular atrophy (SMA). The purpose of this study was to characterize GS and gait speed reserves (GSR), and explore associations with strength and fatigability in SMA and healthy controls (HC). Methods Data were collected from ambulatory individuals with SMA ( n = 14) and controls (HC) ( n = 10). Using custom‐engineered instrumented insoles, stride velocity (SV) was collected during the Six‐Minute Walk Test (6MWT) and 10‐m walk/run (10MWR). Three GS variables were identified; SV50th Centile 6MWT (SV50C 6MWT ), 10MWR SV, and SV95th Centile 6MWT (SV95C 6MWT ). Gait speed reserve (GSR) was calculated from 10MWR and SV50C 6MWT . Repeated measures analysis of variance assessed differences in GS and GSR across groups. Spearman's Rho was used to assess associations between speed variables and clinical assessments. Results All speed variables were different within HC ( p < 0.001) and SMA ( p = 0.002). There was a significant Group × Speed interaction ( p < 0.001) with greater differences in HC. GSR was lower in SMA ( p < 0.001, d = 2.42). In SMA, thigh strength was associated with all three GS variables and inversely associated with fatigability ( p < 0.05). In HC, associations between GS and strength or fatigability were not observed. GSR was not associated with strength, fatigability, or GS in either group. Discussion GS is diminished in SMA and correlated with strength and fatigability. While reduced in SMA, GSR was not associated with GS, strength, or function. GS is a key vital sign of health and may be a useful biomarker in SMA.
authors: Carly Magun; Ton T. H. Duong; Cara H. Kanner; Rafael S. Rodriguez-Torres; Elizabeth R. Harding; Sally Dunaway Young; Rabia Farooquee; Constance de Monts; Amy Pasternak; Maria A. Fragala-Pinkham; Damiano Zanotto; Jacqueline Montes

title: Glow Up: a single-centre observational study protocol to develop digital biomarkers for prediabetes screening and digital phenotyping
abstract: Introduction Prediabetes, a key precursor to type 2 diabetes, is highly prevalent and underdiagnosed, particularly among adults aged ≥45 years with elevated body mass index (BMI). Early detection is critical because lifestyle interventions can delay or prevent progression to type 2 diabetes. The Glucose Observation and Wearable Use for Prevention (Glow Up) study aims to (1) test the feasibility of a digital biomarker for pre-diabetes screening using wearable- and smartphone-derived lifestyle factors (eg, sleep, physical activity and nutrition patterns) in daily life and to (2) characterise individual- and metabolic subgroup-level variability in lifestyle factors and glycaemic control. Specifically, we aim to examine how lifestyle factors relate to glycaemic status and identify personalised predictors of early metabolic dysregulation. Methods and analysis Glow Up is a prospective, single-centre, observational case-control study conducted in Switzerland. Adults (n=200) aged ≥45 years with body mass index (BMI) ≥25 kg/m² will be recruited, including n=100 individuals with pre-diabetes and n=100 age- and sex-matched normoglycaemic controls. Participants will undergo 4 weeks of continuous monitoring using a blinded continuous glucose monitor (CGM) and commercial- and medical-grade wearables; for example, capturing physical activity, sleep and physiological markers (heart rate variability, heart rate and skin temperature), in addition to completing daily image-based meal logs using smartphones. Glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c), fasting plasma glucose (FPG) and body anthropometrics will be collected at the enrolment visit (T0) and repeated at follow-up (T3), approximately 5 weeks apart. The primary outcome is glycaemic status at T3, classified from HbA1c and FPG using prespecified thresholds. Secondary outcomes include CGM metrics, lifestyle profiling (sleep, physical activity, stress and nutrition) and adherence to image-based meal logging. Ethics and dissemination The study received ethics approval from the Ethics Committee of Eastern Switzerland on 15 May 2025 (BASEC ID: 2025–00972). Written informed consent is obtained from all participants before any study procedures are performed. Findings will be disseminated as articles in international peer-reviewed journals and as posters and oral presentations at national and international conferences. Summaries will be provided to funders and collaborators, and personalised reports to participants. Trial registration number NCT07373418.

title: HIV prevention and care in the afterlife of the HIV/AIDS crisis
abstract: Introduction Queer and trans individuals face stark inequities in HIV prevention and care. Existing theories and models explain how individual- and interpersonal-level stressors shape health among queer and trans populations, but less theoretical attention has been paid to how histories of structural violence continue to shape contemporary HIV-related inequities.Theory Drawing on Saidiya Hartman’s conceptualization of the “afterlife of slavery,” we conceptualize contemporary HIV-related inequities among queer and trans populations within an “afterlife of the HIV/AIDS crisis.” This framework considers how normative logics surrounding gender and sexuality that structured responses to the HIV/AIDS crisis persist within contemporary institutions, policies, and practices.Method We conducted an interdisciplinary critical narrative review examining historical and contemporary scholarship on the HIV/AIDS crisis and the health of queer and trans populations. We synthesized literature across disciplines to identify recurring conceptual frameworks and cross-disciplinary themes through which historical responses to HIV/AIDS continue to shape contemporary conditions.Results Three dominant themes emerged: (1) pathologization contributed to the stigmatization of queerness and transness; (2) rhetoric employed by the media, political actors, and the scientific community demoralized and dehumanized queer and trans people; and (3) the codification of homophobia and transphobia in laws and policies contributed to the criminalization of queerness and transness. Across these themes, historical responses to the HIV/AIDS crisis established and reinforced structural conditions that continue to shape HIV prevention and care.Discussion Contemporary HIV inequities among queer and trans populations cannot be fully understood without attention to the historical processes through which they were produced and sustained. Situating present-day HIV prevention and care through the framework of the afterlife of the HIV/AIDS crisis highlights the persistence of structural violence and provides a framework for identifying and addressing its contemporary manifestations.
authors: Tyler D. Harvey; Bryce Puesta Takenaka

title: Healing cascades and infections in wounds monitored using a wearable sensor of gaseous flux
abstract: Abstract Capabilities for quantitative monitoring of chronic wounds remain an unmet clinical need, as existing diagnostic approaches rely on semiquantitative evaluation of symptoms that lack sensitivity especially during early stages of infection. Here we present a scheme for tracking wound physiology that leverages a miniature, wireless skin-interfaced device for non-contact, transient measurements of the flux of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and water vapor from the wound microenvironment. Unlike emerging smart bandage platforms that rely on physical contact with the fragile wound bed to interrogate liquid-phase biomarkers, this strategy uses an engineered microclimate and suspended suite of sensors to measure the diffusive transport of wound-derived gases across the wound surface but separated from it. The result enables quantitative evaluation of metabolic activity and healing progression without perturbing the healing tissues. In biofilm growth models of Staphylococcus aureus , measurements demonstrate that trends in VOC flux correlate strongly with bacterial growth kinetics and precede any visible biofilm formation. Longitudinal monitoring in infected murine wound healing models shows that concurrent measurements of water vapor and VOC flux provide complementary physiological insights, capturing both the trajectory of barrier restoration and the dynamics of bacterial burden. The findings establish this non-contact sensing scheme as a distinct and clinically translatable paradigm for wound monitoring, with broad implications for non-invasive surveillance of disease states in which tissue metabolic activity and skin barrier integrity serve as actionable physiological readouts. Significance Statement Limited capabilities in continuous, quantitative assessment of a wound make early diagnosis and effective management challenging, particularly in cases of infection that rapidly progress before symptoms appear. Non-contact approaches for wound monitoring that preserve fragile tissue can transform wound care. In this context, gaseous flux from the wound bed provides an integrative measure of microbial activity and barrier restoration. This study establishes a wearable sensing platform that quantifies these fluxes in real time, enabling early infection detection and temporal tracking of wound healing. These results highlight a path toward personalized treatment strategies and reduced reliance on episodic clinical evaluation.

title: Higher explanation-necessity scores are associated with longer written explanations of autonomous driving scenes
abstract: Explanations of automated-vehicle behavior may help occupants understand what prompted a maneuver, but how much an explanation should say remains an open design question. Retrospective annotation of recorded driving scenes can supply candidate content. We analyzed 1,103 training and test records from the release, matching the source-described corpus size; each paired human-written text with an aggregate perceived explanation-necessity score. Explanations contained 9,541 whitespace-delimited tokens (mean 8.65; range 2–20) before lexical preprocessing. Higher scores were associated with longer explanations (Pearson’s \(r=0.374\) ; template-cluster bootstrap 95% interval [0.266, 0.448]), including after score-1.0 observations were excluded. We call this corpus-level length association progressive elaboration . Bounded-model comparisons did not identify a unique latent-category count. For groupwise summaries, we used four descriptive partitions: three below-ceiling regions and 59 records scored 1.0. Record-weighted and unique-template analyses showed higher within-partition lexical distinctiveness in upper than in lower partitions. In template-grouped cross-validation of these exploratory partitions, the unweighted text model exceeded token-count and stratified-dummy baselines in balanced accuracy (0.382 versus 0.327 and 0.247). The 1,280-record rerun preserved the score—length, lexical, and predictive findings and left the latent-category count unresolved. These results motivate prospective studies of how annotation-derived content should be selected, compressed, and delivered in real time.
authors: Gwangbin Kim; Dohyeon Yeo; Yumin Kang; Minwoo Oh; SeungJun Kim

title: Hip Mobility Is Associated with Isokinetic Hip Adduction Torque in Recreationally Active Females: An Exploratory Study
abstract: This exploratory study examined whether trunk and hip mobility are associated with isokinetic hip torque in recreationally active females. Twenty-two women completed standing isokinetic hip testing at 60°·s⁻¹, yielding peak torque (PT; normalised to body mass), time to peak torque, and joint angle at peak torque for hip flexion–extension and abduction–adduction. Segmental (lumbar, thoracic, hip) and global mobility indices, composites of active range of motion, were quantified with inertial measurement units. Ninety-six Spearman correlations were computed with Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery-rate (FDR) control; regression models were fitted post hoc. Two associations survived FDR correction: dominant hip adduction PT was related to hip mobility (r = .70, 95% CI .36 to .87) and to global mobility (r = .66, 95% CI .34 to .84). A segmental model accounted for 49% of the variance (adjusted R² = .485), with hip mobility the only stable predictor (β = 0.57, 95% CI 0.13 to 1.00). Sensitivity analyses indicated that this finding was robust to the construction of the indices and was carried mainly by hip flexion range of motion, which is unrelated to the fixed testing excursion. A side-matched analysis weakened the dominant-side association (r = .57). Associations of global mobility with the timing and angle of non-dominant adduction torque did not survive correction. The global index contains the hip index (r = .85), so the two are not independent constructs. Hip mobility is associated with hip adduction torque magnitude; the findings are hypothesis-generating and require confirmation in larger, preferably longitudinal studies.

title: Human Digital Twins: A Paradigm Shift in Personalized Healthcare and Predictive Medicine
abstract: Human Digital Twins (HDTs) are rapidly emerging as a transformative innovation in personalized healthcare and predictive medicine. Through the integration of real-time, high-resolution data from multiple sources like genomics, wearable devices, electronic health records, and behavioral inputs, HDTs create virtual replicas of individuals that can simulate, predict, and optimize health outcomes. This article explores the conceptual framework that underpins HDTs, their current and potential applications in personalized healthcare, as well as their role in advancing predictive medicine and population health. It also addresses the technological and ethical challenges associated with HDT development, including data privacy, interoperability, algorithmic bias, and regulatory gaps. Furthermore, the article outlines future directions, and emphasizes the importance of multi-omics integration, cognitive modeling, edge computing, and interdisciplinary collaboration. Through a comprehensive analysis, this study highlights HDTs as a paradigm shift with the potential to revolutionize healthcare delivery, improve patient outcomes, and enable a more proactive, data-driven model of care.

title: Hybrid intelligent modeling for enhanced surface integrity, process dynamics, and sustainable performance in finish ultra-precision hard turning of AISI D2 under dry conditions
abstract: Abstract This study presents a hybrid intelligent modeling framework for improving surface quality, process dynamics, and sustainable performance in ultra-precision hard turning of AISI D2 steel of 62 HRC under dry conditions. To address gaps in material-specific modeling and the omission of dynamic process variables in sustainable machining, tool vibration ( V rms ) was integrated with cutting speed, feed, and depth of cut using a full factorial experimental design. ANOVA and Sobol sensitivity analyses identified feed as the most influential factor affecting surface roughness ( R a ) and resultant cutting force ( F R ), while tool vibration exhibited significant interaction effects. Three machine-learning models, Bayesian regularization neural network (BRNN), GA-BRNN, and PSO-BRNN, were developed and compared. BRNN demonstrated the best overall performance based on predictive accuracy and computational efficiency. External validation showed highly accurate prediction of F R with an R 2 of 80.35% and a MAPE of 9.30%. For R a , BRNN achieved an R 2 of 70.43% and a MAPE of 38.41%, corresponding to satisfactory predictive performance according to the adopted MAPE criteria. The comparatively lower R a accuracy reflects the greater complexity and variability of surface generation compared with cutting force formation. The BRNN model was analytically formulated and integrated with a multi-objective particle swarm optimization algorithm to determine Pareto-optimal machining parameters. The optimal conditions ( v c = 75 m/min, f = 0.025 mm/rev, a p = 0.06 mm) yielded predicted F R and R a values of 119.87 N and 0.58 µm, respectively. Confirmation experiments produced an average minimum error of 6%, supporting the framework''s applicability for sustainable machining optimization and intelligent decision support in smart manufacturing.
authors: Ugonna Loveday Adizue; Vahid Pourmostaghimi

title: Hydrogel Microneedles for Perioperative Applications: Drug Delivery, Biosensing, and Theranostic Translation
abstract: Hydrogel microneedles provide access across the skin barrier for drug delivery and interstitial-fluid sampling. Their perioperative use depends on whether that access remains reliable during skin preparation, surgical positioning, and changes in tissue perfusion. This narrative review examines how material design affects delivered dose, measurement accuracy, and clinical feasibility. Human sampling studies establish feasibility for selected measurements; most therapeutic and integrated sensing applications remain at the preclinical stage or have been investigated in other clinical settings. The review distinguishes these findings from evidence in surgical patients. Particular attention is given to insertion and adhesion on disinfected or compromised skin, the relationship between interstitial and plasma measurements, and drug exposure after delivery is interrupted. Short-duration superficial procedures and observational drug or wound-adjacent monitoring offer focused questions for initial studies with standard care maintained. Progress toward treatment requires validation of the complete product, including sterilization, batch consistency, shelf life, and safeguards against uncontrolled release. Clinical studies should report failed applications and adverse events alongside patient outcomes. Autonomous anesthetic administration remains a development goal whose safety cannot be inferred from separate demonstrations of sensing and drug release.
authors: Yue Qi; Cong Wang; Jinyue Chen; Dalong Wu

title: INTELLIGENT INTRUSION DETECTION USING MACHINE LEARNING FOR SECURE DIGITAL INFRASTRUCTURE
abstract: The growing interconnectivity of digital infrastructure has increased exposure to cyber threats and strengthened the need for effective intrusion detection. Machine-learning techniques offer promising capabilities for recognizing malicious network behavior from structured traffic observations. However, differences in the representation of benign and attack traffic can affect the development and interpretation of intelligent detection systems. This study characterized the dataset and examined the distribution of legitimate and malicious network traffic, with particular attention to major intrusion groups and less frequently represented attack categories. A secondary descriptive analysis of the original CIC-IDS2017 network-flow dataset was conducted. Dataset structure, traffic attributes, class labels, and traffic-category distributions were systematically examined. Network observations were organized into benign traffic and broader intrusion groups to describe their relative representation. The analysis identified substantial variation across traffic categories. Legitimate network communication represented the largest component, whereas malicious observations comprised multiple attack types with different levels of occurrence. Denial-of-service-related activities represented a major portion of intrusion traffic, while port scanning, brute-force, web-based, botnet, infiltration, and other attack categories contributed additional security-relevant observations. Several specialized attack classes were sparsely represented, demonstrating notable class imbalance. These findings indicate that CIC-IDS2017 provides a diverse foundation for machine-learning-oriented intrusion-detection research. The observed traffic diversity supports analysis of multiple malicious behaviors, while class imbalance highlights the importance of appropriate evaluation strategies and careful interpretation of future predictive models. The study provides a structured basis for subsequent intelligent cybersecurity research and model development.
authors: Mohammad Majharul Islam Jabed; Bhanu Pratap Singh

title: IOT- BASED WOMEN SECURITY SYSTEM
abstract: The safety of women in public places, workplaces, and while travelling remains a serious social concern. Incidents of harassment, stalking, and assault often take place in situations where the victim cannot reach a phone, unlock it, and dial for help in time. Even when a call is made, the person receiving it may not know the exact location of the victim. This paper presents an IoT-based women security system in the form of a small wearable device that can raise an emergency alert with a single action and share the live location of the wearer with trusted contacts and the nearest police control room. The device is built around an ESP32 microcontroller connected to a GPS receiver, a GSM module, a pulse sensor, a three-axis accelerometer, a small microphone, and a concealed push button. When the button is pressed, or when the device detects a combination of an abnormally high heart rate and sudden violent movement, it enters the emergency mode. In this mode it obtains the current coordinates from the GPS receiver and sends SMS messages containing a map link to preconfigured contacts. At the same time it places an automatic voice call to the first contact so that someone is alerted even if messages are not read immediately. Where Wi-Fi or mobile data is available, the device also publishes its location and sensor readings to a cloud platform using the MQTT protocol. A companion mobile application and a web dashboard display the live track of the wearer, the time of the alert, and the recorded audio clip captured by the microphone during the first seconds of the emergency. The location is updated every few seconds until the alert is cancelled by the wearer with a secret button sequence or closed by a responder, so that contacts can follow the movement of the victim if she is being taken away. The system also includes deterrent features. A loud buzzer can be activated to attract the attention of people nearby, and an optional shock circuit provides a means of selfdefence. A fake call feature on the mobile application allows the user to leave an uncomfortable situation without confrontation. All alerts are logged in the cloud with time, place, and sensor data, which can later assist police investigation and help authorities identify locations where incidents occur repeatedly.

title: Implementation of Door Security System Using Machine Learning
abstract: ABSTRACT: Safety comes first in an Ambient Intelligent environment. The primary goal of this paper work is to provide a high-level security solution for various organizations. Recently, the rate of crimes involving robbery in hostels and houses is increasing. There is need to enhance home security systems to make them more sophisticated, effective in order to keep up with the increasing crime rate. This paper presents a Voice Recognition-Based Door Security System that utilizes a trained voice recognition module through supervised machine learning to authenticate authorized users and prevent unauthorized access. The system works by recording and storing the voice of a particular authorized user and compares incoming voice with the stored voice for authentication. Upon successful voice match, the system triggers a relay or servo motor to unlock the door. However, if the incoming voice does not match the stored authorized voice, the system immediately alert the person via voice call through GSM module to alert the owner about the unauthorized access attempt. As the SMS alert has sent the camera which is installed is activated and we can generate a OTP through GSM module. If we want to allow the unauthorized person to go inside then we can directly establish a communication between GSM module and the controller. This provides real-time security monitoring, allowing the owner to take immediate action.
authors: A. Gangadhar

title: Infectious skin diseases in athletes, with particular reference to contact and combat sports: a narrative review of epidemiology, prevention and treatment
abstract: Introduction and purpose. The skin is the body's largest organ and its principal barrier against the external environment. In athletes—especially those in contact and combat sports—continuous mechanical, thermal and microbial stress predisposes to cutaneous infection and to team-wide transmission. This review synthesises current evidence on the epidemiology, clinical features, diagnosis, prevention and treatment of infectious skin diseases in athletes, with emphasis on wrestling, judo, boxing and mixed martial arts. Material and methods. A narrative review of peer-reviewed reviews, epidemiological and microbiological studies, outbreak investigations and case reports addressing bacterial, viral, fungal and parasitic skin infections in athletes. Results. Bacterial infections—chiefly Staphylococcus aureus, including community-associated methicillin-resistant strains, and Streptococcus pyogenes—together with herpes gladiatorum (herpes simplex virus type 1) and dermatophytoses (tinea gladiatorum, predominantly Trichophyton tonsurans) dominate the clinical picture. Transmission occurs mainly through direct skin-to-skin contact, with fomites playing a secondary role. Diagnosis is largely clinical but is strengthened by potassium hydroxide microscopy, culture and polymerase chain reaction. Management combines targeted antimicrobial therapy, incision and drainage of purulent lesions, isolation and, for herpes gladiatorum and tinea gladiatorum, chemoprophylaxis; return to competition is governed by defined criteria. Conclusions. Early recognition, accurate diagnosis, prompt treatment and isolation, rigorous hygiene, environmental disinfection and evidence-based prophylaxis are the cornerstones of minimising morbidity and interrupting transmission of skin infections in athletes.
authors: Jakub Palian; Szymon Kurzyński; Katarzyna Czernecka; Igor Smędowski; Kacper Kazimierczuk; Natalia Mordko; Mateusz Góras; Łukasz Mazelanik; Wojciech Tokarczyk; Julia Pawlak

title: Informing personalization of technologies for promoting physical activity: bridging the knowledge, attitude and practice model and human-centered design
abstract: Background Although the benefits of physical activity (PA) are well established and inactivity poses substantial risks, encouraging adults to change and sustain PA behaviors remains a challenge. Mobile technologies have emerged as accessible and cost-effective tools to encourage healthier behaviors. Personalization is a key factor for improving user engagement and adherence, but current approaches often rely on surface-level data and overlook cognitive and motivational aspects. Objective This study explores how mobile exercise- and health-related technologies can be personalized to support PA behavior change by integrating the Knowledge, Attitude, and Practice (KAP) model with a human-centered design approach. Methods We conducted semi-structured interviews with 24 adults aged 34–66 years to explore their PA habits and use of exercise- and health-related technology. Interview recordings were transcribed, reviewed, and analyzed using deductive thematic analysis guided by the three domains of the KAP model: knowledge, attitude, and practice. Results Participants demonstrated varied knowledge of PA, ranging from general health benefits to specific exercise practices. General awareness of the benefits of PA was not always accompanied by practical knowledge about planning exercise or interpreting activity data. Attitudes toward PA and mobile exercise- and health-related technology were influenced by motivation, convenience, and emotional responses, with some participants reporting guilt or stress related to use of mobile exercise- and health-related technology. Practices reflected diverse PA routines, from structured exercise to incidental daily movement. These practices were shaped by work, family responsibilities, physical limitations, preferred environments, and differing needs for social or solitary activity. Engagement with mobile exercise- and health-related technology varied widely, with some participants relying on wearables and apps, while others reported irregular or discontinued use. Together, the findings informed a framework of 20 dimensions describing how individual differences in knowledge, attitudes, and practices can guide the personalization of mobile exercise- and health-related technology for PA promotion. Conclusions Personalization of mobile exercise- and health-related technologies for PA promotion should extend beyond surface-level data to include cognitive, emotional, and contextual factors that influence behavior. Applying the KAP model within human-centered design can inform adaptive, empathetic, and context-sensitive solutions that better resonate with users’ lived experiences and support sustainable PA engagement.
authors: Agnieszka Jaff; Mia Folke; Annica Kristoffersson

title: Interactive Industrial Metaverse Platform based on Digital Twin and Extended Reality for Real-time Process Monitoring
abstract: The transition toward Industry 4.0 and the emerging Industry 5.0 paradigm highlights the need for real-time integration of heterogeneous machines, human-machine collaboration, and interoperable data flows. Modern factories frequently combine advanced machines with legacy systems, leading to inconsistent data structures and limited process visibility. To address these challenges, a DT-XR-based industrial metaverse framework was developed to enable standardized data acquisition, cloud-centered information management, and immersive visualization across diverse manufacturing environments. The framework provides a multilayer architecture that consolidates heterogeneous controller and sensor data into a unified structure, processes them on edge devices, stores them as cloud-based time-series records, and delivers them to digital twin and XR interfaces for real-time monitoring. This approach supports the cyber-physical integration emphasized in Industry 4.0 and the human-centered decision-making prioritized in Industry 5.0. The framework was validated through two case studies. In a hybrid additive-subtractive testbed, heterogeneous controller data and sensor signals were synchronized within a digital twin with an end-to-end latency of approximately 33.00ms. In an industry-scale blow molding system operating with PLC-based legacy machine, standardized data management and AR-based visualization of heater temperatures, mold timing, environmental conditions, and inline states were achieved, with an average round-trip latency of approximately 1040.92ms. These results demonstrate that the proposed DT-XR framework enhances interoperability, process transparency, and operator-centered decision-making, and shows strong potential for scaling to larger production systems and future Industry 5.0 applications. © 2026 The Authors. title: Invasive species detection from high resolution aerial photographs
abstract: This project focuses on the automatic detection of invasive plant species along railway tracks. Initially, the project targets two highly invasive species: Asian Knotweed (Fallopia japonica) and Giant Hogweed (Heracleum mantegazzianum). ProRail, the Dutch railway infrastructure manager, collects yearly high-resolution helicopter imagery covering all railway tracks in the Netherlands. A deep learning-based classifier is applied to this imagery to detect the aforementioned invasive species. This work was presented as a poster at the 25th anniversary event of the Ambient Intelligence research group.
authors: Bram Ton; Etto L. Salomons; Ronald Visser

title: Investigating effects of day-to-day variations in environmental exposure on the human brain: study protocol for the Day2Day Environment project
abstract: BACKGROUND: Understanding how daily environmental exposures influence the human brain and mental health is increasingly important in the context of global urbanization and climate change. Previous studies have focused primarily on long-term environmental factors or isolated features like green space and air quality, neglecting the interaction between multiple exposures encountered in everyday life. This protocol paper describes the study design and dataset of the Day2Day Environment project, an ongoing study investigating how real-world, day-to-day environmental variability affects brain structure, function, and well-being. METHODS: This dense longitudinal study collects multimodal data from 30 participants over 25 testing sessions, including neuroimaging and tracking of physiological, behavioral, and environmental variables. Using wearable devices, geographic ecological momentary assessments, and GPS-based geospatial tracking, we collect data on air quality, noise, light exposure, physical activity, stress, cognition, and affect. Neuroimaging measures include T1- and T2*-weighted images during rest and tasks, quantitative multi-parameter mapping, high-resolution proton density imaging of the hippocampus, and diffusion tensor imaging sequences. CONCLUSION: The Day2Day Environment dataset offers a unique opportunity to study short-term neuroplasticity in response to the dynamic interplay between multiple environmental exposures. Furthermore, the diversity of measurements in this dataset may be valuable for addressing research questions beyond environmental neuroscience.
authors: Kim Falkenstein; Claire Pauley; Simone Kühn

title: IoT-Based Sleep Apnea Prevention, Detection, and Emergency Alert System
abstract: Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) is a common sleep disorder that often goes undiagnosed. It causes breathing to stop and restart repeatedly during sleep, which can increase long-term risks for heart and metabolic health. Polysomnography is the standard method for diagnosing OSA. However, it relies on lab equipment, overnight supervision, and trained technicians, making it expensive and mostly impractical for use at home. This work proposes an IoT-based system for preventing, detecting, and alerting about sleep apnea. The goal is to allow affordable, continuous monitoring a t home. The design uses a n ESP32 microcontroller connected to a MAX30102 pulse oximetry sensor, an INMP441 digital MEMS microphone, and an MPU6050 motion sensor. Together, these devices capture data on SpO₂ levels, heart rate, snoring, body posture, breathing movement, and respiratory rate. The system filters and normalizes these signals, converting them into Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCC) and Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) features. This data goes to a hybrid CNN-BiLSTM-XGBoost model, which evaluates sleep quality and the severity of apnea, categorizing it as Normal, Mild, Moderate, or Severe. If a Severe episode is detected, the system uploads the information to Firebase Cloud, retrieves the patient's location from a NEO-6M GPS module, and sends a n emergency SMS to registered caregivers via a SIM800L GSM module. It also gently wakes the patient using a micro speaker that plays a softly rising tone and activates a relaycontrolled mini air pump for additional support. A thematic review of related IoT, wearable technology, deep learning, contactless systems, a n d cloud-based monitoring supports the proposed design and explains the integrated sensing- to-response process. Since this paper discusses a proposed system instead of one that has been built and tested, it emphasizes design intent and expected functionality, rather than actual results

title: Irish giants: from myth to medicine
abstract: The archetype of the 'Irish giant' in folklore appears to be rooted in historical individuals afflicted by pituitary gigantism. This review compiles and critically assesses the veracity of historical accounts, primarily from the late 17th to the early 20th century, for a group of individuals with gigantism that had Irish origins. Clinical and, in some cases, osteological data (e.g., Charles Byrne, Cornelius Magrath, and Patrick Cotter) confirm a diagnosis of pituitary gigantism, a rare disease that is caused by excess growth hormone secretion from a pituitary adenoma. In the pre-scientific era, the effects of the unopposed hormone excess resulted in extreme tall stature, debilitating morbidity, and usually premature death. This aligns with our modern understanding of the potential severity of hormonal excess and tumour growth in pituitary gigantism. The high concentration of cases in Ulster is explained by a founder germline pathogenic variant (c.910 C > T, p.(R304*)) in the AIP gene, that was identified in multiple contemporary families, later in the skeleton of Charles Byrne and most recently, among the Irish diaspora. Estimated to have arisen around 2500 years ago, this variant established a direct medical explanation for a regional phenomenon. In this review we provide a detailed compilation of historical Irish giants and discuss the evidence linking myth and folklore to the modern medical reality of pituitary gigantism as a rare, severe genetic disease.
authors: Wouter W. de Herder; Paul Benjamin Loughrey; Márta Korbonits; Adrian Daly

title: LLMs as Narrators of Lived Experience: A Study of Generative Hermeneutical Epistemic Injustice in ADHD Sense-Making
abstract: Large language models (LLMs), as non-human actors, do not have access to first-hand experiences. Yet they are increasingly consulted in processes of making sense of them, from mental health chatbots to reflexive journals. As a result, complex lived realities risk being distorted or flattened through second-order representations. In this paper, we expand on conceptual work to empirically examine narrative mechanisms through which LLMs as narrators give rise to hermeneutical epistemic injustice. We foreground narration as a key interpretive process through which experience is made intelligible. Focusing on ADHD as a motivating case, we compare first-person narratives from online ADHD communities with narratives generated by LLMs. Using an interpretive, reflexive analysis, we examine how these forms of narration construct lived experience. We find that generated narratives organise ADHD experience through recurring modes that individualise, standardise, and stabilise interpretation, reducing messiness, complexity and ambiguity present in community narration. More situated and unresolved accounts remained possible when foregrounded through prompting. We argue that the epistemic concern lies not only in what models can represent, but in which interpretations they make readily available and which require prior conceptual and prompting work.
authors: Anne Arzberger; Dongying Zhang
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI Ethics and Society

title: LOng COvid Multidisciplinary consortium: Optimising Treatments and servIces acrOss the NHS (LOCOMOTION) - COV-LT2-0016
abstract: Plain English Summary Long COVID affects over two million people in the UK, it has various symptoms and impacts daily life. Although there are over 90 long COVID clinics in England, most people have not had access to them, and waiting times to be seen are long. Our research aimed to produce a ‘gold standard’ for care by analysing existing practices, creating new systems of care and establishing best practices nationally. This research has been developed with patients with lived experience and a wide range of NHS professionals in ten long COVID clinics across the UK and led by academics (universities) with links to other long COVID funded studies. Key priorities were understanding and improving: clinical assessment; advice and treatment; NHS pathways and costs; and returning to work and other roles. Comparing findings across our partnership of ten clinics, we learnt more about treatment, provided real-time education to other healthcare staff and patients, and established best practice guidance that was shared with clinics outside our study group. We identified the disadvantages experienced by those from ethnic minority and faith backgrounds and explored ways these could be reduced. We understood the barriers at the workplace and produced guidance to improve returning to previously held roles. An ideal way of engaging patients in supporting each other by sharing experiences (peer support) was put forward. Variations in symptoms on a daily and weekly basis were understood using wearable technology. We showed the value of using an objective 10-min Lean test in clinics for detecting dysautonomia. We tested a questionnaire instrument that we had developed to measure change in long COVID and approved its use for future studies. The impact of the condition on caregivers and the country's economy was estimated. In summary, we established how the condition of long COVID needs to be recognised and how the condition should be ideally managed, and we helped improve the NHS pathways for the condition. Executive Summary Background: Long COVID, a novel condition of persistent symptoms beyond 4 weeks after COVID-19 infection, affects more than 2 million people in the UK. The NHS in England invested in starting specialist clinics for the condition. Many patients did not have access to these specialist clinics, there were long waits to be seen, and there was considerable variation in practice and pathways. There was a need for more recognition of the condition, peer support and informing national policy for the condition. Aims and objectives: We sought to optimise and standardise long-term COVID care both within and outside NHS specialist clinics, including improving access, reducing inequalities, helping patients manage their symptoms effectively at home, and providing guidance and decision support for primary care. We aimed to systematically analyse variation in symptom presentation and current practices, iteratively improve pathways and systems of care, standardise outcome measurement, and disseminate better practices. Methods and analysis: This mixed-method, multi-site study was informed by the principles of applied health services research, quality improvement, co-design, outcome measurement and learning health systems. It was developed in close partnership with patients (whose stated priorities were prompt clinical assessment; evidence-based advice and treatment; and help with returning to work and other roles) and with front-line clinicians. Workstreams and tasks to optimise assessment, treatment and monitoring were based in three contrasting settings: [1] specialist management in 10 long COVID clinics across the UK, via a quality improvement collaborative (QIC), experience-based co-design and targeted efforts to reduce inequalities of access, analyse vocational problems and develop a vocational rehabilitation programme, recommend a framework for peer support groups; [2] patients self-management at home, with wearable sensors and technology-supported symptom monitoring, and regular completion of outcome measures including the C19-YRS (COVID-19 Yorkshire Rehabilitation Scale) on our digital outcome measures platform; and [3] harnessing electronic record data from primary and secondary care to study referral pathways, analyse primary care coding and referrals at the primary-secondary care interface, along with analysis of productivity loss and healthcare burden. Study governance included a 9- member active patient advisory group (PAG) and patient advisory network (PAN). The PAG co-designed and co-produced all steps of the study from concept to dissemination. An external advisory group (EAG) provided strategic oversight and access to stakeholders independent of the study. We also undertook additional service evaluation studies from NHS England and Public Health Scotland analysing outcomes of long COVID clinics in their respective nations. Results and key findings: Some of the key findings were: The goal of accessible, holistic, multidisciplinary assessment and management was met by different services using different service models and staff mix. Most topics prioritised for quality improvement had a weak or contested evidence base, but even in the absence of high-quality research evidence, much learning and improvement occurred. The dual burden of having to fight to be heard in a context of structural inequalities takes its toll and could be part of the reason why so few people from ethnically minoritised communities attend long COVID clinics. A roadmap resource has been developed to address many people’s experience of multiple poorly planned return-to-work attempts and inadequate adjustments. Peer support in long COVID in the form of online networks has benefited many long COVID patients already but does not suit everyone in its current format. Clinical severity types (mild/moderate/ severe) have been identified, which fluctuate longitudinally. Understanding the triggers help patients make adjustments to physical/cognitive/emotional exertion and minimise the fluctuations in daily life. C19-YRSm was shown to be a valid, reliable, responsive, and easy-to-administrate measure for the condition. The Minimal Important Difference (MID) (2 points) and Minimal Clinically Important Difference (MCID) (4 points) values for C19-YRSm have been determined to be used in clinical and research settings to reliably capture the condition trajectory and the effect of interventions and also help inform clinical policy. Primary care coding for the condition was found to be inadequate. The average aggregate value of productivity loss since incident infection nationally was £5.7 billion per year and the corresponding value for informal caregiving was £4.8 billion annually. The 10-min Lean Test (active stand test) must be undertaken as a regular objective test on all patients to detect and manage orthostatic intolerance (dysautonomia). The NHS England and NHS Scotland service evaluation studies showed specialist clinics led to some improvement in condition severity, but many patients continued to have symptoms and disability similar to a long-term condition. Conclusions and recommendations for future research: The care of long COVID in the UK has been improved and optimised. We need further research on longer term outcomes in the condition, continued investment in clinical services and further development of integrated services to manage long COVID and related post-infection conditions. An integrated pathway at the interface of primary and secondary care enabled management by a multidisciplinary team. A whole systems approach is needed that can take into account the interaction of multiple elements that ultimately impact the experiences of minoritised groups living with long COVID. This may enable better recognition, treatment and support for people from minoritised groups living with the symptoms of this condition. title: Let there be music: Prompt, command, and cultural capital in the AI music generator Suno
abstract: This paper examines the role of language in prompt-based music production through the case of the AI music generator Suno and questions the widespread claim that such systems democratize music production. Building on Agamben’s (2022) concept of command, the paper conceptualizes the prompt as a command that initiates production. Drawing on Bourdieu’s (1986) concept of cultural capital, the paper considers how linguistic competence may shape prompt construction. The paper adopts an interpretive case study approach. For Suno, the paper tested one minimal and one elaborated text-based prompt in the platform’s freely accessible v4.5 Simple mode and compared the first musical output presented for each prompt. The minimal prompt consisted of a brief, general description, whereas the elaborated prompt included linguistic detail and musical terminology specific to the selected genre. The analysis focused on rock music because its well-established terminology – such as riff, distortion, power chord, pre-chorus, and guitar solo – enabled a clearer comparison of how linguistic and musical specifications were reflected in the musical outputs. The findings indicate that, in these two examples, the minimal prompt is accompanied by a more detailed style description displayed by the platform, whereas the description associated with the elaborated prompt selectively retains, renames, and restructures elements of the original prompt. Thus, algorithmic interpretation is defined as a theoretical account of how the platform maps the user’s command to the resulting musical decisions. The paper concludes that the musical output can be understood as the asymmetrical co-production of the user’s command, shaped by cultural capital, and the platform’s algorithmic interpretation, with the latter occupying a structurally dominant position in this relationship. These findings suggest that the widespread discourse presenting AI music generators as democratizing music production may overlook the distinction between access to production and control over the production process.
authors: Selim Tan

title: Lifefulness - feasibility and acceptability of a self-guided digital intervention promoting mental health among older adults in Sweden
abstract: Background: The number and proportion of older adults (≥65 years) is increasing worldwide, already exceeding 20% in Sweden. The growing number of older adults with concurrent physical and mental health issues, pose a major challenge for healthcare, rendering a critical need for low-cost, easily accessible behavioural interventions. Methods: This single-group feasibility trial evaluated a transdiagnostic digital self-help intervention, "Lifefulness", specifically adapted for older adults and designed to promote behaviour change and mental health. Content was based on cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) and healthy ageing principles. Older adults were recruited from the community (age range 65-85) and were assigned to the six week intervention, which included three brief phone interviews focusing on program adherence. Outcomes included program use and acceptability as well as preliminary effects on quality of life and mental health outcomes. Results: A total of 73 individuals were included. Program utility was high on average, with 72% of participants engaging with the intervention daily or several times a week. The average time spent on the three interviews was 33 min per participant. The program was associated with favourable changes in various mental health symptoms and higher ratings of quality of life and the participants reported high satisfaction and credibility. Conclusions: These findings support the feasibility and resource-efficiency of a digital self-help intervention for older adults. The intervention warrants further testing in a randomized trial with long-term follow-up assessments of both outcomes and healthcare consumption.
authors: Martin Kraepelien; Karin Romberg; Neda Agahi; Nitya Jayaram‐Lindström; Amit Chakrabarti; Arun Kandasamy; Indranil Saha; Christopher Sundström

title: Lightweight Blockchain Enabled Privacy-Preserving IoT Framework for Secure Parkinson’s Disease Fall Detection and Healthcare Monitoring
abstract: The increased number of PD patients has increased the adoption of the Internet of Things (IoT)-based wearable devices for remote monitoring and automatic fall detection, which helps to notify caregivers and clinicians immediately. Unfortunately, the continuous transmission of patients' physiological and movement data through wireless sensor networks increases their vulnerability to risks of unauthorized access, poor authentication, and privacy loss. Most importantly, current automatic fall detection systems offer low levels of data verification and protection. To overcome this issue, the proposed study introduces the Cross-Layer Lightweight Starvation Blockchain Security scheme with the Provable Master Seeding Authentication Policy (LWSBS-PMSAP) for preserving privacy in the PD monitoring system. The data collected from the IoT wearable devices is first encrypted with the Advanced Shuffle Standard Starvation Encryption Cryptography (ASS-SEC) and packaged in the form of blockchain blocks, which are then stored on the encrypted servers; a controller node performs the verification and validation of the policy to prevent any unauthorized interference, while a zero-knowledge proof-based Provable Master Seeding Authentication (PMSA) protocol verifies devices and users. The framework was tested on the PD monitoring dataset of 100 patients having 1,500 sensor samples. LWSBS-PMSAP obtained a 98.7% throughput rate, 180 ms latency, 99.2% security rate, and 96.8% privacy preservation, and performed better than Ethereum-based, Hyperledger-based, and general lightweight blockchain frameworks. In the context of fall detection, the proposed framework attained 98.7% accuracy, 97.4% precision, 99.0% recall, and 98.2% F1-Score, performing better than CNN-based, LSTM-based, and ensemble-DNN-based models. The ablation study also proved that the contribution of each component in terms of security and privacy gain is measurable. Further, the statistical validation (mean, standard deviation, 95% confidence interval) revealed that there is low variation in performance of the proposed framework among the multiple trials. It can be concluded that LWSBS-PMSAP provides a computationally lightweight, secure, and privacy-preserving solution for real-time fall detection and remote monitoring of Parkinson's Disease, with clear potential for extension to broader IoT-based healthcare applications.
authors: M Rakhee; M. Sudheep Elayidom; Baiju Karun
