title: A coordinated paracrine islet cell network regulating β-cell Ca2+ dynamics
abstract: Pulsatile insulin secretion originates from oscillations in cytosolic free Ca 2+ in pancreatic islet β-cells. Decades of work have identified multiple determinants of these oscillations, including glucose metabolism, ion channels, ER Ca 2+ handling, cellular heterogeneity, and paracrine and neurohormonal signaling. Yet their relative contributions under physiological conditions remain unresolved because each experimental preparation preserves only a subset of these regulatory layers. Here, we review evidence that intercellular paracrine signaling, in addition to cell-autonomous β-cell machinery, is an important determinant of oscillation frequency and coordination. Simultaneous Ca 2+ imaging of α-cells and β-cells reveals tightly coordinated activity, with α-cells following β-cells after a conserved ∼20-s delay. Perturbation of glucagon signaling further indicates that α-cell signaling can modulate β-cell oscillation frequency. In vivo imaging of islets engrafted in the anterior chamber of the eye shows that α-cell expansion enhances β-cell Ca 2+ coordination in a glucagon-receptor-dependent manner. Extending this circuit to δ-cells, somatostatin limits oscillation frequency primarily by suppressing α-cell glucagon release, allowing the δ-cell–α-cell–β-cell paracrine circuit to shift β-cell oscillations between fast, mixed, and slow regimes. In vivo , a glycemia-dependent slow-to-fast transition is lost in diabetic mice and rescued by GLP-1 receptor agonism. Under anesthesia-free conditions, however, islets occupy a slow, highly synchronized oscillatory regime in which glucose modulates amplitude, period, and plateau fraction without altering network coordination. Together, these findings suggest that the δ-cell–α-cell–β-cell circuit represents an important regulatory layer shaping β-cell Ca 2+ oscillations alongside intrinsic β-cell mechanisms and extrinsic physiological inputs. β-cell dysfunction may therefore involve not only altered oscillation frequency and coordination, but also disrupted paracrine regulation by glucagon and somatostatin.
authors: Philip Tröster; Montse Visa; Martin G. Köhler; Per‐Olof Berggren

title: A critical review of microfluidic dielectrophoresis technology in microparticle separation chips
abstract: Abstract In recent years, dielectrophoresis (DEP) technology based on microfluidic chips has become a key method for the efficient manipulation of particles, owing to its advantages of being non-contact, highly precise and highly controllable. This paper reviews the latest advancements, fundamental principles, mixing mechanisms, application fields, and future challenges associated with DEP particle separation technology. It provides a detailed overview of the structural design, separation efficiency, voltage, frequency and other parameters of electrode-based and insulator-based DEP, and discusses the challenges currently facing this technology. Furthermore, the paper proposes a novel classification scheme for synergistic strategies combining DEP with other separation mechanisms. These are categorized into sequential separation, synergistic separation, and multi-stage separation, with a discussion of the respective advantages and limitations of each approach. Finally, the paper summarizes recent progress in the application of DEP particle separation across fields such as biological cell identification, environmental particle monitoring, and chemical particle analysis. It concludes by outlining future directions for the development of DEP and hybrid separation technologies, thereby offering theoretical and technical references for achieving high-precision, high-throughput, and multifunctional capabilities within the field of microfluidic separation.
authors: Yu Liu; Wenbo Han; Haoyu Yue; Xinran Wang; Siqi Zhang; Guo Wenxuan; Xiaotong Mu; Wei Li; H.O.N.G.P.E.N.G. Zhang

title: A dielectric spectroscopic measurement of single Saccharomyces pastorianus growth and heat-shock response
abstract: Cell growth and heat shock response (HSR) are central to cellular adaptation, fate determination, and survival under fluctuating environments, yet their continuous quantification in individual suspended microbial cells remains challenging. Here, we present microwave dielectric spectroscopic cytometry (DiSC) for real-time, label-free monitoring of single-cell growth and HSR in budding yeast, Saccharomyces pastorianus , under physiological culture conditions. Integrated optical microscopy enabled simultaneous tracking of morphological dynamics during growth, heat shock, and apoptosis. At 32 °C, cells exhibited continuous biomass accumulation with fluctuating growth rates but relatively conserved molecular composition profiles (MCPs). Upon heat shock (from 32 °C to 42 °C), cells displayed discontinuous biomass accumulation, rapid mass fluctuations, and dynamically varying MCPs across all 17 cells analyzed. A subset of cells subsequently underwent apoptotic collapse, with onset times ranging from ~ 20 min during temperature ramping to more than 60 min at 42 °C or remaining absent throughout the 340 min observation window, revealing pronounced cell-to-cell heterogeneity. Post-apoptotic cells exhibited stabilized MCP dynamics. Analyses of two- to four-cell lineages further demonstrated divergent apoptotic outcomes among closely related progeny. These results establish DiSC as a promising platform for continuous single-cell quantification of growth, stress adaptation, and phenotypic heterogeneity while highlighting opportunities for further improvements in system performance and analytical capability.
authors: Md Saiful Islam; Thomas P. Caldwell; Pingshan Wang

title: A discrete generative model of neuronal spiking activity on microelectrode arrays
abstract: Generative models of neural activity could help characterize tissue dynamics, compare experimental conditions, and simulate population activity for applications ranging from disease and drug-response studies to closed-loop experimentation. Existing approaches, however, typically assume a fixed set of sorted neurons, whereas high-density microelectrode arrays produce extremely sparse, array-wide binary spike volumes in which the observed subset of electrodes varies across assays. We introduce a discrete generative model that represents this activity using a shared vocabulary of spatiotemporal motifs. A residual vector-quantized autoencoder learns the motif vocabulary, while a factorized masked transformer predicts where activity occurs and which motif appears at each active location. We evaluate the model on 31 assays spanning human brain organoids and acute \emph{ex vivo} human hippocampal tissue. The learned motifs are broadly reused: assay identity explains only $9%$ of the entropy in motif use, and motif overlap across tissue types is comparable to overlap within them. When representation quality is evaluated independently of the generative prior, our approach achieves $5.2\times$ the voxel-level reconstruction average precision of a matched flat tokenizer. For masked completion and free generation, the full model achieves $1.4$--$2.6\times$ the site-level average precision of the matched generative baseline and outperforms it across all four families of generation metrics. These results establish a compact, reusable representation for array-wide spiking activity without learned assay-specific parameters, providing a scalable foundation for generative modeling across diverse neural preparations.
authors: Md. Sayed Tanveer; Mohammed A. Mostajo-Radji; Ge Wang

title: A multiplex droplet digital PCR assay for chromosome copy-number determination in Candida albicans.
abstract: Chromosome copy-number variation is a major contributor to genome plasticity and adaptation in Candida albicans, a leading fungal pathogen of humans. Aneuploidy, defined as deviations from the normal diploid chromosome set, rapidly alters gene dosage and is often observed during exposure to host-imposed and antifungal stress. Accurate detection and quantification of chromosomal copy-number changes are thus essential to dissect the mechanisms by which C. albicans adapts and evolves. Here, we describe the development, optimization, and validation of a 6-color, 16-plex droplet digital PCR assay for simultaneous quantification of all C. albicans chromosome arms in a single reaction. Each target is detected by a unique dual-color or single-color combination of probes, enabling high-order multiplexing through binary fluorescence encoding. Following optimization of probe concentrations, PCR cycling parameters, genomic DNA extraction, and pretreatment with restriction enzymes, the assay provides accurate, reproducible chromosome-level copy-number estimates that correlate closely with whole-genome sequencing results across euploid and aneuploid isolates. Compared to whole-genome sequencing, the assay is rapid, cost-effective, and scalable, requiring minimal DNA input and allowing high-throughput analysis of large collections of isolates. The 16-plex assay thus provides a platform for dissecting genome instability and adaptive evolution in C. albicans.
authors: Eli Isael Maciel; Sylvain Ursuegui; Sana Ahmed-Seghir; Corinne Maufrais; Stéphanie Roy; Cécile Gautier; Philipp Brandt; Cécile Jovelet; Laras Pitayu; Iuliana V Ene

title: A practical guide to Bayesian optimization for organic chemists
abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) is a strategy for global optimization, based on iterative refinement of a machine learning model. This algorithm can aid chemists in finding the highest possible reaction outcome (e.g., yield, er , or turnover frequency) from a relatively small number of experiments. In recent times, BO has garnered great interest in the organic synthesis community as a computer-guided method to increase the efficiency of reaction optimization. This method complements design of experiments (DoE) and traditional "one variable at a time" (OVAT) experimentation. However, beginning a BO campaign can be an intimidating prospect to an organic chemist. To lower the barrier of entry, we wish to share some insights gleaned from experience using BO for reaction optimization.
authors: Rachel Shey; Sven Roediger; Abigail G. Doyle; Julian G. West

title: A review on monitoring orthodontic treatment: from traditional approaches to innovative point-of-care tools
abstract: Orthodontic treatment is performed to treat malocclusions by improving oral functions, tooth alignment, and facial esthetics that impact the quality of life of patients significantly. Nevertheless, various factors like complexity of malocclusions, patient compliance, and dental hygiene can influence treatment outcomes. Traditional diagnostic methods such as clinical evaluation, radiography techniques, and dental casts have played a major role in orthodontics and have remained a standard diagnostic method in dentistry to date. On the other hand, these methods are associated with major disadvantages like radiation exposure and invasive procedures. To address these limitations, recent diagnostic methods have identified various biomarkers in gingival crevicular fluid and saliva as non-invasive diagnostic methods. These biomarkers can help clinicians in planning orthodontic treatment at the optimal time and determine the appropriate initiation of the treatment. Point-of-care diagnostic tools such as lateral flow assays, Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay, Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats and microfluidic devices, and wearable technologies are emerging as promising alternatives for orthodontic treatment monitoring by offering rapid, cost-effective, and non-invasive alternatives to traditional methods. Recent developments such as incorporation of artificial intelligence and machine learning into orthodontic software attempt to improve the overall monitoring of orthodontic treatment. This review aims to present various traditional and innovative methods that have shown promising outcomes in research, along with insights into emerging areas that serve as potential game changers in orthodontic treatment monitoring.
authors: Ananya Nair; Prajwal Shetty; M.S. Ravi

title: AI Agents for CRISPR Diagnostics: From Automation to Bounded Autonomy
abstract: Recent years have witnessed rapid advances in clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) diagnostics, artificial intelligence (AI), and self-driving laboratories for automation. CRISPR diagnostics have emerged as a promising strategy for earlier disease detection, with Cas12a and Cas13a targeting DNA and RNA, respectively, and converting that recognition into collateral reporter cleavage. In parallel, different subsets of AI have advanced rapidly, with machine learning (ML) interpreting biosensor readouts, and large language models (LLMs) and AI agents applied to automation. Laboratory automation and self-driving platforms reduce the workload of human experimentalists and enable scale-up, having run long unattended campaigns in materials discovery. However, how these advances in AI, CRISPR diagnostics and automation could be integrated to enable a future of autonomous biosensing remains unresolved. In this perspective, we evaluate CRISPR diagnostics as autonomous systems, where analytical metrics alone cannot ensure robustness, failure-mode predictability, recoverability and auditability. We then propose a bounded-autonomy layer in which multimodal evidence, scored by ML, gates a Sense, quality control (QC), Decide, Act and Report loop, with guardrailed LLM agents invoked only when QC flags a run, selecting pre-validated actions under deterministic validation. By tying detectable failure modes to validated recovery actions, we outline a path toward bounded autonomy in CRISPR diagnostics, where a device unable to act safely abstains and escalates.
authors: Sina Jamalzadegan; Mahsa Bagi; Sepehr Soltani; Zahra Joudaki; Akhil Penumudy; David H. Haussler; Mohammed A. Mostajo-Radji; Mircea Teodorescu; Qingshan Wei

title: AI Driven Multidomain Research: New Frontiers in Science, Business and Technology
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is no longer confined to computer science. The same families of learning algorithms now predict protein structures, price financial assets, design semiconductor layouts and personalise customer journeys. This diffusion has created a new kind of scholarship in which methods, data and problem formulations move rapidly between science, business and technology. Yet the literature that documents this shift remains organised by discipline, and there is little integrative guidance on how AI-enabled knowledge actually travels across domains or on the institutional conditions under which such travel is productive. This paper addresses that gap through an integrative review and conceptual synthesis. We first consolidate representative evidence on how AI is reshaping inquiry in the natural sciences, in business and management, and in engineering and technology. We then propose the Multidomain AI Research Integration (MAIRI) framework, which explains cross-domain research value through three interacting layers: a foundation layer of shared data, compute and models; a translation layer comprising four transfer mechanisms (method, data and representation, problem-structure, and talent and tool transfer); and a governance layer that secures reproducibility, explainability, ethics and equitable access. Five propositions are derived to guide empirical testing, and a forward research agenda is set out. The paper contributes a common vocabulary for multidomain AI research and offers practical direction for universities, funding agencies and industry partners, particularly in emerging research systems such as India.
authors: Prof. (Dr.) Devanand Chavan Prof. (Dr.) E. B. Khedkar; Dr. Chetan Khedkar; Prof. Dasharath Suryavanshi Prof. Sapna R. Chavan
venue: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology

title: AI in Neuro-Oncology: An Overarching Review
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied across neuro-oncology domains to analyze complex, high-dimensional, multimodal data. Despite major advances in the biological understanding and classification of CNS tumors, clinical outcomes for many of them remain poor, reflecting intra- and inter-tumor heterogeneity and limitations of conventional reductionist approaches. AI offers a paradigm shift to capture this heterogeneity and provide quantitative, reproducible diagnostic, predictive, and prognostic insights. This article describes a joint effort across the Response Assessment in Neuro-Oncology (RANO) working groups to provide an overarching review of the AI use across six key domains of neuro-oncology: neuroimaging, neuropathology, laboratory medicine, neurosurgery, drug discovery, and clinical trials. Applications closest to clinical use include imaging segmentation and quantification, AI-assisted image reconstruction, DNA methylation-based classification, and workflow optimization. Radiogenomics, WSI-based molecular prediction, AI-guided surgical targeting, liquid biopsy interpretation, AI-guided drug discovery, digital twins, and in silico trials remain promising but require stronger prospective validation. Key challenges include limited availability of large diverse datasets, variability in data acquisition and reference standards, and limited external validation. This review provides a unifying framework for understanding the role of AI across neuro-oncology and highlights key considerations for its responsible implementation, emphasizing standardization, reproducibility, multi-institutional validation, and human oversight.
authors: Carla Pitarch-Abaigar; Philipp Lohmann; Patrick Aloy; Fátima Al‐Shahrour; Omar Arnaout; Wenya Linda Bi; Norbert Galldiks; Jason T. Huse; Philipp Karschnia; MacLean P. title: AI-Assisted Risk and Incident Analysis: Advances and Future Opportunities
abstract: Operational risk and security incidents now unfold across distributed, cloud-native estates that generate volumes of telemetry no human team can manually triage at speed. Over the past decade, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) have moved from experimental log-mining prototypes to production components of security operations centres, site reliability engineering practices, and enterprise risk functions. This paper synthesises the advances that have made AIassisted risk and incident analysis viable and examines the opportunities and limitations that will shape the next phase of adoption. We organise the state of the art into five capability areas: anomaly and detection analytics over logs, metrics, and traces; alert triage, deduplication, and correlation; natural language processing (NLP) and large language models (LLMs) for incident summarisation, knowledge retrieval, and postmortem authoring; automation and orchestration of response workflows; and human–AI collaboration in the analyst loop. We map these capabilities to established incident-handling and risk-management frameworks and present a structured capabilities table describing typical inputs, methods, and outputs. We then interrogate the open challenges that temper enthusiasm: model hallucination and reliability, the sensitivity and governance of incident data, the immaturity of evaluation methodology, and the operational hazards of over-automation. Finally, we propose a research agenda spanning benchmarking, retrieval-grounded and explainable reasoning, evaluation of human–AI teams, and resilienceaware automation. We argue that the near-term value of AI in this domain lies less in autonomous decision-making than in augmenting scarce expert attention, and that trustworthy deployment depends on grounding, evaluation, and human oversight rather than on model scale alone.
authors: Uchechi Mary-Linda Unamma
venue: WORLD JOURNAL OF INNOVATION AND MODERN TECHNOLOGY

title: AI-Driven Approaches in Pyridine-Based Drug Discovery: Implementation, Challenges and Future Perspectives
abstract: Pyridine is a heterocyclic scaffolds in medicinal chemistry and serves as a key structural component in many approved drugs used to treat cancer, viral infections, bacterial diseases, inflammatory disorders, and neurological conditions. Owing to its biological activities, pyridine continues to attract significant attention in drug discovery research. However, approaches for the identification and optimisation of pyridine-based drug candidates are often labour-intensive, time-consuming, and costly. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a tool capable of transforming the drug development process by accelerating the discovery of novel agents and improving decision-making throughout stages of research. This chapter explores the role of AI technologies, including machine learning, deep learning, and generative models, in the discovery and development of pyridine-based therapeutics. Particular emphasis is placed on AI-assisted virtual screening, quantitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR) modelling, molecular property prediction, de novo molecular design, and ADMET evaluation. The integration of AI with computational techniques such as molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, and network-based analyses has enhanced the identification of pyridine derivatives with improved biological activity and safety profiles. Additionally, applications and success stories demonstrating the practical implementation of AI in pyridine drug discovery are highlighted. The chapter further discusses limitations, including challenges related to data quality, model transparency, and experimental validation. Finally, developments such as explainable AI, foundation models, autonomous laboratories, and personalised medicine are examined as opportunities for advancing pyridine-based drug discovery. these advances underscore the potential of AI to reshape the development of pyridine-derived therapeutics and facilitate the discovery of safer, more effective medicines.
authors: Pratima Katiyar; Kalpana Kushwaha; Suprabha Nishad

title: AI-Driven Optimization of Electrochemical Fertilizer Processes
abstract: Conventional fertilizer production relies on centralized, fossil-fuel-intensive processes such as Haber–Bosch ammonia synthesis, with high energy demand and associated carbon emissions. Electrochemical routes to nitrogen and phosphorus fertilizers offer a potentially decentralized, renewable-powered alternative, but their practical performance remains limited by the interaction of catalyst structure, electrolyte composition, reactor architecture, and operating conditions. These variables do not act independently: fertilizer synthesis is fundamentally a coupled, high-dimensional optimization problem that is difficult to address by varying one factor at a time. This chapter argues that artificial intelligence becomes genuinely useful for this problem not as an isolated computational tool, but as a layer connecting experimental and sensor data with prediction, optimization, and control. The chapter examines four electrochemical fertilizer pathways nitrogen reduction, nitrate reduction, urea synthesis, and phosphorus recovery alongside the functional materials and electrode architectures used to catalyze them. It then considers the reactors, analytical instrumentation, and real-time, in-situ sensors that generate the data on which these AI applications depend, treating this measurement infrastructure as inseparable from AI-enabled optimization. Three distinct roles for AI and machine learning are developed: discovering and screening catalyst candidates across combinatorial design spaces; predicting process behavior under coupled and time-varying operating conditions; and identifying and maintaining optimal conditions through Bayesian optimization, multi-objective search, and autonomous control. Techno-economic and life-cycle assessment are introduced as additional decision criteria, since chemical performance alone cannot define an optimal process once cost and environmental impact are considered. A fully integrated, autonomous electrochemical fertilizer platform has not yet been demonstrated in the literature reviewed here. Instead, the chapter shows that individual components of such a system, together with several partial integrations from adjacent process industries, already exist and provide a technically credible foundation for future integration. Data scarcity, the DFT–experiment gap, sensor reliability, reproducibility, interpretability, and scale-up nevertheless remain major barriers to realizing this integration in practice.
authors: Muhammad Qamar Bilal

title: AI-Driven Scientific Computing Workflows: A Systems Review of Orchestration, Execution, Reproducibility and Provenance
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded within scientific computing workflows that combine simulation, data processing, optimisation, visualisation and experimental or observational components. Learned models may serve as explicit workflow components, retain persistent state and, in adaptive settings, influence subsequent computation. Existing work has characterised scientific workflow management systems, dynamic and steered workflows, AI--HPC coupling motifs and the machine-learning lifecycle, although these areas are often discussed separately. This review brings them together from a systems perspective. We distinguish conventional scientific workflows, machine-learning pipelines, AI-coupled high-performance computing (HPC) workflows and broader automated research workflows, and propose a continuum describing the depth of AI participation from a computational stage to co-adaptive workflow control. The associated systems requirements are organised around five concerns: control and orchestration; compute and execution; data and model state; reproducibility and provenance; and governance and assurance. Representative systems and applications include AI-steered molecular simulation, drug and materials discovery, simulation--surrogate coupling and distributed self-driving laboratories. Workflow-level evaluation is considered in terms of scientific progress, execution cost, data movement, resource use, resilience and decision traceability. We conclude by identifying open problems in dynamic workflow representation, state-aware recovery, heterogeneous scheduling, interoperable data planes, model-mediated decision provenance and reproducible adaptive execution.
authors: Jamie J. Alnasir

title: AI-enabled CVD synthesis, quality control, and autonomous manufacturing of 2D materials
abstract: Abstract Two-dimensional materials exhibit extraordinary properties for next-generation electronics, optoelectronics, and biosensors, yet industrial adoption remains limited by challenges in scalable chemical vapor deposition (CVD) synthesis and consistent quality control. This review examines how artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are shifting CVD synthesis from empirical trial-and-error toward data-driven manufacturing. Key engineering bottlenecks address large-area uniformity, nucleation control, batch-to-batch reproducibility, and precursor delivery. ML workflows for feature engineering, predictive modeling, and real-time in situ monitoring were also reviewed, while AI-assisted quality control via Raman/photoluminescence classification (random forest, XGBoost) and CNN-based image analysis is discussed alongside emerging autonomous laboratories, closed-loop feedback, and FAIR data ecosystems, offering a practical roadmap for reliable, reproducible 2D material manufacturing.
authors: Musa Ibne Mannan; Premesh Mistry; Varin Kansal; Victoria Estrada; Juyoung Leem

title: AI-facilitated analytical chemistry technologies: Advancing liquid biopsy for early cancer detection
abstract: Cancer remains one of the leading causes of morbidity and mortality worldwide, and many solid malignancies are still diagnosed at advanced stages, when curative-intent therapies are less feasible and prognosis is substantially poorer. This diagnostic gap underscores the need for sensitive, minimally invasive approaches to early tumor detection. As an emerging alternative to tissue biopsy, liquid biopsy enables minimally invasive analysis of tumor-derived circulating biomarkers, including circulating tumor cells, circulating tumor DNA, extracellular vesicles, proteins, and metabolites. Its compatibility with repeated sampling enables longitudinal application across early detection, recurrence monitoring, prognostic assessment, and precision oncology. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) with analytical chemistry technologies, including solid-phase microextraction, spectroscopy, mass spectrometry, electrochemical sensing, and microfluidics, can improve the detection, interpretation, and clinical translation of liquid biopsy-derived molecular data. This review critically evaluates AI-assisted analytical chemistry approaches for liquid biopsy-based early cancer detection, with an emphasis on multi-omics analysis. Specifically, this review examines (1) the biological relevance of circulating biomarkers, (2) isolation, enrichment, separation, and detection methods across the pre-analytical and instrumental stages, and (3) the evolution of AI from machine learning-based classification toward deep learning-based representation learning, self-supervised and transformer-based modeling, and multimodal and foundation-model approaches for molecular signal recognition, multi-omics integration, cancer classification, and cancer signal origin prediction. Furthermore, it discusses applications in cancer detection, recurrence monitoring, and multi-cancer early detection (MCED), as well as treatment-response assessment and AI-assisted clinical decision support, together with challenges involving assay standardization, model interpretability, false-positive management, and prospective validation. This review aims to provide an integrated framework that bridges analytical chemistry and AI to support the clinical translation of AI-assisted liquid biopsy for early cancer detection.
authors: Shengdong Ran; Chunjie Shi; Wanyi Chen; Lixian Li; Janusz B. Pawliszyn

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN MENTAL HEALTH: BENEFITS AND CHALLENGES OF ELECTRONIC HEALTH RECORDS
abstract: A incorporação de novas tecnologias de inteligência artificial aos electronic healthcare records (EHRs) tem proporcionado um forte aumento na capacidade de acumular e analisar dados dos pacientes. E a área de saúde mental tem sido uma das beneficiárias deste potencial de melhorias, proporcionando aos seus profissionais ganhos de tempo e eficiência na gestão de informações médicas. Entretanto, há relatos de problemas que estão surgindo na medida em que a utilização das tecnologias de IA se intensifica. Este quadro inclui questões referentes à gestão de informações sensíveis dos pacientes, à falta de padronização dos dados de saúde mental, prejudicando a interoperabilidade dos mesmos, o receio de que o relacionamento terapêutico paciente-profissional seja prejudicado, além da preocupação que os profissionais estão tendo pela possibilidade de serem substituídos pelas tecnologias de IA. Considerando este contexto, o presente artigo tem por objetivo identificar e analisar a dinâmica de incorporação das tecnologias de IA à área de saúde mental. Para realizar este objetivo, foi realizada uma revisão de literatura envolvendo publicações sobre o tema dos últimos seis anos. Ao final, são oferecidas algumas sugestões para desenvolvimento de futuras pesquisas que possam explorar mais possíveis soluções para os problemas identificados, ao longo do processo de adoção de novas tecnologias de IA na área de saúde mental que está em curso.
authors: Bento Alves Costa Filho; Daniel Sousa Jorge; Felipe Luiz de Morais

title: Abstracts From the 2026 Health Care Systems Research Network (HCSRN) Annual Conference, Dallas, Texas
abstract: The Health Care Systems Research Network (HCSRN) comprises 18 learning health systems with integrated care delivery and embedded research units. The network's annual conference serves as a forum for research teams from member institutions to disseminate project findings, explore scientific collaborations, and share insights about population-based research practices that can measurably improve health and health care for all. The theme of this year's conference was "Scaling Learning Health Systems: Data-Driven Pathways to Better Outcomes." Abstracts presented at HCSRN 2026 are published in this issue supplement of the Journal of Patient-Centered Research and Reviews, the journal of record for HCSRN's annual conference proceedings.
authors: Health Care Systems Research Network
venue: Journal of patient-centered research and reviews

title: Abstracts From the 2026 Health Care Systems Research Network (HCSRN) Annual Conference, Dallas, Texas:How Can Community Mental Health Provision for Working-Age Adults in England Be Improved? An Accelerated Parallelised Realist Literature Review
abstract: Background: Community mental health services in England face persistent challenges in access, capacity, and equity, exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic. The 2019 Community Mental Health Framework aimed to deliver integrated, personcentred care, but implementation has been hindered by resource constraints and systemic inequalities. These pressures compromise safety and outcomes, particularly for minoritised groups. Understanding the conditions under which services succeed or fail is critical for improving care delivery and informing strategies that address disparities in mental health systems. Methods: We developed a novel accelerated parallelised realist-informed literature review methodology to deliver this research in under one month to inform policy decision-making by a health regulator in England. We examined contexts and mechanisms influencing safe and effective community mental health provision for working-age adults to identify what worked about existing policies, for whom, and why. Sources included grey literature, systematic searches of Medline and PsycINFO, and expert peer input. Inclusion criteria focused on UK-based studies relevant to adults aged 18-65 accessing community mental health services. Review processes were streamlined to deliver findings within four weeks while maintaining rigour. From 81 sources, we developed initial programme theories and 26 context-mechanism-outcome configurations (CMOCs). Results: Capacity constraints and entrenched inequalities emerged as dominant factors shaping service quality and safety. Strict referral criteria and fragmented care pathways were associated with disengagement and deterioration of patient condition. CMOCs clustered around three themes: learning from practice and safety, medicine optimisation, and research gaps. Key recommendations include to (1) develop culturally appropriate, co-produced measures of risk encompassing patient, public, and systemic perspectives; (2) expand service capacity to reduce transition risks and improve timeliness of care; and (3) strengthen engagement and trust among minoritised communities to address disparities and improve outcomes. Conclusions: Findings highlight the interdependence of patient safety and systemic resilience. Practices that restrict access amplify risks and perpetuate inequities. Implementing these recommendations can help health systems adapt to changing demands, reduce inequalities, and deliver safer, more responsive care for working-age adults. While focused on England, these insights offer transferable lessons for health systems globally seeking to strengthen community mental health provision under resource constraints and evolving challenges.
authors: Justin Avery Aunger; Bianca Ungureanu; Rachel Posaner; Christian Bohm; Ross Millar; S. M. Fenton
venue: University of Birmingham Research Portal (University of Birmingham)

title: Acute loss of PLIN5 in brown adipocytes reveals its indispensable role in maintaining mitochondrial function and cold tolerance.
abstract: Cold exposure induces adaptive molecular and mitochondrial remodeling in brown adipose tissue (BAT) of mice to sustain thermogenesis. We previously showed that the lipid droplet protein Perilipin 5 (PLIN5) is strongly induced in BAT by cold exposure and promotes thermogenic gene expression, mitochondrial remodeling, and uncoupled respiration. However, constitutive BAT-specific PLIN5 deletion impaired mitochondrial function without causing cold intolerance, suggesting physiological compensation, likely via induction of thermogenic genes in white adipose tissue (WAT). To test this possibility, we generated mice with doxycycline-inducible BAT-specific PLIN5 deletion. Acute PLIN5 deletion in adult mice during cold exposure reduced BAT thermogenic gene expression, mitochondrial cristae density, and uncoupled mitochondrial respiration, which resulted in cold intolerance. Unlike constitutive PLIN5 knockout mice, mice acutely rendered deficient of PLIN5 in BAT failed to mount a compensatory thermogenic response in inguinal WAT. Together, these findings demonstrate that PLIN5 is required for mitochondrial homeostasis in brown adipocytes and for adaptive thermogenesis during cold exposure. Notably, by cell fractionation and protease protection assay, we observed that PLIN5 enriches on the outer mitochondrial membrane in BAT during cold exposure. We also observed that the absence of PLIN5 in BAT is not associated with reduced contacts between lipid droplets and mitochondria, thereby suggesting that the role of PLIN5 in adaptive thermogenesis may depend on its translocation to the mitochondrial outer membrane for a purpose unrelated to the formation of contacts between lipid droplets and mitochondria.
authors: Violeta I Gallardo Montejano; Chaofeng Yang; Hannah Hurtado; Perry E Bickel

title: Adaptive Integrated Microfluidic System with Real-Time Dielectric Feedback for Deterministic Micro-Manipulation
abstract: Abstract Conventional microfluidic particle sorting systems predominantly rely on static, open-loop operational principles, rendering them highly vulnerable to performance deterioration induced by cellular phenotypic heterogeneity and localized hydrodynamic fluctuations. Here, we introduce an adaptive integrated microfluidic system (AIMS) that implements a closed-loop sensing−decision−actuation−verification control framework via on-chip integration of dual-frequency impedance cytometry (IFC) and tunable traveling surface acoustic waves (T-TSAW). An upstream IFC array (1#IFC) performs real-time, label-free electrical interrogation of single-cell dielectric phenotypes. These transient signals are processed in real time by a custom finite-state machine (FSM) algorithm to dynamically modulate the downstream T-TSAW field. Concurrently, a downstream IFC array (2#IFC) performs post-sorting verification and feeds real-time state metrics back to the FSM core. This initiates an adaptive hill-climbing optimization loop to enable continuous acoustic frequency calibration. The system performance was rigorously evaluated using monodisperse polystyrene microspheres and biologically relevant colloidal models. The closed-loop architecture successfully isolated target MCF-7 cells from an erythrocyte-dominated simplified blood model, achieving an acoustic sorting efficiency of 95 ± 1.5% and a purity of 94 ± 2.5%. Furthermore, continuous adaptive sorting of primary mouse immune cell populations (PBMCs and neutrophils) was demonstrated, achieving a sorting efficiency of 92 ± 1.8% and a purity of 93 ± 6.7%. Ultimately, the seamless integration of transient electronic sensing algorithms with multiphysics mechanical actuation establishes a highly robust architectural framework for autonomous microelectromechanical manipulation platforms.
authors: Y Zhang; Zihe Guo; Langlang Yang; Zihao Li; Zhimeng Zhang; Wenping Geng; Zhangbin Ji; Ruiying Wang; Jian He; Xiujian Chou

title: Advanced configurations of needle and ring electrode arrays (NREAs) for superior EHD micropump efficiency
abstract: Abstract Electrohydrodynamic (EHD) micropumps generate fluid motion by applying a high DC voltage to electrode pairs, enabling direct conversion of electrical energy into hydraulic output. To improve power density, this study proposes a novel EHD micropump architecture, termed needle and ring electrode arrays (NREAs). Owing to their three-dimensional multilayer structure fabricated by MEMS technology, NREAs overcome limitations of previous designs, such as low integration and large device footprints. To further enhance pump performance, the effects of key geometric parameters (electrode gap, needle height, needle diameter, and ring inner diameter) were systematically investigated through numerical simulations and experimental validation. The results showed that a smaller electrode gap significantly increased the local electric-field intensity, resulting in higher pressure and flow rate. In particular, an electrode gap of 151 µm achieved a pressure of 1.53 kPa and a flow rate of 261.7 mm³/s at 2 kV. Increasing the needle height also improved both pressure and flow rate, whereas a smaller needle diameter mainly enhanced pressure generation with a relatively limited effect on flow rate. In contrast, ring inner diameter exhibited a trade-off between pressure and flow rate: smaller ring inner diameters increased pressure, while larger ring inner diameters promoted higher flow rates by reducing flow resistance. These findings demonstrate the importance of geometric optimization in tailoring EHD micropump performance for specific microfluidic and microrobotic applications. The proposed NREA architecture provides useful design guidelines for the development of high-performance, compact, and highly integrated EHD micropump systems.
authors: yichuan zhu; Su Jin Heo; Michael F. L. De Volder; Kazuhiro YOSHIDA; Joon-wan KIM

title: Advances In NLP-Driven Analytics for Automated Detection of Regulatory Liabilities in High-Volume Contracts
abstract: Contract portfolios at large enterprises now routinely exceed tens of thousands of active agreements, and the regulatory obligations attaching to those agreements have multiplied faster than legal review capacity. In 2025 this gap became acute: the EU Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) became applicable on 17 January without a transition period, forcing thousands of financial entities into large-scale contract remediation, while the general-purpose AI obligations of the EU AI Act took effect on 2 August. Both events created demand for systems that can read an entire contract portfolio and flag, with evidence, where regulatory liability exists. This paper reviews the state of natural language processing for automated regulatory liability detection as of the end of 2025 and sets out a layered architecture for production deployment. Regulatory liability detection is distinguished here from the better-studied task of clause extraction, on the argument that the former is a normative verification problem requiring a rule base, an evidence retrieval mechanism, and an adjudication step, rather than a span-labelling problem. Four technical shifts that reshaped the field during 2025 are surveyed: the maturation of long-context models beyond the length of most commercial contracts, the emergence of legal-specific retrieval evaluation, the arrival of explicit reasoning models capable of rule-grounded justification, and the closing but still material gap between proprietary and open-weight models on clause-level risk identification. Evidence is also drawn from compliance analytics research in financial audit, cybersecurity governance, critical infrastructure protection, procurement, supply chain assurance, payments, pharmaceutical regulation, aviation safety oversight, and enterprise systems engineering, on the argument that the design problems in regulatory liability detection are not confined to legal NLP and that adjacent literatures have already resolved several of them. A metric suite appropriate to the asymmetric cost structure of compliance work is then set out, in which a missed mandatory clause is not commensurate with a false alarm, and the F1 scores dominant in the literature are argued to be a poor proxy for deployment value. The paper closes on a reflexive governance question specific to this application: a system that classifies legal risk may itself fall within the scope of the regulation it is deployed to manage.
authors: Uchechi Ngonadi
venue: RESEARCH JOURNAL OF PURE SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY

title: Advances and perspectives in genetically encoded biosensors for biomarker detection and theranostic circuits
abstract: Effective biomarker detection is critical for timely and accurate clinical disease diagnosis. However, conventional analytical methodologies are often constrained by laborious procedures, reliance on specialized equipment, and an inherent inability to perform continuous in situ monitoring. To circumvent these limitations, synthetic biology has pioneered the development of genetically encoded biosensors as a rapid, highly sensitive, and cost-effective alternative. This review specifically focuses on transcriptional regulation-based biosensors, primarily those utilizing allosteric transcription factors (aTFs) and two-component systems (TCSs). By integrating these regulatory sensing modules into engineered microbial chassis, researchers can achieve continuous, real-time biomarker monitoring even within complex and otherwise inaccessible physiological environments. This review particularly focuses on microbial chassis rather than mammalian systems due to their highly tractable genetics, rapid response kinetics, and their unique potential to be deployed as autonomous living probiotics for in situ theranostics. Furthermore, coupling these sensors with engineered actuator genes enables the construction of intelligent therapeutic genetic circuits. This closed-loop theranostic paradigm facilitates simultaneous, real-time diagnosis and autonomous, localized therapeutic interventions, paving the way for personalized and dose-adaptive precision medicine. Finally, we summarize recent advancements in these biosensor platforms, explore their applications in targeted disease interventions, and discuss the contemporary challenges alongside future perspectives for their clinical translation.
authors: Jianping Xu; Qingsheng Qi; Qian Wang

title: Advances in engineering organ-on-a-chip models of angiogenesis
abstract: Angiogenesis plays a central role in embryonic development, tissue repair, tumor progression and cardiovascular remodeling.Because vascular growth involves a series of closely coordinated dynamic events, it is difficult for traditional in vitro and in vivo models to resolve the underlying mechanisms.Angiogenesis-on-a-chip (AoC) platforms provide microphysiological systems that can recapitulate key aspects of vascular growth in vitro, while enabling precise spatiotemporal control of the local microenvironment.These platforms combine microfluidic structures, three-dimensional hydrogels and relevant cell populations, so that biochemical gradients, mechanical cues and multicellular interactions can be regulated independently or in combination.When the relevant conditions are properly reproduced, endothelial sprouting, lumen formation and barrier function can be directly monitored and quantified.This review summarizes the recent progress of AoC design and discusses how these platforms can be used to study pathophysiological mechanisms, evaluate candidate therapeutic drugs and engineer vascularized tissues.The article also discusses persistent challenges, including platform standardization, characterization of the immune microenvironment, model validation and quantitative phenotypic analysis.By integrating engineering design with biological applications and an assessment of current limitations, this review provides a practical framework for advancing the application of AoC systems in vascular biology, therapeutic development and regenerative medicine.
authors: Yijun Tao; Ting Liu; Yi Zhang; Hongyan Yue; Huaiyi Zhang; 赁可; Chenxi Wu; Yasi Huang; Xiaran Liu; Xiaoli Wang; Fei Fang; Yang Shen

title: Advancing Multidisciplinary Research for Sustainable Innovation and Global Excellence
abstract: The rapidly changing global landscape is characterized by technological advancement, environmental challenges, social transformation, economic uncertainty, and evolving human needs.Addressing these complex challenges requires more than isolated disciplinary approaches.It calls for collaboration, integration of knowledge, and innovative thinking across diverse fields of study.Advancing Multidisciplinary Research for Sustainable Innovation and Global Excellence is conceived as a scholarly platform that brings together diverse perspectives, ideas, methodologies, and
