title: Autonomous Science Bench: Evaluating AI Agents for Autonomous Scientific Discovery
abstract: AI agents for autonomous scientific discovery must decide which experiments to run under a limited budget. Most benchmarks for science agents provide fixed datasets, while others that support active experimentation largely rely on simulation. We introduce Autonomous Science Bench, an initial release comprising six budgeted design-build-test-learn campaigns grounded in published experiments across biology, chemistry, and materials science. Agents select batches of designs, receive measurements from a lab service, and use the results to guide subsequent experiments before delivering a predictive model. Success requires passing two calibrated gates: a discovery gate, which evaluates the designs the agent measured, and a learning gate, which evaluates its model's ranking of held-out designs. In a pilot evaluation of eight agent-model configurations and 144 trials, the best configuration succeeds in 67% of trials, while the hardest campaign is solved in only three of 24 attempts. The two gates reveal different weaknesses: some agents build accurate rankings but find too few promising designs, while others find promising designs but fail to predict which unseen designs will perform well. These differences are obscured by overall success rates alone. We release version 0.1 of the campaigns, lab runtime, and public leaderboard at https://yibow.me/autonomous-science-bench.
authors: Yibo Wen; Han Liu

title: Autonomous adaptive spectral analysis with an LLM agent for self-driving laboratories
abstract: Self-driving laboratories accelerate materials exploration through autonomous closed-loop integration of synthesis, characterization, and next-experiment selection. However, characterization does not always directly provide the target property; measured spectra or images often require automated analysis to extract quantitative descriptors based on physically motivated assumptions and predefined criteria. Such procedures can fail for measurements outside these criteria, requiring a decision on whether a reliable value can be recovered or no numerical value should be reported. Here, we implemented an autonomous adaptive spectral-analysis agent using a large language model (LLM) to supervise a deterministic numerical-analysis routine. For each spectrum, the agent executes the predefined analysis script and assesses the result using the measured spectrum and fitting diagnostics. Valid results are accepted unchanged, recoverable failures are reanalyzed through bounded adjustments of predefined fitting parameters, and NaN (not a number) is returned when no scientifically defensible value can be obtained. We evaluated the workflow on optical transmittance spectra from 203 epitaxial beta-Ga2O3 films grown during a previously reported self-driving thin-film growth campaign. The predefined optical analysis script returned Urbach energy, an optical-quality metric, for 183 spectra and failed for 20. The agent retained those 183 values and evaluated 20 exception cases, recovering 16 through bounded parameter adjustments and returning NaN for 4 when the spectral evidence did not support a reliable Urbach tail. The audit records captured spectral features, parameter changes, and rationale for each decision. These results demonstrate autonomous scientific exception handling by an LLM agent while leaving quantitative property extraction to deterministic numerical analysis.
authors: Yuki K. Wakabayashi; Yui Ogawa

title: Bio-Inspired Self-Healing Nanostructures for Environmental Pollutant Degradation and Biomedical Diagnostics
abstract: Bio-inspired self-healing nanostructures mimic biological repair processes skin regeneration, bone remodeling, plant vascular reconnection using dynamic covalent chemistry, supramolecular assembly, hydrogen bonding, and metal-ligand coordination to recover mechanical strength, conductivity, and catalytic activity after damage. In environmental remediation, they resist the catalyst deactivation and fatigue limiting conventional photocatalysts, adsorbents, and membranes, sustaining degradation of dyes, pharmaceuticals, pesticides, and heavy metals over far more cycles. In biomedical diagnostics, the same repair logic enables biosensors, wearables, implants, and wound dressings that tolerate repeated mechanical deformation without losing sensitivity. AI and computational modeling are now accelerating design by predicting healing efficiency before synthesis, though scalable fabrication, long-term stability, nanotoxicity, and regulatory approval remain unresolved. This review covers the biological inspiration, material classes, healing mechanisms, applications, and key challenges facing this field.
authors: Sawera Malik Albina; Neelam Zeb; Hafsa Urooj; Kiran Fatima; Atiqa Parveen; Rabiya Bashir
venue: Scholars Journal of Medical Case Reports

title: BioNICs: Biomaterial-enabled neural interfaces with closed-loop control for brain disorders
abstract: Biomaterial-enabled neural interfaces with closed-loop control (BioNICs) integrate neural sensing, state estimation, and responsive intervention within one therapeutic framework. Material composition and architecture influence tissue coupling, signal transduction, therapeutic actuation, and chronic stability. Mechanically compliant polymers and hydrogels can reduce interfacial strain; conductive and mixed ionic-electronic materials can improve electrical and electrochemical coupling; and stimulus-responsive materials can enable localized energy conversion or controlled drug release. BioNICs are therefore relevant to brain disorders requiring continuous physiological monitoring and state-dependent treatment. However, substantial translational gap remains. Clinically established closed-loop therapies rely mainly on metallic electrodes, polymer insulation, and hermetic packaging, whereas conductive polymers, nanocomposites, hydrogels, microbubbles, biohybrid interfaces, and integrated drug-delivery systems have been evaluated chiefly in vitro , in rodents, or over short implantation periods. Greater complexity in materials and functionality does not necessarily enhance therapeutic performance and may, in fact, give rise to delamination, electrochemical degradation, stimulation artifacts, calibration drift, and packaging failure, as well as additional safety risks. This review examines BioNIC architecture, including sensing, intervention, control algorithms, biomaterials, and system integration, and illustrates applications in episodic network disorders, psychiatric conditions, neurodegenerative diseases, and structural brain injury. We focus on trade-offs in combining high-fidelity electrophysiological recording, neurochemical and physical sensing, localized electrical, optical, acoustic, or magnetic actuation, and microenvironment-responsive drug delivery. Ultimately, this review emphasizes that translating the intrinsic advantages of intelligent biomaterials into clinical benefit requires moving beyond isolated component innovation toward long-term system-level validation linking material performance to reliability, biological safety, algorithmic interpretability, and clinically meaningful outcomes.
authors: Yongxu Ju; Zheng Dou; Yiyuan Yang; Fang Yang

title: Biocompatible Microscale DNA Hydrogels with Programmable Swelling and Sequence-Specific Dissolution.
abstract: Stimulus-responsive DNA hydrogels with swelling capabilities are a promising class of materials for biomedical applications such as drug delivery and biosensing. However, translation of these systems to microscale applications requires fabrication methods that are both biocompatible and material-efficient, while enabling precise control over stimulus-induced swelling and its impact on molecular transport. Here, we present a biocompatible fabrication and characterization platform for microscale DNA-hydrogels (μSDs) with tunable isotropic swelling and dissolving properties. Our approach includes a biocompatible, material-efficient fabrication workflow that conserves valuable DNA reagents by minimizing dead volume and process loss. We then demonstrated modular control over isotropic swelling in μSDs, achieving up to a two-fold size increase through programmable DNA design parameters. We further established a quantitative reaction-diffusion workflow to estimate effective diffusivity and characterize swelling dependent transport of a DNA binding fluorescent probe in spherical μSDs. Finally, we demonstrate the dissolution of μSDs using a DNA strand and find that dissolution kinetics are governed by the rates of coupled strand-displacement reactions and diffusive transport. This platform enables programmable swelling and structural disassembly in μSDs. Swelling-induced network expansion further modulates transport of a DNA binding fluorescent probe within the μSD network, highlighting the potential of programmable structural remodeling for future biosensing, controlled release, and single-cell assay applications.
authors: Corinna Torabi; Takayuki Suzuki; Emily Helm; Harrison Khoo; Sophie Tanenbaum; Rebecca Schulman; Soojung Claire Hur

title: Bioelectronics beyond proof-of-concept demonstration
abstract: Biomedical electronic devices are developed to monitor physiological activity and deliver interventions at specific sites in the body. Their operation requires stable biological interfaces, suitable power delivery and reliable interpretation of electrical signals. These requirements become particularly important during movement and prolonged use, when changes in the interface can affect device performance. Developing clinically useful systems therefore requires an understanding of how materials and device architectures preserve the intended function under these conditions. Recent contributions to APL Electronic Devices address these requirements through advances in wearable sensors, biomolecular detection, soft actuators and power sources. We argue that the next stage of development requires closer integration of these capabilities around defined clinical needs. This Editorial examines the resulting design priorities for biological interfaces, feedback control, functional lifetime and reproducible fabrication.
authors: Yeon Sik Choi

title: Bioinspired Surface Enabled by Anisotropic Pyramid Structure Arrays for Directional Liquid Self‐Transport
abstract: ABSTRACT Inspired by the phenomenon of directional liquid transport in natural organisms, various bionic surfaces with customized topological structures have been designed and fabricated, contributing to advances in such fields as microfluidics, microreactors, energy harvesting, biomedicine, etc. Despite extensive progress, bionic surfaces with directional liquid self‐transport capabilities still suffer from high technical thresholds, cumbersome fabrication processes, and contamination‐induced failure, limiting their widespread applications. In this work, a bioinspired surface with anisotropic inverted pyramid groove arrays was developed to achieve directional self‐transport of diverse liquids, from water to blood. Bioinspired by the nepenthes alata peristome, a discretely anisotropic inverted pyramid model was theoretically constructed, and then the surface with inverted pyramid groove arrays was efficiently and simply prepared via three‐dimensional (3D) printing and cast molding. This bioinspired surface exhibited rapid, long‐distance, and continuous liquid self‐transport with high unidirectionality under the optimal structural parameters. Moreover, this bioinspired surface was innovatively applied to achieve efficient removal of blood cells from diluted blood without complex operations, providing a proof‐of‐concept foundation for future applications of bioinspired surfaces in microfluidics, plasma separation, and biomedical detection.
authors: Yi‐Ke Wang; Chaowei Sun; Pin Lv; Shengjun An; Zhao Meng-qian; Hu‐Chen Zhang; Si‐Yu Tian; Yan‐Yan Sun; Jun‐Yue Chen; Yu‐Yin Xu; Fan Zhang; Li‐Yun Zheng; Shegan Gao; Hong‐Xing Xu

title: Biological-Digital-Twin-Driven Microrobotic Sampling Decisions at the Limit STARLI Research Institute XXIX — Flagship Research Monograph 10 What if the next scientific sample could be selected not merely to collect more data, but to distinguish between competing explanations of biological behavior? Biological-Digital-Twin-Driven Microrobotic Sampling Decisions at the Limit explores a prospective research architecture combining versioned biological digital twins, active learning, microrobotic sampling, uncertainty quantification, and mechanistic model discrimination. The central question is whether a computational twin can identify safe, informative sampling actions that distinguish competing biological mechanisms more effectively than conventional experimental schedules, while retaining the ability to recognize model inadequacy and abstain from unsupported decisions. The proposed framework treats biological digital twins as revisable scientific models rather than exact replicas of living systems. Its reference environment is a controlled, nonclinical microfluidic platform containing two declared dynamical mechanisms and a third withheld mechanism reserved for evaluating open-world uncertainty and model failure. The research architecture is organized around five interconnected layers: versioned biological modeling, explicit prior assumptions and knowledge gaps, physically constrained predictive interrogation, comparative adaptive experimentation, and independent requalification. The manuscript develops thirty candidate mathematical research plates covering Bayesian mechanism inference, conditional information gain, experimental identifiability, observation uncertainty, transport dynamics, calibration, model discrepancy, and decision safety. These mathematical structures are connected to eighty-two research chapters, five independently paginated investigation sections per chapter, two hundred detailed Research Gates, and thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos. Each Research Gate is intended as a transferable research question that future investigators may test, challenge, refine, or reject. The proposed evaluation compares twin-guided sampling against optimized fixed schedules, established experimental-design approaches, and alternative active-learning policies under matched physical constraints and experimental budgets. Particular attention is given to blinded mechanism identification, probabilistic calibration, out-of-distribution rejection, specimen integrity, model-version accountability, and explicit stopping conditions. The volume includes DOI-linked methodological literature and a staged nonclinical verification pathway. Scientific status and limitations: This manuscript presents a conceptual methodological research program, not completed experimental validation. Its integrated hypotheses, mathematical proposals, and experimental architectures remain subject to independent technical review and empirical testing. The manuscript does not establish clinical efficacy, diagnostic reliability, therapeutic benefit, or proven superiority of microrobotic digital-twin systems. The work also acknowledges remaining editorial limitations, including recurring methodological language that requires further substantive review before the manuscript can be regarded as a fully refined scientific monograph. The broader purpose of this research is to develop scientific systems that can remain useful even when their initial models are incomplete. Rather than demanding certainty from a digital twin, the proposed framework asks whether future autonomous research tools can become more transparent, corrigible, experimentally accountable, and capable of recognizing the boundaries of their own knowledge. Within the STARLI research continuum, this volume is intended as an evolving research inheritance for future human and artificial-intelligence investigators. title: Biomimetic mineralization for bone-tissue repair
abstract: The increasing global burden of bone tissue injuries and disorders, particularly in aging populations, demands advanced therapeutic strategies beyond traditional methods. While autologous and allogeneic bone grafts remain clinical standards, they are constrained by donor-site morbidity, limited availability, infection risks, and disease transmission. Conventional synthetic materials, including metals, ceramics, and polymers, often fail to fully recapitulate the structural and functional complexity of native bone tissue, resulting in suboptimal repair outcomes. This review aims to systematically summarize the principles, methodologies, material systems, and technological innovations of biomimetic mineralization for bone-tissue repair, and to provide a forward-looking perspective on its clinical translation. We conducted a comprehensive literature search and systematic review of studies on biomimetic mineralization for bone tissue engineering, covering publications from 2015 to 2026. The reviewed studies were categorized according to mineralization methodologies (simulated body fluid immersion, template-guided mineralization, and ion-dynamic regulation), material systems (inorganic materials, organic-inorganic composites, and bioactive molecular composites), and enabling fabrication technologies (electrospinning, three-dimensional/four-dimensional printing, and microfluidics). Key findings were synthesized to chart the conceptual evolution from static structural mimicry to dynamic, responsive mineralization systems. Biomimetic mineralization offers significant advantages over conventional approaches, including enhanced bioactivity, tunable degradation kinetics, and the capacity for sustained release of bioactive molecules such as growth factors and therapeutic ions. Material development has evolved from single-component scaffolds to sophisticated hierarchical composites that mimic the extracellular matrix of natural bone. Advanced fabrication techniques, particularly four-dimensional printing and microfluidic-based platforms, have enabled precise spatiotemporal control over mineralization processes and scaffold architecture. In vivo studies across multiple animal models have demonstrated improved bone regeneration outcomes, with enhanced mechanical properties and functional integration. However, challenges remain in replicating the hierarchical organization of native bone, matching scaffold degradation rates with heterogeneous regeneration kinetics, and ensuring long-term biosafety. Biomimetic mineralization represents a rapidly advancing alternative that addresses many shortcomings of traditional bone grafts. Future breakthroughs will require integration of real-time sensing, feedback-controlled ion delivery, and immune-modulating strategies to achieve not just structural repair but true functional and physiological reconstruction. Close collaboration among materials scientists, mechanobiologists, and clinicians will be essential to translate these promising strategies from bench to bedside.
authors: Quanjiong Wang; Jiandi Qiu; Bingju Xie; Minghai Dai; Chuchu Sun

title: Biomolecular condensates containing RNA: Nuclear magnetic resonance to the rescue
abstract: Liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) drives the formation of membraneless organelles that are crucial for the spatial organization of eukaryotic cells. Given the critical role of biomolecular condensates in health and disease, it is important to gain a quantitative understanding of this phenomenon. Here, we summarize recent progress on elucidating the biophysical properties of RNA-containing condensates with a focus on the use of nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, which allows label-free characterization of these complex biomolecular condensates. We further review how our understanding of condensate formation, properties and function has advanced in recent years based on NMR and complementary methods, which are likely to provide a lot more in the future.
authors: Johannes Schmoll; Nina C. Kathe; Mihajlo Novakovic; Frédéric H.‐T. Allain

title: Blood test on a chip: Sample-to-answer immunoassay on a structurally programmed microfluidic chip
abstract: During COVID-19, rapid antigen tests (RATs) have demonstrated their enormous potential to relax and decentralize the healthcare system for timely results. However, disease diagnosis mostly requires blood tests with quantitative readouts, which are hardly achieved by conventional lateral flow strips. Here, we report a concept of “Blood Test on a Chip” (BTOC) that streamlines the entire sample-to-answer immunoassay process on a single microfluidic chip. Without any external processes, the BTOC can operate independently based on a series of structurally programmed capillary events, including automated blood plasma separation, on-chip reaction, and a length-based quantitative result displayed on the chip. This platform demonstrated a limit of detection (LOD) of 3.78 ng/mL of prostate-specific antigen (PSA) in whole blood, which is below the clinical threshold of 4 ng/mL for PSA abnormality. Clinical validation involving 77 volunteer samples showed strong agreement between the BTOC and standard hospital tests (Lin's concordance correlation coefficient ρ ̂ c = 0.932 ). This all-in-one, self-contained chip eliminates the need for peripheral laboratory settings, offering a simple, affordable, and quantitative at-home test for telemedicine, large-scale screening in primary care and disease self-management.
authors: Jiaheng Li; Zhuoting Han; Hogi Hartanto; Lin Pang; Jianpeng Wu; Zhibing Chen; Lok Ting Chu; Ting-Hsuan Chen

title: Breaking Bottlenecks in Solid Electrolyte Discovery With Large Artificial Intelligence Models
abstract: Solid electrolytes (SEs) are central to next-generation metal batteries, yet their discovery remains constrained by fragmented data, limited transferability of simulations, and slow experimental iteration. Unlike catalysis, where surface reactivity dominates, SEs require simultaneous optimization of bulk ion transport, defect chemistry, mechanical integrity, and interfacial stability. Here, we outline a framework for autonomous SE discovery enabled by large artificial intelligence (AI) models, including machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) and large language models (LLMs). We discuss the evolution from static materials databases to dynamic, self-updating knowledge systems, the role of MLIPs in bridging density functional theory (DFT) and long-timescale ion migration, and the emergence of LLMs as engines for literature mining, hypothesis generation, and scientific reasoning. We further describe a closed-loop architecture integrating AI-driven candidate design, multiscale simulation, uncertainty-aware selection, and experimental validation. Such systems shift SE research from intuition-guided exploration to data-informed, self-improving cycles. We conclude by highlighting challenges in data standardization, interfacial complexity, and reproducibility, and we propose design principles for building autonomous laboratories for solid-state battery materials.
authors: Eric Jianfeng Cheng; Min Hong; Zhiquan Zeng; Chuanyu Liu; Qian Wang; Melissa Jane Meadowcroft; Vlad Badilita; Carlos Miguel Costa; Senentxu Lanceros-Méndez; Ying Li; Chenyao Ma; Weibo Gong; Surendra Martha; Aloysius Soon; Piao Ma; Di Zhang; Teguh Ariyanto; Sudaryanto; Hiroshi Kakinuma; Jie Zhao; Jie Peng; Pengfei Ou; J Lu; Shin-ichi ORIMO; Hao Li

title: Building the Rural Nursing Workforce of the Future: Education, Research, and Partnerships to Address Persistent Health Challenges
abstract: Background: Rural populations experience healthcare disparities, including workforce shortages, geographic isolation, limited access to specialty services, and adverse social determinants of health. These challenges are particularly evident in South Dakota, where nearly half of the population resides in rural or frontier communities. Because of these unique challenges associated with rural life, preparing nurses to work in rural America is critical in preparing a workforce capable of meeting the unique healthcare needs of this population. Methods: This article describes how South Dakota State University College of Nursing, located within a rural land-grant institution, has developed and adapted educational programs, workforce initiatives, community partnerships, and re-search programs to address persistent rural health challenges across the state and region. The College of Nursing (CON) includes three campus locations: Brookings, Sioux Falls, and Rapid City and includes undergraduate and graduate nursing education. Nursing education is designed to allow students to blend their nursing education with South Dakota's unique rural environment. Results: The CON offers multiple pathways into the profession, including traditional and accelerated Bachelor of Science in Nursing (BSN) pro-grams, an online BSN option utilizing a train-in-place model, master's-level nursing education and administrator programs, Doctor of Nursing Practice (DNP) programs, and PhD education. Through strategic academic-practice partnerships and federally funded work-force initiatives, the college prepares nurses for rural practice across primary care, acute care, long-term care, and underserved settings. Additional initiatives support Native American student success, rural workforce recruitment and retention, oral health outreach, care coordination for children and youth with special healthcare needs, and research focused on workforce well-being, workplace violence, and healthcare access. Conclusions: A multi-site college of nursing can serve as a model for improving rural healthcare access, strengthening the nursing workforce, and addressing the complex and persistent health needs of rural and frontier populations. South Dakota State Universi-ty CON demonstrates how innovative educational delivery models, community partnerships, and targeted workforce initiatives can contribute to sustainable rural healthcare solutions.
authors: Lea Niederbaumer; Michelle Lichtenberg; Danielle M. Schievelbein; Abby O. Seydel; Nicole Carlson; Theresa Garren-Grubbs; Danielle Currier; Brian Williamson; Amanda Mehlhaff; Marie Schmit; Sarah Mollman

title: CRISPR‐Scan: Cas13a Mismatch Tolerance Enabled Ultra‐Multiplexed Detection of Same‐Site Indels in Acute Myeloid Leukemia
abstract: Detection of gene mutations related to acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is crucial for its early diagnosis, personalized treatment, and recurrence monitoring. However, accurate detection of diverse mutations occurring at the same locus remains technically challenging. The CRISPR/Cas system, with its unique programmable nucleic acid recognition capabilities, provides a promising solution. Here, we elucidated that CRISPR/LwaCas13a is tolerant to consecutive substitutions but highly sensitive to insertions or deletions (indels) at specific positions of the spacer sequence, enabling rational CRISPR RNA (crRNA) design for multiplex detection of same-site indels. Guided by these principles, we achieved effective detection of ultra-multiplex nucleophosmin 1 (NPM1) c.863_864 4-bp insertions with a single crRNA, while maintaining specificity against the wild-type transcripts. We further established a one-pot CRISPR system, CRISPR-Scan, by integrating recombinase polymerase amplification with LwaCas13a cleavage. CRISPR-Scan enabled detection of mutations in backgrounds as low as 0.01%. In clinical validation, it identified NPM1 mutations in 43 of 120 AML patients, consistent with next-generation sequencing (NGS). Continuous monitoring of four AML patients indicated early recurrence with higher sensitivity than first-generation sequencing (FGS) and full concordance with NGS. A microfluidic chip and portable device further facilitate accurate AML mutation detection. This platform offers an efficient and convenient approach for early AML diagnosis and measurable residual disease (MRD) monitoring.
authors: Linlin Bai; Bei Wang; Mingmin Shi; Dianwei Liu; Huimin Ji; Ting Wang; Ziwei Wang; Kaiming Guo; Xinyang Dou; Chunyan Qian; Fang Zhang; Yongming Wang; Hongju Mao; Rui Wang

title: Cascade-Amplified Microfluidic Detection of Tumor Biomarkers via Metal-DNA Nanospheres Activating CRISPR-Cas12a Assay.
abstract: The development of ultrasensitive protein detection platforms is pivotal for early cancer diagnosis, yet existing methods are often constrained by inefficient "protein-to-signal" conversion and complex instrumentation. While CRISPR-Cas-based biosensors offer higher sensitivity for nucleic acids, their application in protein analysis is fundamentally limited by the low nucleic acid loading capacity and tedious functionalization of traditional inorganic signal carriers such as gold nanoparticles and metal-organic frameworks (MOFs). Herein, we report a highly efficient signal-transduction strategy utilizing Fe-coordinated DNA nanospheres (FDNSs)─a programmable, metal-nucleic acid assembly─as a high-capacity DNA reservoir for amplified biomarker sensing. Unlike conventional surface-modified inorganic nanoparticles, the solid-core FDNSs achieve an unprecedented DNA loading density and exhibit specific stimulus-responsive degradation. In this FACC (FDNS-activated CRISPR chip) platform, the recognition of tumor biomarkers triggers the rapid collapse of FDNSs, releasing a massive flux of barcode DNA that subsequently activates the CRISPR-Cas12a system within a microfluidic device. This dual-amplification architecture enables the ultrasensitive quantification of prostate-specific antigen (PSA) and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) with detection limits of 0.028 fg/mL and 0.0265 fg/mL, respectively. By replacing complex inorganic carriers with this programmable DNA assembly, our platform simplifies the sensing workflow and significantly enhances sensitivity, providing a robust and portable solution for cancer screening in resource-limited settings.
authors: Wenjian Zhao; Xiaowei Luan; Wenxiu Long; Zhi Li; Ping Dong; Bangshun He; Yanfeng Gao; Hongmei Liu; Yi Yin; Yujun Song

title: CircuitATLAS: Agentic reasoning over a systems neuroscience knowledge graph for target discovery in circuitopathies
abstract: Drug discovery for neurological disease has traditionally centered on the molecules altered by disease. But the molecules that cause pathology are not necessarily the best points from which to reverse it. Here, we ask which otherwise unaltered molecular control points can be engaged to restore pathological neural circuits toward functional states. We present CircuitATLAS, a provenance-grounded systems-neuroscience knowledge graph and agentic framework for target discovery in circuitopathies. It structures literature-derived relationships across diseases, phenotypes, electrophysiology, circuits, brain regions, cell types and molecular effectors, while deliberately excluding direct disease-gene and disease-protein edges to reduce shortcut reasoning. The graph contains 3.83 million nodes and 7.66 million edges, including 5.31 million LLM-extracted relations, and incorporates structured datasets such as the Human Cell Atlas and new multimodal in vivo measurements. We then introduce an agentic workflow that reasons from measurable disease phenotypes through their circuit and cellular substrates to molecular interventions, therapeutic feasibility and clinical constraints. Finally, we introduce a human-governed in vivo lab-in-the-loop linking hypothesis generation to experimental iteration. Within this framework an agent nominated ATP1A3, the neuronal alpha3 Na+/K+-ATPase, as a control point on cortical excitability; interneuron-restricted expression of ATP1A3 abolished the beta- and gamma-band response to a focal 4-aminopyridine challenge in vivo, and the validated target was then carried into a structure-guided small-molecule campaign terminating in a defined assay to resolve the direction of modulation. CircuitATLAS thus provides a framework for discovering therapeutics based not only on what is molecularly disrupted in disease, but on what can be controlled to restore circuit function.
authors: Gabriel Ocana-Santero; Marko Tvrdic

title: Closing the Empirical Loop: Autonomous AI Agents Conduct End‐to‐end Research With Human Participants
abstract: Artificial intelligence systems are transforming scientific discovery by accelerating specific research tasks, from protein structure prediction to materials design, yet remain confined to narrow domains requiring substantial human oversight. Exponential growth of scientific literature and increasing domain specialization constrain researchers' capacity to synthesize knowledge across disciplines and develop unifying theories, motivating exploration of general-purpose AI systems for science. Here we show that a domain-agnostic, agentic AI Scientist system can independently navigate the scientific workflow -from hypothesis generation through data collection to manuscript preparation. The system autonomously designed and executed three psychological studies on visual working memory, mental rotation, and imagery vividness, executed online data collection with 288 participants, developed analysis pipelines through 8h+ continuous coding sessions, and produced completed manuscripts. The results demonstrate the capability of AI scientific discovery pipelines to conduct research with theoretical reasoning and methodological rigor comparable to experienced researchers, though with limitations in conceptual nuance and theoretical interpretation. This is a step toward embodied AI that can test hypotheses through real-world experiments, accelerating discovery by autonomously exploring regions of scientific space that human cognitive and resource constraints might otherwise leave unexplored. It raises important questions about the nature of scientific understanding and attribution of scientific credit.
authors: Gabrielle Wehr; Reuben Rideaux; Amaya J. Fox; David R. Lightfoot; Jason M. Tangen; Jason B. Mattingley; Shane E. Ehrhardt

title: Closing the Loop Between Synthetic and Living Cells
abstract: Synthetic cells are moving beyond compartmentalised microreactors to become integrated components of biological networks that physically and chemically merge with their hosts. Existing reviews classify this field by mode of emission, by chemistry, or by architecture, and so describe the construct rather than its effect. This review takes the receiver's side, treating the functional adaptation of the living host as the readout of bio-hybrid function: how living cells probe their synthetic partners mechanically and adapt to them metabolically. We consider the bio-hybrid interface by how far the feedback loop (sensing-actuation) is closed and set out the evidence that would place a study in each of four tiers: open-loop, half-loop, partial feedback, and closed-loop. Read against these criteria, sixteen of the eighteen studies surveyed here are half-loop, two reach partial feedback, and none is closed-loop. Both partial-feedback systems work the same way, by metabolic interception, which the existing taxonomies have no category for. The one construct that comes closest to closed-loop operation contains no living cell at all. We then trace how single-cell coupling is scaling into hybrid prototissues that act as discovery platforms for pathological microenvironments, and we outline the translational barriers these constructs must survive to reach the clinic.
authors: Ion A. Ioannou

title: Coacervates in the Era of Autonomous Experimentation:From Empirical Formulation to Self-Driving Laboratories
abstract: Liquid-liquid phase separation provides a route for organizing molecules into dense, dynamic, water-rich compartments. In cells, such compartments are known as biomolecular condensates or membraneless organelles; in synthetic and reconstituted systems, related droplets are commonly studied as coacervates. These materials can concentrate, exclude, stabilize, and organize molecules within distinct liquid microenvironments, making them relevant for studies of cellular organization as well as applications in encapsulation, delivery, catalysis, separation, and soft-matter design. Their rational design, however, remains challenging because phase behavior and material properties depend on coupled variables such as molecular structure, charge, concentration, stoichiometry, salt, pH, additives, and time. This dissertation addresses this challenge by combining molecular engineering with automated and data-driven experimentation. Chapter 1 introduces the scientific background of complex coacervation and biomolecular condensates. It describes how liquid-liquid phase separation generates dense liquid phases with compositions and properties that differ from the surrounding solution, and discusses the molecular driving forces underlying coacervation, including electrostatic interactions, counterion release, hydrophobic and aromatic contributions, and multivalent sticker-spacer interactions. The chapter also presents phase diagrams as the central language for describing coacervate behavior, while highlighting the limitations of manually mapping high dimensional formulation spaces. Chapter 2 investigates how coacervate interfaces can be stabilized without converting dynamic droplets into static membrane-bound compartments. Polypeptide coacervates composed of oppositely charged polymers are useful model systems for membraneless organelles, but can suffer from fusion, wetting, and dissolution. Engineered surface-active fusion proteins were therefore designed to interact with the coacervate interface. These proteins combine a charged intrinsically disordered region with a folded globular domain, allowing them to bind to the droplet surface while remaining excluded from the dense phase interior. Cryo-TEM and single-molecule super-resolution microscopy revealed a densely packed but highly dynamic interfacial protein layer, establishing transient protein insertion as a dynamic mode of coacervate stabilization. Chapter 3 describes the construction of an autonomous experimental platform for coacervate research. Self-driving laboratories depend on reliable integration of experimental design, execution, analysis, and decision-making. This chapter describes a self-driving module that combines liquid handling, microscopy, plate reading, robotic transport, device control software, data handling, and workflow orchestration. The emphasis is on the practical infrastructure needed for autonomous experimentation in a real laboratory environment, including metadata tracking, logging, failure handling, and the balance between automated execution and human interpretation. Chapter 4 applies this platform to the automated navigation of condensate phase behavior. Automated liquid handling, confocal microscopy, image analysis, and active machine learning are combined to reconstruct multidimensional phase diagrams of polypeptide198coacervates. The workflow updates a predictive model from previous results and selects new experiments in informative regions of formulation space, especially near phase boundaries. In addition to classifying samples as phase-separated or non-phase-separated, microscopy-based analysis extracts droplet-level properties such as morphology, particle count, size, and volume fraction, extending phase-diagram mapping beyond a binary description. Chapter 5 extends autonomous experimentation from phase mapping to property-driven discovery and optimization. Using automated formulation, confocal microscopy, image analysis, and Gaussian process-based optimization, the platform navigates multicomponent coacervate spaces and identifies formulations that generate desired droplet properties. The workflow is used to optimize droplet size, study ion-specific effects across a Hofmeister salt series, and investigate protein additives that generate nonlinear stability landscapes. The epilogue places these results in a broader perspective by discussing future directions in function-driven condensate design, including molecular recruitment, catalytic coacervates, and condensate-assisted molecular diagnostics. Overall, this dissertation shows that complex coacervates can be approached as both molecularly engineerable materials and experimentally navigable formulation systems. Dynamic protein insertion stabilizes condensate interfaces while preserving liquid-like exchange, whereas automated formulation, quantitative imaging, and active learning make high-dimensional coacervate spaces experimentally accessible. Together, these strategies provide a practical route from mapping where droplets form toward engineering what they do.
authors: Yannick Henricus Astrida Leurs

title: Code-multiplexed multi-frequency impedance cytometry with a unified deep-unfolding network
abstract: Impedance flow cytometry (IFC) is a label-free, single-cell measurement technique that captures biophysical properties beyond traditional biochemical markers. Code-multiplexing allows parallelization of IFC with simple hardware but requires advanced signal processing algorithms to resolve overlaps in signals originating from different channels. Existing methods, however, rely on multiple task-specific networks with template-based linear fitting, which loses accuracy under nonlinear or unstable conditions common in microfluidic experiments. Prior studies have also been restricted to demultiplexing single-frequency impedance measurements. To this end, we develop a unified deep-unfolding network for analyzing code-multiplexed, multi-frequency IFC data. We unfold the successive-interference cancellation (SIC) algorithm into a deep-learning network, where repeated stages of a single multitask network implement iterative signal estimation and interference cancellation that reflect the structural prior of SIC. To mitigate nonlinear signal stretching and amplification, our network recognizes events by predicting bit-level intensity and duration. For multi-frequency impedance profiling, we apply least-squares fitting to the predicted single-frequency real-impedance trace to map the real and imaginary impedance traces at other frequencies. On the cell-bead mixture evaluation dataset, our pipeline resolves overlaps from singlets to triplets reliably, reconstructs impedance-intensity distributions accurately, and enables multi-frequency impedance profiling. As a demonstration of principle, we use our pipeline to perform label-free quantification of basophil activation from code-multiplexed, multi-frequency IFC measurements. Consistent with our previous study, impedance opacity correlates well with activation levels measured by fluorescence flow cytometry. In summary, our study demonstrates the feasibility and utility of a deep-unfolding network that extends code-multiplexed, multi-frequency IFC to label-free single-cell functional assays.
authors: Wonjun Lee; Sindy K. Y. Tang

title: Collaborative control of deposition width and height for thick-walled parts in arc-directed energy deposition via integrating arc voltage and vision sensing
abstract: Gas tungsten arc-directed energy deposition (GTA-DED) offers significant potential for producing large-size metal components. However, the precise automatic control of process stability and dimensional accuracy of components with multi-layer multi-bead characteristics in GTA-DED remains a huge challenge. This study develops a collaborative control system for deposition width and height in GTA-DED of thick-walled parts. An arc voltage (AV) and vision collaborative sensing framework is established. The peak AV signal is filtered via an ant colony optimization-based wavelet threshold algorithm to monitor the deposition height stability. The image processing algorithm is applied to extract the deposition width from molten pool images captured at base current periods. Three peak AV-arc length-current relationship models are constructed based on the arc morphologies under different deposition positions. The AV signal is used to calibrate the vision sensing system for the accurate monitoring of deposition width, and the width monitoring error is less than 0.04 mm. A model reference adaptive controller is developed to adjust the wire feeding speed for improving the deposition height stability, while a self-tuning fuzzy controller is designed to regulate the peak current for maintaining deposition width uniformity. The total height and width deviations of the thick-walled parts are no more than 0.5 mm. The present work provides important guidance and feasible solutions for promoting the automated manufacturing level and forming accuracy in GTA-DED of thick-walled parts.
authors: Yuhua Cai; Dashuang Chen; Hui Chen; Guangjun Zhang; Zengxi Stephen Pan; Jun Xiong

title: Colorectal cancer organoids: a developmental trajectory from Matrigel embedding to AI-empowered precision medicine
abstract: The high heterogeneity and complex microenvironment of colorectal cancer (CRC) represent critical bottlenecks contributing to treatment resistance and clinical translation failure, and the iterative development of organoid technology provides a key driving force for precision oncology. This narrative review systematically outlines the four-stage developmental trajectory of CRC organoid technology-while recognizing that these stages are not strictly sequential replacements but rather long-term coexisting and complementary approaches. The first-generation Matrigel embedding method established the foundation for three-dimensional culture but lacked adequate microenvironment simulation. The second generation achieved preliminary tumor-stromal interactions through optimized culture media and co-culture systems. The third generation integrated engineering technologies such as microfluidic chips and bioprinting, overcoming bottlenecks in high-throughput standardization and dynamic regulation in dedicated platforms. The fourth generation leverages artificial intelligence (AI), achieving substantial advances in intelligent phenotypic analysis, drug-response prediction, and initial exploration of digital twin systems. By comparing differences in heterogeneity retention, throughput, clinical potential, and cost-effectiveness among the four generations, this review emphasizes their core clinical value in individualized medication guidance and novel target discovery. Despite persistent challenges-including insufficient microenvironment simulation, poor AI explainability, and lack of standardization-current evidence suggests that interdisciplinary integration and intelligent platform development can transform organoid technology into a key hub bridging basic research and clinical practice. We therefore recommend accelerating the establishment of standardized organoid biobanks, embedding AI-driven predictive models into clinical workflows, and formulating regulatory frameworks to facilitate the translation of organoid-based precision medicine for colorectal cancer.
authors: Muxin Tang; Lin Shaoyi; Qian Liang; Di Long

title: Comparative dynamics of radiative tetra- and penta-hybrid nanofluid flows subject to Joule heating and mixed convection: local non-similar solution and statistical analysis
abstract: nanoparticles offer enhanced heat transfer, stability, and realistic modeling of blood's microstructure. These properties enable improved control of thermal and flow behavior, making them suitable for applications such as cancer hyperthermia, targeted drug delivery, biomedical devices, and advanced cooling systems. The primary objective of the present study is to investigate the comparative dynamics of radiative tetra- and penta-HNFs under the influence of Joule heating. Blood is taken as the base fluid, while the Micropolar fluid model (MFM) is adopted for the analysis. The inertial effects are considered through the Darcy-Forchheimer relation. Mixed convection effects are accounted in the momentum equation. Instead of the conventional Fourier law, the Cattaneo-Christov model is utilized for heat conduction in tetra- and penta-HNFs. Physical aspects of thermal radiation are accounted to enhance the surface heat flux. To amplify the buoyancy forces in the flow, heat generation aspects are considered. Internal frictional forces and Joule heating impacts are further considered. The obtained governing equations are made dimensionless using non-similarity transformations and solved using the built-in function (NDSolve) of Mathematica. The effects of various factors on tetra- and penta- HNF velocities, as well as their thermal fields, are presented alongside a comparative analysis of tetra- and penta- HNFs. Surface drag force and heat transfer analyses for tetra- and penta- HNFs are examined using regression analysis. The results indicate that the velocity of tetra- and penta- HNFs decreases with Hartmann number and surface porosity, while it increases with mixed convection. The temperature rises with heat source, Hartmann number, viscous dissipation, and thermal radiation, but decreases with the Prandtl number. Additionally, the Nusselt number decreases with heat source, thermal conductivity, Eckert number, and Hartmann number, whereas it increases with the Prandtl number.Clinical trial number: Not applicable.

title: Comprehensive Analysis of Laboratory Automation Systems in Evaluating Efficiency, Accuracy, and Workflow Optimization in Diagnostic Testing Through Critical Review
abstract: The given paper is meant to discuss laboratory automation systems in greater detail. It is from the point of view of efficiency, accuracy, and how the processes can be automated. The essence of the study is to critically examine different laboratory automation systems and their respective functions. These components make up the various systems, as well as how the systems affect laboratory operations. A detailed analysis weighs multiple critical factors, including cost-effectiveness, implementation, and potential outcomes. The results of this laboratory automation study demonstrate this invention's significance in enhancing existing diagnostic efficiency, achieving diagnostic accuracy, simplifying workflow processes with eased workflow, and enhancing patient care outcomes.

title: Continuous Downstream Processing in Biopharmaceutical Manufacturing: A Review
abstract: Abstract Purpose Continuous manufacturing has emerged as a promising alternative to conventional batch processing, offering potential improvements in efficiency, product quality, and sustainability. This review evaluates the economic, quality, sustainability, and scalability implications of continuous downstream processing in biopharmaceutical manufacturing and identifies lessons applicable to life-science industries. Methods A literature review was conducted using PubMed, ScienceDirect, and SpringerLink databases to identify peer-reviewed articles, industrial case studies, and regulatory guidance documents published between 2010 and 2025. Results Continuous downstream processing reduces manufacturing costs and improves equipment efficiency. Process Analytical Technology (PAT) enables real-time quality control, reducing variability and improving product purity and yields. Continuous systems lower material, water, and energy consumption while improving scalability and operational flexibility across life-science industries. Conclusions Continuous downstream processing is a technically viable and cost-effective technology for biopharmaceutical production. Implementation challenges, including validation complexity and workforce readiness, can be mitigated with emerging technologies such as digital twins and AI-enhanced PAT systems. Cross-industry evidence supports modular adoption strategies to accelerate implementation.
authors: Srinivasulu Katakam; Erik Hefti

title: Continuous Molecular Monitoring Using Electrochemical Aptamer‐Based Sensors: Remaining Challenges for Long‐Term In Vivo Deployment
abstract: In vivo continuous molecular monitoring represents a long-standing, transformative objective in medicine, with the potential to fundamentally reshape disease diagnostics, therapeutic decision-making, and long-term patient management by providing dynamic biochemical information that is currently inaccessible. Electrochemical aptamer-based biosensors offer a particularly promising and generalizable platform, as engineered aptamers can selectively bind diverse molecular targets and transduce binding-induced conformational changes into robust electrochemical signals. Recent studies have demonstrated encouraging progress toward extended in vivo operation, including early examples of week-scale functionality, highlighting the growing feasibility of this approach. Nevertheless, achieving robust and broadly applicable long-term in vivo deployment remains an ongoing challenge due to factors such as sensor degradation and limitations in fully integrated device architectures. To address these challenges, multiple strategies have emerged, including drift-canceling calibration, non-natural nucleic acids, antifouling coatings, nanoengineered electrodes, advanced immobilization and ultralow-power wireless systems, which are beginning to converge to enhance overall device performance. This review examines principles of aptamer-based biosensing, delineates mechanisms of signal degradation, and surveys emerging strategies for stability enhancement and system-level integration, outlining pathways toward longitudinal continuous molecular monitoring in personalized medicine.
authors: Shibo Liu; Xiangling Li; Wei Ouyang

title: Controlled Assembly and In Situ Reconfiguration of Multiphase DNA Droplets in a Vibration-Induced Local Vortex Microfluidic Platform
abstract: Liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS) of sequence-designed DNA nanostructures offers a powerful route toward dynamic artificial cells and intelligent molecular robots. However, conventional bulk synthesis suffers from stochastic polydispersity in terms of droplet size and topology, and physical compartmentalization restricts continuous chemical exchange with the external environment. This study reports an upgraded vibration-induced local vortex (VILV) microfluidic platform featuring secondary trapping pillars that decouple a localized microvortex-driven assembly from a global convective flow. This architecture enables highthroughput parallel manufacturing of uniform multiphase DNA droplets and their anchoring within micropillar arrays without washout. By systematically tuning the stoichiometry of the interphase hexavalent DNA linker, precise array-wide programming of the surface valence of the multiphase droplets is achieved, driving predictable structural transitions from monovalent Janus artificial cells to highly connected multivalent patchy networks. Notably, under continuous open perfusion, introducing invader strands rationally engineered to mimic clinically diagnostic microRNA (miRNA) biomarker sequences triggers toehold-mediated strand displacement (TMSD) across phase boundaries. This non-invasive tracking demonstrates linker-density-dependent morphological alterations. This study establishes a versatile foundation for mass-producing synthetic organelles and one-pot molecular diagnostic devices by bridging uniform multiphase artificial cell manufacturing with sequence-specific miRNA responsiveness under continuous fluidic flow.
authors: Zhitai Huang; Naoki Asai; Tomoya Maruyama; Masahiro Takinoue; Hiroaki Suzuki

title: Controlling water-in-water droplets and extracellular environments in microfluidics
abstract: Many biological and soft-matter processes take place in water-rich environments. In cells, biological fluids, and polymer-rich materials, molecules do not always remain evenly mixed. Under suitable conditions, a homogeneous aqueous solution can separate into two liquid phases through liquid–liquid phase separation. In aqueous two-phase systems, this process can produce water-in-water droplets, in which both phases are water-rich but differ in polymer or salt composition. These droplets are attractive for biological studies because they provide mild, fully aqueous, and cell-compatible microenvironments. They can also serve as simple models for membraneless compartments, artificial cells, and extracellular microenvironments. However, water-in-water droplets are difficult to control. Their aqueous–aqueous interface has an extremely low interfacial tension, which makes droplet formation and stabilization much more difficult than in water-in-oil systems. Conventional droplet microfluidics often relies on interfacial breakup under controlled flow, but this method becomes less effective when the interface is very weak. As a result, water-in-water droplets are often hard to generate reproducibly, trap stably, and observe over long periods. Their size, composition, and surrounding chemical environment are also difficult to adjust in real time. These limitations restrict their use in biological studies that require stable and tunable aqueous microenvironments. This thesis addresses this challenge by developing a microfluidic platform for the controlled formation, trapping, and manipulation of water-in-water droplets. The central idea is to shift water-in-water droplet control from a flow-breakup problem to a diffusion-and-confinement problem. Instead of generating droplets upstream by shear, active perturbation, or oil-assisted emulsification, the platform forms droplets directly inside dead-end microchambers connected to a main channel. The main channel provides a controlled aqueous solution, while diffusion between the main channel and the chambers changes the local polymer composition and induces liquid–liquid phase separation. In this way, droplets form in place, remain physically confined, and stay chemically connected to the surrounding aqueous phase. This allows the droplet microenvironment to be changed during the experiment without oil, surfactants, or complex flow control. Chapter 1 introduces the background and motivation of the thesis. It explains liquid–liquid phase separation, aqueous two-phase systems, and water-in-water droplets, and places them in the context of soft matter and biological studies. Compared with water-in-oil droplets, water-in-water droplets avoid oil and surfactants and are therefore better suited for cells and biomolecules. At the same time, their weak aqueous–aqueous interface makes them difficult to produce and control. Chapter 1 identifies a key gap in the field: many existing platforms can generate water-in-water droplets, but fewer can combine droplet formation, stable trapping, long-term observation, and dynamic environmental control in one system. The chapter also introduces the biological motivation of the thesis. Cells are not only regulated by biochemical signals, but also by physical properties of their surroundings, such as viscosity, confinement, and the material state of the extracellular environment. Chapter 2 develops the core microfluidic platform. A fused-silica device is fabricated using femtosecond laser micromachining. The device contains a main channel connected to multiple dead-end microchambers. When aqueous polymer solutions are supplied through the main channel, solute diffusion into the chambers changes the local composition and induces liquid–liquid phase separation. As a result, water-in-water droplets form directly inside the chambers and remain trapped at the same location. Using the PEG/dextran aqueous two-phase system, Chapter 2 shows that droplet size and composition can be controlled in a stable and reproducible way through solute diffusion, phase equilibrium, and chamber geometry. The same platform is then extended to associative phase-separating systems, including coacervate droplets with internal structures. The main technical conclusion of Chapter 2 is that weakly interfacial aqueous droplets can be controlled without oil, surfactants, or complex flow breakup, by using diffusion-driven phase separation and geometric confinement instead. Chapter 3 extends the platform from droplet control to cell manipulation. For cell studies, cells first need to be positioned inside the dead-end chambers. This is achieved by using a dextran concentration gradient to drive cell capture. In this process, dextran mainly acts as a neutral macromolecular solute that creates a concentration gradient and an osmotic pressure imbalance near the cell surface. The interaction between dextran and cells is mainly physical and non-specific, rather than biochemical. Because dextran molecules are partly excluded from the thin interfacial region around the cell surface, the polymer gradient can generate a driving force that moves cells into the chambers. This method allows cells to be captured without direct mechanical pushing or strong flow through the chambers. By adjusting the gradient, the initial cell density, and the chamber geometry, the number of cells in each chamber can be controlled. The method is demonstrated with both fission yeast and leukemia cells. After capture, cells can be enclosed inside PEG/dextran water-in-water droplets. This creates a controllable three-dimensional extracellular environment around the cells and integrates cell capture, droplet formation, and extracellular-environment control in one microfluidic system. Chapter 4 uses this integrated platform to study how cells respond to changes in extracellular fluid viscosity. This question is relevant because many biological environments, such as tissues, mucus, and biofilms, are not simple dilute liquids but crowded and physically complex materials. In conventional cell-culture systems, it is difficult to isolate the effect of extracellular viscosity from other factors, such as osmotic pressure, nutrient transport, and biochemical composition. In Chapter 4, the PEG/dextran aqueous two-phase system is used as a reductionist physical model to tune extracellular fluid viscosity under controlled microfluidic conditions. It should not be understood as a chemical mimic of a specific extracellular matrix or biological fluid. Instead, it provides a defined system for testing how cells respond to extracellular viscous resistance. Using fission yeast as a model organism, Chapter 4 examines how extracellular fluid viscosity affects cell-division progression, glucose uptake, plasma membrane tension, and cytosolic viscosity. The results show that extracellular viscosity can strongly influence cell growth and division. When the surrounding fluid becomes too viscous, cells can no longer divide normally. Below this threshold, however, cells can adapt. The central adaptive response is an increase in cytosolic viscosity. This internal material-state change links the physical condition outside the cell to the cell-cycle outcome. It is also associated with preserved glucose-transporter activity and continued growth. Further experiments show that β-1,3-glucan and trehalose contribute to this adaptation. When these components are disrupted, cells lose part of their ability to tolerate high extracellular viscosity. These findings suggest that cytosolic viscosity is not only a passive physical property of the cell interior. Instead, it can behave as a regulated material state that helps cells maintain function under physical stress. At the same time, the biological interpretation must remain specific. The quantitative viscosity threshold measured in the PEG/dextran system is system-dependent and should not be treated as a universal threshold for all cells or extracellular environments. The broader conclusion is that cells can respond to physical changes outside the cell by tuning their own internal material properties. Chapter 5 brings together the technical and biological findings of the thesis. At the technical level, this thesis provides a fully aqueous microfluidic platform for generating, trapping, observing, and controlling water-in-water droplets over time. The platform differs from conventional droplet methods because it does not rely on flow breakup, oil phases, or surfactants. Instead, it uses diffusion-driven phase separation and geometric confinement. At the biological level, the thesis shows that the same platform can be used to create controlled extracellular microenvironments for cell studies. It also shows that extracellular viscosity is not merely a passive background condition, but a physical factor that can affect cell growth, division, and intracellular material state. Overall, this thesis connects water-in-water droplet microfluidics with the study of cellular adaptation to physical environments. It provides a technical strategy for controlling weakly interfacial aqueous droplets and a biological strategy for studying how cells respond to extracellular physical constraints. By bringing together soft matter physics, microfluidic engineering, and cell biology, this work offers a new experimental framework for studying aqueous microenvironments and the adaptive behavior of living cells.

title: Covalent Immobilisation of PVA‐MA Hydrogels on Plasma‐Activated Coatings: Achieving Superior Adhesion by Reagent‐Free Formation of a Nanoscale Primer Layer
abstract: Hydrogel coatings provide a promising pathway to tailor and improve cell culture surfaces, maintaining bulk material properties desired for handling and optical measurement while providing cell–surface interactions vital for optimising cell behaviour. For immobilised hydrogels to be useful, layers of this structure must be robustly adhered to the substrate and able to withstand strain from sources such as tensile forces exerted by adherent cell lines and fluid streams in microfluidic devices. Plasma‐activated coatings (PAC) are investigated here as a method for robust and translatable hydrogel immobilisation. Results show that embedded radicals within the PAC can immobilise methacrylated poly‐vinyl alcohol hydrogels, forming nanometer‐thick (reagent‐free) to millimeter‐thick (photoinitiator‐assisted) hydrogel layers. Utilisation of the nanometer reagent‐free layer as a ‘primer layer’ before forming photoinitiator‐assisted millimeter‐thick layers is a novel approach that results in superior adhesion of the thicker gel layers. When used as a cell culture surface for MCF‐7 cells, E cadherin and vinculin signalling significantly ( p < 0.05) increased (for physiologically relevant High MA hydrogel compared to the glass control). This work therefore outlines the novel reagent‐free primer layer approach as a method for creating hydrogels with superior adhesion for in vitro culture of cells.
authors: Sophia C. Franklin; Clara Tran; Matthew Hadden; David Martínez-Martín; Laura Anne Poole-Warren; Marcela Bilek; Ulises Alejandro Aregueta Robles; Aaron D. Gilmour

title: Co‐Evolution of Humans, AI, and Robotics in Autonomous Materials Manufacturing
abstract: ABSTRACT Materials manufacturing has entered into a new era with the rapid development of technologies. The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics technologies is transforming materials manufacturing from a traditional human‐centered practice into a human, AI, and robotics co‐evolution paradigm. Here, co‐evolution extends beyond conventional human‐in‐the‐loop supervision through reciprocal adaptation: Humans define objectives and constraints and refine them in response to new discoveries; AI translates these objectives and accumulated knowledge into testable hypotheses and experimental plans, then uses new evidence to refine its models and research strategy; and robotic platforms execute experiments and are reconfigured in response to emerging experimental requirements. Such intelligent autonomous materials manufacturing not only accelerates the discovery‐to‐production cycle but also enhances reproducibility and resource efficiency. In this perspective, we discuss the evolution of materials manufacturing, highlighting the roles of robotic platforms and AI in enabling autonomous materials manufacturing, and present a general framework for the human‐AI‐robotics collaboration and co‐evolution paradigm. We further outline the key challenges and future pathways, including effective AI‐driven design, reconfigurable robotic systems, and the critical role of automated characterization.
authors: Yixuan Zhao; Wenlong Li; Xiaodong Chen

title: Cure-induced viscoelastic effects in in-air photopolymerized droplets for microfluidic droplet-based 3D printing
abstract: Motivated by droplet-based additive manufacturing processes, this work presents a multiphysics numerical framework for in-air photopolymerization of resin droplets and their subsequent impact, spreading, and recoil on a solid substrate. The model couples two-phase incompressible flow with energy and species transport, incorporating radiative transport through the Beer–Lambert law to describe free-radical photopolymerization. This formulation enables prediction of core–shell droplet morphologies, in which a partially or fully cured outer shell encapsulates an uncured liquid core prior to impact. The key novelty of the proposed framework lies in the introduction of a cure-induced viscoelastic shell model, described using an Oldroyd-B-type constitutive formulation. The evolving stress response during photocuring is decomposed into equilibrium (elastic, spring-like) and non-equilibrium (viscous, Maxwell-type) contributions. The viscoelastic properties of the shell – including relaxation time as well as equilibrium and non-equilibrium moduli – are explicitly linked to the local degree of cure, allowing the progressive evolution of material stiffness and elasticity to be captured. Using this approach, we systematically quantify how cure-dependent viscoelasticity governs droplet-substrate interaction for micro-scale droplets across various UV intensity exposures with a specific impact velocity. Particular emphasis is placed on the role of viscoelasticity in post-impact recoil and rebound suppression. The proposed model provides a predictive tool for understanding and controlling droplet dynamics in UV-curable, droplet-based additive manufacturing processes.
authors: Saquib Rouf; Johnny Moughames; Arnaud Bertsch; Hang Jerry Qi; Frédéric Demoly

title: Current Perspective on Three-Dimensional In Vitro Models for Bone-Related Diseases
abstract: Bone-related diseases – including osteoporosis, osteosarcoma, osteoarthritis (OA), and bone metastasis – represent a major global health challenge that impairs patients’ quality of life. Addressing these challenges requires a comprehensive understanding of the complex intercellular networks and dynamic microenvironments within bone tissue. Traditional experimental setups, specifically two-dimensional (2D) monolayer cultures and animal models, have long driven bone research. However, they frequently fail to accurately replicate the structural complexity and functional hierarchy of native bone. To bridge this gap, three-dimensional (3D) in vitro models designed to mimic the physiological bone environments have emerged as vital research tools. By synergistically integrating advanced biomaterials, stem cells, microfluidic systems, and biofabrication strategies, these platforms successfully recreate natural bone architecture, extracellular matrix (ECM) interactions, and localized mechanical stimulation. This review provides a critical overview of recent breakthroughs in 3D bone modeling, with particular emphasis on scaffold-based systems, multicellular spheroids/organoids, bone-on-a-chip platforms, and 3D bioprinting technologies. Additionally, we analyze how these technologies are applied in bone regeneration, cancer modeling, osteoporosis research, and high-throughput drug screening, while highlighting current technological bottlenecks and future milestones.
authors: Seon Young Choi

title: Current Translational 3D In Vitro Models of Human Placental Tissue
abstract: Cellular models of placental tissue have the potential to recapitulate normal physiology, model disease, and facilitate therapeutic drug testing. In vivo or two-dimensional (2D) in vitro models of placental conditions have not been sufficiently representative of whole human tissue, thus have limited physiological relevance. This can be attributed to interspecies differences in placental physiology or a lack of structural complexity. In comparison, three-dimensional (3D) multicellular model systems provide a more sophisticated analogue of human placental tissue. Newer models of human placenta include 3D organoids, placenta-on-a-chip and organoid-on-a-chip, employing a range of materials and methods including pluripotent or trophoblast stem cells, microfluidics and 3D bioprinting. Accurately mimicking in vivo human tissue is crucial to the success of these translational 3D models of the placenta.In turn, a reliable representation of placental tissue architecture will allow discovery of the mechanisms underlying abnormal placental development and inform the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of pregnancy-related disorders such as preeclampsia and fetal growth restriction. Here, we provide a comprehensive critical appraisal of recent advances in 3D placental models, which aim to elucidate placental physiology, development and dysfunction. Additionally, we discuss how these platforms can accelerate the development of better monitoring and treatment strategies for pregnancy complications induced by a dysfunctional placenta.
authors: A.S. Raman; Niamh E. P. Mills; Louise Cole; Claire Richards; Lana McClements

title: Deep learning-based analysis reveals patient-level cancer therapy trajectories using single-cell PBMC chromatin images
abstract: Abstract Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) profiled in different data modalities have emerged as diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers for cancer. Here we demonstrate that PBMC chromatin images contain sufficient information to track patients’ trajectories during and after radiation therapy. We collected images from 150 patients across a variety of cancer types including Central Nervous System (CNS) cancer, Head & Neck cancer, Chordoma and Chondrosarcoma, Sarcoma, and Lymphoma, and adapted a multiple instance learning-based framework, which effectively enhanced the patient-level classification and interpretation of images from diverse samples compared to simpler cell-level neural network-based classifiers. We found that patients whose PBMCs returned to a state more similar to healthy after the therapy had more favorable outcomes. Moreover, our framework could indicate whether Head & Neck cancer patients’ PBMCs would likely return to a state similar to healthy after radiation therapy using solely chromatin images from before the treatment. These findings motivate further study of PBMC chromatin images to be used as a non-invasive, easily obtained, and inexpensive biomarker for cancer detection, treatment monitoring, and treatment response prediction.
