title: Integrating artificial intelligence into medical laboratories: A structured implementation framework
abstract: This article presents a structured framework for integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into medical laboratory workflows. As laboratories face increasing demands, workforce shortages, and technological complexity, AI offers promising solutions to enhance efficiency, diagnostic accuracy, and predictive capabilities. The paper outlines key benefits of AI, including automation, quality assurance, and administrative optimization, while also addressing critical challenges such as bias, legal and ethical concerns, workforce disruption, and over-reliance on automated systems. A multi-level implementation strategy is proposed, spanning international, national, and organizational domains, with emphasis on standards, guidelines, training, and oversight. Importantly, the article underscores that AI is a supportive tool, not a replacement for laboratory professionals, whose expertise remains essential for validation and interpretation. The framework aims to guide responsible AI adoption while safeguarding quality and patient safety.
authors: Avi Peretz; Hanoch Goldshmidt; Sari Peretz; Marielle Kaplan; Orna Schwartz; Ronit Marco; Maya Azrad

title: Integration of liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry into total laboratory automation: technical challenges and clinical advantages
abstract: The clinical laboratory is undergoing a paradigm shift toward the integration of liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry(MS) into Total Laboratory Automation workflows. While historically relegated to specialized satellite units due to manual pre-analytical requirements, recent technological advancements have enabled the development of fully automated, 'sample-to-result' MS modules. This review provides an authoritative analysis of the technical integration of systems such as the Roche cobas® i 601 and Shimadzu CLAM-2040 in core laboratories. We examine the role of intelligent middleware and artificial intelligence-assisted algorithms in ensuring standardized data validation and quality control tracking and real-time operational monitoring. Furthermore, we evaluate the clinical impact of this integration on diagnostic accuracy for low-concentration analytes in endocrinology and therapeutic drug monitoring. By transitioning from batch-based processing to continuous automated streams, MS establishes itself as a robust, high-throughput tool for routine clinical diagnostics.
authors: Carlos José Sánchez Ovejero; Sergio Luis Lima; Irene Chaves‐Coira; A. Rey-Catena

title: Intelligent drone-based biosensor for the detection of dengue virus antigen towards smart unmanned aerial-vehicle platform-based virus diagnosis
abstract: In the current work, we established a smart system for dengue diagnosis that enables on-site detection while removing the need for human intervention and continuous monitoring in difficult-to-reach areas. The system comprises of 4-smart technologies: i) drone, ii) biosensor, iii) Yolov5 AI-module, iv) a QR-code-derived digital website linked patient E-Prescription barcode, where the biosensor acts as a smart detector, and the drone as a vehicle for transporting the biosensor to the testing zone. Deep learning analysis was done by an expert using an artificial intelligence module; additional QR-code-based websites were added to the system, allowing users to scan the code and send detection data to laboratory authorities, and the patient got a medical e-prescription from the doctor. The proposed system has lightweight materials, optimized power sources, and weather-resistant housing to ensure reliable on-site diagnostics. However, practical challenges associated with drone-based diagnostic deployment, including environmental conditions, flight stability, battery capacity, payload constraints, and reliable operation in remote settings, should be considered when evaluating the field applicability and scalability of the proposed system. The suggested detection platform used the instrument-less lateral flow colorimetric approach, enabling naked-eye detection of dengue virus antigen with an LOD of 0.91 µg/mL within 5 s. As a consequence, the Drone-based approach allows clinicians to monitor the dengue virus antigen in remote populations. Accordingly, governments and non-profit organizations can utilize this technology to monitor the red alert zone, receiving precise and reliable data for informed decision-making.
authors: Mohd. Rahil Hasan; Sameer Khan; Dakshita Naithani; Pradakshina Sharma; Yashomita Mehta; Samra Ansari; Sushil Kumar; Ubaid Mushtaq Naikoo; Anupam Baliyan; Mohamed Abbas; Muneer Parayangat; Shaeen Kalathil; Jagriti Narang

title: Intelligent material recognition from thermal signatures using hybrid deep learning frameworks
abstract: Accurate material identification using thermal infrared signatures has significant implications for industrial inspection, autonomous systems, and non-contact diagnostics. In this study, we propose a physics-informed deep learning framework for intelligent material recognition based on transient thermal behavior. A large-scale dataset, ThermalMat-85K, comprising 85,000 long-wave infrared (LWIR) images across ten material classes, was constructed under controlled multi-angle, multi-distance, and multi-environment conditions. Each sample was validated through Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy and X-ray diffraction (XRD) to ensure chemical and structural integrity prior to thermal acquisition. Seven deep learning architectures were systematically evaluated, including VGG-16, ResNet-50, MobileNet-V3, DenseNet-121, EfficientNet-B4, a CNN+LSTM temporal hybrid, and a proposed Hybrid Net integrating convolutional, transformer, and recurrent modules with cross-modal attention gating. EfficientNet-B4 achieved the highest Top-1 accuracy (93.1%) and macro F1-score (92.8%), demonstrating superior class-wise stability. Residual and dense connectivity architectures also exhibited strong performance, while lightweight and temporal hybrids revealed trade-offs between efficiency and discriminative power. Class-wise confusion analysis indicates that misclassification trends correlate strongly with thermophysical proximity, particularly thermal conductivity and emissivity overlap. These findings confirm that transient thermal decay dynamics encode physically meaningful features suitable for material discrimination. The results establish a robust benchmark for physics-informed thermal material recognition and provide guidance for selecting architectures based on deployment constraints and robustness requirements.

title: Interconnected Macroporous GelMA Scaffolds for Cell Culture through Temperature Controlled Spinodal Decomposition
abstract: Abstract Developing biomaterials that faithfully recapitulate the complex architecture of native tissues is central to tissue engineering. Conventional hydrogels typically exhibit nanoscale porosity, which limits mass transport and cell migration and thereby constrains tissue development. Here, we exploit liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS) to generate interconnected macroporous gelatin methacryloyl (GelMA) scaffolds with tunable pore sizes ranging from 2 to 50 µm under physiological pH conditions. By mapping the GelMA/dextran phase diagram, we identify a composition range in which LLPS occurs through spinodal decomposition, resulting in a spontaneous bicontinuous, trabecular-like architecture. Pore size can be further tuned by varying polymer concentrations and temperature. We advantageously combined thermal gradients and photopatterning to enable spatial control over pore morphology to fabricate hierarchically structured materials. The biological relevance of these architectures is assessed using fibroblasts cultured within controlled porosity gradients. We show that pore size strongly influences cell infiltration, growth, and spatial organization, with larger pores providing sufficient space for cell migration while reducing the dependence on matrix degradation. Pore size of 7–15 µm is identified for maximizing fibroblast growth. Overall, our approach provides a versatile platform for porosity screening, enabling the engineering of biomimetic hydrogels with optimized microarchitectures tailored to specific biological contexts for three-dimensional cell culture.
authors: Simon Dumas; David González Martínez; Adriene Peixoto De Oliveira; Daniel Ferri-Angulo; Lisa Bacchin; Alexis Arcas; Marie-Charline Blatché; Dominique Goudounèche; Raphaelle Paounov; Marie Hut; Marwan Puaud; Jose Manuel Moran-Mirabal; Julie Foncy; Laurent Malaquin

title: Intestinal Villi‐Inspired Living Biobatteries via Habitat‐Engineered Conductive Hydrogel Architectures
abstract: ABSTRACT Microbial bioelectrocatalysis demands more than electron‐conducting surfaces—it demands living microenvironments that hydrate, protect, and nourish whole‐cell biocatalysts. This biological imperative remains unaddressed by conventional electrode design. Here, we fundamentally reframe microbial biobattery architecture through living habitat engineering, drawing inspiration from the human small intestine—a biological interface evolutionarily optimized to sustain dense, metabolically active microbial communities through high‐surface‐area villi, mucus‐mediated hydration, and short‐path nutrient exchange. We translate these principles into spore‐programmed conductive hydrogel pillar arrays, in which dormant Bacillus subtilis endospores are embedded within poly(3,4‐ethylenedioxythiophene):poly(styrenesulfonate)–poly(vinyl alcohol)/reduced graphene oxide hydrogel villi that simultaneously serve as microbial reservoirs, bioelectrochemical scaffolds, and electron‐harvesting conduits. Upon nutrient contact, spores germinate on demand into electroactive cells. This villi topology delivers an 8.3‐fold volumetric power density enhancement (8.04 to 66.45 µW cm − 3 ) over planar controls under volume‐matched conditions. A 24‐device geometry matrix uncovers a coupled radius–height design rule, with peak single‐villus power of 8.35 µW at optimal dimensions. Conformable villi patches demonstrate nutrient‐triggered electricity generation in a simulated pipe environment using a wastewater‐mimicking nutrient/electrolyte solution, while a separate self‐powered array achieves spatially resolved bioelectrochemical sensing. This work establishes living habitat engineering as a transformative paradigm for activatable, architecture‐programmed, and potentially shelf‐stable microbial biobatteries.
authors: Ruohan Zhang; Botian Wang; Seokheun Choi

title: Intraoperative electromyography (EMG): an updated position statement by the American Society of Neurophysiological Monitoring
abstract: Electromyography (EMG) is used to assess the functional status of peripheral motor axons during surgical procedures and can help protect patients' neurological integrity intraoperatively. This is a position statement on intraoperative EMG monitoring from the American Society of Neurophysiological Monitoring (ASNM) and updates prior ASNM position statement on EMG from 2005. This position statement is endorsed by ASNM and serves as an educational service to the neurophysiological community on the recommended use of EMG as a neurophysiological monitoring tool. It presents the rationale for EMG utilization and its clinical applications. It also covers the relevant anatomy, technical methodology for setup and signal acquisition, signal interpretation, anesthesia and physiological considerations, and documentation and credentialing requirements to optimize EMG monitoring to aid in protecting the peripheral nervous system during surgery.
authors: Kent S. Rice; Stanley A. Skinner; Ernest M. Hoffman; Tatsuya Oishi; Lanjun Guo; Ronald E. Leppanen
venue: Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing

title: Investigating nozzle-based additive manufacturing dynamics with high-speed imaging and machine learning
abstract: Abstract Additive manufacturing (AM) offers great design flexibility but remains constrained by the complexity of tuning processing parameters from a vast parameter search space either by traditional trial-and-error experimental approach or expensive computational fluid dynamics simulations. Further, AM processes involve critical transient phenomena at very small timescales ranging from microsecond to millisecond, which are difficult to observe and characterize experimentally. This work presents a novel approach that combines high-speed photography with machine learning (ML) to model and predict dynamic printing behavior. We used jet printing data obtained from Electrohydrodynamic (EHD) jet printing as a representative AM process. A Gaussian Process (GP) classifier is trained on 123 high-speed video sequences captured at 15,000 frames per second accurately predicts five printing regimes, including cone-jetting, micro-dripping, dripping, unstable, and no-print, across a wide range of parameters. Further, a deep learning model combining a 3D convolutional encoder and transformer-based temporal predictor provided highly accurate quantitative estimation of frame-by-frame droplet dynamics at a computational cost orders of magnitude less than equivalent computational fluid dynamics simulations. These results establish a data-driven framework for the simulation, predictive control, and rapid optimization of EHD printing dynamics, demonstrating the potential of high-speed imaging-informed machine learning as a computationally efficient surrogate for complex AM processes.
authors: Stanford White; Damian L. Stoddard; Prashant Ghimire; Joshua Russell; Yiwei Han; Samrat Choudhury

title: Judgment by agents, numbers by code: auditable automated speciation analysis towards a chemistry world model
abstract: Chemical speciation governs the reactivity, solubility, and toxicity of a solution, yet assembling speciation calculations from evaluated thermodynamic data remains a manual expert task whose reasoning is discarded once the figure is drawn. To mirror real-world research, automation belongs within a chemistry world model (CWM) where language agents curate and analyze data. As a first module, our agentic framework converts plain-language questions into deterministic equilibrium calculations grounded in NIST Standard Reference Database 46 (SRD-46). Agents resolve intent, curate records, adjudicate duplicates, design calculations, and estimate values beyond database coverage through induction-deduction-validation loops, while deterministic code validates every agentic commitment before it reaches the solver and compacts diagram topology into text readable without a vision stage. Across four case studies of escalating difficulty, quoted constants, patched records, and boundary coordinates reproduced their sources essentially exactly, whereas the same model without the framework missed phases or failed to build a solver. Residual errors surfaced only as auditable narration flaws, from misread topology to a sign-flipped hydrogen-evolution argument. The framework serves as a human-in-the-loop instrument delivering consensus-grade starting points, turning evaluated databases into active discovery instruments, mapping where language-model chemical reasoning still fails, and providing a general agentic template for finetuning.
authors: Yunkai Sun; Adwaith Ravichandran; Hassan Harb; Rajeev S. Assary; Brian J. Ingram; Zhenzhen Yang

title: LLM-IDEA: Identifiability-Driven Experimental Agent for Autonomous Discovery of Mechanistic World Models
abstract: Large language model agents are being increasingly deployed as autonomous scientists, designing experiments and inferring mechanistic world models with minimal human oversight. Yet identifiability is often overlooked: when a plateau is reached, the agent needs to know whether it is not yet capable enough or the model simply is not identifiable from the data, in which case no amount of further experimentation of the same kind can help. We propose the Identifiability-Driven Experimental Agent (LLM-IDEA) for closed-loop discovery with an identifiability engine that returns a three-way plateau verdict: capability limit, resolvable within the design class, or certified exhausted. On ODEBench, 60 of the 62 systems with free constants are identifiable at round 0; the RC circuit is certified exhausted for every experiment that protocol can run, and a harvesting model is resolvable by one added initial condition. The identifiability engine reproduces known verdicts on Lotka-Volterra, Van der Pol, Lorenz, and a pharmacokinetic model, where it recommends the intravenous arm pharmacologists use, and it ranks the depth scorer of our own benchmark last among four observation designs. On the DiscoverPhysics benchmark, it finds two public worlds whose explanation rubric rewards a distinction no legal experiment can make, and every model there with accurate trajectories failed the explanation grade (15 of 15, against 5 of 9 in identifiable worlds, p = 0.012). On the Alien Universe, a two-body testbed we propose in which a force law switches between a provably non-identifiable and an identifiable protocol, LLM-IDEA on the identifiable protocol reaches discovery depth at least three on 8/8 seeds versus 1/8 without it. An autonomous discovery agent can thus compute, rather than guess, whether a plateau calls for more search, a better experiment of the same kind, or a different kind of experiment.
authors: Surya Shetty; Ulisses Braga-Neto

title: LabCompiler: A Framework for Verifiable Human-Machine Laboratory Execution from Imperfect Protocols
abstract: Closing the loop of AI-driven science requires reliably translating natural-language protocols into executable laboratory workflows despite protocol defects and heterogeneous hardware. Existing approaches often couple scientific interpretation with device-specific code generation, making errors difficult to localize and limiting reuse across laboratory platforms. We introduce LabCompiler, a robust protocol-to-execution framework that transforms imperfect natural-language protocols into verifiable human-machine workflows. Its protocol firewall diagnoses and repairs defects before compilation while preserving unaffected content, guided by troubleshooting knowledge accumulated through perturbation-guided self-evolution. A two-level, device-agnostic graph representation separates experimental semantics from hardware-specific implementation and supports capability-based device assignment with coordinated human execution. We further introduce a protocol recovery benchmark covering four controlled perturbation types and naturally occurring errors collected from protocols written by iGEM participants. Experiments show that LabCompiler outperforms frontier LLMs in protocol error correction while enabling coordinated human-machine execution across heterogeneous, partially automated laboratory settings.
authors: Jingyuan Li; Dongzhan Zhou; Minting Pan; Yujie Liu; Yuan Gao; Yankai Jiang; Xinyu Gu; Zhe Liu; Yang Li; Bo Zhang; Lei Bai; Tong Si; Weinan Zhang

title: Laboratory 4.0: on the path to the fourth generation of laboratory medicine
abstract: Abstract Laboratory medicine has witnessed three generational paradigm shifts over the past 75 years – from manual work to early automation, from batch processing to patient-oriented selective analysis, and from human perianalytics to Total Laboratory Automation (TLA). Drawing on a personal trajectory spanning half a century of the discipline, this essay argues that a fourth generation, called “Laboratory 4.0”, is not a distant utopia but an expected reality, just like the so-called “Industry 4.0,” which is emerging in other areas of technological development. Three converging forces are driving this transformation: miniaturization (microfluidics, lab-on-a-chip platforms, and painless capillary sampling), decentralization (pervasive diagnostics available at any point and time without a central laboratory as intermediary), and artificial intelligence (from classical decision-support systems to generative large language models). A hybrid model is proposed in which incremental modernization within existing structures (until ∼2035) gives way to genuine decentralization and democratization of diagnostic services (∼2035 to 2045), followed by a fundamental redefinition of the discipline’s role in society from 2045 onwards. Underlying these technical developments is a new epistemic responsibility: as AI transforms raw data into medical knowledge autonomously, laboratory professionals must claim their irreplaceable role as the sole legally and professionally qualified institution responsible for translating laboratory data into medical insight. The future of laboratory medicine is not a swan song, it is an invitation to actively shape the laboratory 4.0.
authors: Georg Hoffmann

title: Laser-induced local wetting on self-assembled monolayers for microscale fluid control
abstract: Precise spatial control of surface wettability is central to emerging technologies in microfluidics, biosensing, and medical applications. However, current methods for wetting control can be limited by low spatial resolution, a narrow range of achievable wettability modulation, or reliance on masks that are time-consuming to fabricate. Here, we introduce Laser-Induced Local Wetting (LILoW), a maskless technique that uses nanosecond ultraviolet laser pulses to selectively change the wettability of self-assembled monolayer (SAM) coated surfaces. By locally irradiating the SAM coating near its ablation threshold to expose selected regions of the underlying substrate, LILoW combines the broad wetting tunability of coating-based approaches with the high-resolution patterning capabilities of laser systems. We describe the principle of the technique and analyze the contrast in wettability—up to nearly 90 ° —as a function of laser parameters, including laser pulse energy and irradiation pitch, all without inducing damage to the substrate. As a proof of concept, we fabricated an open-air, pumpless Y-shaped microfluidic guide that facilitates capillary-driven laminar co-flow, with high interfacial stability in the absence of physical wall confinement. The rapid and cost-effective platform represented by LILoW can pave the way to democratizing high-resolution wettability patterning for bioanalytical sensing and surface-guided chemical applications.
authors: Lidia Lozano‐Martín; Olga Bantysh; José María Gómez; Jordi Ignés‐Mullol; Martí Duocastella

title: Laser-matter interactions in intrinsically soft materials for biointegrated systems
abstract: Abstract Biointegrated systems are emerging as a new class of technology that redefines how electronic devices interact with the human body and surrounding environments through intimate integration with biological tissues. To establish such interfaces, intrinsically soft materials, including liquid metals, conducting polymers, hydrogels, elastomers, and composites, have attracted significant attention because their low modulus minimizes mechanical mismatch with soft tissues. However, conventional fabrication strategies are often incompatible with intrinsically soft materials due to harsh processing conditions. In this regard, laser processing has emerged as a powerful manufacturing strategy for soft biointegrated systems by delivering highly localized and programmable energy with exceptional spatial and temporal precision. Depending on the laser-matter interaction mechanism, laser irradiation can induce localized heating, structural reconfiguration, chemical conversion, and interfacial reconstruction within soft materials. In this article, we explore the fundamental mechanisms of two representative laser-matter interactions, photothermal and photochemical. Then we deal with laser processing strategies for soft materials, followed by representative biointegrated systems enabled by laser-based approaches. Finally, we discuss current challenges and future opportunities for scalable, adaptive, and intelligent biointegrated systems. Collectively, these discussions highlight the emerging role of laser processing in tailoring structural properties and generating conductive functionalities in intrinsically soft biointegrated systems.
authors: Jung Jae Park; Minwoo Kim; Seung Hwan Ko

title: Liquid Metal Resistive Sensing Architectures for Measuring Diaphragm Strain Responses on Obstructed Surfaces
abstract: ABSTRACT The mechanical response of diaphragm actuators for microfluidics and soft robotics is typically characterized on flat surfaces rather than the obstructed interfaces encountered in practical devices. Upon diaphragm actuation on textured or obstructed interfaces, geometric constraints redirect the strain from uniform bending to a constrained draping mode, which is not transduced by standard strain sensing. We formulate a liquid metal‐based strain sensing architecture integrated on a circular diaphragm to measure and control diaphragm deformation on even and uneven surfaces, using a rigid bead to create an obstructed diaphragm interface. Using finite element simulations, the electrical readouts from the strain sensor on the actuated diaphragm are correlated to its progression from symmetric diaphragm deformation to constrained geometry‐induced nonlinear diaphragm deformation and eventually to saturated diaphragm deformation at the bead center, with the predicted bead‐constrained deformation showing close agreement to the cross‐sectional confocal measurements across the diaphragm. The electrical readouts from the strain sensor reflecting the deformation regimes under geometric interruptions are utilized to control diaphragm‐induced confinement on an array of beads, which is validated based on its biomolecular immobilization level. This electromechanical basis for transducing diaphragm displacement on obstructed surfaces provides a roadmap to control actuation in microfluidic and soft‐robotic systems.
authors: Abdullah‐Bin Siddique; Jui‐Hong Weng; Deng‐Kai Yang; Chia‐Fu Chou; Nathan S. Swami

title: Livestock disease monitoring using artificial intelligence, machine learning and deep learning algorithms: A review
abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), and Deep Learning (DL) in livestock disease detection has ushered in a new era of precision farming. These technologies facilitate early detection and diagnosis of diseases, thereby minimizing the impact on livestock health and improving overall farm productivity. AI-driven systems analyse vast datasets from various sources such as images, videos, and sensor data to identify patterns and anomalies indicative of disease. Machine Learning algorithms enhance the predictive accuracy by learning from historical data, while Deep Learning models further refine disease detection by analysing complex patterns in real-time. In this article an attempt was made to review the detection of different livestock diseases using several machine and deep learning algorithms. An array of livestock disease conditions such as mastitis, cardiovascular diseases, diseases during postpartum period, and animal skin ailments were detected using different machine learning and deep learning algorithms and among them, decision tree model, ResNet101, Support Vector Machine (SVM), Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), YOLOv5, EfficientNetB7 and EFMYOLOv3 were found to be most efficient algorithms for detection of the livestock diseases.
authors: Jahnavi AP; Ramesh BK; Harish Menpadi; Srinivasa DK
venue: International Journal of Advanced Biochemistry Research

title: Lookahead Bayesian Optimisation for Molecular Growth in Self-Driving Laboratories
abstract: Self-driving laboratories can autonomously execute iterative design-make-test-analyse cycles, but molecular optimisation presents a distinctive challenge: selecting which compound to elaborate determines not only the next experiment, but also the chemical space accessible in subsequent rounds. Conventional molecular Bayesian optimisation typically evaluates compounds without considering how their selection changes what can subsequently be synthesised. Here, we introduce Lookahead Bayesian Optimisation (LABO), which instead values candidate molecules according to the predicted value of the synthetically accessible chemical space they unlock, enabling optimisation to account for future experimental opportunities. We evaluate LABO in simulated five-round molecular optimisation campaigns across 30 lead-like starting compounds and five kinase targets. LABO outperformed established molecular optimisation strategies from the literature across all 30 optimisation landscapes, as well as random, greedy and Bayesian optimisation controls. LABO was shown to improve ligand-lipophilicity efficiency by 1.25 units over random selection, equivalent to approximately 18-fold greater potency at equal lipophilicity, and by 0.34 units (2.2-fold) over greedy elaboration. These results demonstrate a general principle for autonomous molecular optimisation: under synthetic constraints, the value of a molecule depends not only on its predicted properties, but on the future experiments that selecting it makes possible. By explicitly incorporating this future experimental value into molecular selection, LABO provides a framework for planning successive rounds of molecular growth in self-driving laboratories.
authors: Connor J. Taylor

title: MACHINE LEARNING-ASSISTED COMPUTATIONAL CHEMISTRY FOR ACCELERATED MOLECULAR DESIGN AND SUSTAINABLE CHEMICAL INNOVATION
abstract: Machine learning-assisted computational chemistry has emerged as a transformative approach for accelerating molecular design and promoting sustainable chemical innovation by integrating data-driven algorithms with computational modeling techniques. This review provides an overview of the principles, methodologies, and applications of machine learning in computational chemistry, highlighting its role in molecular property prediction, quantitative structure–activity and structure–property relationship modeling, virtual screening, de novo molecular design, and structure-based drug discovery. The review further discusses key molecular representation strategies, including molecular descriptors, fingerprints, SMILES, SELFIES, graph-based representations, and biomolecular features, which serve as the foundation for predictive modeling. Major machine learning algorithms, including regression models, support vector machines, random forests, artificial neural networks, graph neural networks, transformer models, and generative artificial intelligence, are examined with respect to their contributions to computational chemistry workflows. In addition, the review explores the expanding applications of machine learning in molecular biology and genetics, including drug target identification, protein structure prediction, pharmacogenomics, biomolecular interaction analysis, disease-associated molecular discovery, and precision medicine. The role of artificial intelligence in advancing green molecular design, sustainable catalyst discovery, reaction optimization, eco-friendly material development, and sustainable pharmaceutical manufacturing is also highlighted. Finally, emerging trends such as generative AI, large language models, explainable artificial intelligence, multi-omics integration, and autonomous molecular discovery platforms are discussed alongside current challenges and future perspectives. Collectively, machine learning-assisted computational chemistry represents a powerful interdisciplinary framework for accelerating molecular discovery while supporting sustainable and biologically informed chemical innovation.
authors: Anil Kumar Singh; Kedar Prasad Meena; Balaji Maroti Pulchwad; Texin Joseph; Chayannika Singh; Dr. Dinesha H E

title: MICROROBOTIC SAMPLING AND QUANTUM BIOSENSING CO-DESIGN AT THE LIMIT An Exploratory Engineering Monograph on Sample Handling, Reference Control, and Biological Risk Boundaries This research monograph examines whether controlled micromanipulation can improve the positioning, transport, recovery, and reproducibility of biological research samples without increasing sample alteration, cross-contamination, thermal exposure, or misleading biosensor signals. The guiding three-coupling is Sample Handling × Reference Control × Biological Risk Boundary. Its guiding question is not whether an autonomous microrobot can move a sample, but whether the resulting measurement remains traceable to an authentic, independently verifiable sample state. The work synthesizes three mother research architectures: (S) Swarm Manufacturing and Robotic Matter at the Limit, particularly chapters 9–16 and 33–40, for embodied manipulation and collective transport; (QH) Autonomous Quantum Health Infrastructure at the Limit, especially chapters 9–24 and 67–74, for raw-to-result lineage, uncertainty-aware decisions, human authority and recovery; and (QB) Self-Calibrating Quantum Biosensing Networks at the Limit, particularly chapters 57–73, for fabrication variation, reference transfer, calibration, drift and measurement integrity. These sources contribute methods rather than evidence that the cross-domain integration is already demonstrated. Across 82 chapters and 12 single-section research studies per chapter, the monograph examines non-clinical microfluidic sample environments, magnetic and acoustic micromanipulation, optical and electrokinetic methods, nanoscale surface chemistry, quantum-enabled and classical biosensing, correlated uncertainty, sample-to-signal provenance, authorized closed-loop control, physical damage and carryover detection, interlaboratory replication, lifecycle burden, and successor reconstruction. Thirty mathematical and physical derivation plates introduce assumptions and validity boundaries. Every chapter presents a distinct candidate engineering relation and a geometric three-dimensional research portrait. The validation approach prioritizes synthetic phantoms and permitted ex-vivo research standards in closed non-clinical environments. It calls for blinded comparison of skilled manual pipetting, passive microfluidics, and robotic operation under matched sample identity, measurement time, contamination constraints, and independent calibration. A perceived improvement in robotic throughput or algorithmic readout quality does not establish improved sample authenticity. Any claim of quantum advantage must be compared against an appropriate, strong classical sensing baseline end to end. The research architecture closes with 200 independently framed Research Gates and 33 provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos, each accompanied by one of 233 indexed equation eggs. Gates specify questions, comparators, pass criteria, and veto conditions; answer embryos can be challenged, decomposed, recombined or retired. An accompanying Research Gates spreadsheet maps these questions to chapters, physical relations, evidence packets and future experiments. The study is explicitly exploratory and non-clinical. It does not establish the existence of mature autonomous in-body nanorobotic medicine, grant permission for diagnosis or therapy, or imply that quantum-enabled detection is intrinsically superior. Candidate indices and equations are design hypotheses unless identified as established physical relations; many passages use a recurring structured research grammar and require independent experiments, domain expert review, and peer assessment. The aim is to leave a reproducible and falsifiable research architecture that subsequent investigators are free to revise, reject, or extend. title: MOF-VERIFY: A Failure-Aware Agentic Harness for MOF Hypothesis Verification
abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as reasoning components in AI-driven materials Co-Scientists, yet the reliability of the resulting verification pipeline remains unclear. Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) provide a particularly challenging setting because structures may appear under different identifiers, synthesis outcomes depend strongly on experimental conditions, evidence is distributed across heterogeneous sources, and some hypotheses require computation rather than literature alone. We introduce a diagnostic benchmark with four task families covering structural grounding, synthesis-condition verification, evidence-sufficiency verification, and MLIP-based computational verification. T-MOF-1-3 are evaluated under closed-book, retrieval-enabled, and oracle-evidence settings to localize failures in knowledge access, evidence acquisition, and reasoning, while T-MOF-4 separately evaluates computational verification. Guided by these diagnosed failure modes, we develop MOF-Verify, a failure-aware agentic harness that targets structural, literature, evidence-sufficiency, and computational bottlenecks before producing a final verdict. Across multiple backbone LLMs, MOF-Verify substantially improves hypothesis-verification performance over direct inference and retrieval-based baselines. Benchmark datasets are released at https://github.com/IMMS-Ewha/MOF-Verify-Benchmark.
authors: Donghyun Lee; Taehoon Lee; Geonhee Ahn; Jieun Kim; Jihyun Park; Suyeon Cho; Yoona Kim; Chaerim Shin; Hoi Ri Moon; Jonggeol Na; Sukho Hong; Jihwan Oh; Soo Kyung Kim

title: Machine Learning-Based Taylor Cone Analysis for Electrospinning Process-Window Identification and Cell-Laden Nanofiber Scaffold Fabrication
abstract: Electrospinning is a powerful biofabrication technique for constructing fibrous scaffolds that mimic extracellular matrix architectures. However, the process is highly nonlinear and involves strongly coupled parameters, making fiber architecture and biological performance difficult to control empirically and limits reproducibility. Most machine learning (ML) studies still focus on static correlations between processing parameters and outcomes rather than on dynamic modeling of electrospinning evolution and regulation, thereby hindering real-time, precise process control. Here, we establish a data-driven framework that links process parameters, Taylor cone geometry, and nanofiber/cell outcomes through high-speed imaging and ML. A custom image-processing pipeline is developed to automatically extract cone angle, height, and width from in situ images with improved accuracy via a rotating-ray-based geometric algorithm. Using datasets collected from three representative polymer systems (PVDF, PVB, and PEO), random forest models outperform support vector machine and minimum description length, achieving moderate-to-good prediction of Taylor cone descriptors (R²≈0.57-0.83) across varied voltages, flow rate, and needle-collector distances. We further extend this framework to PEO-based cell electrospinning. By correlating predicted cone geometries with experimentally measured viability of 293T cells and umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells, we identify a Taylor cone "safe window" that simultaneously stabilizes jet formation and preserves cell survival (>95%). Guided by this window, a bilayer cell-laden scaffold comprising a PVB support layer and a PEO-cell layer is fabricated with improved process robustness. This enables stable delivery of high-density, highly viable cells and facilitates the fabrication of three-dimensional cell-laden nanofiber scaffolds. Overall, this Taylor cone analysis, ML-guided strategy provides a quantitative framework for process-window identification in polymer and cell electrospinning, and may support future integration with real-time monitoring, online inference, and closed-loop control in intelligent biofabrication.
authors: Huazhen Liu; Kaidi Luo; Jiayao Gu; Wenbin Sun; Xiaoyi Wang; Yongjun Zheng; Zhijian Li; Su Xiao; Yuanyuan Liu

title: Machine Learning–Assisted Fluorescent Eu@ZnMOF for the Enoxacin and Glyphosate Detection in Food by Suppressing Sensitization and Ligand–Metal Charge Transfer
abstract: ABSTRACT The antibiotics and pesticides in the ecosystem environment, owing to their extensive application in veterinary medicine and insecticides, present a significant hazard to public health. Herein, we developed a novel bimetallic metal‐organic framework (MOF) as a ratiometric fluorescent sensor for the simultaneous monitoring of enoxacin (ENX) and glyphosate (GLY). To fabricate a dual‐responsive probe, we synthesized the ZnMOF by reacting Zn 2+ ions with the ligands (2,2′‐bipyridine‐5,5′‐dicarboxylic acid, 8‐hydroxyquinoline, and 2‐aminoterephthalic acid). Subsequently, the bimetallic Eu@ZnMOF was synthesized by loading europium (Eu 3+ ) ions into the ZnMOF based on the coordination with the 2,2′‐bipyridine‐5,5′‐dicarboxylic acid sites. The Eu@ZnMOF‐based detection system exhibits a distinct green emission due to the suppression of excited‐state intramolecular proton transfer in 8‐hydroxyquinoline by Zn 2+ ions. In the detection system, ENX enhances the red emission of Eu@ZnMOF by sensitizing Eu 3+ ions. Accordingly, the ENX fluorescent sensing system was fabricated. Moreover, ENX‐modified Eu@ZnMOF was fabricated. Upon the addition of GLY, suppression of sensitization and ligand‐to‐metal charge transfer (LMCT) occurs, which quenches the red emission of Eu 3+ and boosts the blue emission, resulting in a distinct color transition from red to blue. The ratiometric fluorescent sensor allows detection limits of 0.05 and 0.10 mg/L for ENX and GLY, respectively. Moreover, we integrated this material into a microfluidic chip. By combining this platform with smartphone imaging and machine learning algorithms, we constructed a rapid detection protocol capable of simultaneous multi‐sample analysis. These results demonstrate the promising application potential of Eu@ZnMOF for advanced environmental and food‐safety testing.
authors: Ze Li; Yan Man; Qingju Liu; Jilong Han; Zhikun Zhang

title: Machine-Vision-Assisted Automated Closed-Loop Manipulation of Open-Surface Droplets.
abstract: Automated manipulation of open-surface droplets is important for microscale sample handling, reaction assembly, and biochemical analysis, yet existing systems often lack obstacle-aware planning, control-state monitoring, and disturbance recovery. Here, we present a machine-vision-assisted closed-loop system for programmable, noncontact droplet manipulation on a photogated corona microfluidic (PGCM) platform. The system integrates real-time localization, rapidly exploring random tree planning, robotic laser actuation, and hierarchical feedback control. An inner loop guides the laser spot along the planned path, while an outer loop monitors the droplet-laser binding state. Obstacle changes trigger online replanning, whereas loss of binding triggers laser return, droplet recapture, and task recovery. The system transported 1-50 μL droplets, performed sequential coalescence, static and dynamic obstacle avoidance, complex-path manipulation, multistep reactions, and droplet-mediated transport of a flexible porous solid target. Following a manually imposed voltage interruption, it automatically detected loss of binding and resumed the task after actuation was restored. This work provides a programmable and disturbance-tolerant visual closed-loop framework for automated open-surface droplet manipulation.
authors: Biao Cheng; Jialin Yang; Chengjun Wang; Yongliang Sun; Lei Zhou; Qiang Zhao; Huanyu Li; Yifan Meng; Qiang Tang
venue: Langmuir : the ACS journal of surfaces and colloids

title: Magneto-electrochemistry: A tool for sustainability and green chemistry
abstract: Magnetic fields provide a versatile and energy efficient strategy for modulating electrochemical processes without adding chemical reagents, mechanical stirring, or complex reactor designs. By coupling ionic currents with external magnetic fields, the resulting Lorentz-driven magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) convection accelerates mass transport and regulates interfacial kinetics at the micro- and macro-scale. These transport phenomena govern reaction rates, metal nucleation and growth, electrodeposition quality, and the long-term stability of electrochemical systems. This review examines recent advances in magnetic field assisted electrochemistry through the lens of process intensification and the 12 Principles of Green Chemistry. We discuss how magnetic fields influence fundamental processes, including electrodeposition, electrocatalysis, electrochemical energy storage, and emerging applications such as microfluidics, sensing, and dynamic autonomous systems, with a specific emphasis on the use of permanent magnets as zero-operating-energy tools for controlling transport. By evaluating sustainability metrics and life-cycle considerations, we highlight opportunities to enhance turnover frequencies and reduce the industry's reliance on critical minerals, chemical additives, or mechanical agitation. Finally, we identify key challenges that must be addressed to translate magnetic control from laboratory demonstrations to scalable electrochemical technologies. These include the need for quantitative transport models and reactor designs that can be implemented at industrially relevant scales. Overall, magnetic field assisted electrochemistry is positioned as an emerging approach for improving efficiency and circularity in the next generation of electrified chemical manufacturing.

title: Mapping the technology–demand interface: how brain organoid evolution is reshaping the translational landscape of stroke
abstract: Stroke research faces a dual modeling barrier: interspecies divergence and oversimplified 2D cultures have contributed to the failure of many neuroprotective trials. Brain organoids, which provide human genetic backgrounds and 3D neural networks, offer a promising but incomplete solution. Existing reviews often address isolated technological aspects without linking them to stroke-specific demands. This narrative review establishes a “technological iteration–clinical demand” mapping matrix (Figure 1). We trace organoid evolution from static oxygen–glucose deprivation models to vascularized, assembloid, and microfluidic chip-integrated systems, and toward multi-organ coupling. We highlight how these advances may uncover human-specific neuroinflammation, proposed PANoptosis-like spatiotemporal cascades, and synaptic deficits mediated by human-specific genes such as SRGAP2C. We argue that the inability of animal models to resolve certain human-specific targets is driving organoids from static endpoint models toward dynamic platforms with perfusable vasculature and immune integration, although current systems remain at an early stage. We critically evaluate the preclinical role of organoids, defining scenarios where they may partially replace animal testing and where they cannot. Major bottlenecks include fetal-like organoid maturity (transcriptome approximately equivalent to gestational weeks 12–20) versus the average stroke onset age of about 70 years, and the absence of peripheral immune infiltration, which mediates a large fraction of secondary injury. We outline potential solutions including multi-omics integration, inducible aging, gene editing, and multi-organ chip coupling, and emphasize that standardized evaluation frameworks are needed to translate organoid findings into personalized stroke therapy.

title: Mathematical analysis of electromagnetically driven squeezing flow in confined microchannels
abstract: Abstract Nanofluids flowing through confined channels are widely used in micro-cooling systems, miniature pumps, and other microfluidic technologies, where the combined effects of electromagnetic forces and variable fluid properties play an important role in transport phenomena. This study explores the squeezing flow of a nanofluid between two parallel plates, specifically focusing on a stretching, porous lower plate. We examine how external electric and magnetic fields influence flow transport. Temperature-dependent viscosity and thermal conductivity are included in the model to obtain a realistic thermophysical behaviour of the nanofluid flow. The novelty of the study lies in simultaneously considering electro-magnetohydrodynamic effects together with variable fluid properties within the Buongiorno nanofluid model. The governing equations are transformed using similarity transformations and solved by the Optimal Homotopy Analysis Method (OHAM). The results reveal that squeezing, electroosmotic, and electric field parameters enhance the forward flow, whereas suction and magnetic field intensity oppose the fluid motion. Brownian motion and thermophoresis increase the fluid temperature, while increasing the thermophoresis and Lewis number leads to a reduction in the nanoparticle concentration. The combined influence of electromagnetic effects and variable fluid properties demonstrates their importance in controlling flow and heat transfer in confined microfluidic systems.

title: Matrix-Based Specific T-Cell Activation Reporter for Nearly-Digital Mapping of Antigen-Specific T Cells via Heterotypic Cell Micro-Communities and Digital Microfluidics.
abstract: Antigen-specific T cells constitute a low percentage of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and require antigen presentation by autologous antigen-presenting cells for activation and cytokine secretion. Conventional interferon-γ release assay (IGRA) averages rare activation events beyond cellular resolution, while single-cell compartmentalization disrupts the intracellular synapses for T cell immunity. Here, we developed mSTAR (matrix-based Specific T-cell Activation Reporter), an active-matrix digital microfluidic platform that partitions microliters of PBMCs into a nanoliter-scale matrix of 16 cell microcommunities (CMCs), each retaining tens to hundreds of PBMCs in their native heterotypic composition to preserve the natural physiological immune response. In a proof of concept, mSTAR executes parallel IGRA for a tuberculosis disease model, including CMC stimulation and magnetic-bead-based immunofluorescence assay. The IGRA of the mSTAR system achieves a limit of detection of 3.70 pg/mL, yielding 16 interferon-γ quantification readouts and ratios between CMCs incubated with different stimulants (negative, positive, or specific antigen). This enables the mapping and reporting of activated antigen-specific T cells in the matrix, thereby achieving functional phenotyping of each CMC. Poisson-based modeling of the droplet matrix converts rare T-cell activation events into a nearly digital estimation, and the positive CMCs encapsulating target cells can be retrieved for further characterization without loss. By bridging functional phenotyping and molecular features without prior cell sorting or engineering, mSTAR provides a programmable immunoanalytical infrastructure for broad downstream applications such as antigen-specific immunotherapy development or T-cell receptor discovery.

title: Mesenchymal stem cells and their exosomes modulate sebocyte fate and lipid-associated proteomic-lipidomic remodeling.
abstract: Sebocytes regulate skin lipid production and inflammatory homeostasis, yet how mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) and MSCs-derived exosomes reshape sebocyte function remains unclear. This study compared the effects of indirect MSCs co-culture and MSCs-derived exosome treatment on MTS-associated metabolic activity, intracellular lipid droplet accumulation, proteomic remodeling, and lipidomic profiles in sebocytes. Human sebocytes were indirectly co-cultured with bone marrow-derived MSCs using transwell inserts or treated with MSCs-derived exosomes under proliferative or low-serum, lipid accumulation-promoting conditions. MTS-associated metabolic activity was assessed using the MTS assay, intracellular lipid droplet accumulation using Nile Red staining, proteomic remodeling using label-free LC-MS/MS, and lipidomic changes using untargeted LC-MS lipidomics. Indirect MSCs co-culture reduced MTS-associated metabolic activity, particularly under low-serum conditions, while markedly increasing intracellular lipid droplet accumulation. Proteomic analysis indicated that MSCs co-culture promoted cytoskeletal, adhesion-related, and lipid-handling remodeling. Lipidomics further revealed broad lipid-class reprogramming, characterized by increased phospholipid-associated features and reduced lysophospholipid-associated features. In contrast, MSCs-derived exosomes increased MTS-associated metabolic activity under low-serum conditions, while intracellular lipid droplet accumulation remained largely comparable to control levels. Exosome treatment induced more selective proteomic changes related to proteostasis, mitochondrial adaptation, and vesicular trafficking/signaling, with limited lipidomic alterations that did not remain significant after FDR correction. MSCs co-culture and MSCs-derived exosomes exert biologically distinct effects on sebocytes. Whole MSCs co-culture drives extensive lipid-associated remodeling, whereas isolated exosomes mainly increase MTS-associated metabolic activity and induce adaptive proteomic responses, suggesting that exosomes transmit only part of the broader MSCs paracrine influence on sebocyte biology.
authors: Maryam Adelipour; Mohamed A Gab-Allah; Mingyu Kim; Sangsoo Lee; Kee K Kim; Ga Seul Lee; Jeong Hee Moon; David M Lubman; Jeongkwon Kim

title: Micro/Nanostructured Materials and Microfluidic Diagnostic Platforms Enable Multimodal Detection of Circulating Tumor Cells
abstract: Circulating tumor cells (CTCs), as pivotal targets in liquid biopsy, offer dynamic, multidimensional insights into tumor heterogeneity and metastatic progression. However, their extreme rarity, pronounced heterogeneity, and the complexity of the blood microenvironment severely constrain detection accuracy. Advances in micro/nanomaterials and functional device engineering have enabled substantial improvements in CTC enrichment efficiency by refining the topographical and chemical properties of capture interfaces. These innovations also provide a compatible foundation for multimodal molecular profiling. This review systematically outlines the structure-function relationships of functionalized nanomaterials, microfiltration substrates, and biomimetic microfluidic devices, highlighting how material parameters-such as nanoscale architectures and membrane pore sizes-govern CTC capture performance. We further explore the integration of micro/nanomaterials with functional platforms for multidimensional molecular analyses across DNA, RNA, and protein levels. Coupled with emerging digital PCR technologies, these systems show promise in overcoming the sensitivity barriers associated with rare mutation detection and protein quantification, enabling multi-omics data fusion. We also discuss how artificial intelligence (AI)-driven feature selection, clustering, and prediction integrate multidimensional data to decode tumor heterogeneity and guide disease monitoring. Despite rapid progress, key challenges remain-including the lack of standardization, limited integration of multi-omic datasets, and the need for robust clinical validation. Future directions may lie in the convergence of microfluidic-integrated materials, single-cell multi-omics, and AI-driven analytics to establish dynamic, high-resolution monitoring platforms that bridge the gap between fundamental research and clinical precision oncology.
authors: Hao Li; Jiaojiao Sun; Kunguo Liu; Shijie Wang; Bowen Fu; Hong Zhu; Peng Cao; Xin Han

title: Microbial quality control management in industry : approaches for assessing bioburden and community composition
abstract: Microbial contamination of industrial products and processes can endanger the health and safety of consumers and workers and negatively affect businesses by causing product spoilage and decreases in process efficiency. Major microbial contamination events can result in financial losses from product recalls, unplanned production downtime, loss of sales and litigation. Effective microbial monitoring is essential for detecting the presence of microorganisms and helps businesses control and maintain product quality. This thesis first examines the challenges in achieving accurate assessments of microbial load, which is defined as the quantity of viable microorganisms within a given sample matrix (Chapter 2). Classical culture techniques remain the most widely utilized and approved methods but their major shortcomings have limited their applicability in Quality Management systems employed to control contamination throughout product processing, handling, and distribution. Issues such as the long incubation times to achieve a result, the selective bias of culture conditions on species recovery, and the inability to detect damaged or injured cells are discussed. Rapid microbiological methods (RMMs) offer increased sensitivity and accuracy, can deliver results in near real-time, and could enable more effective and proactive management of microbial contamination problems. Nevertheless, their uptake in industry has been hindered by their higher operating costs and time-consuming proof-of-equivalency studies to the reference culture methods, which are required for approval by the relevant regulatory bodies. An overview of commercially available RMMs is provided and the suitability of each method is application- and industry-dependent. An industrial case study of microbial monitoring methods was performed with Omya AG (Switzerland) the top global producer of calcium carbonate (CC) slurries (Chapter 3). CC slurries are used as manufacturing fillers in a wide range of industries including paper, paints, construction and food. High microbial loads have been shown to adversely effect slurry quality and performance and negatively impact on customers’ finished products (Schwarzentruber, 2003). Quality Assurance (QA) managers rely on culture dip slides for detecting microbial load and directing biocide treatment to manage excessive population growth. RMMs offer Omya the potential for cost savings from effective biocide management and could help QA managers uncover and remedy microbial-related product spoilage sooner. The viability-based RMM CellFacts II (CFII) (CellFacts2014 Ltd., UK) combines electrical flow impedance and viable cell specific fluorescent staining to produce an accurate, real-time measurement of the contaminating population. To improve its usability and desirability to Omya the technology was optimized by streamlining sample preparation steps, the cost per test was reduced, and data presentation and interpretation was simplified. During this study CFII showed increased sensitivity and reliability compared to dip slides and highlighted the differences in preservation efficiency and bioburden levels in slurries preserved with biocide blends or by pHstabilization. Although pH stabilizers are added to slurries during production, Omya still relies upon biocides for managing any uncontrolled microbial growth detected during product storage or upon delivery to customers. The biocide-preserved slurries that were analyzed were maintained at pH 8.5-9.0 while the pH-stabilized slurry were pH 9.5-10.0. It was hypothesized that this 1-log difference in pH impacted upon microbial community composition and it was necessary to ensure that these populations were still susceptible to post-production biocide treatments. A multifaceted approach was used to characterize the communities and assess the coverage and limitations of each method (Chapter 4). Samples were collected and microbial load was determined by plate culture and CFII, and population diversity was elucidated by the recovery of species in culture and by 16S rRNA gene analysis by Terminal-Restriction Fragment Length Polymorphism (T-RFLP) and sequencing on the Illumina MiSeq (USA). A comparison of direct and indirect DNA extraction methods was performed to observe the efficiency and differences in DNA recovery from microbial species. In addition, DNA from the viable population was selectively amplified by treating isolated microbial cells with propidium monoazide (PMA), a dye that enters non-viable cells, binds DNA and inhibits PCR amplification. Biocidepreserved slurry showed lower diversity in culture compared to pH-stabilized slurry but displayed a higher number of operational taxonomic units (OTUs) by T-RFLP and sequence analysis in the microbiome analysis platform Quantitative Insights in Microbial Ecology (QIIME). The microbial communities were significantly different with Pseudomonas spp. associated with biocide-preserved slurry and alkaliphilic Bacillus spp. dominating in pH-stabilized products. The culture media conditions were inadequate for recovering the highly abundant alkaliphilic population in pHstabilized slurry and future culture work must be optimized on alkaliphilic media. 16S rRNA gene analyses produced a more truthful representation of the community and DNA extracted from PMA-treated cells revealed changes in population structure after 48 hours of incubation and in response to biocide addition. Slurry populations are dynamic; regular sample collection at various time points is necessary to achieve accurate detection and monitoring of microbial communities.

title: Microcapillary-assisted acoustoelectric platform for selective single-cell isolation and in situ transfection
abstract: Single-cell transfection technologies hold tremendous promise for precision cell and immunotherapies. However, monolithic integration of cell isolation with targeted intracellular delivery remains technically challenging, especially within complex biological matrices. Herein, we present a microcapillary-assisted acoustoelectric single-cell selective isolation and sonoporative transfection platform (μC-ASSIST), which seamlessly sequences microcapillary-assisted dielectrophoresis (μC-DEP) for deterministic single-cell trapping with high-frequency surface acoustic waves (SAWs) for transient membrane poration within a unified workflow. We demonstrate the label-free, high-efficiency extraction of human non-small cell lung cancer (A549) cells from a complex white blood cell (WBC) background with a capture efficiency of 95%. Furthermore, we validate the highly efficient, contact-free intracellular delivery of diverse cargoes ranging from small dyes (PI) to functional small interfering RNA (siRNA) and large plasmid DNA (mRFP-C3), maintaining a high cell viability of 83.7% alongside a 78.1% transfection efficiency. Crucially, the targeted delivery of siBcl-xL significantly suppressed target mRNA expression and profoundly inhibited tumor cell motility. By circumventing off-target effects and cumbersome manual handling, the μC-ASSIST platform establishes a highly versatile, streamlined paradigm for precision single-cell engineering, holding immense potential for advancing functional genomics and next-generation gene therapies.

title: Microchemical Strategies and AI-Enabled Biosensing for Non-Invasive Liquid Biopsy in Precision Oncology
abstract: Traditional blood-based liquid biopsy platforms have established crucial paradigms in precision oncology by enabling the longitudinal tracking of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs). However, blood sampling remains minimally invasive, requires dedicated clinical infrastructure, and is restricted by physiological boundaries such as the blood-brain barrier (BBB). Non-Invasive Liquid Biopsy (NILB) addresses these limitations by utilizing painlessly collected alternative biological matrices, including saliva, urine, breath, stool, sweat, sputum, tears, and cervical secretions. From a microchemical and analytical perspective, these biofluids present extreme analytical challenges: target biomarkers exist at attomolar-to-picomolar concentrations within dense, highly variable chemical matrices containing high background noise and interference. This review outlines the microchemical, physical, and bio-sensing strategies developed to overcome these pre-analytical and analytical barriers. We evaluate advanced microfluidic architectures, nanoscale deterministic lateral displacement, functionalized surface chemistry, isothermal signal amplification, and label-free optical spectroscopy. Furthermore, we evaluate how Artificial Intelligence (AI) and chemometric algorithms—such as Support Vector Machines (SVM), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), and multivariate spectral extraction—decode low-abundance, fragmented multi-omic signatures from complex noise. Finally, we propose a standardized analytical framework to bridge point-of-care microchemical devices with routine clinical diagnostic pipelines.

title: Microfluidic Fabrication of Functional Micro-/Nanoparticles: From Structural Regulation to Scalable Integration
abstract: Ran Tian,1,* Jiani Liu,2,* Tao Liu,3 Hanyu Du,1 Geng Dou,2 Juan Tong,4 Xinyu Qiu,4 Linqian Hou,2 Xiaoju Lu,1 Yuting Su51School of Advanced Materials and Green Chemical Engineering, Hubei Polytechnic University, Huangshi, People’s Republic of China; 2State Key Laboratory of Oral & Maxillofacial Reconstruction and Regeneration, National Clinical Research Center for Oral Diseases, School of Stomatology, The Fourth Military Medical University, Xi’an, People’s Republic of China; 3Center of Biodiagnosis and Biotherapy, Precision Medical Institute, The Second Affiliated Hospital of Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an, Shaanxi, People’s Republic of China; 4Department of Preventive Dentistry, State Key Laboratory of Oral & Maxillofacial Reconstruction and Regeneration, National Clinical Research Center for Oral Diseases, Shaanxi Clinical Research Center for Oral Disease, School of Stomatology, The Fourth Military Medical University, Xi’an, People’s Republic of China; 5Center of Clinical Aerospace Medicine, School of Aerospace Medicine, Air Force Medical University, Xi’an, People’s Republic of China*These authors contributed equally to this workCorrespondence: Yuting Su, Center of Clinical Aerospace Medicine, School of Aerospace Medicine, Air Force Medical University, Xi’an, People’s Republic of China, Email sssusyt@163.com Xiaoju Lu, School of Advanced Materials and Green Chemical Engineering, Hubei Polytechnic University, Huangshi, China, Email luxiaoju@hbpu.edu.cnAbstract: Functional particles play critical roles in biomedicine, sensing, catalysis, energy storage and conversion, and environmental remediation. Conventional bulk synthesis can provide limited control over local reaction environments when narrow size distributions, complex morphologies, or hierarchical architectures are required. Microfluidic synthesis addresses these limitations by confining reactions within microscale channels, droplets, or flow segments, thereby enabling controlled multiphase flow, rapid heat and mass transfer, and precise regulation of local reaction conditions. This review is organized around a particle formation/process control/particle properties/scale-up framework, linking microfluidic design and operating parameters to nucleation, growth, phase separation, interfacial assembly, and solidification, and subsequently to particle size, morphology, dispersity, and hierarchical structure. Representative strategies, including droplet microfluidics, hydrodynamic focusing, co-flow systems, structured microchannels, and integrated microreactors, are critically compared in terms of particle-quality control and manufacturing feasibility. Particular attention is given to scalability, productivity, process robustness, clogging, downstream processing, and internal and external integration. Although microfluidic processing can improve control and reproducibility, many reported systems remain at the proof-of-concept or laboratory scale. Future development therefore requires quantitative process-structured relationships, robust device engineering, in-line monitoring, feedback control, and validated scale-up strategies.Keywords: functional particles, microfluidic synthesis, micro-/nanoparticles, particle regulation, chip integration

title: Microfluidic Technologies for Seminal Fluid Analysis: from Sperm Selection to Liquid Biopsy in Prostate Cancer
abstract: Microfluidic technologies, which enable precise manipulation of cells and biological fluids at the microscale, represent a promising platform for reproductive medicine and urologic oncology. This review examines the operating principles, engineering features, and clinical potential of microfluidic systems for seminal fluid analysis, sperm selection, and liquid biopsy in prostate cancer. The reviewed domestic and international literature addresses microfluidic sperm selection, sperm DNA fragmentation, rheotaxis, inertial microfluidics, circulating tumor cells, and molecular biomarkers in seminal fluid. Microfluidic devices can facilitate gentle processing of spermatozoa, enrichment of samples with progressively motile cells, and isolation of tumor cells, extracellular vesicles, and cell-free DNA. Particular attention is paid to the potential for standardized processing of viscous and heterogeneous samples prior to molecular analysis and cytological evaluation in specialized laboratories. A particularly promising area is the development of integrated platforms suitable for clinical validation and subsequent incorporation into diagnostic pathways for patients with prostate diseases.
authors: S. P. Sametov; R. F. Gizatullin; R. I. Tukhvatullin

title: Microfluidic technology: from historical development to modern applications
abstract: Microfluidics is a rapidly evolving interdisciplinary field focused on the precise manipulation and control of fluids at the micrometre scale. The kingdom of microfluidics is ruled by tiny fluid volumes through the development of novel applications that benefit from the use of these small samples. Typical manipulations involve small volumes of fluid (microliters or sub-microliters) leading to improved capability to manipulate fluids, increased accuracy over traditional methodologies, and many successful implementations in diverse domains including health care, environmental capabilities, and chemical processing. Examples of microfluidic implementation that have significantly improved testing efficiency, effectiveness, and portability include lab on chip & point of care testing appliances. The primary advantages of microfluidics include lower sample use, faster analysis times, improved sensitivity, and the ability to combine with other systems for automated operation and control. This review highlights the historical development and fundamental principles of microfluidics along with its growing importance in modern science and engineering. Various applications of microfluidic systems in healthcare diagnostics, environmental monitoring, chemical synthesis, and biological analysis are comprehensively discussed. In addition, the review outlines the current limitations and challenges associated with microfluidic technologies, including fabrication complexity and scalability issues. Overall, this review offers a comprehensive understanding of both possible opportunities and existing limitations of microfluidics. Therefore, it is concluded that further development and improvement of this area are of significant importance, as it may become the basis for future scientific and engineering breakthroughs. Finally, future perspectives and trends in microfluidics are discussed, highlighting its potential to enable revolutionary approaches in subsequent analytical and biomedical technologies.
authors: Sourav Ghosh; Jit Chakraborty; Avishek Saha; Arijit Das; Kalachand Mahali; Sanjay Roy

title: Microfluidics to assess the impact of transfused blood components
abstract: Assessing the function of transfused blood components within the dynamic environment of the vascular system remains challenging, as conventional assays are largely static and poorly represent the dynamic mechanical and biochemical interactions between blood cells and the vessel wall. Microfluidic approaches, which study blood flow within small-scale channels, provide an opportunity to bridge this gap by introducing physiologically relevant flow and shear rates into experimental models. This review synthesises the current literature describing the application of microfluidic technologies to the assessment of transfused blood components, with particular emphasis on platelet concentrates, red cell concentrates and plasma-derived products. Across existing studies, microfluidic models have demonstrated differences in component function related to storage conditions, manufacturing methods and emerging transfusion products that are not always detected using conventional bulk assays. These approaches have provided new insights into platelet haemostasis at defined shear rates, red cell deformability and gas exchange, and plasma-mediated coagulation in trauma and critical illness. However, substantial diversity in device design, experimental conditions and analytical endpoints limits direct comparison between studies and constrains translation into routine practice. The development of more standardised platforms, alongside integration with endothelialised and organ-on-a-chip models, may help to overcome these challenges. Overall, microfluidics represents a promising tool for improving functional assessment of blood components and supporting future advances in transfusion medicine research and personalised transfusion strategies.
authors: Edward John Sayers; Jamie Nash; E. M. Davies; Christine V. Saunders; Chloë E. George

title: Miniaturized Multifunctional Valves for Intelligent Pneumatic Systems in Soft Robotics
abstract: Soft robotics stands to benefit significantly from advances in pneumatic circuit‐based actuation, sensing, and on‐board logic. Soft pneumatic valves serve as vital components; however, existing implementations remain limited by insufficient function versatility, constraining their use in intelligent pneumatic architectures. Here, we present a unified framework for miniaturized functional pneumatic valves that provides both normally open (NO) and normally closed (NC) configurations. These valves can execute logic operations (AND, OR, NAND, and NOR) and can be rapidly reconfigured and programmed without physical replumbing or hardware modification. Fast dynamic response is achieved, with time constants as low as 5.2 and 6.1 ms for NO and NC valves, respectively. These valves enable embodied intelligence, as demonstrated in two representative robotic systems. First, we realize a reflexive response with an electronics‐free autonomous soft gripper capable of regulating grasping force. Second, we demonstrate a robotic gripper that integrates valve‐based tactile sensing to classify objects and support higher‐level intelligent control. Together, these results establish multifunctional pneumatic valves as foundational building blocks for intelligent pneumatic systems, enabling decentralized sensing, decision‐making, and adaptive control through physical embodiment. This approach advances soft robotics toward autonomy by embedding intelligence directly into the material and fluidic architecture of the system.
authors: Jing Xu; Xuezhi Niu; J. Andersson; D./G. Broo; Klas Hjort

title: Miniaturized biosensor platforms for early detection of neurodegenerative diseases and their potential for clinical translation
abstract: Neurodegenerative disorders (NDs), such as Alzheimer’s disease (AD), Parkinson’s disease (PD), and prion diseases, are defined by the gradual deterioration of neurons that frequently occurs prior to the onset of clinically observable symptoms. The early diagnosis of these conditions relies on analytical systems that are capable in detecting disease-related biomarkers at low concentrations within complex biological fluids. This analysis extensively evaluates miniaturized biosensor systems aimed at disease-specific biomarkers, such as amyloid-β and tau for Alzheimer’s disease, α-synuclein (α-syn) and DJ-1 for Parkinson’s disease, and prion protein isoforms for prion disorders. Electrochemical, optical, surface plasmon resonance, field-effect transistor, surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy, microfluidic lab-on-a-chip, portable, and wearable systems are assessed concerning their biorecognition methodologies, signal-transduction processes, linear ranges, detection thresholds, selectivity, sample matrices, and suitability for point-of-care applications. Recent research indicates that nanostructured sensing interfaces and microfluidic integration can improve analytical sensitivity, minimize sample needs, and facilitate biomarker identification in blood, plasma, cerebrospinal fluid, saliva, and other therapeutically pertinent matrices. However, remarkably low detection thresholds alone do not establish clinical significance. Biofouling, matrix influences, intricate production, prolonged stability, insufficient clinical validation, and the absence of standardized multicenter research persist in limiting clinical application. This review evaluates the development of biosensors for the diagnosis of neurodegenerative diseases towards miniaturized and portable systems based on current studies. It also comprehensively addresses the key limitations in the clinical validation, standardization, scalable production, and commercialization processes. Graphical abstract
