title: Minimally Invasive In Vivo Fabrication of Multiscale Biohybrid Systems
abstract: Multiscale biohybrid systems integrating living materials with minimally invasive in vivo fabrication offer new opportunities for precise diagnosis, physiological monitoring, and tissue regeneration. This review provides a unified perspective on their design and therapeutic integration, organizing recent advances across multiscale material design, minimally invasive fabrication, spatiotemporal co-engineering, and functional applications. Three emerging principles are identified: multiscale coupling bridges material architectures with cellular and tissue responses; spatiotemporal coordination integrates precise in vivo construction with dynamic material and biological evolution; and sensing-regeneration feedback extends biohybrid systems from passive repair toward responsive therapeutic regulation. Building on these principles, we highlight machine learning-assisted material discovery, multi-site fabrication, and intelligent feedback control as key directions for developing adaptive, closed-loop therapeutic systems. Together, these insights provide design guidance for translating minimally invasive multiscale biohybrid systems toward next-generation patient-centered healthcare.
authors: Zhixing Ge; Yuji Gao; Elgene Chng Junyuan; Truong‐Son Dinh Le; Liang Lanfeng; Yu Zhang; Chwee Teck Lim

title: Modular Bio‐Integrated Materials and Devices for Advanced Theranostic Healthcare
abstract: Bio-integrated theranostic systems that combine sensing, analysis, interaction, and therapy are emerging as powerful platforms for personalized healthcare. Unlike conventional diagnostic or therapeutic devices, modular bio-integrated systems integrate body-conformal or implantable interfaces with analytical units, user-interaction platforms, and therapeutic modules to enable continuous monitoring, feedback-guided decision-making, and on-demand intervention. In this review, we summarize progress in modular bio-integrated theranostic systems (MBTS) from four functional perspectives. First, we discuss biophysical, biochemical, and multimodal sensing modules that provide physiological and molecular inputs across skin-interfaced, wound-integrated, ocular, oral, and implantable formats. We review analysis modules that convert sensor-derived signals into health-state assessments, risk estimates, and intervention guidance. Interactive interfaces and feedback modules are discussed, focusing on visual and graphical interfaces for data presentation and interactive feedback for user engagement and therapeutic response. Finally, programmable therapeutic modules for controlled drug delivery and nonpharmacological intervention are summarized, followed by biomedical implementations in drug delivery, neuromodulation, diabetes management, wound care, blood pressure regulation, and other healthcare scenarios. We further discuss engineering challenges related to module integration, bio-interface stability, power supply, data security, and cost-effective manufacturing. This review provides a modular framework for designing next-generation bio-integrated theranostic systems that connect sensing, analysis, interaction, and therapy within healthcare platforms.
authors: Zhenyou Ge; X Q Li; Bingbing Gao; Chwee Teck Lim; Yukun Ren

title: Modular construction of osteochondral organoids: Recapitulating gradients and microenvironment
abstract: In recent years, bone and cartilage organoid technology has attracted increasing attention and undergone rapid development, offering emerging approaches and broad prospects for osteoarthritis (OA) treatment, tissue engineering, regenerative medicine, and related fields. Despite the documented progress of bone and cartilage organoid models in structural biomimetic design, their limitation in the holistic reproduction of osteochondral unit, including interface gradient and physiological functions, remains a challenge for clinical application. Based on cutting-edge research, this review summarizes modular construction strategies of bone and cartilage organoids, targeting three types of signals in the osteochondral unit microenvironment: mechanical, metabolic, and immune. First, this review analyzes the microenvironment characteristics of the osteochondral unit, including the interface gradient and major signal pathways, then discusses the essential requirements for construction of osteochondral organoid. Then, based on different emphases, various osteochondral or cartilage organoid examples are classified and reviewed. Furthermore, this paper analyzes their advantages, bottlenecks, and feasibility, thereby outlining a design framework for modular organoids. Next, the technical pathways for functional coupling between modules are discussed, mainly including 3D bioprinting, organoid assembly, and microfluidic chips, in an attempt to provide solutions to the integrated challenge of osteochondral organoids. Then, the monitoring of multidimensional signals in organoids culture system is discussed. Finally, feasibility of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning in this field is discussed, with the aim to establish a closed-loop system for intelligent organoid culture.
authors: Zihan Xu; Yixing Ren; Xiaoming Li

title: Molecular point-of-care: technological evolution, clinical applications, and future perspectives
abstract: The landscape of clinical diagnostics is undergoing a fundamental shift from centralized laboratories toward decentralized point-of-care testing (POCT) models. Conventional molecular diagnostics often suffer from prolonged turnaround times, high operational costs, and a strict reliance on sophisticated infrastructure. To overcome these limitations, modern POCT platforms have deeply integrated advanced molecular techniques. These include diverse isothermal nucleic acid amplification methods (such as LAMP, RPA, and RCA) and highly specific CRISPR/Cas recognition systems. Furthermore, coupling these biochemical reactions with microfluidic chips and smartphone-based digital platforms has enabled fully automated, "sample-in, answer-out" diagnostic capabilities. This review systematically summarizes the technological evolution of these molecular POCT platforms. It highlights their transformative clinical applications across diverse fields, including infectious disease containment, early oncology screening, cardiovascular emergency triage, and metabolic disease management. Despite remarkable progress, several critical bottlenecks still prevent the widespread clinical translation of molecular POCT. These challenges include cross-interference in multiplexed detection, enzyme stability outside strict cold chains, high costs of core components, and the lack of tailored regulatory frameworks. Addressing these barriers via synthetic biology, robust system integration, and artificial intelligence is critical to advancing the core vision of delivering rapid, accessible, and precise healthcare solutions in resource-limited settings.
authors: Danfeng Zhang; Xin Cui; Ruijie Zhang; Wenlong Cai; Wang Li; Jichun Yang

title: Multi-Agent Scheduling of Instrument-Time for High-Throughput Palladium-Catalysed Cross-Coupling
abstract: NMR time and a shared liquid-handling robot are scarce, noisy and only partially observable, so the practical question is which experiment to run next on which instrument. Existing reaction-optimisation benchmarks measure budgets in experiments rather than instrumenthours, and they learn chemical feasibility only by paying for infeasible runs. We present CHASE, a centralised-training decentralised-execution scheduler with three coupled modules: a belief encoder (PEB) infers per-instrument throughput and channel health from local event histories and exchanges only low-bandwidth summaries; a chemistry feasibility gate (CFG) masks chemically impossible actions with a four-layer compatibility graph; and a counterfactual attribution module (CFA) converts delayed campaign reward into per-step credit through leave-one-experiment-out surrogate scoring. On the Buchwald–Hartwig (3,955 reactions) and Suzuki–Miyaura (5,760 nanomole-scale conditions) HTE datasets, the ten Olympus benchmarks and a plant-wide Tennessee Eastman process, CHASE reaches 94.1% best-found yield under a shared 60 instrument-hour budget, +3.3 points over the strongest same-setting baseline, attains 90% of the attainable optimum with 25.6% fewer experiments, and cuts infeasible actions to 0.7–1.6% across plate, flow and fault-injection settings.
authors: Yuhang Shao; Siqi Meng; Yutian Luo; Jiawei Tan; Chengyu He

title: Multi-mode droplet splitting on active-matrix digital microfluidics: quantitative boundaries and optimal sequential generation
abstract: Precise generation of microdroplets at picoliters to microliters scale is critical for advancing microfluidics technologies and precision life sciences research. Digital microfluidics enables programable individual droplet, however, there still lacks comprehensive characterization and analysis on optimal splitting modes, hindering its further application requiring extreme volume accuracy and splitting. Here, we report a systematic quantitative investigation of four droplet splitting strategies: symmetric splitting, asymmetric splitting, deformative splitting, squeezing, leveraging the high programmability advantage of large-scale active-matrix digital microfluidics. Droplet splitting is experimentally tested across varying droplet sizes, shapes, ratios and sub-droplet motion modes. Based on extensive experimental results, quantitative analysis is conducted to comprehensively characterize the splitting accuracy and effective ratio ranges. From these statistical results and optimal splitting modes, we establish an optimal sequential splitting decision framework. Aiming at precise generation for ultra-low-ratio sub-droplet through sequential splitting, the proposed framework can efficiently screen reasonable splitting paths from the combinatorial solution space. Ultra-low-ratio droplet generation at 0.78125% is realized, which is unattainable by any single-step method, with a cumulative accuracy of 1.05868 upon a target droplet of 12 nL. This work clarifies the quantitative performance boundaries of multi-mode droplet splitting strategies and demonstrates the capability of standardized optimal splitting sequence generation. These findings provide a theoretical and technical basis for customized multi-step droplet preparation and high-stability microfluidic manipulation.
authors: Chenxuan Hu; Hanbin Ma

title: Multimodal LLM-Assisted Diagnosis of Cryptic Failure Modes in High-Throughput Experimentation: A Case Study in Gold Nanorod Synthesis
abstract: Self-driving labs typically optimize experiments within a predefined design space. Yet high-throughput campaigns can fail for reasons outside this design space, in-cluding reagent state, stock solution quality, and handling history. Here, we present a case study of a five-plate high-throughput gold nanorod synthesis campaign in which a multimodal large language model (LLM) helped diagnose such cryptic failure modes. We used low-cost camera images for rapid assessment of seed and synthesis state, with UV–vis spectroscopy when the images were insufficient for failure diagnosis. The campaign included an abnormal seed batch, a visually plausible synthesis with hidden spectroscopic defects, and a plate-wide failed synthesis in which most wells showed weak spectra with a strong rise toward the near-infrared. In response, the LLM intervened by questioning the seed preparation step and reagent handling instead of optimizing the screened concentrations of silver nitrate and ascorbic acid. To quantify recovery, we defined a UV–vis spectral roughness metric based on local spectral interpolation across the synthesis grid. The final synthesis had the lowest roughness, Rspec = 0.636 compared with ∼ 0.772 for earlier successful runs, and the highest median longitudinal-window absorbance. Our results show the potential of multimodal LLMs upstream of autonomous optimization in self-driving labs to identify when an experiment has failed for reasons outside the nominal design space and when additional characterization is needed before optimization should continue.
authors: Riya Patel; Gabriela Briceno; Amirali Aghazadeh; Vida Jamali

title: Multimodal wearable biosensors in sports: integrating physical and chemical sensing for performance and health
abstract: Wearable technologies have emerged as essential tools for monitoring athletes’ performance and physiological states in real time. This review systematically examines advances in biosensing and wearable systems for sports applications, highlighting their design, sensing modalities, and integration strategies. Athlete tracking and data acquisition form the foundation for personalized training, injury prevention, and performance optimization. Biopotential sensors, including electrocardiography (ECG), electromyography (EMG), electroencephalography (EEG)/electroneurogram Electroneurography, and biopotential electrodes, provide insights into cardiac, muscular, and neural activity. Physical sensors, such as temperature, piezoresistive, piezoelectric, balance and acceleration, pressure, optical, and galvanic skin response (GSR) sensors, enable real-time assessment of movement, mechanical load, body posture, stress, and environmental interactions. Chemical sensors, including sweat and glucose sensors, facilitate non-invasive metabolic monitoring, supporting hydration and energy management. Integrated and hybrid biosensor systems combine multiple sensing modalities, offering comprehensive real-time feedback and personalized analytics for athletes. Despite these advances, challenges remain in sensor miniaturization, power efficiency, data accuracy, wireless communication, and user comfort. Future directions focus on artificial intelligence-driven data analysis, flexible and durable materials, multi-modal integration, and fully personalized wearable platforms. Collectively, wearable biosensing technologies present a transformative approach to sports monitoring, enabling enhanced performance evaluation, injury prevention, and long-term health management.
authors: Burhan Adıgüzel; Mansour Ghorbanpour; Begüm Sarac; Seydanur Yücer; Fatih Çiftçi

title: Multiscale mechanobiology of circulating tumor cells: microfluidics and atomic force microscopy
abstract: Cancer progression is shaped by coupled molecular, biochemical, and mechanical changes across multiple scales, from altered signaling and cytoskeletal organization to cellular deformation, adhesion, and metastatic dissemination. Circulating tumor cells (CTCs) are rare and heterogeneous in blood, occurring as single cells and multicellular clusters that provide access to evolving tumor phenotypes through liquid biopsy. Their apparent elasticity, deformability, adhesion, and viscoelastic behavior may reflect invasive potential, treatment response, and phenotypic state, while cytoskeletal proteins, membrane lipids, cell surface glycans, and receptors provide molecular context for these mechanical signatures. This review examines the complementary roles of microfluidics and atomic force microscopy (AFM) in multiscale CTC mechanobiology. Microfluidic platforms support label-free and affinity-based enrichment, capture, positioning, and recovery of viable cells. AFM provides localized measurements of apparent elasticity, deformation, adhesion, viscoelastic response, and nanoscale surface architecture in liquid, while functionalized probes enable molecular recognition and molecule-specific force measurements. We evaluate physical, affinity-based, cluster-preserving, open-space, and artificial intelligence-assisted microfluidic strategies together with reversible device assembly, automated AFM targeting, fluidic probes, advanced mapping modes, and treatment-response applications. Existing studies establish feasibility, including direct AFM measurements of individual patient-derived CTCs and automated analysis following microfluidic enrichment in model rare-cell mixtures. Clinical evidence remains limited, many integrated workflows rely on cultured cells or spiked samples, and within the literature identified in this review, direct AFM characterization of intact patient-derived CTC clusters was not found. Clinical translation will require confirmation of tumor identity, standardized acquisition, analysis, and reporting, increased throughput, statistical analysis that preserves the hierarchy of patients, cells, and force curves, and validation in independent patient cohorts. Integrated AFM-microfluidic platforms could extend CTC liquid biopsy beyond enumeration toward functional mechanobiological analysis relevant to metastasis, therapeutic response, and biomarker development.
authors: Ayoub Glia; Muhammedin Deliorman; Mohammad Ameen Qasaimeh
venue: Frontiers in Lab on a Chip Technologies

title: Multiscale wavelet Hurst analysis of pressure fluctuations in a jet impact negative pressure reactor
abstract: Abstract This work investigated the multiscale fractal dynamics of a jet impact‐negative pressure reactor (JI‐NPR) using an integrated wavelet‐Hurst methodology tailored to the JI‐NPR geometry. The analysis of pressure signals revealed a significant spatial diversity in the Hausdorff dimension (Dh). The negative pressure zone exhibited distinct spatial distribution characteristics of Dh compared to the slow flow zone, indicating that the turbulent sub‐atmospheric interaction resulted in characteristic flow complexity within the negative pressure zone. Two distinct Hurst exponent ( H ) regimes were identified: a persistent mode reflecting self‐similar flow patterns, and an anti‐persistent mode which at small scales reflects high‐frequency fluctuations yet re‐emerges at the largest scale (d8) in the negative‐pressure zone as low‐frequency vortex‐shedding structures. Furthermore, the evolution of the persistent H accurately captured hydrodynamic stability transitions. Dimensional convergence at the d4 scale served as a quantitative indicator of this transition. Through the parameter analysis, the targeted combination of wavelet and fractal analysis reveals flow dynamics specific to the coupled jet‐impingement and negative‐pressure environment. In a post‐hoc comparison, the regimes characterized by a persistent Hurst mode with H > 0.9 were found to coincide with the optimal operating conditions reported in our prior independently conducted trials. On this basis, the persistent Hurst exponent threshold is proposed as a candidate diagnostic indicator of favourable operating states, rather than as a validated efficiency criterion. The plausible rationale‐that persistent, self‐similar flow structures may reduce unnecessary turbulent dissipation relative to highly disordered states‐requires confirmation through future simultaneous measurement of pressure signals and process performance metrics.
authors: Fei Long; Yingying Dong; Zhongjun Li; Lingxing Hu; Facheng Qiu
venue: The Canadian Journal of Chemical Engineering

title: Nanofluid transport in Taylor bubble flows
abstract: Taylor bubble flows with nanoparticle suspensions are regularly encountered in non-isothermal chemical synthesis and microfluidics. Despite this, a complete mechanistic insight into the coupled thermal and hydrodynamic interactions remains unresolved. Here, a Eulerian-Lagrangian framework has been developed to address this, capturing two-way momentum, energy exchange, and nanoparticle interactions under non-isothermal conditions. We find that Brownian motion acts in two opposing ways, enhancing local particle-fluid energy exchange yet driving a thermophoretic drift away from the heated wall that strengthens as particle diameter is reduced below 100 nm. At particle volume fractions of $ϕ\sim 10^{-2}$, Taylor flow departs from the Nusselt scaling with dimensionless slug length, $\tilde{L}_s$, observed for particle-free flows. This coincides with alterations to bubble topology that co-benefit nanoparticle momentum and energy exchange with the carrier fluid. Examining both Poiseuille and Taylor flow problems, we observe contrasting, often opposing dimensionless heat transport behaviours, questioning the suitability of traditionally accepted mixture approaches. This work reveals that, in the visco-inertial regime ($Re > 500$), it is the interplay of hydrodynamic, Brownian, and interfacial forces, combined with the Taylor bubble and slug flow topology, which determine positive or negative $Nu$ outcomes. Interestingly, short-range particle forces at the liquid-gas interface work synergistically with the convective motion in the slug to alter local particle concentration and energy exchanges within downstream thin film and near-wall regions. The intensity of this convective flow was found to impact both slug and film transport phenomena, improving the redistribution of nanoparticles when $\tilde{L}_s \leq 1.6$ and with increasing $Re$.
authors: Fahad Al-Gburi; Faysal Khaleel; Yulong Ding; Jason Stafford

title: Nanomaterials in Solid-State Physics and Engineering: Synthesis Strategies, Structure-Property Relationships, and Emerging Applications
abstract: Nanomaterials often deliver impressive laboratory metrics, yet translation is weakened when the path from synthesis to operating-state behavior is poorly documented. This review asked whether performance claims could be traced consistently from controllable processing to verified structure, mechanism, function, and a stated translation boundary. Peer-reviewed literature published mainly from 2021 to 31 March 2026 was examined through a narrative review. During major revision, a structured OpenAlex and Crossref audit was added for operando and active-state characterization. The literature showed that size alone rarely determined performance. Surface chemistry, defects, interfaces, and process history often changed the outcome, and in many systems the functional state differed from the pristine or post-mortem structure. Translation problems were most visible when these changes were not connected to realistic measures of loading, yield, stability, or manufacturing compatibility. Stronger studies combined controlled processing with complementary characterization and measurements made under relevant operating conditions. They also made clear where the evidence stopped. Comparison across application areas showed markedly different levels of readiness, from manufacturing-scale evidence in a few device platforms to predominantly laboratory demonstrations in others. On this basis, the review treats the evidence chain as a practical traceability tool rather than a new materials theory and translates it into a domain-adaptable minimum evidence package for engineering claims.
authors: Thanh Van Nguyen
venue: Indonesian Journal of Modern Science and Technology

title: New Era of Biosensors - Integration of Artificial Intelligence and Technology in Healthcare
abstract: The connection between biological systems and electronic devices has developed beyond simple glucose tests or pregnancy checks. It is now a transformative area in modern science. This chapter looks at the “New Era of Biosensors,” where molecular biology, materials science, and information technology come together to provide a clear view of our integration of Artificial intelligence in biosensors. We follow the transition from large, lab-based equipment to decentralized, patient-focused diagnostics. By moving the process from hospital beds to homes, these technologies change healthcare from a reactive approach to a proactive approach. Three advances enable this shift. Microfluidics and nanotechnology bring lab-grade sensitivity to chip-scale devices. Epidermal electronics maintain signal quality on flexible, skin-conformable substrates. Artificial intelligence removes noise from real-world recordings, identifies patterns that precede clinical symptoms, and tunes predictions to individual baselines. Translation from prototype to clinical deployment remains difficult. This chapter examines the technical, regulatory, and ethical barriers to implementation, including data privacy under Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) and General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), algorithmic bias arising from non-representative training data, and power constraints in implantable and energy-harvesting devices. Drawing on clinical applications such as smart bandages and remote cardiac monitoring, the chapter outlines how continuous, AI-supported sensing can shift healthcare from episodic consultation toward sustained physiological monitoring and earlier intervention.
authors: Sagar Pralhad Kanekar; Sahil Vaghole; Aarya Kamat; Anirjit Kartha

title: Next-Generation Liposomes for Drug Delivery: Engineering Strategies and Therapeutic Applications
abstract: Liposomes are versatile nanocarrier systems widely investigated for pharmaceutical drug delivery because of their biocompatibility, biodegradability, and ability to encapsulate both hydrophilic and lipophilic drugs. Since their discovery in the 1960s, liposomes have evolved into advanced nanomedicine platforms with applications in cancer therapy, antimicrobial treatment, gene delivery, vaccines, and personalised medicine. Advances in lipid chemistry, nanotechnology, and pharmaceutical engineering have enabled the development of long-circulating, targeted, stimuli-responsive, and multifunctional liposomal formulations. Several liposome-based products have received regulatory approval, demonstrating their clinical and translational potential. However, challenges related to formulation stability, encapsulation efficiency, large-scale manufacturing, storage, and regulatory requirements remain. Emerging approaches, including microfluidics, artificial intelligence-assisted formulation development, precision nanomedicine, and personalised drug delivery, are expected to address these limitations. This review discusses the historical development, structural characteristics, classification, preparation methods, therapeutic applications, clinical status, and future perspectives of liposomal drug delivery systems, with particular emphasis on recent innovations driving the development of next-generation liposomal therapeutics. Keywords: Liposome, Nanomedicine,Drug Delivery System, Phospholipid Vesicles, Targeted Drug Delivery, Nanotechnology, Lipid Nanocarriers, Controlled Drug Release.
authors: Shubham Sachdeva; Vikramjit Singh; Kaur Harwinder; Fairy Fairy; Jitender Singh
venue: Journal of Drug Delivery and Therapeutics

title: Next-generation point-of-care diagnostics for urinary tract infections: a systematic review of rapid pathogen detection methods
abstract: Background: Urinary tract infections are among the most prevalent bacterial infections worldwide, with Escherichia coli as the leading pathogen. Conventional diagnostic methods, including urine culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing, require 48–72 hours, often delaying targeted therapy and promoting empirical antibiotic use, thereby exacerbating antimicrobial resistance. Objective: This review summarizes advances in point-of-care diagnostic technologies for rapid detection and antimicrobial susceptibility testing in localized or uncomplicated urinary tract infections. Methods: A comprehensive literature review of studies published between 2008 and 2025 was conducted using MeSH and free-text searches for “point-of-care testing”, “urinary tract infection”, “rapid diagnostics”, and related terms. Included studies described the mechanisms, performance, and clinical applicability of emerging point-of-care systems. Results: Thirty-four studies met inclusion criteria. Paper-based assays, lateral-flow tests, microfluidic devices, and hydrogel biosensors demonstrated rapid bacterial detection (from <5 min to 6 h) with variable sensitivities (10–106 CFU/mL). Among commercial devices, the Sysmex PA-100 antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) system provided phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility testing within 30–45 minutes and achieved over 95% specificity compared with standard microbiology, while the Lodestar DX (LAMP-based) and Bosch Vivalytic (PCR-based) systems enabled molecular identification of uropathogens and resistance genes within 40–146 minutes. Conclusions: Point-of-care diagnostic platforms substantially reduce diagnostic turnaround, improve antibiotic stewardship, and offer cost-effective alternatives to conventional culture. The Sysmex PA-100 system currently represents the most clinically validated phenotypic point-of-care tool for uncomplicated urinary infections management. Future research should focus on expanding diagnostic panels, validating clinical outcomes, and facilitating integration into primary care and antimicrobial stewardship programs.
authors: Silvia Juste-Álvarez; José Medina‐Polo
venue: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)

title: Nucleic acid synthesis screening at an inflection point: U.S. policy momentum and global implications
abstract: This article examines the positioning of nucleic acid synthesis screening (NASS) policy within the current U.S. political landscape, tracing its evolution from voluntary industry practices to executive and legislative action across administrations. We analyze the sources of NASS’s political momentum, including the rare convergence of bipartisan national security imperatives, industry support for codified screening requirements, and biosecurity-related incidents. We assess key policy challenges, including navigating jurisdictional limitations and congressional gridlock, the risk of regulatory capture, and ensuring regulatory frameworks remain adaptive to evolving technologies. We situate U.S. efforts within an international context, examining parallel initiatives in the United Kingdom, the European Union, and New Zealand, noting how U.S. market-access requirements may promote de facto global screening adoption through economic incentives rather than multilateral diplomacy. We recommend specific policy instruments, such as expanding the U.S.-based third-party screening industry, leveraging federal procurement requirements, aligning with ISO standards, and building on NIST’s maturing capability-based benchmarks, to establish enforceable domestic requirements while extending global reach.

title: Open-well compartmentalized microfluidic devices for reconstituting brain region connectivity
abstract: Microfluidics-based in vitro models provide powerful platforms for investigating disease mechanisms and screening therapeutic compounds. However, fabrication protocols for microfluidic devices that enable precise control over the directional connectivity between three-dimensional tissue models remain limited, restricting their applications in studying inter-regional interactions. In this study, we present an open-well polydimethylsiloxane microfluidic device that enables unidirectional axon connectivity between region-specific spheroids. We show that the combination of axon-diode microchannels and time-delayed spheroid plating effectively suppresses reverse projections and biases activity propagation. Using human midbrain and striatal spheroids, we further demonstrate that the platform reconstitutes 6-OHDA-induced dopaminergic axonal degeneration in vitro.
authors: Mamoru Sakaibara; Hideaki Yamamoto; Sota Endo; Kotaro Murata; Shigeo Sato; Yoshito Masamizu; Kaneyasu Nishimura; Ayumi Hirano-Iwata

title: Opportunities and Challenges of Generative AI for Cybersecurity in Sub-Saharan African Organizations: A Systematic Literature Review
abstract: Generative AI (GAI) is increasingly used and studied across various fields in different countries; however, its implications for cybersecurity in Africa remain underexplored. This study investigates the opportunities and challenges of GAI on cybersecurity within the Sub-Saharan African organizations through a systematic literature review. Peer-reviewed journal articles and conference proceedings papers were retrieved from five databases, yielding 51 relevant publications, which were synthesized. The literature review was guided by the PRISMA flow diagram to ensure a structured review. Thematic analysis informed a taxonomy of GAI-related challenges and opportunities, aligned with the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0. Key challenges include the absence of context-specific governance frameworks, technical and model-related limitations, data quality issues and people-related challenges. It was found that the reliance of GAI models on a few dominant languages limits their effectiveness in cybersecurity tasks such as threat detection within Sub-Saharan Africa’s multilingual context. Conversely, GAI presents opportunities to mitigate the region’s cybersecurity skills shortage by automating functions such as cybersecurity awareness and training, log analysis and continuous auditing. The findings provide valuable insights for policymakers, practitioners, and governments seeking to harness GAI for cybersecurity in Sub-Saharan Africa, while also highlighting avenues for future research.
authors: Thembekile O. Mayayise

title: Optimal Control and Closed-Loop Stability of Droplet Transport in a Microchannel
abstract: Understanding the efficient transport of fluid droplets in confined geometries has been a domain of interest for industrial applications in recent times. In the present work, we focus on designing control strategies that optimally steer droplet motion. Here, we apply optimal control framework to the droplet transport problem in a microchannel based on lubrication theory that minimizes viscous dissipation. Two complementary modeling routes are adopted: a reduced-order ordinary differential equation (ODE) model optimized via Pontryagin's Maximum Principle, and a full nonlinear partial differential equation (PDE) model optimized using a Covariance Matrix Adaptation-Evolutionary Strategy. By parameterizing target displacement, droplet size, and capillary number, we uncover two distinct optimal transport regimes: a "translate-relax" strategy for short distances and a "compact-translate-relax" strategy for longer targets. In continuum mechanics, the competition between surface forces and cumulative viscous dissipation decides the optimal transport strategies. We further show that the displacement range over which the reduced-order controller transfers to the continuum model is governed by capillary stiffness. We finally address closed-loop stability by adapting a control Lyapunov function (CLF) framework to the reduced-order dynamics. We demonstrate that the terminal cost which penalizes deviation from the target, serves as a cost-compatible CLF on the physical domain, and prove that the CLF-compatible feedback exponentially stabilizes the target state.
authors: Rajneesh Anand; Mayuresh V. Kothare

title: Optoelectronically Enabled Simultaneous and Decoupled Navigation and Selective Pairing of Electrically Driven Janus Particles for Multi-Agent Microrobotics
abstract: Self-propelled Janus particles are promising active agents for microscale manipulation and microrobotic applications. However, when powered by a global external energy source, such as an electric, magnetic, or optical field, all particles respond simultaneously, preventing their independent and concurrent control. Achieving parallel, decoupled control without continuous particle-specific feedback, while preserving intrinsic self-propulsion, remains a significant challenge. Here, we present an optoelectronic (OE) strategy for simultaneously and independently controlling electrically driven, self-propelled metallo-dielectric Janus particles (JPs) using spatially programmable virtual electrodes. These electrodes are generated by projecting a single predefined illumination pattern from a digital micromirror device onto a photoconductive surface. The resulting confinement landscape enables multiple JPs to follow distinct trajectories without continuous monitoring, feedback, or pattern reconfiguration. We demonstrate controlled pairing of JPs with passive polystyrene particles and biological cells. For automated multi-agent operation, an image-based assignment framework identifies optimal agent-target pairs, excludes intersecting trajectories, and generates a single composite pattern for simultaneous, selective pair formation without real-time updating. Finally, we demonstrate independent manipulation of multiple magnetically rolling JPs under a globally applied magnetic field. Overall, this programmable open-loop strategy provides a versatile framework for multi-agent microrobotic manipulation, with potential applications in in-vitro micromanipulation and microfluidic systems.
authors: Srikanta Debata; Ido Rachbuch; Gilad Yossifon

title: Organ-on-a-chip platforms for disease modeling and in vitro diagnostic applications
abstract: Organ-on-a-Chip (OoC) systems, as microphysiological models integrating microfluidic engineering, 3D tissue construction, and sensing technologies, can faithfully recapitulate the barrier functions, dynamic microenvironments, and inter-tissue crosstalk of human organs. They effectively address the inherent limitations of traditional 2D cell cultures and animal models in in vitro diagnostics (IVD), offering a novel avenue to tackle the high failure rate of candidate drugs and biomarkers in clinical translation. This review systematically summarizes the technological advances and application practices of OoC in the IVD field, covering core construction technologies (microfluidic regulation, cell and tissue engineering, material innovation), the integrated optimization of the "online real-time monitoring-offline in-depth analysis" dual-detection system, and typical applications in disease modeling, biomarker screening, drug toxicity evaluation, and personalized diagnosis. It further explores Multi-Organ-Chip (MOC) systems and Artificial Intelligence (AI) empowerment, analyzes core bottlenecks including insufficient physiological complexity, lack of standardization, and barriers to clinical translation and industrialization, and prospects future directions from technological optimization, standardization establishment, and regulatory pathway exploration. By focusing on the IVD-oriented perspective, this review aims to provide theoretical references and practical guidance for the transformation of OoC from laboratory research to clinical IVD tools.
authors: Po Hao; Deng Jingrong; Jian Xu

title: PGC-1α and PPARs cooperatively mediate photoreceptor neuroprotection in rd1 mouse inherited retinal degeneration
abstract: Abstract Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is a group of inherited diseases characterized by primary rod photoreceptor dysfunction and progressive cone cell death. Due to their very high energy demand, the degeneration of photoreceptors may be linked to insufficient energy supply or metabolic imbalance. Critical transcription factors that regulate metabolism, such as peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs) and PPAR gamma coactivator 1α (PGC-1α), have been found to play important roles in neurodegenerative diseases, but their potential roles in RP have yet not been elucidated. Here, organotypic retinal explant cultures derived from retinal degeneration 1 ( rd1 ) mice were used to investigate the effects of PPARα, PPARγ, PPARβ/δ agonists, as well as PGC-1α activation and inhibition. Photoreceptor death was quantified using the TUNEL assay, while in situ activity assays were used to monitor effects of PPARs and PGC-1α on poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) and calpain activity. Generation of poly (ADP-ribose) (PAR) and activation of calpain-1 and calpain-2 were evaluated by immunostaining. PGC-1α/PPAR-associated transcriptional changes were assessed by RT-qPCR. We found that PPARβ/δ agonists had limited effects, while treatment targeting PPARα, PPARγ, and PGC-1α significantly reduced photoreceptor death and PARP activity in rd1 retina. RT-qPCR analysis in treated rd1 retina confirmed upregulation of genes downstream of PGC-1α/PPAR signaling. Stimulation of the histone deacetylase sirtuin-1, an upstream regulator of PGC-1α, had no beneficial effect on photoreceptor viability unless combined with PARP inhibition. Furthermore, PPARγ and PGC-1α effectively suppressed overall calpain activity and overactivation of calpain-2, alleviating photoreceptor degeneration caused by Ca 2+ imbalance. In summary, our data support the concept of a PARP–sirtuin-1–PGC-1α–PPAR–PARP feedback control that connects defective energy metabolism to photoreceptor degeneration. Specifically, our findings suggest that PPARα, PPARγ, and PGC-1α cooperate to preserve photoreceptor viability, highlighting PPAR-signaling as a promising target for future therapeutic interventions.
authors: Lan Wang; Jie Yan; Javier Sancho-Pellúz; Qianlu Yang; zhulin Hu; Kangwei Jiao; Mathias W. Seeliger; François Paquet‐Durand

title: POSTOPER ATIVE COMPLICATIONS AFTER COLORECTAL CANCER SURGERY: RISK FACTORS, IMPACT ON SURVIVAL, AND CONTEMPORARY PREVENTION STRATEGIES (A LITERATURE REVIEW)
abstract: Relevance: Postoperative complications remain major determinants of unfavorable outcomes following colorectal cancer surgery, contributing to increased mortality, reoperation rates, disease recurrence, and reduced long-term survival.The study aimed to analyze current evidence on postoperative complications after colorectal cancer surgery, identify major risk factors, evaluate their impact on long-term survival, and summarize contemporary preventive strategies.Materials and Methods: This structured literature review covered 39 publications from January 1, 2021, through July 31, 2026, including 34 original studies and 4 systematic reviews or meta-analyses; the GLOBOCAN 2022 fact sheet was used only for epidemiological context and was not counted among the included studies.Results: Reported overall postoperative morbidity ranged from 8.1% to 33.3%, while colorectal anastomotic leakage occurred in 4.7% to 15.1% of patients. Wen et al. reported postoperative infectious complications in 95/593 patients (16.0%), including wound infection, anastomotic leakage, intra-abdominal infection, pneumonia, and other infectious events. Severe complications (Clavien-Dindo grades III-V) occurred in 9.7-29.7% of patients. Significant adjusted associations included sarcopenia and postoperative complications (OR = 2.53; 95% CI: 1.45-4.42), three or more linear stapler firings and anastomotic leakage (OR = 2.71; 95% CI: 1.17-6.26), and male sex in a CT-based leakage model (OR = 3.75). In one colon cancer cohort, postoperative complications were associated with a higher adjusted risk of death (HR = 1.70; 95% CI: 1.19-2.45). Multimodal prehabilitation reduced major complications from 29.7% to 17.1%, while diverting ileostomy was associated with fewer leakage-related reoperations.Conclusion: Postoperative complications are consistently associated with adverse short- and long-term outcomes following colorectal cancer surgery. Adjusted analyses identify nutritional, metabolic, patient-related, and technical factors that may support risk stratification. Multimodal prehabilitation, nutritional optimization, structured perioperative pathways, meticulous anastomotic technique, and selective diversion may reduce postoperative morbidity; however, the predominantly observational and heterogeneous evidence does not establish causality.
authors: Ye.M. Zheldibaev; Aman Berkinbay; A. Aitakyn; Dauren A. Nurmakov; A. Raimkhanov; Dauren T. Zhumatayev
venue: Eurasian Journal of Oncology and Radiology

title: Pendant drop microtraps for signal enhancement of microbead-based bioassays
abstract: Reliable fluorescence-based biosensing often requires efficient preconcentration of analytes, but existing preconcentration methods are highly prone to clogging and biofouling. Active methods, on the other hand, demand complex tools and operational steps. In this study, we present a pendant drop microtrap that uses a wall-free and pump-free configuration to preconcentrate microbeads before fluorescence readout. Droplets (0.5–4 μL) containing microbeads were dispensed onto hydrophobic polystyrene substrates and inverted to form stable hemispherical pendant drops. Target non-magnetic microbeads accumulated at the drop apex under gravity alone, whereas magnetic beads were concentrated by gravity and magnetic force. We studied the effects of droplet volume on bead distribution and fluorescence signal intensity. The platform was evaluated with fluorescently labeled magnetic Dynabeads and non-magnetic polystyrene beads, and demonstrated up to a 5.7-fold signal enhancement with 4 μL droplets. The pendant drop microtraps concentrated Dynabeads and non-magnetic polystyrene beads functionalized with various labels and antibodies, specifically streptavidin-Cy5, an anti-TNF-α antibody, and a FITC-conjugated rabbit anti-goat IgG (H + L) antibody. The pendant drop microtrap therefore offers a simple, wall-free, pump-free, and cheap preconcentration platform that can be readily integrated into existing fluorescence-based bioassay workflows.
authors: Amin Ghaffarzadeh Bakhshayesh; Isabella Walker; Huiyan Li

title: Persistent Lipotoxicity Overwhelms Adaptive Capacity in Human Hepatic Cell Line.
abstract: Chronic fatty acid (FA) elevation drives metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease. Hepatocytes buffer transient lipid overload via coordinated adaptive mechanisms, but the temporal limits of this capacity remain undefined. We characterized early, intermediate, and prolonged hepatocellular responses to sustained lipid excess. HuH7 hepatocytes were exposed to an equimolar palmitic/oleic acid (PA/OA) mixture for 1, 14, or 28 d. Viability, lipid accumulation, stress-response pathways, insulin signaling, metabolic regulators, mitochondrial markers, [14C]-PA uptake, and exometabolomic profiles were assessed (n ≥ 3/group). Data (mean ± standard error of the mean) were analyzed by 2-way analysis of variance with Bonferroni post hoc testing; cumulative cell death was analyzed by linear regression. P < 0.05 was considered significant. FA treatment increased lipid droplet accumulation 1.4- to 1.7-fold compared with time-matched bovine serum albumin controls at all time points (P < 0.001) and increased the rate of cumulative cell death ∼4.3-fold (1.556% ± 0.083% compared with 0.365 ± 0.054%/d, P < 0.001). Exometabolomic principal component analysis explained 88.5% of variance (Q2 = 0.758), with peak lactate release at day 14 and progressively rising acetate through day 28. [14C]-PA accumulation at day 28 was ∼30% lower than day 1 (∼800 compared with ∼500 cpm/mg protein), with a declining rather than plateauing profile between 20 and 60 s. By day 28, FA-treated cells showed lower FA synthase (P < 0.001), CD36 (P < 0.05), FABP1 (P < 0.001), SIRT1 (P < 0.005), and CLOCK (P < 0.01) protein levels, and higher carnitine palmitoyl transferase 1A (P < 0.001), phosphorylated AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)/AMPK (P < 0.01), p53 (P < 0.001), Bax/Bcl2 (P < 0.005), and respiratory complex I-V abundance (P < 0.05-P < 0.001) compared with controls. Sustained PA/OA exposure induces a staged hepatocellular response, early lipid-buffering adaptation, intermediate metabolic compensation, and late decompensation, indicating that chronic lipotoxicity reflects progressive loss of regulatory coordination despite persistent metabolic adaptation.
authors: Ilaria Serra; Elisa Bisconti; Francesco Vari; Eleonora Stanca; Federica De Castro; Federica Angilè; Daniele Vergara; Francesco Paolo Fanizzi; Anna M Giudetti

title: Perspectives on the future of biofabrication: insights from the winter school for biofabrication
abstract: Abstract Biofabrication is a multidisciplinary field that integrates diverse technologies to create three-dimensional structures composed of living cells, biomaterials, and other biological components. One of its main goals is the realization of functional tissue constructs with hierarchical architectures, as observed in native biological tissues, for applications in tissue engineering and regenerative medicine, as well as for in vitro modelling. Given its multidisciplinary nature, continued collaboration among experts from various scientific and technological disciplines remains essential to address the challenges ahead and to achieve the ambitious objectives of this rapidly advancing field. Reflecting on the progress made since the first bioprinting attempts, one can only envision the achievements that biofabrication may accomplish in the coming decades. Symposia such as the Alpine winter school for Biofabrication, bring together leading experts and early-stage researchers who collectively shape the future of the discipline through innovation and discussion. During the 2025 edition of the winter school, participants exchanged knowledge on current advances, challenges, and future perspectives in biofabrication. Guided by experts in this field, early-stage researchers discussed and summarized their views on five key topics: (i) the future of devices and technology in biofabrication, (ii) current trends and opportunities in material development, (iii) impact on society, ethics, and communication, (iv) applications and clinical translation, and (v) education and skillsets required for successful research. Their perspectives summarized here, address critical questions about future methodology, material development, and technological improvements that will continue to shape the evolution of biofabrication. Furthermore, aspects such as the impact on society, as well as the required skillset and education for future scientists working in the field are discussed.

title: Phage phenotyping by measuring plaque expansion dynamics
abstract: Abstract Bacteriophages exhibit staggering genomic diversity, yet phenotypic characterization remains bottlenecked by assays that generally yield simple binary infection outcomes. Quantitative traits can be extracted from standard liquid cultures, but many phages fail to produce a measurable effect in these settings, necessitating an improved quantitative approach on semi-solid media. While end-point plaque size is commonly used for quantitative phenotyping, it only provides a static snapshot that fails to disentangle phage performance across changing bacterial growth phases. Here, we report a cost-effective, scalable method to quantify the bacterial killing rates of diverse phages by continuously tracking plaque development using a consumer-grade flatbed scanner and custom open-source computer vision software. By fitting a minimal, phenomenological model to the diverse BASEL collection of Escherichia coli phages, we accurately captured plaque expansion dynamics across all bacterial growth phases. We discovered that plaque expansion parameters vary significantly across individual phages and taxonomic families, with the initial expansion rate demonstrating an inverse correlation with viral genome size. Notably, these plaque expansion dynamics did not correlate with bacterial collapse times in liquid culture, indicating that they represent distinct physiological and kinetic processes. Finally, we demonstrated that phage taxonomic family can be predicted with 72.1% accuracy solely from dynamic plaque parameters using a random forest classifier, whereas conventional endpoint plaque sizes held no predictive power. This time-lapse phenotyping approach yields robust kinetic data superior to end-point measurements, establishing a scalable platform to accelerate phage discovery and genotype-phenotype mapping.
authors: Jonathan Costa; Baltus A. van der Steen; Yuval Mulla

title: Phenomenon-first problem formulation with language models in metal-organic frameworks
abstract: Here we introduce a phenomenon-first framework for materials discovery in which an LLM receives separate descriptions of guest physics, host capabilities and operating context and proposes an unusual qualitative behavior with its mechanism, distinguishing signature and falsifier. Across 80 guest-host combinations in metal-organic frameworks, the model generated 57 proposals that were frozen before evaluation or materials selection; assessment identified nine computationally tractable candidates. In a repeat and guest-only baseline, structured formulation reproducibly broadened mechanistic exploration: the original and repeat runs each covered 21 broad mechanism families versus eight for guest-only formulation despite fewer proposals. From the original run, MC-010 yielded reproducible hydration-driven reorientation of retained ethanol in experimentally reported MOFs, while MC-015 yielded a quantum-corrected reversal of H$_2$ adsorption-region preference relative to the matched classical description. These results show how structured LLM reasoning can move upstream from executing supplied objectives toward prospectively formulating qualitative materials phenomena.
authors: Jihan Kim

title: Photo-guided azopolymer hydrogel actuators
abstract: Amorphous azopolymers are fascinating materials that can be deformed in arbitrary directions by light. However, they are so far used mostly for microfabrication, to anisotropically reshape dry polymer structures - essentially as a post-processing fabrication step. This is because the effect is known to be a plastic deformation, wherein the azopolymer is photo-softened and selectively reflows along the direction of the illumination polarization, owing to its polarization-dependent functional dyes. Crucially, such deformations are retained in the dark and cannot easily be overwritten by subsequent illumination. Once reflowed, there is no memory of the initial state, and sequential photo-deformations are added on top of each other. Consequently, to use the directional photo-deformation of amorphous azopolymers for dynamic and reconfigurable micro-actuators, e.g., in lab-on-chip applications, one would need to face this lack of overwritability, in addition to a lower deformability of larger structures, sticky behavior, and poor mechanical stability in water for some uses. Here, we show how azopolymer-hydrogel composites overcome these issues. By embedding azopolymer nanoparticles in hydrogel matrices, directional photo-deformation is ensured by the particles, while the compliant gel matrix neatly propagates deformations to the overall composite. Elastic restoring forces from the matrix also promote overwritability, such that microfabricated gel cubes display ample and directionally reconfigurable photo-deformations in water. Sequential illuminations with orthogonal linear polarizations produce alternating linear deformations up to twice the pristine cube side length, using illumination intervals down to five seconds. Finally, we introduce polarization-controlled, fully closeable microwells, with potential applications in biotechnology, microfluidics, and drug release.
authors: David Urban; Ryota Toyohara; Marcel Rey; Daniele Martella; Dag Roar Hjelme; Andrea Alessandrini; Toshiro OHASHI; Emiliano Descrovi

title: Plasma protein glycation, oxidation and nitration markers for improved risk prediction of Type 1 diabetes mellitus
abstract: Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) is characterized by hyperglycaemia caused by a deficiency of insulin resulting from autoimmune destruction of insulin-secreting beta cells of the pancreas. T1DM is caused by interaction of complex-trait genetic factors and environmental triggers such as viruses, endotoxin and possibly dietary effects. Recent studies have suggested that increased serum protein content of an advanced glycation endproduct is associated with increased risk of T1DM and also, with increased risk of cardiovascular disease in T1DM patients. The aim of this study is to quantify levels of Nε-Carboxymethyl-lysine (CML), other glycation endproducts, oxidation and nitration adducts in serum protein, in addition to related serum free adducts and amino acid metabolomics of monozygotic twins discordant for T1DM, and T1DM patients with HDL of high and low HAE, and compare these with plasma from healthy subjects. HDL apoA-1 exchange (HAE) – a measure of its ability to release lipid-poor apolipoproteinA-1, an essential step in reverse cholesterol transport. Monozygotic twins discordant for T1DM were studied from a London cohort and studies of T1DM patients with HDL of high and low HAE were based on an Oslo cohort. Major chemically-defined markers of protein damage by glycation, oxidation, and nitration were quantified in samples of plasma protein and in ultrafiltrate (glycated, oxidized and nitrated amino acids) by stable isotopic dilution analysis liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. In monozygotic twins there were increased protein glycation and oxidation markers in plasma and decreased nitration markers of plasma protein for the diabetic twin. However, increased nitration was observed in the second cohort of diabetic twins. In T1DM patients with HDL of high and low HAE, there were increased levels of glycation, oxidation and nitration of plasma protein in both patients groups with HDL of high and low HAE activity. There were changes in the amino acid metabolome in plasma of diabetic patients. This study reveals that dicarbonyl stress is a potential contributory impairment in T1DM and thereby very likely contributes to risk of CVD. Measurement of protein glycation, oxidation and nitration markers provides evidence of protein damage in healthy and patients with T1DM and also provides additional facility in the prediction for developing specific complications of metabolic disease.
authors: Daniah Alamoudi
venue: Warwick Research Archive Portal (University of Warwick)

title: Plasmonic metasurface microfluidic accelerates redox reactions for rapid phenotypic antibiotic susceptibility testing
abstract: Electron-accepting chain reactions play crucial roles in diagnostics for bacterial infections, from nucleic acid amplification for bacterial identification to metabolic assays for phenotypic antibiotic susceptibility testing. When coupled with redox mediators, these reactions can be interrogated using an electroanalytical method. We demonstrate kinetic acceleration of loop-mediated isothermal amplification-based identification and resazurin-based phenotypic antibiotic susceptibility profiling through enhanced electromagnetic fields and modulated hot electron injection at the multilayered plasmonic metasurface-fluidic interface. We systematically investigate rounded versus sharp-apex plasmonic architectures, quantifying near-field magnitude and decay to identify geometries that maximize kinetic amplification under electrochemical readout. This approach is further combined with machine learning-assisted Gaussian fitting to improve data quantification and interpretation. Across diverse bacterial species, we achieved rapid identification with no cross-reactivity and phenotypic antibiotic susceptibility testing without overnight culture. In a prospective pilot clinical study of urine specimens directly from patients with suspected urinary tract infections, we observe high accuracy and strong essential and categorical agreement with standard clinical microbiology assays for bacterial identification and antibiotic susceptibility testing.
