title: A FOCUS-PDCA quality improvement model involving unlicensed assistive personnel for improving clinical effectiveness and efficiency in inpatient physical examination: a quasi-experimental, historical-control study
abstract: The accuracy and efficiency of inpatient examinations depend on a well-collaborated working team that involves doctors, nurses, and unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP). This study aimed to evaluate the clinical effectiveness and efficiency of a FOCUS-PDCA quality improvement model involving UAP in improving inpatient physical examinations. A quasi-experimental, historical-control before-and-after study was conducted among 372 patients who received the FOCUS-PDCA quality improvement examination management (the observation group) and another 385 patients under normal management (the control group). Clinical effectiveness and efficiency were compared between the two groups. Compared to the control group, the FOCUS-PDCA group had significantly lower rates of defect examinations (19.6% vs. 44.7%, p < 0.01), nursing interruption events (14.5% vs. 26.4%, p < 0.01), and nurse referral events (6.1% vs. 24.7%, p < 0.01). Furthermore, the FOCUS-PDCA group had higher patient satisfaction (9.04 ± 0.82 vs. 8.45 ± 0.96, p <0.01) lower hospital cost [Median: 29,434.70 RMB (IQR: 9,705.00–52,451.40) vs. 34,537.60 RMB (IQR: 14,689.98–64,222.12), p < 0.001], and shorter length of hospital stay [Median: 4.00 days (IQR: 3.00, 5.00) vs. 5.00 days (IQR: 4.00, 6.00), p < 0.001]. The FOCUS-PDCA model involving UAP was associated with improved clinical effectiveness and efficiency of inpatient physical examination, which may be applied in hospital management to enhance the quality of care and patient outcomes. Further validation in other clinical settings is needed to test its broader application.
authors: Jing Li; Yixia Zhao; Shi Zhou; Guangyan Lv; Weihong Huang; Jianzhong Hu; Jing Chong; Fang Li

title: A New Current Fingerprinting Sensing Method for Adaptive Protection of PV-Integrated Distribution Networks
abstract: Grid-following photovoltaic (PV) inverters inject fault currents whose magnitude and phase are set by the control mode active during the disturbance, so directional overcurrent relay (DOCR) settings coordinated for one inverter response can miscoordinate after a mode change. This paper proposes a communication-free adaptive protection scheme built on local sensing. A voltage-adaptive current fingerprinting classifier uses local positive sequence measurements to detect current-limiting (CL), active current priority (ACP) and reactive current priority (RCP) operation, as well as momentary cessation (MC) and asymmetrical faults. The classifier activates the relay setting group prepared offline for the detected mode. With pickup currents fixed, the coordination sub-problem is shown to be a linear program (LP), so every setting group is computed at its exact global optimum. Where the grid code droop law makes ACP and RCP indistinguishable by angle, the classifier declares the ambiguity and activates a group that is feasible for both. Under a class-0.5 instrument transformer noise model, the group placed in service is coordination-valid in 99.8% of cases and the expected residual miscoordination is 3.0×10-5 s, 0.01% of the 0.30 s margin. On the CIGRE medium-voltage benchmark, the scheme satisfies the margin in all operating modes for three-phase, line-to-line (LL) and single-line-to-ground (SLG) faults. The same fault types are then verified at three fault locations on a practical Egyptian 11 kV feeder model, where the sensing layer is confirmed on an electromagnetic transient (EMT) model and the scheme removes the violations of single-setting coordination using an estimated 4 kB of relay memory.
authors: Ahmed A. Salem; Emad Eldeen Omran; Azza Ahmed Eldesouky; Hany S. E. Mansour; Mohamed A. A. Mohamed; Eyad S. Oda

title: A Qualitative Case Study on the Implementation of an AI-Powered Gait Rehabilitation Robot Program for Students with Severe and Multiple Disabilities
abstract: This qualitative case study explored how an AI-powered gait rehabilitation robot program was implemented over one semester in a special school and how its participants experienced and made sense of it. The bounded case was the program itself; its participants comprised three students with severe and multiple disabilities, the teacher-researcher (a special education teacher), a collaborating physical therapist, and three guardians. Data were collected from multiple sources, including health-management records and assessment sheets, class documents and Individualized Education Program (IEP) team minutes, robot-recorded gait data, semi-structured surveys and interviews, participant-observation logs, and the researcher’s reflexive journal. The data were analyzed through iterative coding, pattern identification, and cross-source comparison, with attention to discrepant data, and trustworthiness was strengthened through triangulation, member checking, and peer debriefing. Three themes were identified. First, the program was implemented within a co-teaching model that connected the special education teacher and the physical therapist across the boundary of education and therapy, and it was organized as a related service through IEP team consultation under the 2022 revised special education curriculum. Second, the participants moved from initial expectation and concern toward a more nuanced appreciation of the program, while also raising practical concerns about safety, sensor limitations, and the burden of responsibility. Third, the students showed uneven but meaningful changes. Although gains on the ordinal functional indicators (MMT, BBS, FAC) were partial or limited to maintenance, clearer changes appeared in confidence, self-efficacy, and social participation. Rather than verifying effectiveness, this case illustrates the possibilities and conditions of school-based AI gait-robot education and points to the need for a sustainable policy and institutional support framework, including the placement of rehabilitation professionals within schools.

title: A Reproducible Safety Assessment Model for Concurrent Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation with Implanted Intracranial Electroencephalography Electrodes
abstract: BACKGROUND: Concurrent transcranial magnetic stimulation and intracranial EEG (TMS-sEEG) offers a powerful approach for interrogating human brain circuits with high spatiotemporal resolution. However, standardized safety testing procedures for TMS in the presence of implanted electrodes are lacking. OBJECTIVE: To establish and validate a reproducible methodological framework for assessing TMS safety with sEEG hardware, addressing potential risks of electrode displacement, heating, and secondary current induction. METHODS: A conductive agarose phantom implanted with clinical-grade platinum sEEG electrodes was exposed to single-pulse TMS (0.4 Hz), repetitive TMS (1-50 Hz), and intermittent theta burst stimulation. Electrode displacement was quantified via high-speed video and motion tracking. Temperature changes were measured with fiber-optic thermal probes positioned at stimulated electrode contacts. Induced voltages were recorded using an oscilloscope and intracranial EEG hardware, and secondary current and charge density were calculated from oscilloscope outputs and impedance measurements. RESULTS: sEEG lead displacement remained micrometer-scale across stimulation conditions, with a maximum transient displacement of 10.99 μm and a maximum 1-s mean displacement from the pre-TMS position of 16.27 μm. Temperature changes remained well within the 2°C safety threshold across all tested conditions; in the primary temperature series, the maximum observed increase was 0.073°C. Induced voltages and charge densities remained below established safety limits, exhibiting consistent exponential decay with increasing distance from the coil. All stimulation conditions, including those exceeding typical clinical ranges, remained well within safety margins. CONCLUSIONS: Under the tested conditions in a controlled phantom environment, TMS exposure produced micrometer-scale transient and longer-timescale displacement, temperature changes within established safety thresholds, and charge densities within established safety thresholds. This validated methodological pipeline provides a standardized framework for future safety experiments involving TMS and implanted devices and supports continued development of TMS-sEEG as a tool for studying human brain circuitry and neuromodulation.

title: A Retensionable Inlay/Onlay Hybrid Double-Bundle Medial Collateral Ligament Reconstruction Produces Superior Restoration of the Uninjured State When Compared to a Single-Bundle Inlay Reconstruction
abstract: Background: Traditional superficial medial collateral ligament (sMCL) reconstruction techniques have not consistently restored native laxity. Purpose/Hypothesis: The purpose of this study was to develop a retensionable inlay/onlay hybrid medial collateral ligament (MCL) reconstruction through comparison to a biomechanically and clinically validated reconstruction. It was hypothesized that increasing the distal footprint on the tibia through a double-bundle construct and a retensionable construct would better restore native laxity. Study Design: Controlled laboratory study. Methods: A total of 27 cadaveric knees were tested on a 6 degrees of freedom robot system. Knees were tested with valgus and external rotation (ER). Each knee was tested in a native state and an injured state after sectioning of the sMCL. One of 3 reconstructions using an anterior tibialis allograft was then performed: (1) single-bundle inlay reconstruction, (2) double-bundle inlay/onlay hybrid reconstruction with tibial fixation at both the proximal and distal (PD) tibial insertions of the sMCL footprint, or (3) double-bundle inlay/onlay hybrid reconstruction with tibial fixation at the anterior and posterior (AP) aspects of the distal sMCL tibial insertion. The constructs used retensionable variable-loop devices, allowing for retensioning after knee cycling. The constructs were tested after cycling and retensioning. Results: Sectioning of the sMCL resulted in significantly increased laxity compared to the native state for both valgus and ER laxity testing ( P < .001). After flexion cycling and subsequent retensioning, both AP and PD double-bundle reconstructions demonstrated significantly higher restoration of stability compared to cycled single-bundle reconstructions ( P < .001). Both double-bundle reconstructions were significantly closer to the native state than the single-bundle reconstruction for valgus rotation ( P < .001) and ER ( P < .05). For valgus testing, there was no difference between retensioned double-bundle constructs and the native state, with a pooled valgus difference of 0.56° (95% CI, 0.05°-1.06°; P = .032). For ER testing, no differences were found between the retensioned AP double-bundle and the native state ( P = .836), suggesting more complete restoration was achieved by AP double-bundle restoration. Conclusion: A retensionable inlay/onlay hybrid double-bundle MCL reconstruction with a larger femoral footprint and 2 distal anterior-posterior tibial footprints produced superior restoration of the uninjured state when compared to a traditional single-bundle inlay reconstruction. For double-bundle reconstructions, an anterior-posterior tibial fixation achieved mean values closer to the native state than proximal-distal fixation. Clinical Relevance: A double-bundle retensionable inlay/onlay hybrid reconstruction is an effective alternative to a single-bundle inlay reconstruction technique. The double-bundle reconstruction may better withstand early unrestricted range of motion during postoperative phases.
authors: Adam William Anz; Garrett Waller; Jeremy D. Carroll; Gabe Colbrunn; Aiden Cole Magoolaghan; Jessi Truett; Achraf Cohen; Mangesh M. Kulkarni; Mark C. Callanan

title: A Review of Robotic Surgery: Engineering Considerations and Future Directions From Surgeons' Perspectives
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Since its initial inception, robotic-assisted minimally invasive surgery (RAMIS) is continually being applied to a wider array of procedures. However, there are significant limitations in current surgical subsystems, including a large learning curve, lack of effective haptic feedback, decreased surgical intuition, and decreased dexterity. METHODS: A narrative review of the literature was conducted to provide an overview of key developments in the field. Relevant articles were identified through searches of PubMed, IEEE, Google Scholar, and EMBASE, along with manual screening of references. RESULTS: A selection of representative articles covering topics including teleoperation, kinematics, dynamics, and haptic feedback is discussed to highlight major themes and recent advances. CONCLUSIONS: Despite recent advances, limitations to operator experience remain. Numerous strategies and approaches are currently being proposed and explored to further advance surgical subsystems, improving dexterity, haptic feedback, movement time delay, and learning curve.
authors: Noah Shaikh; Walter Fitschen; Abhinaba Bhattacharjee; Dimitrios Stefanidis; Michael W. Sim; Meghan Turner; Sohel Anwar; Muhammad Ashraful Alam
venue: International Journal of Medical Robotics and Computer Assisted Surgery

title: A Review of Strip Shape Prediction Methods Transitioning From Mechanistic Models to Interpretable Deep Learning
abstract: Strip shape prediction is a core task in rolling process control, and its accuracy directly impacts product quality and production efficiency. However, complex multivariable nonlinear couplings, dynamic operating conditions, and strong environmental disturbances severely challenge the accuracy and adaptability of traditional mechanistic models. In recent years, machine learning (ML) has provided new pathways to overcome these limitations. Although research achievements are increasingly abundant, the field still lacks a systematic review that integrates technological evolution with industrial application experience. This paper systematically reviews the research progress of ML in strip shape prediction, tracing the evolution from mechanistic modeling to data‐driven approaches. By detailing the core modeling stages and using strip crown, flatness, and key influencing factors as specific contexts, we systematically categorize the functional positioning and applicable scenarios of various ML algorithms. Crucially, we outline their structural limitations in practical deployment, such as “black‐box” unreliability and a lack of physical consistency. Based on this synthesis, the paper explores current industrial bottlenecks and future development directions, specifically highlighting interpretable deep learning, mechanism‐data fusion, and causal inference. Ultimately, this review aims to provide valuable references and insights for academia and industry professionals striving to advance intelligent steel production and enhance process efficiency.
authors: Fei Shang; Zhijie Zheng; Huilin Chen; Jipeng Zhao; Yonhao Ma; Sifang Wang; Ruilin Miao; Xuegang Zhou; Chunwei Xing; Pengpeng Zhang

title: A TIBIA FIRST GAP BALANCED PATIENT-SPECIFIC ALIGNMENT TOTAL KNEE ARTHROPLASTY TECHNIQUE ACHIEVES BETTER TKA BALANCE THAN MECHANICAL, KINEMATIC, AND FUNCTIONAL ALIGNMENT
abstract: Purpose This study evaluates four different alignment techniques to assess knee TKA balance. Methods A prospective cohort of 1035 patients undergoing primary robotic-cruciate-retaining TKA by a single surgeon were analysed. The Velys TKA robotic system collects a balance curve that enables the surgeon to intra-operatively analyse the balance consequence of a mechanically aligned (MA), kinematically aligned (KA), functionally aligned (FA), and patient-specific aligned (PSA) TKA. FA was determined by starting from the KA position and then making positional implant changes to balance the TKA with equal extension gaps, equal medial gaps, and 3 mm more laxity laterally in flexion. The tibia was then cut robotically, and a ligament tensor was inserted to determine the balance consequence of FA. For PSA, the femoral component position was further adjusted, if necessary to achieve optimal balance. Finally, the femur was resected robotically, and the balance outcome of PSA was assessed in a blinded manner. Balance was determined as ±2 mm from optimal. Results A total of 1035 consecutive patients with a mean age of 67 ± 9 years were included. The proportion of balanced TKAs was 16% for MA, 43% for KA, 35% for FA, and 98% for PSA (P < .05). The proportion of potentially correctable TKAs for MA was 18%, Thus MA balanced TKA 34% of the time With KA, 14% were potentially correctable Thus KA balanced a TKA 57% of the time For FA, the planned pre-resection gaps differed significantly after tibial resection (P < .05), and 19% were potentially correctable. Thus FA balanced a TKA 54% of the time. The factors that showed a significant difference for a unbalanced FA TKA was a greater alignment from neutral p=0.004, a fixed flexion deformity p=0.02 and large posterior osteophytes p=0.04 Conclusion Optimal TKA balance is achieved with a tibia-first, gap-balanced PSA technique
authors: Mark Clatworthy; Guido Wierer

title: A first realization of reinforcement learning-based closed-loop EEG-TMS.
abstract: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is a powerful tool to investigate neurophysiology of the human brain and treat brain disorders. Traditionally, therapeutic TMS has been applied in a one-size-fits-all approach, disregarding inter- and intraindividual differences. Brain state-dependent EEG-TMS, such as coupling TMS with a pre-specified phase of the sensorimotor μ-rhythm, enables the induction of differential neuroplastic effects depending on the targeted phase. But this approach is still user-dependent as it requires defining an a-priori target phase. Here, we present a first realization of a machine-learning-based, closed-loop real-time EEG-TMS setup to identify user-independently the individual μ-rhythm phase associated with high- vs. low-corticospinal excitability states. We applied EEG-TMS to 25 participants targeting the supplementary motor area- primary motor cortex network and used a reinforcement learning algorithm to identify the μ- rhythm phase associated with high- vs. low corticospinal excitability. We employed linear mixed effects models and Bayesian analysis to assess effects of reinforced learning on corticospinal excitability indexed by motor evoked potential amplitude, and functional connectivity indexed by the imaginary part of resting-state EEG coherence. Our results show that reinforcement learning identified the μ-rhythm phase associated with high- vs. low-excitability states, and their repetitive stimulation resulted in long-term increases vs. decreases in functional connectivity in the stimulated sensorimotor network. Our work demonstrated the feasibility of a reinforcement learning-based adaptive closed-loop EEG-TMS approach in a full experimental cohort, enabling user-independent identification of μ-rhythm phases associated with corticospinal excitability states.
authors: Dania Humaidan; Jiahua Xu; Jing Chen; Christoph Zrenner; David Emanuel Vetter; Laura Marzetti; Paolo Belardinelli; Timo Roine; Risto J Ilmoniemi; Gian Luca Romani; Ulf Ziemann

title: A normative torque-profile approach for quantifying elbow and wrist flexor hyper-resistance after stroke: a proof-of-principle study
abstract: Abstract Background Post-stroke spasticity is commonly assessed using the Modified Ashworth Scale (MAS), despite its limited objectivity and variable reliability. This study introduces Score E , a novel isokinetic dynamometry-derived metric designed to quantify elbow and wrist flexor hyper-resistance by comparing patients’ torque-angle profiles with a healthy reference corridor. Methods Thirty-five post-stroke patients and twenty-one healthy controls were included. Elbow and wrist hyper-resistance was assessed using the MAS and an isokinetic dynamometer in two testing conditions: seated on the dynamometer chair (ergo chair) and seated in the patient’s wheelchair. Two dynamometer-derived metrics were analyzed: Score E and peak torque (Peakτ). Feasibility, inter-rater and test-retest reliability, and associations with MAS grades were assessed. Exploratory PRE-POST changes following a 10-min local vibration session were also described. Results Score E showed good to excellent inter-rater and test-retest reliability across joints and testing conditions. Inter-rater ICCs ranged from 0.81 to 0.89, and test-retest ICCs from 0.76 to 0.93. Peakτ showed moderate to good reliability. In contrast, MAS agreement was lower and more variable. Score E showed moderate associations with MAS grades, particularly at the elbow, with weaker and less consistent associations at the wrist. MAS assessment was faster, but all assessments were well tolerated, with median pain ratings of 0/10 in all testing conditions. PRE-POST vibration changes were small and heterogeneous, preventing formal assessment of responsiveness. Conclusion Score E provides a reliable, objective, and visually interpretable quantification of post-stroke elbow and wrist flexor hyper-resistance. By comparing the full torque-angle profile with normative data, this approach preserves information on both the magnitude and angular span of abnormal resistance, supporting its potential for targeted longitudinal monitoring.

title: A scenario-adaptive AHP-FCE framework for lithium-ion battery thermal management: Optimal strategy selection in energy storage, supercars, and marine propulsion
abstract: The suitability of lithium-ion battery thermal management strategies (TMSs) varies substantially across operating conditions and engineering constraints, limiting the effectiveness of single-metric or fixed-weight evaluation methods. This study develops a scenario-adaptive framework integrating the Analytic Hierarchy Process and Fuzzy Comprehensive Evaluation (AHP-FCE). The framework comprises four primary criteria (technical performance, economic viability, environmental safety, and sustainability) and 15 secondary indicators, with scenario-specific weights and evaluation boundaries established for energy storage systems (ESS), electric supercars (ESC), and electric propulsion ships (EPS). Among the evaluated candidates, single-phase immersion cooling, two-phase immersion cooling, and single-phase cold-plate cooling rank first for ESS, ESC, and EPS, with adaptability scores of 0.894, 0.930, and 0.885, respectively, highlighting the scenario dependence of TMS selection. Robustness analyses confirm the overall stability of these recommendations, although the ESC ranking is more sensitive to the weighting method. An external techno-economic benchmark further supports the engineering plausibility of the ESS recommendation. The proposed framework provides a transparent and interpretable quantitative basis for preliminary TMS screening and scenario-specific engineering decision-making.

title: A story for Pepper and Nao: applying the learning by teaching paradigm in children with patterns of neuromotor impairment
abstract: Background Social robots are increasingly used in educational and clinical contexts to enhance engagement and learning, particularly in children with neurological and neurodevelopmental disorders. The Learning by Teaching paradigm, in which children actively teach social robots, promotes cognitive and metacognitive processes such as planning, self-efficacy, and executive functioning; however, controlled and systematic evidence supporting its effectiveness remains limited. Children with neuromotor disorders frequently present with closely intertwined motor and cognitive planning difficulties, which significantly impact learning and everyday functioning. In this context, social robot–mediated interventions based on the Learning by Teaching paradigm may represent a promising approach. The current multicenter randomized controlled trial (RCT) explores the feasibility and effectiveness of this approach to enhance cognitive and motor planning in children with neuromotor impairments, and to examine potential generalization effects on other cognitive domains and engagement. Methods The main aim of this RCT study is to evaluate the feasibility and effectiveness of a social robot-mediated Learning by Teaching intervention in children aged 7–16 years with neuromotor impairments. Eighty participants will be randomly assigned to an Experimental Group (EG) receiving social robot training or to a Control Group (CG) continuing standard care. The intervention consists of 20–25 sessions in which children teach a humanoid social robot (Pepper or NAO) to order picture-based stories of increasing complexity. Assessments will be performed at baseline (T0), post-intervention or control period (T1), and follow-up/post-treatment (T2). Primary outcomes include planning abilities assessed through picture arrangement and an ad hoc motor planning task. Secondary outcomes encompass executive functions, visuo-spatial memory, attention, inhibition, narrative production, visual-perceptual skills, and reading comprehension. Engagement will be measured using a multimodal approach integrating behavioral, cognitive, emotional, and physiological indicators derived from video, audio, and wearable sensors. Results The study will examine improvements in planning and motor programming abilities and potential generalization effects on executive functions and reading comprehension. Additionally, the predictive and mediating role of engagement in intervention effectiveness will be reported. Conclusions This research protocol proposes an innovative, engagement-focused rehabilitation approach integrating cognitive, motor, and narrative processes through social robotics. Findings are expected to inform the development of evidence-based, personalized interventions for children with neuromotor disorders and to advance methodological approaches for assessing engagement in human–robot interaction. title: A study on Critical Factors for Blockchain Adoption in India: Analytic Hierarchy Process
abstract: Blockchain technology (BCT) has attracted a lot of attention because of its technological characteristics that improve the security, transparency, and operational efficiency of organizations. However, several considerations should be taken into account while evaluating its adoption. The aim of this study is to define and prioritize the factors influencing the adoption of BCT by organizations in India using Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) methodology. Five dimensions and nineteen sub-factors were evaluated using a literature review and interviews with experts. The results indicate that technology factors have the greatest impact on the adoption of blockchain, followed by organizational factors and regulatory factors. The most significant sub-factors were: security and privacy, relative advantage, and top management support. The study provides valuable implications for organizations and policymakers to address the challenges of successful implementation of blockchain and digital transformation initiatives.

title: A transdiagnostic framework for neurological intervention in maladaptive repetitive behaviors.
abstract: From daily rituals to pathological patterns of behavior and thought, a wide spectrum of habitual behaviors emerges through repeated reinforcement learning and becomes embedded in cortico-basal ganglia circuits. Once established, these behaviors operate automatically and resist conscious control. This review summarizes neurological intervention strategies for correcting pathological habits (e.g., addiction, obsessive-compulsive disorder) and restoring adaptive behavioral patterns. Pharmacological approaches target the plasticity of habit circuits via modulation of dopamine, serotonin, and glutamate systems. Non-invasive brain stimulation techniques-such as repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), and deep TMS-can modulate cortical control networks and indirectly influence connected subcortical circuitry. Behavioral interventions include extinction learning, reinforcement of alternative actions, contextual modification, cognitive strategies, and memory reconsolidation-based techniques. Recently, hybrid approaches combining AI-based digital therapeutics (DTx) with neuromodulatory devices have gained attention. Invasive techniques such as optogenetics and deep brain stimulation (DBS) enable direct modulation of specific neural circuits, allowing suppression of habitual responses or facilitation of alternative learning. Beyond clinical applications, these approaches elucidate the neural mechanisms underlying habitual behavior. Modulation of habits is most effective when employing multi-level, combinatorial interventions rather than a single technique. Integrating these strategies, this paper proposes a staged framework-habit circuit suppression → alternative learning → consolidation → sustained management-and a neuroscience-based, personalized model for behavioral treatment with implications for future clinical and research applications.
authors: Se Jin Jeon; Darine Froy Mabunga; Chan Young Shin

title: ARAM: a threshold model for understanding occupant acceptance of architectural robot adaptations
abstract: Physical interior elements are increasingly becoming roboticised to support occupant needs. Partitions, ceilings, and furniture can now physically and autonomously change shape or move to architecturally “adapt” indoor spaces, with the aim of improving occupant comfort, satisfaction, and wellbeing. However, occupants sometimes reject these adaptations when they are perceived as disruptive, unpredictable, or difficult to control. Motivated by the goal of making architectural robots more acceptable, we involved an interdisciplinary team of experts in human-building interaction, human-robot interaction, psychology, anthropology, and human comfort to qualitatively re-analyze how occupants accepted adaptations across three previous studies on robotic partitions. We found that an occupant tended to accept an adaptation when they recognized a personal need that the architectural robot was capable of addressing in a socially justifiable way. Accordingly, we developed the Architectural Robot Acceptance Model (ARAM), in which three qualitative thresholds along a continuum of perceived stress severity define four distinct acceptance responses to a specific adaptation. As the positions of these thresholds may vary across occupants and situations, ARAM supports testable estimates of how an occupant may respond to different appraisal states of personal need, adaptation capability, and social justification. Because architectural robot adaptations may simultaneously be experienced as robotic behaviors, building automation, and socially situated environmental adjustments, ARAM is particularly relevant to individual adaptations that enter occupants' spatial experience and may affect co-located others. We then discuss how the model can inform situated estimates of occupant acceptance of architectural robot adaptations, and outline how its broader relevance to other robotic, automated, intelligent, and smart technologies embedded in the built environment may be evaluated in future work.

title: Academic Stress and Self-Regulation Skills among High School Mathematics Learners
abstract: Academic stress is one of the serious issues in mathematics education that is likely to undermine student performance and motivation. This study examines the relationship between academic stress and self-regulation skills among high school mathematics learners, focusing on how self-regulation can prevent the adverse effects of stress and enhance academic performance. With a descriptive-correlational research design, the research sampled 300 high school students from private schools in Davao City for the academic year 2024–2025. Data were collected using validated Likert-scale questionnaires to measure academic stress (e.g., teaching methods, parental expectations, and exam results) and self-regulation skills (planning, self-checking, effort, and self-efficacy). Statistical analysis indicated a significant negative correlation between academic stress and self-regulation skills. Among the stress indicators, only class tests and content difficulty stress showed a considerable relationship with self-regulation. These findings support the necessity to address these particular sources of stress in building resilience and improving performance in mathematics. Therefore, the study recommends that educational institutions emphasize developing interventions for reducing academic stress and enhancing student self-regulation through structured learning strategies, well-rounded support systems, and alternative assessment methods. Moreover, involving parents in nurturing supportive learning environments is essential. Future research should investigate the relative effect of digital tools and institutional policies for maintaining lower stress levels and improving academic self-regulation across diverse educational contexts. Addressing academic stress is crucial for fostering a positive learning environment and improving student achievements in mathematics education.

title: Accelerated TMS is associated with changes of subgenual cingulate–default mode network coupling in depression: an observational 7 Tesla fMRI study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Accelerated transcranial magnetic stimulation (aTMS) is an effective treatment for depression, but its neurobiological mechanisms of action remain to be elucidated. This study used high-resolution 7-Tesla MRI to investigate changes in resting-state functional connectivity (rs-FC) of the subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC) following a treatment series of aTMS. We hypothesized a decrease in sgACC rs-FC with key cortical regions of the default mode network (DMN), reflecting a downregulation of a network that is overactive in depression. METHODS: Twenty-two patients with current depression underwent 7-Tesla MRI scans before and after a two-week aTMS treatment series (24,000 pulses) targeting the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Fourteen healthy participants were also scanned twice as a control group. Longitudinal changes in sgACC seed-based rs-FC were compared between groups. Furthermore, group differences were assessed at baseline and at follow-up. Exploratory correlations between longitudinal changes in sgACC rs-FC, depression severity, mindfulness, and affect were also evaluated. RESULTS: There was a reduction in rs-FC between the sgACC and bilateral precunei, and between sgACC and left frontal pole in patients receiving aTMS. At baseline, patients had increased rs‑FC between the sgACC and a cluster including the left precuneus and a cluster in the right superior frontal gyrus. Exploratory correlations suggest an association between sgACC-precunei rs-FC changes and mindfulness (p = 0.008, uncorrected for multiple comparisons), while no associations were found with depression severity or affect. CONCLUSIONS: Treatment with aTMS is associated with a reduction in rs‑FC between the sgACC and the DMN. Exploratory correlations with mindfulness warrant replication in larger, independent samples.

title: Active Function Improvement with Repeated Injections of Botulinum Toxin A in Upper Limb Spasticity: A Longitudinal Analysis from the ULIS-III Study
abstract: Improvement in active function (making it easier to use the limb) is a common goal following treatment of upper limb spasticity with botulinum toxin (BoNT-A). ULIS-III was a large international, observational, longitudinal study (N = 953) conducted in the context of usual clinical practice over two years. In this secondary post hoc analysis, we examine whether goals for improvement in active function were met over repeated injection cycles. Patients were selected if improved active function (AF) was a primary/secondary goal for at least one cycle of treatment (n = 286/953). They were assessed at the start and end of each cycle using the Goal Attainment T-score alongside the Arm Activity measure (ArmA). Serial changes and predictors of improvement were explored. Across eight cycles, there were 1167 injections for active function, 875/1998 (44%) AF goals were set and 493 (57%) of those goals were achieved. Patients continued to show significant improvement in AF (p < 0.001) for each injection at least up to three cycles, which is likely to be clinically significant, especially in patients with milder spasticity who were naïve to BoNT-A. No statistically significant predictors were confirmed on mixed effects modeling. Conclusions: Repeated BoNT-A continued to produce significant improvement in active function for at least three cycles, regardless of patient- or treatment-related factors in this cohort, but type II errors due to small numbers cannot be excluded.

title: Adaptive Electrochemical Self‐Cleaning via Surface Reconstruction Enables Fluoride‐Free and Batch‐Consistent Cathode Regeneration
abstract: ABSTRACT Direct recycling of spent lithium‐ion battery (LIB) cathodes holds great promise for sustainable materials recovery. However, residual fluorinated impurities, including inorganic fluoride species and polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), remain a persistent challenge due to their chemical persistence and heterogeneous distribution. Here, we report an electrochemically driven self‐cleaning strategy that enables fluoride‐free adaptive direct recycling of spent cathodes. Using LiNi 0.5 Co 0.2 Mn 0.3 O 2 (NMC532) as a model system, anodic polarization activates oxygen‐evolution‐driven surface reconstruction, generating hydroxylated transition metal (TM) interfaces that trigger the cooperative elimination of fluorinated contaminants. Specifically, the reconstruction promotes proton‐assisted dissolution of LiF and related inorganic fluoride species, while simultaneously inducing a hydrophobic‐to‐hydrophilic interfacial transition that weakens PVDF adhesion and facilitates its removal. These coupled redox‐hydrolysis‐interfacial processes synergistically eradicate fluorinated residues while preserving the bulk composition and structural integrity of the cathode. The regenerated NMC532 delivers a high discharge capacity of 145.1 mAh·g −1 , comparable to commercial material. When implemented in pouch cells, this strategy achieves an inter‑batch capacity variation of less than 1.3%, dramatically outperforming the ∼24.1% variation typical of conventional recycling and meeting commercial consistency standards (± 3%–5%). This reconstruction‐enabled self‐cleaning strategy is broadly applicable across diverse cathode chemistries, providing a scalable and chemically selective pathway toward impurity‑free, high‑performance battery material regeneration.

title: Adaptive architecture-aware CT-guided knowledge distillation for low-data lung disease classification from chest X-rays
abstract: Abstract Chest X-ray (CXR) images have been used for screening purposes in thoracic diseases owing to their low cost and wide availability. However, accurate classification of thoracic diseases using CXRs with limited data remains challenging due to poor lesion visualization and overlapping disease-sensitive structures. On the contrary, computed tomography (CT) scans provide better three-dimensional, disease-sensitive detail and more precise visualization of pulmonary lesions. This paper proposes CTGuideNet, an adaptive cross-modality knowledge distillation framework that provides CT-guided feature supervision by transferring disease-sensitive feature representations learned from independently collected CT images to chest X-ray classification models. Contrary to existing approaches to knowledge distillation (KD) where uniform distillation strategies across different architectures are used, we design an approach in which distillation behavior varies with the representational capabilities of various convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures like lightweight CNNs, residual CNNs, and attention-aware CNNs. First, a CT-based teacher model was trained on 8408 CT images of COVID-19, pneumonia, lung tumors, and normal conditions; then extensive experiments were conducted in low-data and large-scale CXR settings containing COVID-19, pneumonia lung tumors, and normal classes. The proposed framework established the largest improvements under limited-data conditions, where CT-Guided supervision improved classification performance by up to 10% over baseline training in the multi-architecture experiments. The lightweight MobileNetV2 demonstrated consistent improvements under multi-seed evaluation. Additional Grad-CAM analysis and external validation on the JSRT lung nodule dataset further confirmed improved lesion-sensitive representation learning and cross-dataset generalization capability. The experimental results demonstrate that CT-guided feature supervision using disease-sensitive representations learned from CT images provides an effective strategy for improving data-efficient thoracic disease classification in CXR images.

title: Agreement and Systematic Differences Between Intraoperative ROSA Hip-Knee-Ankle Measurements and Standing Radiographic Alignment After Robotic-Assisted Total Knee Arthroplasty: A Retrospective Agreement Study
abstract: Background/Objectives: Intraoperative robotic hip-knee-ankle angle (HKA) measurements are obtained with the patient supine under operative conditions and may not directly represent postoperative standing weight-bearing alignment. This study quantified the correspondence and systematic differences between intraoperative ROSA HKA and standing radiographic HKA after robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty. Methods: This retrospective single-center study included 208 knees from 178 consecutive patients, including 30 bilateral patients. The primary comparison was post-trial-component intraoperative ROSA HKA versus postoperative standing radiographic HKA; the secondary comparison was pre-cut intraoperative ROSA HKA versus preoperative standing radiographic HKA. Patient-cluster bootstrap confidence intervals used 10,000 resamples. Agreement was evaluated using Bland–Altman analysis, absolute-agreement ICC(A,1), and weighted kappa; Spearman ρ described association. Results: For the primary comparison, mean bias (ROSA minus radiographic HKA) was −1.75° (95% CI −2.08 to −1.43°), conventional limits of agreement were −6.36° to 2.85°, and ICC(A,1) was 0.472 (95% CI 0.379 to 0.557). Differences were within 3° in 70.2% of knees and exceeded 3° in 29.8%; proportional bias was present (slope −0.569, p < 0.001). The secondary comparison showed bias 0.97° and ICC(A,1) 0.956. Exact femoral and tibial size agreement was 42.3% and 80.8%, respectively. The standardized surgeon-entered 10 mm starting value was retained in 57.7% of knees. These systematic and angle-dependent differences may partly reflect the differing loading, positioning, and measurement conditions between the intraoperative trial construct and postoperative standing radiography. Conclusions: Post-trial-component ROSA HKA showed systematic and angle-dependent differences from postoperative standing HKA and should not be considered interchangeable with, or a fixed patient-level predictor of, postoperative standing alignment.

title: An FBG tactile sensor array and self-supervised contrastive learning transformer for tumor depth estimation in robotic palpation
abstract: Abstract Restoring haptic feedback remains a major challenge in robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery (RMIS), especially for localizing subsurface tumors and estimating their depth. This paper presents a compact, high-density tactile sensor array based on fiber Bragg grating (FBG) sensing for robotic palpation. The array uses a honeycomb topology to increase spatial sampling within an 8.5 mm footprint while preserving high sensitivity. Static and dynamic tests show a linear force-wavelength response across seven channels, an average force resolution of 8.43 mN, and \((<)\)1% full-scale dynamic error. To estimate tumor depth from palpation signals, we propose FBG-PatchFormer. Since depth annotations are scarce and costly to obtain, FBG-PatchFormer leverages contrastive self-supervised pretraining on unlabeled palpation windows to reduce the reliance on dense labels, and is then finetuned for depth classification. On phantom palpation with embedded inclusions, FBG-PatchFormer achieves 99.60% record-level accuracy on a ten-class depth task (blank and 2--10 mm). In vivo tests on porcine liver further demonstrate robust tumor localization under physiological motion and fluid interference, supporting the clinical potential of the proposed sensing system.

title: Anatomic Anterolateral Ligament Reconstruction Using the Iliotibial Band Results in Less Internal Rotation Constraint and Lateral Compartment Joint Loading As Compared With the Modified Lemaire Procedure: A Robotic Biomechanical Study
abstract: Background: While current anterolateral complex knee procedures have been demonstrated to reduce anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) graft failures, concerns about potential lateral compartment overload are present. Purpose: To compare lateral compartment pressures and knee laxity between an anterolateral ligament reconstruction (ALLR) using the iliotibial band and the modified Lemaire lateral extra-articular tenodesis (LET) procedure by biomechanically testing for anterior tibial translation, a simulated pivot shift, and internal rotation (IR). Study Design: Controlled laboratory study. Methods: Seven paired cadaveric knees were utilized for this study. A 6 degrees of freedom robotic system was used to measure anterior tibial translation with an 88-N anterior drawer load, IR with a 5-N·m torque, and a simulated pivot-shift test using 5-N·m IR and 10-N·m valgus torques. Force sensors inserted under the lateral meniscus measured lateral compartment pressure during the simulated pivot shift. All specimens were tested in 3 states: intact, anterior cruciate ligament cut, and ACLR. The specimen pairs were then randomized to either an anatomic ALLR technique or a modified Lemaire LET. Results: When compared with the ALLR cohort, the modified Lemaire LET cohort had significantly increased lateral compartment peak pressure at 30° ( P = .047) and significantly decreased IR at all flexion angles (all P < .05). For the modified Lemaire cohort, lateral compartment peak contact pressures were significantly increased versus the intact and ACLR states at 30° of flexion, and IR was significantly decreased as compared with the intact state at 30°, 45°, and 90° during IR testing (all P < .05). For the ALLR cohort specifically, lateral compartment peak contact pressures were not significantly different from intact and ACLR states, and IR was significantly increased relative to the intact state at 30°, 45°, and 60° during IR testing (all P < .05). Conclusions: Lateral compartment peak contact pressure was restored to near intact values with an ALLR using the posterior third of the iliotibial band, while the modified Lemaire LET led to significantly increased pressures. Additionally, the modified Lemaire LET led to decreased IR at all flexion angles, while the ALLR had significantly increased IR between 30° and 60° of flexion. Clinical Relevance: Reconstruction of the anterolateral ligament using the posterior third of the iliotibial band is an option for knees requiring an anterolateral complex procedure. Modified Lemaire LET leads to increased lateral compartment pressures and decreased IR; however, no negative long-term outcomes of overconstraint have been agreed on in the literature.

title: Aperiodic neural activity predicts cortical excitability in TMS-EEG
abstract:
Background

Fluctuating cortical excitability states are inherent to and critical for brain function. They can be probed non-invasively using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) combined with electroencephalography (EEG) by measuring early local TMS-evoked potentials (EL-TEPs). Pre-stimulus periodic neural activity can predict fluctuating excitability states. To what extent aperiodic neural activity represents a marker of cortical excitability has not been explored.

Objectives

We investigated the relationship between pre-stimulus aperiodic and periodic neural activity and EL-TEP amplitude in both the primary motor cortex (M1) and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC).

Methods

Single-pulse TMS was delivered to the left M1 or left DLPFC in 29 and 11 healthy adults, respectively, while EEG was recorded simultaneously. Pre-stimulus EEG was parameterized into aperiodic and periodic components to extract the aperiodic exponent (slope of 1/f-like activity), alpha power (8–13 Hz), and beta power (13–30 Hz). EL-TEP peak-to-peak amplitudes were extracted from approximately 20-65 ms after the TMS pulse.

Results

Aperiodic exponent showed a strong negative relationship with EL-TEP amplitude in both M1 and DLPFC, with steeper 1/f-like slopes associated with smaller EL-TEP amplitudes. Inconsistent relationships were found between alpha and beta power with EL-TEP amplitude across the two regions.

Conclusions

These findings indicate that pre-stimulus aperiodic neural activity influences cortical excitability in both motor and prefrontal areas. Notably, the aperiodic exponent exhibited stronger associations with cortical excitability compared to periodic alpha or beta power. Brain-state-dependent protocols may benefit from real-time extraction of aperiodic exponent as a target feature to improve the precision and efficacy of TMS.

Highlights

Pre-stimulus aperiodic exponent predicts EL-TEP amplitude in M1 and DLPFC. Larger aperiodic exponent is associated with smaller EL-TEP amplitudes. Periodic alpha and beta power do not consistently influence EL-TEP amplitude. Aperiodic exponent may inform brain-state-dependent and closed-loop TMS.
authors: van Hattem T, Hougland JR, Gogulski J, Gordon PC, Belardinelli P, Ziemann U.

title: AquaMend: Minimal Re-probing and Conditional Rollback for Latent-Belief Failures in Embodied Agents
abstract: Physical changes or sensing errors can invalidate embodied agents' task-relevant beliefs. AquaMend compares re-probing, rollback, and supported continuation on a probe-belief-action graph under an expected-loss objective covering sensing, physical recovery, and uncorrected failures. A joint posterior guides a one-step policy with conditional detection-power screening. The per-belief three-way optimum requires independence, separability, and fully resolving probes; the general policy has no global optimality guarantee. Across 32 paired scenarios in a self-constructed simulation benchmark, AquaMend recovers in 28/32 cases and reduces mean complete loss by 21.6% versus restart. Its paired loss difference from decision-theoretic troubleshooting (DTT) is not statistically significant after Holm correction. Against the all-candidate ablation, online decision time decreases by 12.3% overall but increases by 3.4% in the uncovered late stage.

title: Artificial Intelligence in European Healthcare
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted tools and systems are increasingly being applied and offer substantial potential for innovation across many scientific and societal fields.At the same time, appropriate policy guidance and regulation are crucial to ensure that the benefits of innovation are realised while effectively addressing the risks associated with implementing AI applications.Given this overall challenge of leveraging AI innovations for the benefit of society while simultaneously managing potential risks, AI developments in healthcare and public health bring specific opportunities, questions, and requirements.Therefore, with this report, the European Academies Science Advisory Council (EASAC) and the Federation of European Academies of Medicine (FEAM) aim to present a high-level, accessible overview of the opportunities and risks of AI systems in healthcare and focused recommendations.The intention is to assist European policy-makers -and other policy stakeholders -in promoting responsible innovation by formulating and implementing evidence-based policies, while ensuring appropriate methodological, ethical, security, and regulatory safeguards.The report therefore frames AI in healthcare as both an opportunity and a governance challenge.Its focus is on professional health and public-health uses of AI in Europe, including clinical care, population health, health-system management, and selected policy-relevant parts of medicines development, rather than on every possible consumer or wellness application of AI. Understanding AI systemsFor the purposes of this report, and given that the intended audience includes European Union (EU) policy-makers, we use the definition of an 'AI system' set out in the EU AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 3(1): 'A machine-based system designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy and that may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment, and that, for explicit or implicit objectives, infers, from the input it receives, how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions that can influence physical or virtual environments.'This definition is part of the AI Act, which entered into force on 1 August 2024, with its provisions applying in phases from 2025.It is intended to help determine whether a software system falls under the scope of the AI Act or not.The European Commission (EC) gives non-binding guidelines clarifying how the definition should be applied in practice.The guidelines intend to support developers, providers, and users, including healthcare workers, in understanding whether their systems qualify, and are subject to its rules, as AI systems under the EU AI Act.This definition applies to healthcare; however, there are different regulatory implications from it.Certain healthcare AI systems, including regulated medical-device systems subject to third-party conformity assessment, are classified as highrisk under the AI Act and are consequently subject to stringent safety, accuracy, governance, and oversight requirements (EC 2025).We view this risk-driven definition as essential for balancing regulation (risk mitigation) and innovation (benefit), ensuring that the regulatory approach fosters innovation.For healthcare, the AI Act should be read together with the wider EU legal and regulatory ecosystem, including the Medical Device Regulation, the In Vitro Diagnostic Medical Device Regulation, the General Data Protection Regulation, and the European Health Data Space.The applicable obligations depend on intended use, clinical risk, data use, and whether the system functions as, or forms part of, a regulated medical device. Drivers of change in AI system useAI in healthcare is predicted to increase in application owing to converging drivers such as rising healthcare demand, workforce shortages, digitalisation of health records, and advances in computational power and data analytics.These pressures are prompting a shift towards more data-driven, personalised, and efficient healthcare models.At the same time, policy initiatives across the EU, alongside increased public and private investment, are accelerating AI integration.Together, these trends are reshaping expectations around healthcare delivery, prompting urgent attention to readiness, governance, and equity in implementation.A patient-centred approach should be operational rather than rhetorical.Patient organisations and patient representatives can contribute to priority setting, co-design, validation endpoints, procurement criteria, governance boards, communication materials, and post-deployment feedback.Evaluation should include patient-reported outcomes, patient experience, quality of life, accessibility, and the distribution of benefits and harms across patient groups. Regional/sub-sectoral differences in the use of AI systemsThe use of AI systems varies across Europe and healthcare sectors, reflecting disparities in digital infrastructure, investment capacity, regulatory readiness, and workforce expertise.While some regions and institutions lead in AI adoption, particularly in radiology, pathology, and administrative support, others lag relative to this because of resource constraints or limited technical capabilities.These differences risk deepening existing inequalities in healthcare access and quality.EU-level coordination and targeted support are needed to ensure balanced development and equitable AI integration across all Member States and health system segments.EU-level action should therefore support structured mutual learning across Member States, including identification, comparison, and dissemination of best practices for responsible AI implementation.This is especially important where differences in infrastructure, workforce capacity, data readiness, and procurement expertise risk widening inequalities in access to beneficial AI-enabled care. Current EU policies for AI systemsCurrent EU policies prioritise ethical, trustworthy, and human-centric AI systems, as reflected in initiatives such as the EU AI Act, the European Health Data Space, and Horizon Europe research funding.These frameworks aim to ensure safety, transparency, and equity while promoting innovation.However, gaps remain in harmonising implementation across Member States, aligning health-specific regulations, and addressing sector-specific challenges.Continued policy refinement and cross-sector collaboration are essential to translate these principles into effective, context-sensitive actions within healthcare systems. Policy shifts and integrated frameworks for AI systemsA proactive approach focusing on data protection and privacy, and energy and carbon footprint, is increasingly shaping AI-related policy developments (OECD 2025).To support sustainable and trustworthy AI in healthcare, integrated frameworks are needed that align digital health, environmental, ethical, and industrial strategies.Such coherence will help balance innovation with societal safeguards, ensuring that AI deployment contributes to broader EU goals, including climate neutrality, resilience, and social equity.Harmonised, forward-looking policies are key to managing complexity and fostering responsible AI adoption.Interoperability and sustainability should be treated as implementation conditions, not technical afterthoughts.Procurement, funding, and evaluation frameworks should encourage use of recognised standards such as HL7 (Health Level Seven), FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources), and DICOM (Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine) where relevant, assess cost-effectiveness and opportunity costs, and consider the energy and carbon footprint of compute-intensive AI systems. Urgent key messagesThis report aims to provide recommendations for embedding responsible AI practices into European healthcare, ensuring that AI deployment is managed proactively as part of a sustainable, anticipatory healthcare strategy, rather than merely responding to external factors such as emergencies or market inevitabilities.In the box below, we give the three urgent key messages of this report.1. Responsible AI integration must be proactive, not reactive.AI systems in healthcare should be guided by forward-looking policies that anticipate long-term impacts rather than reacting to crises or market pressures.Embedding responsibility requires early governance, inclusive design, and strategic investment to ensure AI strengthens -not destabilises -health systems.2. Equity and trust are essential for sustainable AI adoption.Without targeted action, AI systems risk widening health disparities and undermining public trust.EU policies must prioritise equitable access, transparency, and community engagement to ensure AI systems support universal healthcare goals and democratic values.3. title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation(TMS) for Autism Spectrum Disorder
abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a complex neurodevelopmental condition characterized by impairments in social communication, repetitive behaviors, sensory processing abnormalities, and variable cognitive deficits. Despite significant advances in behavioral therapies and pharmacological interventions, effective treatments capable of directly modulating dysfunctional neural networks remain limited. Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) has emerged as a promising non-invasive neuromodulation technique that can alter cortical excitability, enhance neuroplasticity, and potentially improve cognitive and behavioral outcomes. Simultaneously, recent developments in Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), Deep Learning (DL), Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), Reinforcement Learning (RL), and Digital Twin technologies have created new opportunities to personalize TMS protocols using multimodal patient data, including structural and functional neuroimaging, electroencephalography (EEG), behavioral assessments, genetic information, and longitudinal clinical outcomes.

title: Atomic cluster expansion potentials for screw dislocations in BCC refractory metals
abstract: Accurate atomistic modeling of screw dislocations in body-centered cubic (BCC) metals remains challenging because their plasticity is governed by complex dislocation glide behavior due to their compact threefold symmetric core structure and a strongly temperature-dependent flow stress induced by the large Peierls barrier. In the context of group 5 (V, Nb, and Ta) and group 6 (Mo and W) refractory metals (RMs), both classical interatomic potentials and some machine-learning potentials consistently fail to reproduce density functional theory (DFT) Peierls barriers and the glide plane. Here, we developed an array of atomic cluster expansion (ACE) potentials for these RMs by extending an existing DFT database. The developed ACE potentials significantly improve the description of screw dislocation properties, showing good agreement with the DFT references for Mo and W and substantial improvement for V, Nb, and Ta. The results show that transferability to screw dislocation behavior depends sensitively on both database composition and element-specific energetics and that achieving a single-humped Peierls barrier alone is not a sufficient validation metric for accurate prediction of dislocation glide. For Nb, Mo, and W, the developed ACE models also enable reliable calculation of kink-pair activation enthalpies, which are well described by both Kocks' law and a line-tension model.
authors: Lei Zhang; Francesco Maresca

title: Attention-Based Surface Representation Learning for Robot State Prediction and Open-Ended Surface Classification
abstract: For ground robots operating in outdoor environments, understanding the properties of the underlying terrain is essential for ensuring reliable operation. In most perception-based studies, this problem is formulated as categorical classification with a fixed number of classes defined during training. We propose an approach that enables new surface classes to be added as trainable vectors, which can subsequently be used to address higher-level tasks. By employing a learning paradigm based on predicting the robot's next state in time and using attention blocks, we improved classification accuracy to 98.56% on the Belyaev-Kushnarev dataset and 94.8% on BorealTC.

title: Author response: Heterogeneity and Ontogeny of Mouse Thymic Macrophages Reveal a Requirement for Csf1r-Expressing Myeloid Cells During Early T Cell Development
abstract: Thymic macrophages (TMs) maintain tissue homeostasis by clearing the large numbers of apoptotic cells generated during T cell development, but how TM heterogeneity relates to their developmental origin and role in thymocyte maturation remains incompletely understood. Using complementary flow-cytometric, single-cell transcriptomic, and genetic approaches, we resolved two major TM populations corresponding to TIMD4+ cortical and CX3CR1+ medullary/cortico-medullary macrophages. TIMD4+ VCAM1+ TMs displayed a prominent efferocytosis and apoptotic-cell-clearance program, whereas TIMD4− VCAM1+ TMs were enriched for antigen-presentation and interferon-response pathways. Fate mapping revealed unequal progenitor contributions to these populations, and CCR2 deficiency selectively reduced TIMD4− VCAM1+ TMs and thymic monocytes, supporting ongoing input from circulating precursors. Exploratory pseudotime analysis further identified a transcriptional continuum from Ly6c2+ Ccr2+ monocytes toward macrophage states. Using MaFIA fetal thymic organ cultures, AP20187-mediated depletion of Csf1r-expressing myeloid cells reduced CD4+CD8+ thymocyte differentiation and produced a coordinated accumulation of DN3 cells, loss of DN4 cells, and reduction in CD27 expression. These convergent changes identify the DN3-to-DN4 transition as a developmental stage that requires an intact Csf1r-expressing myeloid compartment, and establish a functional connection between the thymic myeloid niche and early αβ T cell development. Together, our study refines the phenotypic and developmental organization of mouse TMs and reveals a previously under-appreciated requirement for myeloid-cell support during progression through the β-selection checkpoint.
authors: Helen Wang; Vinothkumar Rajan; Anthony Wong; Slava Epelman; Juan Carlos Zúñiga‐Pflücker

title: Ağız yoluyla endoskopik miyotomide yapay zekâ: Kişiselleştirilmiş miyotomiye, daha güvenli eğitime ve reflü tahminine doğru: AI in POEM
abstract: Peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM) is an established treatment for achalasia and selected spastic esophageal motility disorders, but several aspects of care remain highly operator-dependent. These include early diagnosis, patient selection, procedural planning, myotomy length, intra-procedural safety, training assessment, and prediction of post-procedure reflux. Artificial intelligence (AI) may help address these limitations by integrating endoscopic video, high-resolution manometry, timed barium esophagram, EndoFLIP, clinical variables, procedural data, and follow-up outcomes into more personalized decision-support tools. This narrative review critically examines the evidence for AI across the POEM pathway and distinguishes direct achalasia or POEM evidence from adjacent and conceptual applications. Early AI applications are most likely to emerge in achalasia detection during diagnostic endoscopy, automated motility interpretation, video-based procedural assessment, and prediction of clinical response or post-POEM reflux. More ambitious applications, such as real-time tunnel orientation, vessel recognition, mucosal injury alerts, and personalized myotomy planning, remain largely investigational. Most AI-specific POEM applications remain at an early or conceptual stage and require multicenter validation, standardized outcomes, and careful clinical governance. AI should support, rather than replace, expert judgment, and an AI-derived reflux estimate cannot replace standard follow-up or objective reflux assessment.
authors: MD Ahmed Abdallah Salman; Ahmed Abdallah

title: BIM-Supported green building adoption in the construction industry
abstract: The construction industry is under growing pressure to embrace digital technologies that advance sustainable infrastructure and support the transition toward smart cities. Building Information Modeling (BIM) has emerged as a key enabler of green building practices, yet its adoption across construction organizations remains uneven and the factors shaping this adoption are not fully understood. This study investigates the determinants influencing BIM-supported green building adoption and examines its contribution to smart and sustainable city development. Drawing on the Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework and Diffusion of Innovation (DOI) theory, an integrated model was developed to assess the effects of technological competence, top management support, organizational readiness, external support, environmental sustainability orientation, and relative advantage on BIM-supported green building adoption. Survey data were collected from 389 construction professionals, including architects, engineers, project managers, and BIM coordinators, and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS. The results reveal that technological competence (β = 0.399), top management support (β = 0.378), and relative advantage (β = 0.317) are the strongest drivers of BIM-supported green building adoption, while environmental sustainability orientation, external support, and organizational readiness exert smaller but significant positive effects. More broadly, these determinants of BIM-supported green building adoption are relevant to the wider goal of smart and sustainable city development, given the role of green buildings in enabling data-driven design, lifecycle performance analysis, and environmentally responsible urban decision-making. This study extends technology adoption research by integrating TOE and DOI perspectives within a sustainability-driven construction context offers practical guidance for construction firms and policymakers operating in similar rapidly developing, sustainability-focused markets.
authors: Khaled A. Alrasheed; Abdulaziz Alotaibi; Abdullah O. Baarimah; Aawag Moshen Alawag; Hamad Almujibah; Madhusudhan Bangalore Ramu

title: BOS-TMC Data Set: DFT Properties of 159k Experimentally Characterized Transition Metal Complexes Spanning Multiple Charge and Spin States.
abstract: We present the Boston Open-Shell Transition Metal Complex (BOS-TMC) data set, a set of density functional theory (DFT) properties for 159k experimentally characterized mononuclear transition metal complexes (TMCs) in multiple spin states with a range of formal charges derived from the Cambridge Structural Database (CSD). To curate this set, we carried out an iterative procedure to confidently assign the overall TMC charge. From this information, we then obtained properties in up to three spin states, i.e., low-, intermediate-, and high-spin for 3d metals and low- and intermediate-spin for 4d and 5d metals, depending on compatibility with the metal electron configuration, for a total of 343.8k TMC/spin combinations. At odds with prior sets, we preserved experimental heavy atom coordinates in these structures during optimization. We report all properties using PBE0/def2-TZVP single-point energies for these structures. We introduce a scheme for computing metal-spin-dependent atomization energies, which we report for each TMC. Alongside electronic energies, we report up to seven additional properties, including HOMO and LUMO levels, HOMO-LUMO gap, atomic partial charges, dipole moments, atomization energies, and spin-splitting energies for a total of over 2.9 M TMC-associated properties. For a representative subset of over 10k complexes chosen based on size, we evaluate the sensitivity of computed properties to exchange-correlation (xc) functional choice from a set of 12 xc functionals spanning multiple rungs of "Jacob's ladder," highlighting hotspots of TMC space that have the greatest uncertainty with respect to xc choice. In comparison to prior experimentally derived TMC data sets, BOS-TMC is both larger and more diverse in terms of charge and spin configurations and, as a result, more diverse in its range of properties. This data set is expected to provide a high-fidelity foundation for machine learning model development, DFT benchmarking, and exploration of transition metal chemistry.
authors: Aaron G. Garrison; Jacob Toney; T. P. Nikolaeva; Roland G. St. Michel; Christopher Johannes Stein; Heather J. Kulik

title: BanglaBBQ: A Bias Benchmark for Question Answering in the Bangladeshi Context
abstract: This paper introduces BanglaBBQ, a question-answering bias benchmark designed to capture stereotypes grounded in the Bangladeshi context, in both Bangla and English. Following KoBBQ and PakBBQ, BanglaBBQ adapts the original Bias Benchmark for Question Answering (BBQ) by classifying its templates into three groups: directly translated (DT), modified to align target groups or contexts with Bangladesh (TM), and removed when deemed unsuitable for the Bangladeshi context (SR). This process retains 140 templates across six categories, comprising 76 DT and 64 TM templates. Five newly authored (NA) categories, based on stereotypes common in Bangladeshi society, are then added: marital status, age and political perception, regional origin, educational background, and mental-health status. Native Bangladeshi annotators judged all 466 newly authored templates, and 372 were retained because a strict majority of English annotators identified the intended target and rated the attitude as common enough. Each newly authored template is linked to a documented source and a verbatim quote from it. Each evaluated template also has a counter-stereotypical version of its disambiguated context. The dataset was evaluated using two open-weight models (Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B) and two closed models (GPT-4.1-mini and Gemini 2.5 Flash). All four lean towards the stereotyped person when the context is ambiguous, in both languages, and the effect of language differs by model, so English results do not predict behaviour in Bangla. On the adapted BBQ templates, both Qwen3 models are also less accurate when the context contradicts a stereotype than when it confirms it. On the newly authored templates, the closed models follow counter-stereotypical evidence almost perfectly, and all four models are more biased on the templates that annotators validated than on those they rejected.
