title: Effectiveness of the SEFT teaching model on the clinical practice competence of surgical residents: a retrospective cohort study
abstract: Background This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of the SEFT teaching model in improving surgical residents’ clinical practice competencies, so as to provide a basis for optimizing training strategies.Methods This single-center, non-randomized retrospective cohort study included 38 residents. The 2019 cohort (n = 19) was the control group, receiving traditional demonstration and practice-based training, while the 2020 cohort (n = 19) was the intervention group, trained via the SEFT teaching model. Scores across five core competencies were compared using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test.Results The intervention group scored significantly higher than the control group across all five assessment domains (all p < 0.05): medical history taking (90.43 ± 3.83 vs. 84.29 ± 10.63, p = 0.039), physical examination (91.20 ± 4.88 vs. 83.76 ± 11.51, p = 0.017), initial medical record documentation (90.61 ± 4.98 vs. 84.20 ± 4.97, p < 0.001), and clinical reasoning and decision-making (87.00 ± 3.64 vs. 80.76 ± 9.24, p = 0.039).Discussion The SEFT teaching model, with its closed-loop structure and targeted feedback, showed promising potential to enhance surgical residents’ clinical practice competencies.
authors: Xiang Jin; Weihong Zhao; Xinye Lin; Xiaomei Xie; Xinli Mao; 李卫林

title: Effects of Different Numbers of Stimulations in Single-Session Radial Extracorporeal Shock Wave Therapy on Spasticity Improvement in Individuals With Subacute Hemiparetic Stroke: Protocol for a Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial
abstract: BACKGROUND: Radial extracorporeal shock wave therapy (rESWT) improves lower-limb spasticity after stroke. However, the efficacy of rESWT in individuals with hemiparetic stroke in the subacute phase, in whom neural components of spasticity are thought to predominate, has not been sufficiently investigated. In addition, the effects of different numbers of stimulations on the magnitude and duration of spasticity improvement remain unclear. OBJECTIVE: We aim to explore the effects of different numbers of stimulations during a single rESWT session on lower-limb spasticity in individuals with subacute stroke and assess the feasibility and safety of the evaluation and treatment procedures for future large-scale trials. METHODS: This single-center, open-label pilot randomized controlled trial will enroll 24 individuals with subacute stroke and spasticity who will be randomly assigned to either the rESWT 3000- or 6000-stimulation group for 1 treatment at the triceps surae muscle, with stimulation applied at 3 locations: the medial and lateral heads of the gastrocnemius muscle and the triceps surae muscle-Achilles tendon junction. The stimulation intensity will be the maximum intensity tolerated by the individual (≤3.0 bar), with a 10-Hz fixed frequency. Evaluations will be performed the day before treatment; immediately before and after completion of treatment; at 1 and 8 hours after treatment; and at 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, and 14 days after treatment. The primary clinical outcome is the intergroup difference in the Modified Ashworth Scale score of the triceps surae immediately after completion of treatment. Secondary clinical outcomes include intergroup differences in Modified Ashworth Scale scores at 1 and 8 hours and on days 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, and 14 after treatment, as well as intragroup differences from baseline to each evaluation point. Additional measures include the range of motion, angle of catch, tendon reflexes, and clonus scores. Feasibility will be assessed using the recruitment, enrollment, adherence, and retention rates. Safety will be assessed by recording the occurrence of serious and treatment-related adverse events. RESULTS: This study was approved by the Fujita Health University Institutional Review Board on September 26, 2024 (CR24-033). Participant enrollment commenced on November 19, 2024. By November 25, 2025, a total of 14 participants had been enrolled. Data analysis has not commenced, and the results will be reported in a separate article in 2026. CONCLUSIONS: This exploratory dose comparison pilot study is designed to explore whether the number of stimulations delivered during a single rESWT session influences the extent of short-term improvement in spasticity following subacute hemiparetic stroke and obtain preliminary clinical outcomes and feasibility and safety data for future large-scale trials. title: Effects of QEEG-guided low-intensity transcranial magnetic stimulation on executive network function in an athlete with chronic traumatic brain injury
abstract: Abstract Background Traumatic brain injury (TBI) can cause persistent executive dysfunction, critically affecting athletes’ cognitive control and decision-making. Personalized neuromodulation, guided by quantitative electroencephalography (QEEG), may enhance network function. Methods In this case study, a 33-year-old male athlete with chronic TBI underwent a 12-session individualized low-intensity transcranial magnetic stimulation (Li-TMS) protocol guided by quantitative electroencephalography (QEEG). Stimulation targeted Pz, F4, and F3 using sequential low-delta, infra-low frequency, and sensorimotor rhythm protocols. Resting-state QEEG was recorded before and after the intervention. Results Post-intervention QEEG showed reduced slow-wave activity and normalization of alpha, beta, and sensorimotor rhythm oscillations in frontal and central regions. Connectivity analyses revealed improved intra- and inter-hemispheric organization and enhanced functional integration within executive control networks. Conclusions This case provides preliminary evidence that individualized, QEEG-guided low-intensity TMS may support restoration of executive network organization in chronic TBI. The findings highlight the potential of precision neuromodulation as a targeted rehabilitation strategy for athletes with persistent cognitive impairment.
authors: Ali Nasiri; Mahboubeh Ghayour Najafabadi; Mina Amirian Jahromi

title: Effects of robotic walking on bone and muscle health in youth with neuromotor impairments: a five-participant case series
abstract: Introduction/Background Bone and muscle health is a significant concern among individuals with neuromotor impairments, especially those with the greatest functional limitations. This case series presents the bone and muscle adaptations in response to 13 to 14 weeks of robotic walking in children and adolescents with neuromotor impairments. Methods To ensure that the intervention targeted functionally meaningful outcomes, the Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM) was used to capture family-centered goals and motivations for participating in robotic walking. Peripheral quantitative computed tomography (pQCT) scans of the tibia assessed bone and muscle health at three locations: the 3% (trabecular bone), 38% (cortical bone), and 66% (muscle) of tibia length. Scans were acquired before and following robotic walking in five participants with the greatest functional limitations [Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS) levels III -V and Functional Assessment Questionnaire (FAQ): Functional Walking Scale levels 1 -5; aged 4 -12 years]. Bone and muscle outcomes were converted to age-, sex-, and ethnicity-matched Z -scores relative to a typically developing population, and the change in pre- and post-intervention Z -scores was assessed. The least significant change (LSC) was calculated for each participant in bone parameter units, and a clinically relevant change was defined as one that exceeded both the LSC and the expected growth from available reference data. Results In some participants, clinically relevant improvements were observed in trabecular bone mineral density (BMD) (three participants), total bone mineral content (one participant), and cortical BMD (one participant) following robotic walking, suggesting promising bone adaptations. Conclusions Results underscore the need for larger longitudinal studies to explore the impacts of robotic walking across various GMFCS and FAQ levels.
authors: Erin Hodgson; Jessica L. Youngblood; Christa M. Diot; Benjamin M. Norman; Leigh Gabel; Elizabeth G. Condliffe

title: Electromyography biofeedback therapy for spinal cord injury rehabilitation: a systematic review
abstract: Background Electromyographic biofeedback (EMG-BF) is being increasingly used as an adjunct to rehabilitation after spinal cord injury (SCI), but the available evidence is limited by the small sample size, heterogeneous comparators, and variable outcome reporting. We aimed to systematically identify and narratively synthesize the evidence on the effects of EMG-BF in SCI rehabilitation. Methods We searched the PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, CNKI, Wanfang, VIP and other databases from inception to 8 January 2026. Two reviewers independently screened records, extracted data and assessed the risk of bias using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool. Because of substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity and inconsistent outcome-data types, we did not pool effect estimates; instead, we performed a structured synthesis without meta-analysis (SWiM) and graded the certainty of evidence using GRADE. Results Ten randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 537 participants were included. All 10 studies reported a favorable direction of effect for EMG-BF, but the evidence for every outcome was of low or very low certainty. Across the five RCTs reporting surface electromyography (sEMG), all reported larger signal amplitudes in the EMG-BF arm, although the outcome data types varied (means vs. medians) and the muscle sites and comparators differed. Two RCTs reported greater lower-limb muscle strength with EMG-BF. One RCT reported a higher functional independence measure score, and two reported higher ASIA motor scores with the use of the EMG-BF. Four RCTs reported reduced spasticity (modified Ashworth scale, MAS), but MAS was reported inconsistently as ordinal grade distributions or as grade-derived scores, precluding any pooled estimate. Three RCTs reported higher Berg balance scale scores with the use of the EMG-BF. Only one pilot RCT reported pain, and it permitted only within-group comparisons. Conclusion Low- to very-low-certainty evidence suggests that EMG-BF may improve sEMG signals, lower-limb muscle strength, functional independence, ASIA motor scores, spasticity and balance in patients with SCI, but these findings are preliminary. Large, well-designed RCTs with allocation concealment, blinding of outcome assessors, standardized comparators and prospective registration are needed. Systematic review registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261282923 , Identifier: [CRD420261282923].
authors: Mingwei Liu; Zhong-yuan Liu; Bing-can Zhang; Shu-ji Gao; Hui-de Peng

title: Elevated Levels of Blood Neurofilament Light Chain in Substance‐Using Populations: A Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis
abstract: Substance-use disorders are increasingly linked to structural and functional brain alterations consistent with neuroaxonal injury. Neurofilament light chain (NfL) is a sensitive blood-based marker of axonal damage, but evidence in substance-using populations remains fragmented. We systematically reviewed and meta-analyzed blood NfL levels in individuals who use psychoactive substances compared with controls. This PRISMA-guided systematic review and meta-analysis was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251270728). MEDLINE, PubMed, Embase, and Scopus were searched from inception through August 23, 2026, without language or publication-date restrictions. Eligible observational studies measured blood NfL in plasma, serum, or whole blood among individuals with psychoactive substance use and controls. Effect sizes were calculated as geometric mean ratios (GMRs). Multilevel random-effects models accounted for correlated comparisons within studies, and meta-regression explored demographic, clinical, and methodological moderators. Eleven studies comprising 16 comparisons were included. Overall, individuals who use substances had significantly higher blood NfL levels than controls (GMR = 1.81, 95% CI: 1.49-2.20). Alcohol-specific analyses showed a larger pooled effect (GMR = 2.09, 95% CI: 1.62-2.70). In studies restricted to SIMOA assays, the association remained significant, although attenuated (GMR = 1.64, 95% CI: 1.41-1.91). Meta-regression indicated that higher male representation was associated with larger effect sizes, while most clinical and methodological moderators were nonsignificant. Graphical diagnostics did not suggest marked publication bias. Overall, substance use was associated with higher circulating NfL, a non-specific signal consistent with increased neurobiological burden but not sufficient on its own to establish the presence, anatomical source, or cause of neuroaxonal injury.
authors: Joao Antônio Leal; Thiago Wendt Viola; Rodrigo Grassi‐Oliveira

title: Emotional Intelligence, Personality, Resiliency, and Stress: Basis for Soft Skills Extension Program
abstract: This study intends to examine the emotional intelligence, personality traits, resilience, and stress levels of teachers in the Department of Education (DepEd) Bataan, Dinalupihan West District since educators serve as essential architects in developing the minds of future generations, making their overall wellness—both personal and professional—fundamental to successful educational outcomes. The study looks at how these factors interact to offer suggestions for improving teachers' capacity to handle the challenges of learning settings. Findings indicate that most teachers have low levels of emotional intelligence, with notable differences found on demographic variables such as sex on personality. According to correlation, personality and resilience have a strong positive link. These findings highlight the importance of targeted interventions that prioritize emotional regulation but need to improve resilience and how to manage stress. To address this, a soft skills enrichment program was developed to bolster teachers' psychosocial abilities, equipping them with the necessary tools to thrive in evolving educational settings and enhance their overall teaching effectiveness.

title: End-Effector Robotic Rehabilitation After Spinal Cord Injury: A Systematic Review of Devices, Operational Characteristics Used, Outcome Measures, and Rehabilitation Effectiveness
abstract: Background: End-effector robotic devices are increasingly used in rehabilitation to retrain neural pathways through repetitive, task-specific exercise. However, the influence of movement kinematic variables remains unclear. This systematic review aimed to; (i) identify end-effector robotic systems used in upper- and lower-limb spinal cord injury rehabilitation, (ii) describe their technical specifications and operational use, and (iii) explore associations between device use characteristics and study outcomes. Methods: A systematic review of five databases was conducted from inception to June 2026. Results: Fifteen studies, ten lower-limb and five upper-limb, met the inclusion criteria. These covered five commercially available lower-limb devices and three upper-limb devices. Most lower-limb studies demonstrated moderate-to-large improvements in balance, ambulation (WISCI-II), walking endurance (6mWT), and independence (SCIM-III). End-effector training produced comparable outcomes to both conventional therapy and exoskeleton-based rehabilitation in controlled comparisons. Upper-limb studies showed substantial heterogeneity in outcome selection, reflecting diverse rehabilitation goals. Conclusions: WISCI-II and 10MWT were the most used lower-limb functional assessments, with SCIM-III used to assess independence for both upper- and lower-limb motor impairments. Reporting of kinematic settings are often limited and concentrated at study onset, limiting assessment of their contribution to outcomes. Reporting the progression of session-level metrics is needed to better understand how time-varying kinematics affect intervention effectiveness.
authors: Michael Baldock; Silvia Caggiari; Antonio Capozio; David E. Lunn; Frances Gawne; Ioannis Delis; Sarah Louise Astill

title: Enhanced Adaptive Forwarding Strategy to Reduce Processing Time in Vehicular Named Data Networks (V-NDN)
abstract: Vehicular Named Data Networking (V-NDN) enables data-centric communication for intelligent transportation systems; however, high vehicle mobility and dynamic topology frequently degrade forwarding efficiency and increase processing time. This study aims to enhance adaptive forwarding mechanisms to reduce processing latency and unsolicited data in dynamic vehicular environments. The proposed method introduces an Enhanced Adaptive Smoothed RTT-based Forwarding Strategy (E-ASF) that integrates dynamic Interest lifetime control, duplicate suppression, PIT–measurement synchronization, NACK-aware handling, adaptive probing, and context-aware path validation. Performance evaluation is conducted using ndnSIM integrated with NS-3 and SUMO in an urban intersection scenario involving 61 vehicles and two RSUs. Unlike conventional evaluations that focus solely on macro-network metrics, this study applies a device-metric-based analysis framework measuring CS, PIT, and FIB look-up latency, processing latency, hit/miss rates, and overall processing time. The results demonstrate that E-ASF significantly reduces unsolicited data, improves cache hit ratio, minimizes PIT miss occurrences, and achieves a lower average processing time compared with Best-route, Multicast-VANET, and ASF strategies. The novelty of this work lies in combining an enhanced adaptive forwarding mechanism with a detailed device-level metric evaluation framework, providing deeper insight into internal forwarding efficiency and establishing a more reliable strategy for highly dynamic V-NDN environments.

title: Evaluating longitudinal speed control dynamics approaching work zones: the impact of visual–auditory interventions
abstract: Introduction: Current safety evaluations of highway work zones often focus on cross-sectional speed compliance, overlooking continuous deceleration dynamics. This study evaluates how multimodal warnings combining visual markings and auditory alerts affect spatial deceleration behaviors. Methods: Using a driving simulator, continuous vehicle trajectories were analyzed using a linear mixed-effects model with spatial interaction terms to account for individual driving habits and examine the effects of different warning interventions. Results: The results show that physical barricades and mandatory speed limits largely determine maximum deceleration and absolute speed reduction, regardless of warning type. However, multimodal warnings significantly smooth the microscopic deceleration process. By extending reaction times, they reduce panic hard braking and lower peak negative jerk. Furthermore, while isolated auditory alerts are subject to driver adaptation in far-field zones, multimodal combinations effectively counteract driver laxity in high-workload bottleneck segments, reducing the trajectory speeding exposure rate to 39.9%. Discussion: These findings indicate that multimodal warnings enhance safety primarily by smoothing longitudinal driving trajectories rather than altering absolute braking limits, providing quantitative evidence for spatially differentiated warning layouts.

title: Evaluating the iliotibial band as a biological internal brace in ACL repair surgery: a finite element analysis study
abstract: Introduction: The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) is essential for knee stability but has limited regeneration ability due to low cell density and poor vascularization. Current ACL repair and augmentation approaches aim to preserve native tissue and provide early mechanical stability; however, challenges remain, including variable healing, risk of retear, and inconsistent clinical outcomes. A promising alternative is biological reinforcement using the iliotibial (IT) band, which may provide structural support and biological advantages while permitting a smaller graft harvest and tunnel size. This study evaluates IT band graft biomechanics in ACL repair using finite element analysis (FEA), focusing on graft thickness and tunnel-diameter compatibility. Methods: FE models simulated 10 mm wide IT band grafts of three thicknesses (1, 1.5, 2 mm) in femoral and tibial tunnels of 5, 6, and 7 mm. Knee anatomy was derived from CT data and processed in Blender, Gmsh, and FEBio. Bones were modeled as rigid, cartilage as hyperelastic Mooney-Rivlin, menisci as orthotropic Fung, and ligaments/grafts as fiber-reinforced hyperelastic materials. Contact included tied and sliding elastic formulations. The tibia was fully constrained in all six degrees of freedom, while femoral rotation was prescribed to achieve 30° of knee flexion. This position was maintained as a 100 N posterior femoral force was progressively applied. Von Mises stress and effective Lagrange strain distributions were analyzed to assess graft-tunnel compatibility. Results: Stress and strain increased when thicker grafts were paired with smaller tunnels. The 2 mm graft in a 5 mm tunnel showed peak stress of 11.62 MPa and strain of 2.5%. However, the 1.5-mm graft-6-mm tunnel configuration exhibited a lower maximum effective Lagrange strain of approximately 1.1%, a maximum principal stress of 5.69 MPa, and AP laxity of 3.5 mm, which was close to the intact-knee value of 3.2 mm. Larger tunnels consistently reduced stress and strain for all graft sizes. Peak stress and strain were localized near the femoral tunnel, identifying the region where graft stress and strain were highest. Discussion: FE analysis shows graft-tunnel mismatch compromises ACL repair mechanics. The 1.5-mm IT band graft with a 6-mm tunnel showed comparatively low graft stress and strain while maintaining AP laxity close to the intact-knee value. Tunnel diameter strongly influenced graft stress and strain, with smaller tunnels generally producing higher values. Limitation: A single patient-specific FE model was used, which may not capture anatomical variability. These findings provide computational support for further evaluation of the IT band as a biological internal brace and may inform future graft-selection and tunnel-sizing strategies in ACL repair.

title: Evaluation of high-dose alerts in computed tomography using an automated dose monitoring system: a retrospective institutional study
abstract: Radiation dose monitoring software (DMS) tools are increasingly used to support automated monitoring of radiation dose in medical imaging. This study evaluated the frequency and causes of high-dose events detected by a DMS in computed tomography (CT). All CT examinations performed at one hospital across three CT scanners over a one-year period were retrospectively analysed to establish the frequency and causes of high-dose alerts. Descriptive statistics summarized alert frequency and distribution, and multivariable logistic regression identified factors independently associated with high-dose alerts. Of 11,865 CT examinations, 851 (7%) exceeded predefined dose thresholds. High-dose alerts occurred most frequently in spine (17%), musculoskeletal joint (14%), abdomen/pelvis (8%), vascular angiography (8%), chest/lung (5%), and head/face (4%) examinations. Reasons for high-dose alerts included high body mass index (29%), scan repetition (25%), additional scans (15%), patient malpositioning (12%), excess scan range (11%), and orthopaedic hardware (6%). Multivariable analysis showed that overweight status, scanner model, spine and joint examinations, and patients aged 45-74 years were independently associated with high-dose alert occurrence (P < .05). DMS is an effective tool that enables imaging facilities to automatically identify high-dose events, facilitating investigation of their causes, protocol review, and identification of opportunities for dose optimisation.

title: Excitation-Inhibition Balance and Fronto-Limbic Connectivity Distinguish TMS Treatment Outcomes in Refractory Depression
abstract: BACKGROUND: Intermittent theta burst stimulation (iTBS) targeting the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) is effective for treatment-resistant depression, but outcomes remain variable. The neurophysiological mechanisms underlying response remain poorly understood, limiting precision neuromodulation. METHODS: We combined transcranial magnetic stimulation with electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) and connectome-based Jansen-Rit neural mass modeling to investigate the mechanistic basis of treatment efficacy in 90 patients with treatment-resistant depression. Individualized whole-brain models were fitted to pre- and post-iTBS TMS-evoked potentials, yielding subject-specific estimates of synaptic connectivity, excitation-inhibition (E/I) balance, and cortical dynamics. Brain states were defined by singular value decomposition of the model's population activity, and partial least squares analysis with nested cross-validation identified the brain-state pattern distinguishing responders from non-responders. RESULTS: We identified two neurophysiological signatures associated with treatment response. First, responders showed greater post-treatment reductions in 3-10 Hz oscillatory power, driven by shifts in E/I balance toward greater inhibitory control through reduced excitatory drive and increased inhibitory-to-pyramidal connectivity. Second, a pre-treatment brain state characterized by opposite-polarity dynamics between subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC) and left DLPFC distinguished responders from non-responders, consistent with prior fMRI findings on frontolimbic anticorrelation. Neural trajectory analysis further revealed greater dynamical reorganization and increased attractor stability in responders following treatment. CONCLUSIONS: These findings provide a neurophysiologically-informed framework linking iTBS treatment efficacy to specific changes in cortical E/I balance and frontolimbic circuit dynamics, pointing toward candidate markers that, with subject-specific structural connectivity and independent validation, may inform personalized neuromodulation approaches in treatment-resistant depression.

title: Exploring collaborative problem-solving in AI-assisted robotics education
abstract: Prompt engineering (PE) involves creating, improving, and deploying prompts to improve large language model (LLM) performance. Despite its increasing importance, many students lack skills in this area. Although frameworks for prompt design and process exist, theory-based instructional tools for improving prompt engineering skills are uncommon for developing collaborative problem-solving (CPS) skills in Robotics Education. This study adopted a PE strategy in AI-assisted robotics education, particularly for developing CPS. PE has four scaffolding stages: Alignment, Adaptation, Autonomy, and Innovation, and was analysed through four PE codes: Alignment Specification, Adaptive Refinement, Auditing, and Innovation. This study adopted a non-randomised, multi-site, criterion-group comparative design, with 243 undergraduate students categorised according to their ability group. This study used epistemic network analysis (ENA) to identify the co-occurrences of PE and CPS skills and examine the differences in conversation patterns among ability groups. The findings revealed distinct PE–CPS discourse configurations across ability groups. These results underscore the pedagogical value of scaffolding in developing PE skills and fostering students’ productivity in a synergetic learning environment.
authors: Christian Basil Omeh; Elias Oupa Mashile

title: Exploring data sharing through the lens of open data ecosystems in public-private freight logistics
abstract: Background: The freight transport sector is expected to grow, and with sustainability challenges, there is a need for more efficient solutions. Data sharing has been identified as one approach to increase efficiency in the domain of freight logistics by sharing transport-related information within an Open Data Ecosystem (ODE). This enables involved actors to collaborate towards a common goal, supported by a technological platform. Objective: This thesis aims to develop a conceptual, empirical, and design-oriented understanding of data sharing through the lens of ODEs.Within the context of municipal and regional freight logistics, the thesis investigates how data sharing is organized in practice and explores design insights that may support the development of more efficient and sustainable freight logistics through data sharing solutions.Methodology: The research follows a design science research approach consisting of three interconnected studies. The first paper employs a literature review to develop a conceptual understanding of data sharing in ODEs in relation to logistics. The second paper builds on this understanding through a longitudinal multiplecase study of three cases, involving prolonged participation with stakeholders and validation through a workshop. Drawing on the findings from the first two studies, the third study takes initial steps towards the solution domain by exploring design insights and mechanisms from cross-sector domains.Results: The results show that data sharing emerges as a central mechanism within ODEs, but it takes different forms depending on elements such as technical maturity, organizational structure, and governance arrangements. A conceptual model was developed to illustrate platforms, stakeholders, relationships, and roles. The findings identify recurring socio-technical challenges related to interoperability, data quality, governance, procurement, and sensitive data. Building on these findings, we identified design insights and supporting mechanisms that may contribute to the development of more flexible and interoperable data sharing platforms. Conclusion: The thesis contributes a conceptual understanding of data sharing in ODEs, an empirical understanding of data sharing in municipal and regional freight logistics, and initial design-oriented knowledge in the form of design insights and mechanisms. The research progresses from the problem domain towards the solution domain, where the identified design insights provide a foundation for future research concerning the development and evaluation of TMS platforms.
authors: John Larsson

title: Eye Pain in Dejerine-Roussy Syndrome: A Rare Post-Thalamic Stroke Manifestation – A Case Report
abstract: Introduction: Dejerine-Roussy syndrome presents with contralateral neuropathic pain following a thalamic stroke. Previously reported presentations included contralateral upper and lower extremity pain, along with paralysis, spasticity, and other classic post-stroke manifestations. Facial and eye pain following a stroke is infrequent, and previous reports of facial and eye pain following a stroke are limited to brainstem infarctions. Case Presentation: A 69-year-old male patient reported severe right-sided facial and eye pain following a previous left-sided thalamic hemorrhagic stroke. The patient is positive for multiple vasculopathic risk factors and is continuing residual right arm and leg spastic paralysis management. The patient's neuropathic pain is being treated with gabapentin, amitriptyline, trazodone, and ibuprofen. Interestingly, his facial and ocular pain resolved following cataract removal. Conclusion: The location of this patients' stroke, and his unique presentation, highlight a rare ocular manifestation clinicians should be aware of for their stroke patients' and their post-stroke management. Further, the unique resolution of this pain prompts more exploration into neuropathic pain treatment.
authors: Shravya Yarlagadda; Dietlein W.; Sanjana Jaiswal; Elizabeth O. Arogundade; Ben-David G.; Andrew G. Lee

title: FUNCTIONAL ALIGNMENT REDUCES RESIDUAL LATERAL LAXITY AND IMPROVES PATIENT SATISFACTION COMPARED WITH MECHANICAL ALIGNMENT USING A 3° MEDIALLY INCLINED JOINT LINE IMPLANT IN CONSTITUTIONAL VARUS KNEES
abstract: Purpose This study compared postoperative laxity and clinical outcomes between mechanically aligned total knee arthroplasty (MA-TKA) and functional alignment TKA (FA-TKA) using a 3° medially inclined joint line implant in patients with Coronal Plane Alignment of the Knee (CPAK) type 1. Methods This retrospective cohort study included patients with preoperative CPAK type 1 who underwent primary unilateral TKA for osteoarthritis with ≥12 months follow-up. All procedure used an implant with a 3° medially inclined joint line and a bi-cruciate substituting design, performed using manual MA-TKA (2017–2021) or robotic-assisted FA-TKA (2022–2024). Among 155 eligible patients, 44 matched pairs were generated using propensity matching for age, sex, follow-up duration and preoperative Forgotten Joint Score-12 (FJS-12). Radiographic parameters including the arithmetic hip–knee–ankle angle (aHKA) and joint line obliquity (JLO), were measured pre- and postoperatively. Varus–valgus stress radiographs at 1 year quantified medial and lateral joint opening. Patient-reported outcomes included FJS-12, Knee Society Score (KSS), and Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Scores (KOOS). Results At 1 year, lateral opening under varus stress was smaller after FA-TKA (4.8 ± 1.9 vs 6.0 ± 2.1; p =0.03), whereas medial opening under valgus stress did not differ. FA-TKA produced a more varus postoperative aHKA (−2.4 ± 1.8 vs −1.4 ± 2.6; p = 0.03) and required less coronal correction (ΔaHKA: 3.0 ± 2.8 vs 4.6 ± 3.3; p = 0.01). Greater coronal correction correlated with larger lateral opening (r = 0.39; p = 0.0006). FA-TKA demonstrated greater improvement in KSS satisfaction scores (18.9 ± 8.2 vs 15.2 ± 8.3; p = 0.04). FJS-12 scores were higher after FA-TKA; however, not statisticaly significant. Conclusion In CPAK type 1 knees, robotic-assisted FA-TKA better preserved coronal alignment and reduced postoperative lateral laxity compared with manual MA-TKA, resulting in higher patient satisfaction at 1 year.

title: Fear learning–induced brain dynamics predict individual extinction memory expression following transcranial magnetic stimulation
abstract: Abstract Fear learning and extinction unfold as time-dependent processes. Herein, we examined whether fear learning dynamically reorganizes brain activity and whether such reorganization predicts subsequent extinction-memory expression under transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS)-modulated extinction. Eighty-seven healthy adults completed a three-day Pavlovian threat-learning protocol with resting-state fMRI, TMS-modulated extinction, and extinction-memory fMRI. Using coactivation pattern analysis with a hidden Markov model, we identified a fear-learning–induced brain state characterized by increased engagement and transition uncertainty after conditioning. Functional connectivity reorganization within this state predicted individual differences in extinction recall- and renewal-related brain activation under TMS-modulated extinction (cross-validated; recall r = 0.47, p = 0.001; renewal r = 0.37, p = 0.01; permutation-tested), but not natural extinction. In separate brain–behavior correlation analyses, the neural variates identified in the TMS-modulated extinction were associated with behavioral expression. These findings demonstrate that fear learning reshapes brain-state dynamics and identifies a candidate biomarker of neuromodulation-linked extinction-memory expression.

title: Femoral rotation and medial flexion gap tightness in functional alignment robotic total knee arthroplasty for varus knees
abstract: Functional-alignment (FA) robotic total knee arthroplasty (TKA) combines component positioning and soft-tissue management. This study described the association between medial flexion-gap tightness and surgeon-selected femoral rotation, together with release grades and intraoperative gap asymmetry in varus knees. This observational single-surgeon study included the 65 varus knees in an 89-knee database. Medial tightness was defined as lateral minus medial preoperative flexion gap. Correlation and ordinary least-squares regression used 63 complete observations. Recorded preoperative, planned and final trial gaps were analysed with endpoint-specific denominators. An exploratory model considered tibial coronal positioning and posterior slope. Selected rotation was associated with medial tightness (Spearman ρ = 0.571; p < 0.001). The univariable fit was rotation = 1.93° + 0.343°/mm × tightness (R² = 0.257; slope 95% CI, 0.194-0.492). The adjusted slope was 0.296°/mm (95% CI, 0.131-0.460; n = 60). Release was mild in 64/65 and moderate in 1/65 knees. Mean absolute final asymmetry was 0.38 mm in extension and 0.29 mm in flexion. Asymmetry <1 mm occurred in 50/60 (83.3%) and 55/59 (93.2%), respectively; 53/58 (91.4%) met ≤1 mm in both positions. Greater medial flexion tightness was associated with greater selected femoral rotation. Predominantly mild release and small final mean asymmetry accompanied the combined workflow. The equation describes one surgeon's decisions and is not a validated surgical rule. These observations do not establish an independent release-sparing effect, clinical superiority of submillimetre symmetry, patellofemoral safety or long-term benefit.

title: Financial Reporting Quality Determinants in Indonesia's Religious Affairs Ministry: The Moderating Role of Organizational Culture
abstract: Purpose: This study examines the effects of Human Resource Competence (HRC) and Top Management Support (TMS) on Financial Reporting Quality (FRQ), with the moderating role of Organizational Culture (OC) within the Regional Office of the Religious Affairs Ministry of Jambi Province, Indonesia. Methodology: The study involved data collected through a structured questionnaire distributed to 320 financial management officers at the Religious Affairs Ministry of Jambi Province. The data were analyzed using PLS-SEM with SmartPLS software. Results: Empirical evidence demonstrates that HRC and TMS have positive and significant effects on FRQ. Furthermore, OC significantly strengthened the relationship between HRC and FRQ and between TMS and FRQ. Conclusions: The results demonstrate that improving employee competence and strengthening managerial commitment are essential for enhancing the quality of financial reporting. A supportive organizational culture further reinforces the effectiveness of these factors in producing transparent, reliable, and credible financial statements. Limitations: This study is limited to the Religious Affairs Ministry of Jambi Province and examines only two antecedents of financial reporting quality, namely human resource competence and top management support, with organizational culture as the moderating variable. Contributions: Theoretically, this study extends Institutional Theory by positioning organizational culture as an institutional mechanism that strengthens the effects of human resource competence and top management support on financial reporting quality. Practically, the findings suggest that the Religious Affairs Ministry should integrate competency development and managerial support with its five cultural work values to strengthen the quality of financial reporting.

title: From Underuse to Recovery: Intensive Neurorehabilitation of Deforming Spastic Paresis in Resource-Contrasted Settings - A Unified Physiopathological Framework
abstract: Background: Deforming spastic paresis following stroke remains one of the most disabling sequelae of upper motor neuron injury. The pathophysiological cascade - from neural lesion to spastic myopathy through progressive underuse -is well characterised but systematically under-treated, particularly in resource-limited settings where conventional physiotherapy remains sparse and low-intensity. The concept of therapeutic intensity, formalised through the formula I=(R×L×E)/T (repetitions × load × effort / time), provides a pharmacological-like framework for dosing neurorehabilitation. This paper presents a unified physiopathological model of underuse-driven spastic paresis and its reversal through intensive, task-oriented physical therapy, illustrated by two clinical cases treated in contrasted resource environments.Methods: Two male patients (58 and 52 years) with chronic post-stroke hemiparesis (14 and 22 months post-onset respectively) underwent a 12-week intensive neurorehabilitation protocol combining aggressive prolonged stretching, maximum-amplitude alternating movements, a guided self-rehabilitation contract (CAG), and - in the Cameroonian case -the Cogni-Famille task-shifting protocol engaging trained family members. Case 1 was treated at the private physiotherapy practice in Vitry-sur-Seine, France; Case 2 at the Regional Hospital of Bafoussam, Cameroon.Results: Both patients demonstrated clinically significant functional recovery across all measured domains. The Modified Ashworth Scale (wrist flexors) decreased from 3/4 to 1+/4 (Case 1) and from 3/4 to 2/4 (Case 2) at 12 weeks. The E5E retraction index decreased from 0.62 to 0.31 and from 0.74 to 0.41, respectively. Walking perimeter increased from 300 m to 1,800 m (Case 1) and from 80 m to 1,200 m (Case 2). Therapeutic intensity, measured by I=(R×L×E)/T, increased 6-fold in Case 1 and 17-fold in Case 2 relative to prior conventional treatment. Both patients achieved their primary functional goals: partial return to professional activity (France) and full return to farming (Cameroon).Conclusion: Intensive neurorehabilitation - applied consistently, regardless of resource context -can reverse the underuse-driven pathological cascade and achieve functional recovery well beyond conventional expectations. The therapeutic intensity formula operationalises dosing in a replicable, measurable manner. The Low-Tech, High-Sense paradigm demonstrates that human expertise, not technological equipment, is the primary determinant of neuroplastic recovery in post-stroke spastic paresis.

title: Gait disorders in neurological diseases: clinical significance, assessment methods, and rehabilitation potential
abstract: Gait disturbances are a common manifestation of neurological disorders and a major contributor to functional limitations, increased fall risk, and reduced quality of life. Nevertheless, gait impairment often remains underrecognized in routine neurological practice, and its evaluation is frequently confined to basic spatiotemporal parameters, such as gait speed, without sufficient consideration of the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms. The aim of this review was to summarize current evidence regarding the types and mechanisms of gait disorders in neurological diseases, clinical approaches to gait pattern analysis, and contemporary therapeutic strategies. A literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, EMBASE, and The Cochrane Library, focusing on studies examining the clinical characteristics of pathological gait, methods of gait assessment, rehabilitation interventions, and medication-based management of gait disturbances in patients with neurological conditions. The available evidence indicates that different neurological pathologies can result in comparable alterations in fundamental gait parameters, including decreased walking speed and reduced step length. However, detailed gait pattern analysis enables determination of the specific locomotor pattern and facilitates identification of the predominant mechanisms underlying gait impairment, including muscle weakness, spasticity, sensory deficits, impaired motor control, limited joint mobility, and pain. Furthermore, distinguishing primary gait abnormalities from compensatory adaptations is essential for selecting targeted and effective interventions. Optimal functional outcomes are achieved through comprehensive, mechanism-oriented approaches that integrate physical therapy, orthotic management, and oral medication-based or injection-based therapies.
authors: Yuriy Flomin; Anastasiia Orlovska; A.V. Tsyhanii; M.V. Guliaieva; Mykola Romanyshyn; Anastasiia Honchar; I.R. Havryliv; Maksym H. Tsariapkin

title: Gelişmekte Olan Ekonomi KOBİ’lerinde Üretken Yapay Zekâ Entegrasyonu ve Yönetsel Karar Verme Kalitesi: İstanbul’dan PLS-SEM, NCA ve fsQCA ile Bulgular
abstract: Policy across the emerging world presses small and medium-sized enterprises toward generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), yet enthusiasm has run ahead of firm evidence that channeling managerial reasoning through such tools sharpens the decisions firms actually make. The distinction anchoring the analysis is between holding access to GenAI and weaving it substantively into how managers think; the latter, the depth of integration into managerial cognition, is modeled here as the conduit translating enabling conditions into decision quality within emerging-economy SMEs. Responses from 312 owner-managers and senior managers of Istanbul SMEs are examined through an integrated TOE-TAM lens joining PLS-SEM with Necessary Condition Analysis (NCA) and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA). Depth of integration drives decision quality (β = 0.612) and process innovation performance (β = 0.574) alike. Top management support and perceived usefulness behave as necessary conditions, each carrying an empirical floor (42% and 38%) beneath which high decision quality never materializes, while three sufficient configurations reach that outcome by separate routes.
authors: Haldun TURAN

title: Global Burden of Post-Stroke Wrist Extension Weakness Due to Wrist Extensor Muscle Inactivity: Pathophysiology, Functional Implications, and Rehabilitation Challenges- Systematic review.
abstract: Most stroke survivors experience upper-limb dysfunction, making stroke one of the major causes of long-term disability globally.One of the main causes of chronic hand dysfunction and decreased functional independence Wrist extension recovery has gotten less attention than general upper-limb rehabilitation, despite its vital role in regaining grasp, object manipulation, and activities of daily living.This review will thoroughly examine the global burden of post-stroke wrist extension weakness linked to wrist extensor muscle inactivity.The evidence that is currently available indicates that delayed wrist extension recovery results from a complex interaction between neural and musculoskeletal impairments that compromises the selective activation of the wrist extensor muscles.Conventional rehabilitation methods that improve upper-limb function generally include task-oriented training, strengthening exercises, functional electrical stimulation, mirror therapy, robotic-assisted therapy, and biofeedback; however, recovery of specific wrist extensor activity often fails.Additionally, the lack of studies that specifically target wrist extensor muscle inactivity and the variety of rehabilitation protocols impede the development of standardized, evidence-based interventions.Wrist extension weakness following a stroke is still a major but little-known cause of upper-limb impairment.Selective wrist extensor activation and functional recovery may be improved by placing more of an emphasis on impairment-specific rehabilitation, objective evaluation of wrist extensor function, and the incorporation of cutting-edge technologies like wearable electromyography, intelligent biofeedback, and robotic-assisted rehabilitation.
venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

title: Governance of talent management systems and national innovativeness: The moderating role of culture
abstract: This study conceptualizes talent management (TM) systems as a governance mechanism influencing national innovation performance. Building on contextual talent-management research and the Hofstede (1984) cultural framework, the paper examines the association between country-level talent competitiveness and national innovativeness and assesses whether individualism/collectivism changes this relationship (Gallardo-Gallardo et al., 2020; Hofstede, 2011). Using 2022 Global Talent Competitiveness Index (GTCI) and Global Innovation Index (GII) ranking data, together with The Culture Factor Group (2023) (formerly Hofstede Insights) cultural indicators, the study applies simple regression, moderated regression, independent-samples t-tests, and group-specific regression models for 70 countries. The results show a strong positive association between talent-management rankings and innovation rankings, meaning that countries with stronger talent systems tend to occupy better innovation positions. Cultural context differentiates the level and pattern of this relationship: individualist and collectivist groups show statistically significant differences in GTCI, GII, and related components, although interaction effects require cautious interpretation. The study contributes to governance and regulation literature by positioning TM as an institutional and policy-driven system and by highlighting the need for culturally adaptive human-capital and innovation policies.
authors: Д. Б. Жуламанова; Azamat Zhanseitov; Saule Iskendirova; Aliya Daueshova; Ulagat Yussupov

title: Gut and nasal microbiome trajectories shape respiratory disease severity in calves exposed to antibiotic and pathogen challenge
abstract: ABSTRACT Bovine respiratory disease complex (BRDC) is a multifactorial syndrome resulting from interactions among pathogens, host responses, and environmental stressors. However, substantial variation in disease severity persists among animals exposed to similar infectious challenges. To assess the contribution of the respiratory and gut microbiota to BRDC severity, we experimentally inoculated 28 calves with Mycoplasma bovis , bovine coronavirus (BCoV), and influenza D virus (IDV), with half receiving metaphylactic tilmicosin. Clinical trajectories were classified into mild, moderate, and severe phenotypes using unsupervised clustering of longitudinal health scores. Severe BRDC was associated with higher and more persistent nasal IDV loads, yet pathogen burden alone failed to explain the marked inter-individual variability in clinical outcomes. Tilmicosin-treated calves developed substantially milder disease despite comparable pathogen loads, coinciding with lower systemic inflammation, suggesting that host-pathogen interactions, rather than pathogen replication alone, influenced disease severity. Neither nasal nor faecal microbiota diversity consistently explained BRDC severity. However, calves that later developed severe disease displayed a more homogeneous nasal microbiota before infection, indicating that early microbial community structure may influence susceptibility. In contrast, the strongest disease-associated microbial signatures were observed in the faecal microbiota. Gut antibiotic-induced dysbiosis revealed associations between BRDC severity, specific intestinal bacterial taxa, systemic inflammation, and faecal short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) profiles. Notably, Chlamydia was strongly associated with disease severity, while several other taxa were linked to inflammatory biomarkers and SCFA concentrations. Collectively, these findings support a holobiont-driven model of BRDC in which disease severity emerges from interactions among pathogens, host inflammatory responses, and microbiota-associated functions. The stronger associations observed in the intestinal microbiota, along with links between gut bacteria, SCFAs, and disease outcomes, provide evidence for a functional gut-lung axis in calves and highlight microbial metabolism as a potential target for strategies to improve respiratory health and reduce antibiotic use. Implications Bovine respiratory disease is one of the most costly health and welfare problems in cattle production. This study shows that disease severity is not determined only by pathogen infection but is also linked to changes in the gut microbiome and its metabolic activity. Calves with different microbiome profiles developed markedly different clinical outcomes despite similar pathogen exposure. The findings provide new evidence for a gut-lung connection in cattle and identify microbial functions associated with disease resilience. These results may support the development of microbiome-based strategies to improve animal health, reduce production losses, and decrease reliance on antibiotics in livestock systems.
authors: Maverick Monié--Ibanes; Thomas Peyret; Guenaelle Derolez; Marie Corbin; Florence Mompart; David Bars; Fatima Sikht; Christine Citti; Laurent‐Xavier Nouvel; Éric Baranowski; Gilles Meyer; Mariette Ducatez; Núria Mach

title: Heterogeneity and Ontogeny of Mouse Thymic Macrophages Reveal a Requirement for Csf1r-Expressing Myeloid Cells During Early T Cell Development
abstract: Thymic macrophages (TMs) maintain tissue homeostasis by clearing the large numbers of apoptotic cells generated during T cell development, but how TM heterogeneity relates to their developmental origin and role in thymocyte maturation remains incompletely understood. Using complementary flow-cytometric, single-cell transcriptomic, and genetic approaches, we resolved two major TM populations corresponding to TIMD4+ cortical and CX3CR1+ medullary/cortico-medullary macrophages. TIMD4+ VCAM1+ TMs displayed a prominent efferocytosis and apoptotic-cell-clearance program, whereas TIMD4− VCAM1+ TMs were enriched for antigen-presentation and interferon-response pathways. Fate mapping revealed unequal progenitor contributions to these populations, and CCR2 deficiency selectively reduced TIMD4− VCAM1+ TMs and thymic monocytes, supporting ongoing input from circulating precursors. Exploratory pseudotime analysis further identified a transcriptional continuum from Ly6c2+ Ccr2+ monocytes toward macrophage states. Using MaFIA fetal thymic organ cultures, AP20187-mediated depletion of Csf1r-expressing myeloid cells reduced CD4+CD8+ thymocyte differentiation and produced a coordinated accumulation of DN3 cells, loss of DN4 cells, and reduction in CD27 expression. These convergent changes identify the DN3-to-DN4 transition as a developmental stage that requires an intact Csf1r-expressing myeloid compartment, and establish a functional connection between the thymic myeloid niche and early αβ T cell development. Together, our study refines the phenotypic and developmental organization of mouse TMs and reveals a previously under-appreciated requirement for myeloid-cell support during progression through the β-selection checkpoint.
authors: Helen Wang; Vinothkumar Rajan; Anthony Wong; Slava Epelman; Juan Carlos Zúñiga‐Pflücker

title: Homecage-Like Monitoring Reveals Domain-Specific Rescue of Central SPTAN1 R1098Q Phenotypes by Wild-Type Partner Co-Housing
abstract: Abstract Neurodegenerative disorders manifest with markedly different phenotypes, with motor- and memory impairments dominating both clinical and preclinical phenotyping efforts. However, neurodegeneration in unlikely to be confined to these two functional domains alone, and its broader behavioral consequences, including social alterations remain underexplored. Here, we present a non-invasive, high-content home-cage phenotyping framework to investigate social and exploratory dysfunction in SPTAN1 R1098Q mice, a model of early infantile epileptic encephalopathy (EIEE5). Our pipeline integrates three open-source AI engines: SLEAP.ai for markerless multi-animal pose estimation, DeepOF for automated classification of autonomous and social behaviors, and SAM2 for segmentation and quantification of nest-building material usage. Long-term monitoring revealed that SPTAN1 R1098Q mutants exhibit impaired spatial habituation in mutant-mutant (MUT - MUT) pairs. Mutants also displayed persistent, unreciprocated trailing (following) of cage mates and a pronounced reduction of nest-building behavior alongside. Notably, co-housing with a wild-type littermate (MUT - WT) attenuated mutant hyperactivity and restored more typical rest pattern, suggesting that social context can partially buffer these behavioral abnormalities. By revealing social and exploratory alterations that expand conventional phenotyping, this computational ethology pipeline advances 3R principles while revealing that intrinsic executive state-switching failures in neurodegenerative models can be functionally buffered by social dynamics.
authors: Patrycja Ziuzia; Michał Ślęzak; Arkadiusz Miążek

title: Hubungan Antara Tingkat Spastisitas dengan Kemampuan Motorik Anak Cerebral Palsy Spastik di Pusat Rehabilitasi Harapan Jaya Pematang Siantar
abstract: Spastic cerebral palsy (CP) is a prevalent neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by velocity-dependent muscle hypertonia, which severely hinders motor execution and functional independence in pediatric populations. This study aimed to analyze the correlation between the level of spasticity and gross motor function among children with spastic CP at the Harapan Jaya Rehabilitation Center in Pematang Siantar, Indonesia. A quantitative observational study with a cross-sectional design was conducted involving 33 pediatric patients aged 4–12 years selected through purposive sampling. Spasticity was evaluated using the Modified Ashworth Scale (MAS), while gross motor capacity was classified via the Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS). The cohort was predominantly characterized by spastic quadriplegia (81.8%), elevated spasticity grades (MAS Grade 4: 42.4%; MAS Grade 3: 36.4%), and severe motor limitation (GMFCS Level V: 72.7%). Spearman’s rank correlation test demonstrated a statistically significant, strong positive correlation between spasticity level and gross motor function impairment (r = 0.710, p < 0.001). These findings confirm that higher degrees of muscle hypertonia correlate directly with increased severity of gross motor limitation. This study contributes empirical evidence from a community-based rehabilitation setting, emphasizing the clinical necessity of combining spasticity-reduction strategies with task-specific gross motor functional training to optimize mobility and independence in children with severe spastic CP
authors: Lusianti Simanjuntak; Mustafa Al Haris; Sulaiman

title: Hydration status and repetitive head impacts: neurophysiological responses and functional implications
abstract: Combat sport athletes frequently experience two distinct yet potentially interacting physiological stressors: repetitive head impacts (RHIs) and rapid weight loss through hypo-hydration. While each has been studied independently, limited research has examined their combined neurophysiological consequences. This thesis aimed to investigate how RHIs and hypo-hydration influence neuromuscular and cortical function, using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and motor nerve stimulation (MNS) as assessment tools. An initial survey of over 100 combat sport athletes highlighted widespread engagement in rapid weight loss practices, with many reporting overlapping symptoms of hypo-hydration and concussion. In addition, some athletes reported exacerbation of concussion symptoms after undergoing a weight-cut. A reliability study confirmed that TMS and MNS measures could be used with sufficient precision in ensuring robustness for subsequent investigations. In the first experimental study, exercise and heat-induced hypo-hydration impaired maximal strength and voluntary activation but did not significantly alter corticospinal excitability or inhibition, suggesting preserved central drive under fluid-restricted conditions. In contrast, the following study examined responses to a single sparring session and found significant increases in cortical inhibition and motor thresholds, along with reduced maximal strength and voluntary activation, all of which resolved within 48 hours. A follow-up longitudinal study using instrumented mouthguards revealed that impact magnitude e.g., cumulative angular acceleration predicted the degree of increased cortical inhibition. Finally, a 10-week case series tracked three fighters through their fight camps. Voluntary activation and strength showed the most frequent meaningful changes, and over 200 RHIs were recorded in approximately 35% of their monitored sparring sessions. In summary, repeated head impacts elevated cortical inhibitory activity and central fatigue, while heat-induced hypo-hydration produced a contrasting neurophysiological response. These opposing effects may suggest a complex physiological interplay if they occur concurrently, whereby head-impact-related neural inhibition could disrupt or override compensatory mechanisms associated with fluid loss, potentially increasing vulnerability to injury and impairing athletic performance.
authors: Nasir Uddin
