title: INTRAOPERATIVE ROBOTIC ASSESSMENT OF PATELLAR TRACKING IN TOTAL KNEE ARTHROPLASTY: DOES IT PROVIDE ANY ADDITIONAL BENEFIT?
abstract: Purpose This study aimed to determine the clinical utility of a novel robotic assessment of patellar tracking in TKA. Patellar tracking patterns in osteoarthritic knees were examined to assess the relationship with coronal alignment, as well as investigate correlation of coronal and sagittal tracking of implanted patellae to early patient outcomes. Methods A retrospective analysis was performed on 252 knees that underwent robotic-assisted primary total knee arthroplasty (TKA). Intraoperative patellar tracking was assessed prior to any bone cuts and after trial implantation, using a previously described technique with the CORI robotic system. Preoperative full-length standing radiographs were used to assess coronal alignment parameters, and knees classified according to the CPAK classification. Associations between patellar tracking patterns and radiographic parameters were analyzed. For a smaller subgroup (103 knees) the relationship between coronal and sagittal PF tracking and early (3 month) pain outcomes was analysed. Results The mean age of the cohort was 71.4 ± 7.1 years. Pre-implantation patellar tracking was classified into three patterns: central tracking in 58% (n = 147), lateral tracking in 35% (n = 89), and medial tracking in 7% (n = 16). A significant association was observed between CPAK alignment category and coronal patellar tracking pattern (p = 0.006). Central tracking was more frequently associated with varus alignment, whereas lateral tracking showed a relative predominance in neutral-to-valgus alignment, reflected by lower mLDFA and higher aHKA and mHKA values (p < 0.05). Sagittal tracking analysis post implantation showed higher pain scores in understuffed PFJ, whereas no correlation was found between coronal tracking post implantation and pain scores. Conclusion Three distinct native coronal patellar tracking patterns were identified using robotic intraoperative assessment prior to implantation. Tracking patterns were associated with coronal alignment characteristics and with broad CPAK alignment categories (varus, neutral, valgus), but not with individual CPAK phenotypes. Sagittal but not coronal tracking had correlation to early pain scores. Robotic assessment of patellar tracking needs further study to better understand its utility, but the early experience suggests it provides a more comprehensive analysis of PF dynamics that may help better inform surgical technique and implant design
authors: David A Parker; Takaaki Hiranaki; Andrew Li; Apoorva Praveen Kabra; Jobe G. Shatrov

title: Identifying Neural Source Dynamics from Unknown Local Interventions
abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) records mixtures of brain-source activity. Even with a known anatomical forward model, experiments that excite only part of the source-state space leave the dynamics unidentified, and repetition cannot resolve the ambiguity. We show that unknown local mechanism changes can supply the missing information. We consider linear dynamics among fixed anatomical sources with known source-state initialization patterns. Changing one source's update rule for one transition leaves a rank-one, source-specific signature in subsequent EEG: subtracting matched baseline responses isolates it, and the forward model identifies the source and calibrates its response history. Combining these histories with initialization responses recovers source interactions without baseline reachability and without first identifying the intervention coefficients. We establish sufficient recovery conditions, a direct estimator, and a noise-sensitivity bound conditional on correct source labels. Simulated EEG on anatomy derived from magnetic resonance imaging confirms the information gain: with baseline excitation confined to four of twelve source coordinates, eight unknown changes recover all dynamics in 32/32 systems, whereas baseline realization, baseline regression through an invertible forward model, and changes that leave the tested states unexposed all fail, and explicitly constructed alternative dynamics reproduce every baseline mean. Where baseline information suffices, direct reconstruction is also more reliable than a matched-information spectral estimator. Nonlocal changes and forward-model error limit accuracy even when source labels are correct.
authors: Ayana Mussabayeva; Jiaqi Sun; Anuar Aimoldin; Olivier Oullier; Kun Zhang

title: Immediate cortical responses to transcranial magnetic stimulation of the human motor leg area
abstract: Abstract Background Immediate transcranial evoked potentials (iTEPs) are ultra-early electroencephalographic responses elicited by single-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) of the primary motor cortical hand area (M1-HAND). Their characteristic latency, waveform, and sensitivity to short-interval intracortical inhibition suggest a close relationship to the cortical generators of indirect corticospinal volleys (I-waves). Here, we tested the hypothesis that iTEPs constitute a fundamental physiological response of human motor cortex and therefore generalize across motor representations, including the leg representation (M1-LEG). Methods Single-pulse TMS was delivered over the motor cortical representation of the right tibialis anterior (TA) in 16 healthy volunteers. In a subset of participants (n=10), stimulus–response curves and paired-pulse short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI) measures were obtained. Results TMS of M1-LEG elicited reproducible iTEPs consisting of a slow positive deflection with superimposed high-frequency peaks with topographic maxima in electrodes adjacent to the stimulation site. M1-LEG iTEPs emerged close to active motor threshold and increased in prevalence and amplitude with increasing stimulation intensity. Paired-pulse stimulation produced consistent SICI of the second and third iTEP peaks. M1-LEG stimulation also evoked conventional later TEPs with latencies and polarities closely resembling those recorded after M1-HAND stimulation. Conclusions TMS of the human M1-LEG elicits robust iTEPs that closely resemble those recorded from M1-HAND in their timing, intensity dependence, and sensitivity to intracortical inhibition. These findings indicate that iTEPs are not specific to M1-HAND but reflect a general physiological response of human motor cortex closely linked to corticospinal I-wave generation. This broadens their utility as a non-invasive probe of excitatory and inhibitory circuit dynamics throughout the human motor system. Highlights Single-pulse TMS of the leg motor cortex (M1-LEG) elicits reproducible immediate TMS-evoked potentials (iTEPs). M1-LEG iTEPs emerge near active motor threshold, increase with stimulation intensity, and display selective short-interval intracortical inhibition of late iTEP peaks with paired-pulse TMS. Immediate and later TMS-evoked responses show striking resemblance in leg and hand motor cortex. The shared properties of M1-LEG and M1-HAND iTEPs support iTEPs as a general motor cortex response linked to corticospinal I-wave generation and intracortical inhibition.
authors: Mikkel Malling Beck; Marten Nuyts; Laura Sakalauskaitė; John C. Rothwell; Hartwig Roman Siebner; Lasse Christiansen

title: Impact of hybrid assistive limb on gait ability and quality of life in patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
abstract: Objective Hybrid Assistive Limb (HAL) is a cyborg-type wearable robot that supports gait training based on the wearer’s intended motion. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of HAL treatment on gait ability and quality of life (QoL) in patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Methods Patients with an unsteady gait with the ability to walk ≥10 m with assistance from a caregiver and/or walker were included in this study. Patients underwent nine HAL treatment sessions (20–40 min per session), with no more than one session per day, over a period of at least 4 weeks. Gait ability was evaluated using the distance of the 2-min walk test (2MWT), and the speed (m/s), step length (m/step), and cadence (step/s) of the 10-m walk test. Both tests were performed without HAL assistance. QoL was evaluated using the 36-Item Short Form Health Survey. Results We evaluated 30 patients who completed one course of treatment. To evaluate the effectiveness of HAL, a paired t- test was used for the results of one course. With one course of treatment, the 2MWT improved from 92.27 m (40.46) at baseline to 104.16 m (41.73) ( p < 0.001). Regarding QoL, the mental component summary score was 55.35 (8.27) before HAL treatment, indicating relatively preserved mental QoL. There were no significant changes in QoL before and after treatment. Conclusion Although no curative treatment exists for ALS, HAL treatment may provide short-term improvement in gait ability in patients with ALS. However, no significant changes in QoL were observed after one course of treatment.
authors: Harumi Morioka; Takehisa Hirayama; Mari Shibukawa; Tatsuki Sugisawa; Junpei Nagasawa; Sayori Hanashiro; Junya Ebina; Ryuichi Okamoto; Makiko Ogawa; Ikuko Okuni; Yoshitaka Murakami; Osamu Kano

title: Implementation of RFID Technologies in Logistics and Supply Chain Management
abstract: RFID technology is increasingly used to automate object identification and improve the visibility of warehouse and transportation operations. However, existing studies provide limited sector-specific guidance on selecting appropriate tagging objects, configuring RFID control points, integrating RFID data with warehouse and transportation management systems, and evaluating implementation outcomes in agricultural logistics. This study addresses this gap by developing a phased RFID implementation framework designed for agricultural and warehouse logistics. The research combines an analysis of 20 standards, implementation guidelines, and prior academic studies with an illustrative before-and-after warehouse scenario. The framework covers product-batch and logistics-unit identification, RFID read-zone configuration, integration with WMS, ERP, TMS, and GPS records, employee training, performance measurement, data security, and implementation-cost assessment. The examined scenario compares warehouse inventory operations before and after the introduction of RFID-based identification and automated WMS event recording. In the illustrative scenario, the duration of a warehouse inventory count decreased from 16 hours to 4 hours, representing a 75% reduction. RFID-supported event recording also reduced the need for delayed manual entry of receiving, movement, and shipping data and enabled the automatic verification of tagged logistics units at configured control points. The economic assessment demonstrates that RFID feasibility depends on the selected tagging level, transaction volume, infrastructure and integration costs, tag-replacement requirements, maintenance, exception handling, and the value of measurable operational savings. The study shows that RFID performance depends on the level at which objects are identified, the configuration of read zones, the quality of master data, and the integration of RFID events with warehouse and transportation records. The proposed framework contributes a sector-specific approach that links physical cargo identification, warehouse events, transportation data, documentation, performance measurement, economic assessment, and implementation-risk control.
authors: Krystyna Hulyda
venue: International Journal of Economics and Management Studies

title: Implementing robotic-assisted therapy in stroke rehabilitation: a structured narrative review of evidence and technology adoption barriers in Indonesia
abstract: Introduction Robotic-assisted therapy (RAT) has emerged as a promising intervention for post-stroke recovery; however, its implementation in developing countries such as Indonesia remains limited by economic, technical, and systemic barriers. This structured narrative review summarizes clinical effect reported by systematics review and meta-analyses and examines implementation consideration and potential economic feasibility within the Indonesian healthcare context. Method A structured review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses (2015–2025) was conducted using PubMed, Scopus, PEDro, and Cochrane Library. Studies involving adult with stroke were included. Findings were synthesized narratively because of heterogeneity. Implementation barriers were analyzed, and a scenario-based economic model was developed to assess feasibility of RAT in Indonesia. QALY-equivalent outcomes (QEOs) were estimated using ratio-based value-transfer approach that scaled published reference values according to observed functional effects. Result Evidence from 22 systematic reviews indicated that RAT improved functional outcomes compared with conventional therapy, particularly gait and upper-limb function (effect sizes: 0.02–0.52). Key implementation barriers included limited device availability, inadequate workforce training, and regulatory constraints. Modelled ICERs ranged from US$236.23–752.31 per QEO for upper-limb rehabilitation and US$558.86–4,890 per QEO for gait-related rehabilitation. Most estimates remained below the Indonesian willingness-to-pay threshold ( Conclusion RAT shows potential clinical benefits, but implementation in Indonesia should consider clinical effectiveness, economic feasibility, infrastructure, workforce, technology acceptance, and reimbursement. A phased approach in suitable tertiary-care settings may support wider adoption based on local evidence.
authors: Ezra Bernadus Wijaya; Phyo-Wai Thu; Pao‐Chu Chen

title: Improving undergraduate clinical skills through Generative AI virtual assistants: A pilot study of history taking and physical examination
abstract: Beyond the AI Hype: Evaluating GenAI Virtual Assistants for Undergraduate Clinical Skills Across Kirkpatrick Levels 1 to 3 1. Background & The Educational Problem History-taking and physical examination remain the bedrock of clinical diagnosis, skills developed primarily through experiential practice rather than didactic learning. However, preclinical curricula face chronic structural bottlenecks: students have minimal supervised patient exposure prior to clinical clerkships, while simulated and standardized-patient (SP) encounters demand substantial institutional resources, rooms, trained actors, and faculty time that cannot scale indefinitely. While Generative AI (GenAI) offers scalable, asynchronous simulation, the literature remains saturated with perception-based studies and short-term knowledge recall. Critical questions remain unanswered: Can custom GenAI assistants safely facilitate structured clinical practice? Does performance transfer to authentic human encounters? And crucially, is GenAI truly the active ingredient, or simply an auxiliary tool within structured assessment? 2. The Intervention: Purpose-Built GenAI Assistants We engineered and deployed two specialized, prompt-standardized conversational AI assistants built on Google Gemini (custom Gems) to eliminate instructional variability: Anamnesio : A virtual patient simulating outpatient consultations via free-text dialogue. It remains strictly in character, reveals clinical information only upon structured inquiry, and concludes with automated feedback targeting communication, consultation structure, and diagnostic reasoning. ExplorIA : A Socratic clinical tutor focusing on physical examination. Rather than passively presenting solutions, it introduces diagnostic scenarios where physical findings are pivotal, prompting learners to justify selected maneuvers, interpret signs, and correct procedural reasoning. 3. Study Design & Evaluation Framework We conducted a four-week, multi-phase proof-of-concept study mapped systematically across Kirkpatrick Levels 1 to 3. Participants : Twenty-two third-year medical students (68% women; median age 20) were randomized 1:1, stratified by sex, into sequential training tracks: Group A used Anamnesio only during Weeks 1–2; Group B used ExplorIA only. In Weeks 3–4, all participants accessed both tools concurrently. Assessment Protocol : Students underwent three standardized clinical encounters (Weeks 0, 2, and 4) featuring unseen clinical cases enacted by specialist registrars serving as standardized patients. Objective performance was scored by blinded, trained senior evaluators using validated analytic rubrics (History: 0–9; Physical Examination: 0–7). To isolate independent learning, no human faculty feedback was provided during the intervention period; students received only AI-generated feedback between formal checkpoints. No participants were lost to follow-up) Eight months post-intervention, participants' objective performance was assessed in an authentic hospital clinical practice rotation involving real inpatients, evaluated by clinical faculty entirely blinded to study participation (n=19 vs. n=201 historical/peer controls). 4. Key Findings Kirkpatrick Level 1 (Reaction): Usability and educational acceptability were high: 95.5% found Anamnesio easy to use (81.8% for ExplorIA), and 86.4% reported subjective skill improvement. Crucially, students demonstrated sophisticated pedagogical discernment: 90.9% viewed GenAI as complementary to existing curricular resources, and only 22.7% believed AI could replace real human interactions (63.6% actively disagreed). Kirkpatrick Level 2 (Learning): Objective standardized scores demonstrated statistically significant, large effect-size gains from Week 0 to Week 4: History Taking: Mean baseline increased from 3.0 to 7.0/9 (+4.0 points [95% CI 3.3–4.7], p < 0.001, Hedges' g = 1.5). Physical Examination: Mean baseline increased from 3.3 to 5.5/7 (+2.2 points [95% CI 1.7–2.8], p < 0.001, Hedges' g = 1.3). Kirkpatrick Level 3 (Behavior & Clinical Transfer): In the 8-month follow-up clinical clerkship with real inpatients, participants demonstrated significantly higher median performance than non-participants (9.25 [IQR 9.0–9.5] vs. 9.00 [IQR 8.7–9.5], p = 0.042). Crucially, the primary effect was an elimination of the performance floor: 100% of participants achieved grades > 9.0, whereas non-participant scores ranged widely from 6.0 to 10.0. 5. Critical Nuance: What the Data Actually Reveal In contrast to uncritical portrayals of GenAI in education, our granular analyses challenge AI-centric causation: 1. Absence of Sequence Effect : The initial two-week single-assistant phase yielded no domain-specific advantage; between-group scores did not differ at Week 2 or Week 4. 2. Absence of a Clear Dose-Response Curve: Cumulative usage hours did not correlate with history-taking improvement ($p = 0.729), and physical examination correlated only weakly (\rho = 0.438, p = 0.042), dissolving at subdomain levels. Total platform exposure was remarkably modest (median 3.5 hours for Anamnesio, 2.0 hours for ExplorIA). 3. Rival Explanations :Given the lack of a non-intervention control arm, the observed gains cannot be attributed strictly to GenAI. Instead, the data strongly support programmatic assessment principles: the dominant driver appears to be the *synergistic triad* of autonomous GenAI practice, repeated authentic standardized-patient encounters (testing effect), and rapid-cycle feedback. Furthermore, participant self-selection likely contributed to baseline academic resilience. 6. Curricular Implications: The Tripartite Hybrid Model These findings argue decisively against positioning GenAI as an autonomous replacement for clinical teaching. Instead, we advocate a pragmatic three-tier implementation framework: 1. Asynchronous GenAI Practice: Low-stakes, 24/7 repetitive practice for cognitive framing, communication structure, and procedural justification without patient burden. 2. Standardized Patient Encounters : High-fidelity simulation introducing social realism, non-verbal nuance, and emotional pressure that digital interfaces cannot replicate. 3. Faculty-Led Debriefing : Expert human calibration to contextualize AI feedback, model professional behavior, and prevent diagnostic ossification. Open Science Note: Anonymized participant-level dataset available at DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21207512.
authors: Luís Corral-Gudino; Candela Campo-Martínez; Isabel Herrera Montano; Cecilia Bombin-Escribano; José Pablo Miramontes‐González; Isabel DE LA TORRE-DÍEZ

title: In Vivo Validation of Automated Knee Arthrometry: What Do These Measurements Really Represent?
abstract: Background: Objective assessment of anterior knee laxity (AKL) is important for evaluating graft integrity after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction. Automated arthrometers, such as the GNRB, provide reproducible measurements; however, the in vivo biomechanical meaning and validity of these measurements remain unclear. Hypothesis/Purpose: The primary purpose was to validate GNRB-derived AKL measurements against biplanar videoradiography (BVR)–derived metrics under in vivo postoperative conditions. It was hypothesized that GNRB measurements would differ significantly from BVR-derived measures of tibiofemoral translation and ACL graft elongation. A secondary, exploratory purpose was to examine the relationships between GNRB- and BVR-derived laxity measures. Study Design: Cohort study (Diagnosis); Level of evidence, 2. Methods: Twenty patients (6 months post-ACL reconstruction) underwent simultaneous AKL testing using a GNRB arthrometer and BVR. Six BVR-derived laxity metrics were calculated, including tibiofemoral translation, tibial tuberosity displacement, and ACL graft elongation. Arthrometer accuracy was assessed using a repeated-measures analysis of covariance, and linear regression analyses were used to evaluate relationships between GNRB- and BVR-derived measures. Results: GNRB-derived laxity differed significantly from all BVR-derived measures ( P < .001). Compared with BVR-defined tibiofemoral and graft-based metrics, the GNRB consistently overestimated AKL (bias: 3.4-6.1 mm). The strongest relationship to GNRB was observed in BVR-derived tibial tuberosity displacement expressed in the world coordinate system ( r = 0.93), whereas associations with ACL graft elongation were weakest ( r = 0.51-0.66). Differences between tibial tuberosity displacement expressed relative to the femur versus the world coordinate system indicated a substantial contribution of femoral motion during arthrometric testing. Conclusion: This study provides the first in vivo validation of GNRB-derived AKL measurements following ACL reconstruction. Using BVR as the reference standard, the GNRB consistently overestimated AKL and showed the weakest correlation with ACL graft elongation. These findings highlight the need to better understand how arthrometry relates to knee motion and ACL graft elongation to improve the reliability and clinical interpretation of postoperative AKL assessments.
authors: Tomasz Bugajski; Alonso Figueroa; Bonnie P. Gregory; Walter Richard Lowe; Payam Zandiyeh

title: In silico-guided design, synthesis and in vitro evaluation of thiazolo-pyridines targeting SARS-CoV-2 Nsp13
abstract: In the search for novel antiviral agents targeting SARS-CoV-2 non-structural protein 13 (Nsp13), we applied an integrated in silico drug design workflow combining ADME profiling, molecular interaction field analysis, molecular docking and thermodynamic evaluations to identify thiazolo-pyridine derivatives as promising scaffolds. This computational strategy enabled the rational prioritization of compounds and guided the design and synthesis of a novel series of [1,3]thiazolo[5,4- b ]pyridine-6-carboxamides ( 19 and 20 ) and [1,3]thiazolo[5,4- h ][1,6]naphthyridines ( 21 and 22 ). Among the synthesized compounds, 19h and 19n emerged as the most potent candidates, demonstrating dual inhibitory activity with IC 50 values for unwinding and ATPase activities in the low micromolar range. Kinetic analyses confirmed a competitive inhibition mechanism, as these compounds successfully compete with the natural substrate ATP for the enzyme’s active site. Overall, our findings highlight the effectiveness of integrated computational approaches for accelerating antiviral lead optimization and establish the thiazolo-pyridine core as viable chemotype for further Structure-Activity Relationship (SAR) studies and preclinical development.

title: Induction of interhemispheric visual plasticity by paired associative stimulation
abstract: ABSTRACT Unveiling the plastic mechanisms of the primary visual cortex (V1) is crucial for understanding how visual processing can change and adapt, ultimately informing interventions to promote functional recovery following visual system damage. Paired associative stimulation (PAS) protocols can induce associative plasticity within the human V1. However, previous paradigms used full-field visual stimulation, engaging both hemispheres simultaneously, leaving unclear whether plasticity can be selectively targeted to a single visual pathway and whether it can modulate the non-stimulated hemisphere. Across three experiments in healthy participants, we investigated the neurophysiological, behavioural, and interhemispheric outcomes of a novel lateralized visual PAS protocol (vPAS). Pattern-reversal checkerboards were presented in a single visual hemifield and time-locked to transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) pulses delivered over the contralateral V1. Experiment 1 assessed neurophysiological effects by recording hemifield-lateralized visual-evoked potentials (VEPs) and testing three inter-stimulus intervals (ISIs: 75, 100, and 125 ms) between vPAS-paired stimuli. Experiment 2 evaluated perceptual changes in contrast detection, while Experiment 3 examined vPAS hemispheric specificity and aftereffects on interhemispheric visuomotor transfer. Only the 75-ms ISI consistently modulated visual processing in the non-conditioned hemisphere, reducing N75 amplitude and improving contrast detection for visual stimuli presented contralateral to the TMS side. Longer ISIs were not effective. Furthermore, this protocol altered interhemispheric transfer exclusively when the left, but not the right, V1 was targeted during vPAS. In conclusion, lateralized vPAS induces timing-dependent changes beyond the stimulated cortex, suggesting that associative plasticity can engage contralateral visual circuits and modulate visual processing.
authors: Francesca Crespi; Giacomo Guidali; Eleonora Arrigoni; Nadia Bolognini

title: Infant neurodevelopmental impairment detection via large-scale motion screening with generative learning
abstract: Neurodevelopmental impairments like cerebral palsy are prevalent infant developmental problems in clinical infant healthcare. Early detection of these disorders enables timely intervention and better rehabilitation outcomes. Automated, large-scale screening tools remain scarce, and artificial intelligence offers a promising solution by identifying abnormal infant motion patterns. However, developing a data-driven AI system is challenging due to the scarcity of expert-annotated motion records. To address the challenge, this paper proposed a generative pattern learning method, which achieves sensitive detection of abnormal actions through the training paradigm of temporal auto-regression and reconstruction. We trained and validated the AI model DeepAD with more than 1,300 infant motion videos over a period of 5 years (2019-2024) from three children’s hospitals in China, which contain about 50 infants diagnosed with cerebral palsy. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superior performance of DeepAD over baseline methods and equivalent level to clinical experts, indicating its potential for smart screening of neurodevelopmental disorders.
authors: Ning Ma; Hui Wang; Hui Wang; Xuhui Li; Yonglin Yu; Jiajun Bu; Jiajun Bu; Haifeng Li; Haishuai Wang; Haishuai Wang

title: Integral resonant filter-based chattering reduction in switched human-robot interaction with hybrid admittance-adaptive impedance control
abstract: Physical human-robot interaction (pHRI) is a type of interaction that implies that robots should demonstrate dynamic and compliant behavior that is dependent on the interaction environment. A prominent solution is compliant control, which includes either Admittance Control in the case of soft contact or Impedance Control for stiff contact. However, if the nature of the environment is unknown or dynamic, then a hybrid control scheme that switches between the admittance and impedance regimes is adopted. However, switching from admittance to impedance and vice versa results in discontinuity in the control signal. The discontinuity inherent in the abrupt switching mechanism causes high-frequency oscillations (chattering) in the control signal. The effect of this phenomenon is poor performance of the system, mechanical stress, and high energy consumption. To effectively attenuate this chattering and its negative effects, this work proposes an Integral Resonant Control (IRC) command filter, which is incorporated into the switching loop of the hybrid admittance and adaptive impedance control. The IRC filter, normally employed to damp structural vibrations, is designed here to act as a command filter for robust signal smoothing by damping the high-frequency components of the control signal introduced by the switching action. The proposed hybrid controller is compared to a standard hysteresis (dead-zone) chattering mitigation strategy. Comparative simulation results indicate that the proposed filtering technique can reduce the Chattering Index on average by over 76% for both joints of a planar rehabilitation robot while maintaining trajectory tracking accuracy. The results obtained indicate that the proposed switched hybrid control is Lyapunov stable and can be employed to achieve effective, energy-efficient, and compliant robotic rehabilitation in uncertain environments.
authors: Ado Haruna; Auwalu Muhammad Abdullahi; Ronnapee Chaichaowarat

title: Integrated, adaptive decarbonization strategies for last mile delivery
abstract: The aim of this study is to identify and assess the importance of selected decarbonization instruments in shaping integrated, adaptive, and low-emission last-mile delivery strategies, taking into account consumer behavioural determinants. The study utilised a modelling approach, developing a conceptual model integrating regulatory, organisational, and behavioural factors, which was then subjected to preliminary empirical verification. The obtained results indicate that the decarbonization process is nonlinear and systemic, based on interdependencies between the regulatory, strategic, and consumer levels. Regulatory pressure and enterprise adaptation strategies play a key role, significantly determining operational efficiency and the implementation of low-emission solutions, while the influence of behavioural factors remains relatively limited. Consequently, the research hypothesis was partially confirmed, indicating an asymmetry in the interactions between ”top-down” and ”bottom-up” mechanisms. A limitation of the study is the need for further in-depth empirical verification, particularly using operational data and a broader consideration of the demand side. Practical implications include the need to develop integrated adaptation strategies, intensify digitalisation processes, and apply behavioural economics tools to logistics demand management. In the social dimension, the importance of strengthening the role of consumers in the low-carbon transition process is emphasised. The study's originality lies in its integration of systems and behavioural approaches in the analysis of last-mile delivery decarbonization, which significantly complements existing research, which focuses primarily on technological and regulatory aspects.
authors: Urszula Motowidlak

title: International Multi-Centre Validation of Unsupervised Domain Adaptation for Precise Discrimination between Normal and Abnormal Retinal Development
abstract: Arrested retinal development can cause childhood visual impairment, but grading optical coherence tomography scans is difficult to standardise across devices and centres. We developed and evaluated an unsupervised domain adaptation model to classify normal and abnormal retinal development across different OCT systems. This retrospective multicentre study used OCT scans from five centres in four countries and the UK Biobank. Data covered four OCT devices, including table mounted and handheld systems. A ResNet50 based Domain Adversarial Neural Network was trained using labelled images from a source device and unlabelled images from a target device. We evaluated six source to target pairings and compared model performance with seven clinician graders. A separate Heidelberg Spectralis dataset was reserved for external evaluation. Across validation sets, accuracy ranged from 87.75% to 96.06%, sensitivity from 88.68% to 98.38%, and specificity from 78.00% to 98.02%. The best performing model, adapted from TM OCT1 to HH OCT1, achieved 96.06% accuracy and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.994, with a 95% confidence interval from 0.981 to 0.999. Several models also maintained discrimination on the unseen Heidelberg device. Unsupervised domain adaptation enabled OCT classification across devices without labelled target device data. The approach may support more consistent assessment of retinal development and large scale analysis of existing imaging datasets.

title: Invariant-Governed Adaptive Systems: Delayed-Commit Stability and Return Without Erasure
abstract: Abstract This research record presents two related proposed frameworks for invariant-governed adaptive systems: the Morrison Delayed-Commit Stability Principle and RETURN WITHOUT ERASURE — Causal Correction Under Invariant Preservation. The first studies the separation between proposal dynamics and committed-state dynamics. A candidate-generating process may remain exploratory, oscillatory, drifting, or nonconvergent while a distinct governance layer determines which proposed transitions are permitted to enter committed history. Under explicit Lyapunov-descent, admissibility, and invariant-preservation assumptions, the committed trajectory remains non-increasing in the chosen Lyapunov functional, preserves its protected invariant component, and has square-summable accepted increments even when convergence of the proposal process itself is not assumed. This formalizes the distinction PROPOSAL ≠ PERMISSION ≠ COMMIT. The second framework addresses retrospective invalidation. When later evidence establishes that an earlier committed transition was invalid, conventional rollback may discard valid subsequent evolution simply because it occurred later in time. RETURN WITHOUT ERASURE instead introduces a causal dependency relation between commits, removes the invalid commit and its dependency cone, preserves independent surviving commits, and reconstructs a minimally disturbed admissible state subject to exact preservation of a protected invariant. A central open problem is repair confluence: determining conditions under which independent retrospective corrections produce the same repaired state regardless of correction order. Disjoint causal dependency alone may be insufficient where admissibility geometry, invariant constraints, or reconstruction operators couple otherwise independent repairs. Characterising the sufficient and necessary conditions for confluence—and constructing minimal counterexamples where those conditions fail—is therefore identified as a primary research target. Together, the papers investigate a common principle: exploration, authorization, commitment, correction, and invariant preservation can be treated as mathematically distinct operations. The results are presented as proposed mathematical frameworks under active investigation; broader novelty and relationships to supervisory control, runtime assurance, truth-maintenance systems, belief revision, event sourcing, CRDTs, viability theory, and related fields remain subjects for formal comparative review. title: Joint line obliquity change was associated with femoral and tibial resection patterns and smaller final flexion imbalance after robot‐assisted total knee arthroplasty
abstract: Abstract Purpose Associations between preoperative‐to‐post‐operative changes in arithmetic hip–knee–ankle angle (aHKA) and joint line obliquity (JLO) and final balance after robot‐assisted total knee arthroplasty (TKA) were evaluated. Relationships with resection redistribution and tibial‐varus reduction were also examined. Methods A retrospective single‐surgeon series of 402 primary robot‐assisted TKAs was analysed. Preoperative and post‐operative aHKA, JLO and coronal plane alignment of the knee (CPAK) type were determined from full‐length radiographs. Final extension and flexion imbalance and laxity ranges after trial implantation were the primary outcomes. Signed and absolute changes were assessed in multivariable models; resection redistribution and a varus‐only tibial‐boundary subgroup were examined in supportive analyses. Results A change in CPAK type was observed in 300 knees (74.6%), including a JLO‐zone change in 221 (55.0%). Greater ΔJLO was associated with smaller final flexion imbalance (β = −0.060; p < 0.001) and a narrower final extension laxity range ( β = −0.055; p = 0.002). Corresponding associations were found for |ΔJLO| ( β = −0.046; p = 0.018 and β = −0.070; p = 0.004). Neither signed nor absolute aHKA change was associated with final extension or flexion imbalance. In varus knees, tibial‐varus reduction was associated with greater JLO and aHKA changes, coronal femoral adjustment and smaller final flexion imbalance. Neither |ΔaHKA| nor |ΔJLO| was associated with improvement in the Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score for Joint Replacement. Conclusions Greater JLO change was associated with smaller final flexion imbalance and a narrower extension laxity range rather than impaired balance. In varus knees, JLO change accompanied tibial‐varus reduction and coordinated femoral adjustment. JLO change may therefore reflect specific aspects of the final balancing state rather than an unintended deviation from the native phenotype. Level of Evidence Level III, retrospective cohort study.
authors: Yugo Morita; Jonggu Shin; Mohammed El-Hassan; Ittai Shichman; William John Long; Peter Keyes Sculco

title: Knee proprioception in children with spastic cerebral palsy: an observational study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Proprioception, the sense of body position and movement, is vital for motor control but has been sparsely explored in children with cerebral palsy (CP), particularly in the lower extremities. This study explored proprioception as the capacity to reproduce and maintain a knee flexion angle in children with CP. METHODS: Fifty-seven children aged 6-18 years with spastic CP; 20 unilateral (USCP), and 37 bilateral (BSCP), at Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS) I-IV, and 42 typically developing (TD) children participated. Three-dimensional motion analysis was used to capture knee movements during a joint position sense test performed in sitting with occluded vision. The test consisted of (i) the criterion angle (CA) trial; the leg was passively elevated to a knee flexion angle of 45 degrees (CA) by an examiner and the position was maintained by the child, and (ii) the reproduced angle (RA) trial; the angle was actively reproduced (RA) and maintained by the child. Joint position sense errors were evaluated as the difference between CA and RA. The children's capacity to maintain the leg position was measured as the difference in knee angles, fluctuations (root mean square error) and drift (linear regression). Data were analysed with non-parametric statistics. RESULTS: Joint position sense errors were greater in the USCP-group than the BSCP-group (p = 0.037), with a more extended knee in the USCP-group (p = 0.012). When maintaining the passively positioned knee angle for 2.5 s, the CP-group compared to the TD-group, showed increased knee flexion and greater movement fluctuations (p = 0.006). Within-group analysis showed increased knee flexion at the passively assumed position (CA vs. maintained for 2.5 s) compared to at the actively assumed position (RA vs. maintained for 2.5 s) in the BSCP-group (p = 0.015) and the GMFCS II-group (p = 0.028). The BSCP-group also showed increased drift over time towards knee flexion when the leg was passively compared to actively positioned (p = 0.040). CONCLUSIONS: The results reveal a divergence in proprioceptive function: while the USCP-group had greater difficulty than the BSCP-group in reproducing a knee angle, the BSCP-group demonstrated greater difficulty in maintaining the knee position during passive positioning of the lower limb. TRIAL REGISTRATION: This study was observational and was therefore not registered as a clinical trial.
authors: A Ericson; Åsa Bartonek; Israel Luis; Marie Hjelm-Eriksson; Cecilia M. Lidbeck

title: Knowledge Sharing Behavior among Vietnamese Academics: The Dominant Roles of Organizational Culture and Leadership
abstract: Background/ problem: While knowledge sharing is vital for academic innovation and institutional performance, its behavioral determinants in emerging higher education systems remain inconclusive, particularly regarding the assumed facilitating role of information technology (IT). Objective/ purpose: Grounded primarily in social exchange theory, this study investigates the effects of organizational culture, top management support, and personality traits on knowledge sharing behavior among university lecturers, while also examining the moderating role of IT. Design and Methodology: A cross-sectional quantitative survey was administered to 185 academic staff across universities in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. Hypotheses were tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) and multigroup analysis (MGA). Results: The model explains 56.0% of the variance in knowledge sharing behavior (R2 = .56). Organizational culture (β = .42, p < .001, f 2 = .34) and top management support (β = .38, p < .001, f 2 = .32) emerged as dominant drivers with medium-to-large effect sizes. Extraversion exerted a significant positive impact (β = .32, p < .001, f 2 = .20), whereas introversion exhibited a small negative effect (β = -.11, p = .03, f 2 = .03). Conversely, IT had neither a significant direct effect (β = .09, p = .07, f 2 = .02) nor a moderating effect on organizational relationships. MGA revealed no significant gender differences. Conclusion and Implications: Findings demonstrate that knowledge sharing is fundamentally a socially embedded behavioral process. Technological infrastructure cannot substitute for interpersonal trust, collaborative norms, and supportive leadership in fostering academic knowledge exchange.
authors: Bao-Huy Dinh; Ngoc-Thin Chau

title: LIVE-GaitNeuroKids: A multimodal and Longitudinal Gait dataset with Inertial, Video and surface Electromyography in Neuromotor conditions and typically developing children
abstract: Precise characterization of gait patterns is essential for the clinical assessment of motor disorders, such as cerebral palsy (CP) and idiopathic toe walking (ITW). While laboratory-based motion capture remains the gold standard, its operational complexity often limits its use in daily clinical practice. In this work, we present a comprehensive, multi-modal dataset of pediatric gait comprising 59 participants: 22 with CP, 12 with ITW, and 25 typically developing (TD) controls. The dataset provides synchronized time-series of 3D kinematics, derived from a body-worn inertial measurement unit (IMU) system ( Xsens™) , and four-channel surface electromyography (sEMG) ( Delsys Trigno™ ) targeting the tibialis anterior and gastrocnemius muscles. Additionally, regular video recordings from three views (front left, front right, and sagittal) are provided as quality visual references. A distinguishing feature of this repository is the inclusion of pre- and post-treatment sessions for pathological cohorts, enabling the evaluation of clinical interventions over time. The records include (i) raw acquisition files, (ii) processed clinical joint angles and sEMG signals, and (iii) segmented gait cycles time-aligned across wearable sensors. This dataset facilitates the development of automated gait analysis algorithms, clinical decision-support methods, and digital gait biomarkers, bridging the gap between laboratory-based gait analysis and portable monitoring in pediatric clinical settings.
authors: Carmen Fernández-González; Hichem Saoudi; Celia Mazariegos-Iglesias; Beatriz De la Calle García; Francisco Javier Díaz Pernas; Míriam Antón‐Rodríguez; David González‐Ortega; Daniel Iordanov Lopez; Mario Martínez‐Zarzuela

title: Lack of vision shifts occipital dynamics toward a frontal-like regime and enhances top-down connectivity
abstract: ABSTRACT The human occipital cortex is robustly repurposed for non-visual cognition after blindness, yet it remains unknown whether this functional reassignment is accompanied by a fundamental retuning of its intrinsic neural dynamics. Here, we recorded the electroencephalographic (EEG) responses to transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) of frontal and occipital areas to causally probe local cortical reactivity and large-scale effective connectivity in 16 blind individuals and 16 sighted controls. Direct perturbation of the occipital cortex revealed a profound shift in its intrinsic operating regime: compared with sighted participants, blind individuals exhibited faster, lower-amplitude TMS-evoked potentials that closely resembled the electrophysiological signature of the frontal cortex, which turned out to be comparable in the two populations. At the network level, source analyses further showed a specific enhancement of frontal-to-occipital effective connectivity, whereas occipital-to-frontal propagation remained unchanged. Importantly, among blind participants, faster occipital dynamics were associated with stronger frontal-driven occipital recruitment, directly linking local temporal retuning to enhanced top-down network influence. Together, these findings indicate that blindness reshapes both the intrinsic dynamics and large-scale integration of the occipital cortex. We propose that successful functional reassignment of the occipital cortex requires not only changes in cortical connectivity but also a tuning of the temporal operating regime toward a faster dynamics, enabling its embedding into distributed cognitive networks and providing a mechanistic framework for the functional reassignment of deafferented cortex.
authors: Gabriel Hassan; Isabella De Cuntis; Gianluca Gaglioti; Giulia Furregoni; Elena Focacci; Francesca Baglio; Davide Bottari; Giulio Bernardi; Alessandra Calcagno; Pietro Pietrini; Emiliano Ricciardi; Marcello Massimini; Mario Rosanova; Silvia Casarotto

title: Large language models as collaborative learning partners in higher education: a theoretical framework
abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into higher education environments reveals notable challenges within existing educational technology frameworks. Current theoretical models conceptualize artificial intelligence as an instrumental tool that supports human learning processes, yet numerous empirical studies demonstrate that LLMs function as collaborative learning partners with reciprocal agency, dynamic adaptation capabilities, and shared knowledge-construction behaviors. Research in Hungarian higher education contexts provides compelling evidence for this partnership phenomenon, with studies revealing that students primarily use AI systems for collaborative tasks such as brainstorming, information exploration, and iterative problem-solving rather than simple tool operation (Folmeg et al., 2024). I pro-pose the Collaborative Learning Partnership Model as a theoretical framework that reconceptualizes LLMs as active learning agents rather than passive educational instruments. Drawing from systematic analyses of recent implementation research across multiple educational domains, my model identifies four core components: reciprocal agency, dynamic contextual adaptation, shared knowledge construction, and transparent collaboration protocols. This frame-work addresses challenges in AI integration, including academic integrity concerns, assessment innovation, and pedagogical role transformation. The model provides a theoretical foundation for effective LLM integration while maintaining educational rigor and human agency in learning processes. Furthermore, I present a four-stage partnership development progression that guides practical implementation strategies.
authors: Zoltán Biczó

title: Left-DLPFC theta-burst stimulation produces delayed effects on musical pleasure without affecting piano-melody learning
abstract: Abstract Reward operates as a cycle in which a stimulus produces a pleasure response, and the degree of pleasure experienced reinforces the behaviours that lead back to it. Music provides a useful model for examining this cycle because it is intrinsically pleasurable, can be learned, and engages reward-related frontostriatal circuitry that overlaps with circuitry involved in primary and secondary rewards, such as food, sex, and money. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), a non-invasive stimulation method, has been shown to produce bidirectional effects on music-evoked pleasure by increasing or decreasing activity in cortical regions, such as the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), that are functionally connected to subcortical regions, including the striatum. Here, we further characterize the reward cycle by incorporating TMS into a paradigm that combines musical pleasure ratings with an early musical skill acquisition task. In a within-subjects, counterbalanced crossover design, 23 participants with 2-10 years of musical experience received intermittent TBS (iTBS; excitatory) and continuous TBS (cTBS; inhibitory) over the left DLPFC in separate sessions. Participants rated the pleasantness of short piano melodies before stimulation (T0), immediately afterwards (T1), and 24 hours later (T2). After stimulation, they learned to play the melodies, and pitch and rhythm accuracy were assessed during three performance phases, namely acquisition, immediately after acquisition, and 24 hours later. Liking did not differ between conditions at T1; however, the increase in liking from baseline (T0) to T2 was significantly larger following iTBS than cTBS, a divergence that emerged across the 24-hour interval spanning both learning and sleep. Pitch and rhythm accuracy did not differ between conditions at any phase, despite improvement across trials in both. These results indicate that TMS to the left DLPFC can produce delayed, condition-dependent shifts in musical liking without a parallel change in early skill acquisition.
authors: Sofia Simonetto-Rizk; Yang Liu; Jérémie Ginzburg; Robert J. Zatorre; Emily B. J. Coffey

title: Long-term robot-assisted gait training in patients with cerebral palsy: meaningful changes in gait parameters require time
abstract: Introduction Robot-assisted gait training (RAGT) is increasingly used in children with cerebral palsy (CP), but evidence regarding the timing and persistence of meaningful changes in gait remains limited. This study aimed to describe long-term changes in spatiotemporal gait parameters, gait kinematics, and walking endurance in ambulatory patients with CP undergoing systematic, repetitive RAGT, and to determine whether the timing of clinically meaningful change differs between ambulatory levels. Methods A study group consisting of 211 patients with hypertonic CP (93 females, 118 males; mean age 10.33 ± 3.80 years) classified at Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS) levels I–III underwent a structured 2-year RAGT program comprising four therapy sets and 40 sessions in total. Gait was assessed five times: at baseline (pre-intervention) and at 6-month intervals over 24 months. Outcomes included the Gait Deviation Index (GDI), spatiotemporal gait parameters obtained from three-dimensional gait analysis, and six-minute walk test (6MWT) distance. The follow-u p values were compared with the baseline. Clinical meaningfulness was evaluated using the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) thresholds. Results In the entire group, step length and stride length increased significantly from T2 onward, walking speed from T3 onward, and 6MWT distance at each follow-up assessment. At T5, individual improvement exceeding the relevant MCID thresholds was observed in 61.61% of participants for step length, 62.09% for stride length, 52.13% for walking speed, and 51.66% for 6MWT distance. Cadence increased significantly only at T5, whereas GDI increased throughout follow-up; however, the corresponding MCID thresholds were exceeded by 32.23 and 46.92% of participants, respectively. GMFCS III showed the earliest and largest gains, while changes in GMFCS II generally emerged later. Effect sizes increased over time and reached their highest values at T5. Repeated-measures ANOVA confirmed significant time effects for most outcomes. Significant time-by-GMFCS interactions for cadence, step length, and 6MWT distance indicated that selected longitudinal trajectories differed across functional levels, although the interaction effect sizes were small. Conclusion Systematic, repetitive gait training based on RAGT in patients with CP was associated with long-term positive changes in spatiotemporal gait parameters and walking endurance. In contrast, clinically meaningful changes in gait kinematics, as quantified by the GDI, were limited across all GMFCS levels. The effects of systematic and repeated RAGT developed progressively over time, with selected outcomes following different trajectories according to the participants’ functional level.
authors: Paweł Chmara; Sabina Brazevic; Marek Jóźwiak; Faustyna Manikowska

title: Longitudinal Gait Improvement With Multimodal Treatment and Repeated Hybrid Assistive Limb Gait Training in Hereditary Spastic Paraplegia: A Case Report
abstract: Hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by lower-limb spasticity and gait impairment.Although spasticity management, including botulinum toxin injections, intrathecal baclofen therapy, and orthopedic surgery, can reduce spasticity and improve limb alignment, translating these improvements into meaningful gains in walking remains challenging.Robot-assisted gait training with wearable exoskeletons, such as the Hybrid Assistive Limb (HAL), may facilitate task-specific gait practice by assisting voluntary movements based on the user's motor intention.We report the case of a 64-year-old man with spastic paraplegia type 4 (SPG4), a subtype of HSP associated with pathogenic variants in the SPAST gene, who underwent stepwise spasticity management combined with repeated HALassisted gait training over long-term follow-up.Botulinum toxin injections were initiated at presentation, followed by intrathecal baclofen therapy during follow-up and tendon lengthening surgery.HAL-assisted gait training was performed repeatedly from Month 29 to Month 49.Over the course of treatment, walking speed and 2-minute walk distance gradually improved, whereas cadence remained relatively stable.These functional gains persisted despite a temporary decline.These sequential interventions may have provided a therapeutic foundation for subsequent gait reconstruction through repeated task-specific gait training using the HAL.Although the individual effects of each intervention cannot be determined from a single case, this clinical course suggests that integrating impairment-oriented interventions with repeated HAL-assisted gait training can optimize functional walking outcomes in patients with HSP.
authors: Taiyo Kawaguchi; Takatoshi Hara; Yuta Miyazaki; Ayano Matsui; Yuki Hara; Keiko Sone; Takeshi Matsuura; Yuji Takahashi; Tetsuya Tsuji; Masahiro Abo

title: Longitudinal spatial changes of the contralesional corticospinal tract in high-grade glioma: a within-patient DTI tractography study
abstract: PURPOSE: The contralesional corticospinal tract (CST) is often used as an internal reference in glioma tractography, but its longitudinal stability remains poorly understood. We explored within-patient changes in contralesional CST characteristics between primary and recurrent high-grade glioma. METHODS: Twenty-nine patients with paired preoperative diffusion tensor imaging at primary and recurrent assessments were retrospectively analyzed. The contralesional CST was reconstructed using anatomically guided deterministic tractography at fractional anisotropy thresholds (FATs) of 0.10 and 0.15. Tract-averaged fractional anisotropy (FA), tract length, and tract volume were compared longitudinally. Spatial changes were assessed using patient-level slice-wise centroid trajectories and paired voxel-wise analyses in standardized space, with HCP842 used as a fixed normative spatial reference. RESULTS: No longitudinal differences in FA, tract length, or tract volume remained significant after BH-FDR correction. In contrast, slice-wise analyses showed a predominantly anterior CST displacement at recurrence, with mean paired Y-axis differences of 2.576 mm at FAT 0.10 and 2.078 mm at FAT 0.15; 57 and 21 slices, respectively, remained significant after correction. Mediolateral changes were smaller and less consistent, and no voxel-wise differences survived correction. Relative to HCP842, both assessments were posterior to the reference trajectory, while the recurrent CST was less posterior. CONCLUSION: The contralesional CST showed longitudinal spatial displacement without corresponding corrected changes in tractography-derived FA, tract length, or tract volume. These findings indicate that its spatial position may not remain fixed between primary and recurrent glioma assessments.

title: Lower limb orthotics in cerebral palsy
abstract: Uvod: Cerebralna paraliza je neprogresivna nevrološka motnja, ki nastane kot posledica okvare osrednjega živčnega sistema v obdobju razvoja. Zanjo so značilne trajne motnje v nadzoru gibanja, koordinacije in telesne drže, ki lahko pomembno vplivajo na posameznikovo samostojnost in funkcionalnost v vsakdanjem življenju. Pri osebah s cerebralno paralizo so najpogosteje prizadeti spodnji udi, kjer se pojavlja spastičnost, zmanjšana stabilnost, slabša kontrola gibov in patološki vzorci hoje, ki lahko sčasoma vodijo v razvoj deformacij in drugih sekundarnih mišično-skeletnih sprememb. Pomemben del obravnave predstavlja ortotična oskrba, katere cilj je izboljšanje biomehanike gibanja, stabilizacija sklepov in preprečevanje napredovanja deformacij. Namen: Namen diplomskega dela je predstaviti ortotično obravnavo spodnjih udov pri osebah s cerebralno paralizo in prikazati vpliv različnih ortotičnih rešitev na biomehaniko hoje in funkcionalno mobilnost. Metode dela: V diplomskem delu je bila uporabljena deskriptivna metoda dela s pregledom domače in tuje znanstvene ter strokovne literature. Za iskanje literature smo uporabili bibliografske podatkovne baze: ScienceDirect, PubMed, ResearchGate, Journal of Prosthetics and Orthotics in Google Scholar. Rezultati: V pregled literature je bilo vključenih šest raziskav, ki so obravnavale uporabo ortoz za spodnje ude pri osebah s cerebralno paralizo. Analizirane raziskave poročajo o izboljšanju parametrov hoje, predvsem hitrosti hoje, dolžine koraka, stabilnosti in poravnave sklepov. Stopnja izboljšanja se je med raziskavami razlikovala glede na klinične značilnosti preiskovancev, vrsto uporabljene ortoze in cilje ortotične obravnave. Razprava in zaključek: Uporaba ortoz za spodnje ude pri osebah s cerebralno paralizo pomaga omiliti patološke gibalne vzorce in preprečuje dolgoročni razvoj deformacij. Z ustrezno ortotično oskrbo osebi omogočimo učinkovitejše gibanje, ki je bolj varno in energijsko učinkovito. Uspešnost zdravljenja je odvisna od individualnih značilnosti uporabnika, vrste patologije ter izbire ustrezne ortoze, njenih komponent in materialov. Za doseganje optimalnih rezultatov je potrebno dobro poznavanje biomehanike gibanja, klinične slike cerebralne paralize in principov delovanja ortotičnih pripomočkov.

title: MIRROR THERAPY COMBINED WITH REHABILITATION INTERVENTIONS FOR POST-STROKE UPPER LIMB MOTOR DYSFUNCTION: CURRENT EVIDENCE, MECHANISMS, AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS
abstract: Post-stroke upper limb motor dysfunction is a common cause of long-term disability. Mirror therapy (MT) is a generally safe, accessible, and low-cost rehabilitation intervention, and its combination with other rehabilitation modalities has attracted growing clinical interest. This narrative review synthesized targeted literature available up to September 2026 on MT combined with electrical stimulation, non-invasive brain stimulation, task-oriented training, acupuncture, robot-assisted therapy, and electromyographic biofeedback. Higher-level clinical evidence and relevant mechanistic studies were prioritized, while no PRISMA-style systematic screening, de novo risk-of-bias assessment, or meta-analysis was undertaken. Across the six combined approaches, evidence suggests potential additional benefits for upper limb motor function and activities of daily living (ADL), but certainty varies substantially. Moderate-quality evidence supports major motor and ADL outcomes for robot-assisted MT, whereas evidence for several electrical stimulation outcomes remains low-certainty. Recent meta-analyses also support potential benefits of MT combined with tDCS and acupuncture, although protocol heterogeneity remains substantial. Patient selection, intervention dose and sequencing, and adverse-event reporting remain inconsistent across studies. MT combined with other rehabilitation interventions is a promising adjunctive strategy for post-stroke upper limb recovery, but current evidence does not support uniform superiority across all modalities or patient groups. Future studies should prioritize standardized reporting, stronger comparative trials, patient stratification, safety monitoring, and clinically meaningful outcome measures.

title: MOVING TOWARD ROBOT FRIENDLY CITIES
abstract: Advances in artificial intelligence, autonomous navigation, sensing, and robotics are accelerating the deployment of autonomous robots in streets, buildings, and public spaces. Yet existing research remains fragmented across robotics, human–robot interaction, architecture, engineering, and policy, leaving an integrated urban planning framework for human–robot coexistence underdeveloped. This study conceptualizes the Robot-Friendly City as an urban environment capable of accommodating autonomous robots while supporting safe, inclusive, and responsible coexistence with humans. Through a systematic literature review and thematic analysis, the study identifies and synthesizes key considerations for integrating autonomous robots into urban environments. The analysis identifies five interdependent dimensions: (1) physical and spatial environment, (2) environmental sustainability, (3) digital and technological environment, (4) social and human–robot interaction, and (5) governance and institutional arrangements. Together, these dimensions provide an integrated framework for understanding the urban conditions and design considerations associated with human–robot coexistence. By shifting the focus from adapting individual robots to existing environments toward considering how urban environments should accommodate robots, this study positions robotic integration as a multidimensional urban planning challenge and provides a conceptual foundation for future planning strategies and urban design guidelines for Robot-Friendly Cities.
authors: Sung Jin Park; Taeyun Lim; Hyein Kim; Yejin Kim

title: MRI-guided navigated TMS protocol for language production lateralization in right- and left-handed individuals
abstract: Hemispheric language lateralization has been assessed using various neuroimaging techniques in both basic research and clinical settings. The use of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) for this purpose, however, has shown low to moderate concordance with other neuroimaging techniques, particularly in cases of atypical lateralization and when studying the right hemisphere. The present study aimed to develop an MRI-guided navigated TMS protocol based on a verb-generation task to identify optimal conditions for determining language lateralization. Thirty healthy participants were classified into three groups according to hemispheric dominance during the verb-generation task: right-handers with left-hemisphere dominance, left-handers with left-hemisphere dominance, and left-handers with right-hemisphere dominance. TMS was applied at four predetermined locations within the inferior frontal gyrus while participants performed a picture-based verb generation task outside the scanner. Results showed a larger proportion of error responses when TMS was applied to the dominant language hemisphere, as defined by fMRI, across all groups. Concordance values between fMRI and TMS language lateralization ranged from 89 % to 100 %. Naming times were slower when the dominant hemisphere was stimulated, but only in the left-handed group. Trials more likely to induce TMS-related errors were characterized by longer reaction times, a greater number of response options, lower word frequency, and the absence of a clearly dominant response. These findings support the reliability of the proposed navigated TMS protocol for individual-level assessment of language lateralization during verb generation task as well as identify task-related conditions that increase the likelihood of verbal errors following TMS interference.
authors: Cristina Cano-Melle; Miriam Lluesma-Martín; Cristina Narganes-Pineda; Joaquín J. Ramírez-Guerrero; Ana B. Chica; César Ávila

title: Macro-Cybernetic Architecture of Planetary Systems: Integrating Quantum Epidemiology, Thermodynamic Hysteresis, and Dimensional Topologies
abstract: The complex interplay between microscopic pathogenic emergence, macroscopic geological events, and global sociopolitical shifts presents a significant challenge to classical, isolated scientific disciplines. This paper introduces a unified, interdisciplinary theoretical model—the Macro-Cybernetic Framework—which analyzes the terrestrial biosphere as a highly integrated computational and immunological network. By applying principles of cryptography, non-equilibrium thermodynamics, and quantum mechanics to biological and sociological phenomena, this framework proposes several novel mechanisms for planetary-scale events. First, we define "Pathogenic Steganography" and "Interferometric Illumination" to explain the camouflage and subsequent systemic unmasking of pervasive parasitic architectures. Second, we introduce the concept of the "Kinetic Echo" and "Pathological Hysteresis," utilizing classical mechanics and control systems engineering (PID overshoot) to model the thermodynamic lag between the cessation of systemic biological triggers and the physical dissipation of disease, offering a new etiology for post-acute infection syndromes. Third, we propose "Quantum Epidemiology," moving beyond classical vector-based transmission models to account for the simultaneous, non-local activation of pre-distributed dormant pathogens (the biospheric botnet), heavily modulated by the "Friction of Manifestation"—a localized ecological shield comprising climatic, nutritional, and microbial variables. Furthermore, this paper models historical macroeconomic and geopolitical isolationist shifts (the Khaldunian cycle) not as independent political events, but as automated "Geopolitical Tourniquets" and network edge deletions executing planetary autoimmune responses. Finally, the framework applies wave shoaling physics to multidimensional topologies, highlighting the critical vulnerability of modern 2-dimensional transactive memory systems (digital infrastructure) to impending high-kinetic electromagnetic events. Ultimately, this comprehensive matrix provides a robust theoretical foundation for predicting epidemiological trajectories, executing comparative shield extraction via subtractive genomics, and ensuring the resilience of complex civilizational networks.

title: Mapping the current evidence on mirror therapy, soft robotic gloves, and their combined use in upper limb rehabilitation after stroke: a scoping review
abstract: Abstract Background Upper-limb impairment after stroke can restrict hand use, activities of daily living, and functional independence. Mirror therapy (MT) and soft robotic glove (SRG)-based rehabilitation represent technology-enabled approaches to upper-limb rehabilitation. The extent and characteristics of evidence examining these approaches individually and in combination have not been mapped. Objective To map the literature on MT, SRG-based rehabilitation, and their combined use after stroke, with emphasis on study characteristics, intervention dosage, outcome measures, technological integration, safety reporting, and evidence gaps. Methods This scoping review followed Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and CENTRAL were searched in the original review. The Scopus strategy was rerun using OR between the MT and SRG concept blocks, and IEEE Xplore was searched to improve engineering-literature coverage. Eligible interventional studies involved adults with stroke receiving MT, SRG-based rehabilitation, a direct MT + SRG combination, or a direct MT-versus-SRG comparison. Data were charted using a standardized form and synthesized descriptively; study-level fields were rechecked against accessible full-text articles or primary records to resolve classification and reporting discrepancies. Results The evidence map included 84 studies reporting 2,634 stroke participants. Fifty-four studies were MT-only (64.3%), 27 were SRG-only (32.1%), two directly combined MT + SRG (2.4%), and one directly compared MT with SRG (1.2%). Randomized controlled/clinical trials accounted for 53 studies (63.1%) and pilot/feasibility studies for 16 (19.0%). Chronic stroke was explicitly represented in 31 studies (36.9%), subacute stroke in 15 (17.9%), acute stroke in five (6.0%), and mixed acute/subacute populations in two (2.4%); stage was unspecified/other in 31 (36.9%). FMA was charted in 35 studies (41.7%), ARAT in 12 (14.3%), and ADL/independence outcomes in 19 (22.6%). Safety was not reported in 52 studies (61.9%); 23 (27.4%) explicitly reported no serious/adverse safety signal. Conclusion The evidence base is substantially larger for MT or SRG studied separately than for their direct combination. Considerable heterogeneity exists in study design, stroke stage, intervention dosage, outcome selection, technology integration, and safety reporting. The review provides an evidence map and identifies areas requiring further investigation without making claims of comparative treatment superiority.

title: Mediolateral Joint Balance Assessment Is Reproducible Between Surgeons, Under No Standardized Varus–Valgus Stress, During Robot-Assisted Total Knee Arthroplasty
abstract: Objective: To evaluate inter-surgeon variability in mediolateral joint balance assessment during robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty (TKA) using the robotic surgical assistant (ROSA) Knee System, and to determine whether such variability influences the surgical planning generated by this system. Methods: An observational study was conducted including 101 patients undergoing primary robotic-assisted TKA. Two experienced surgeons independently assessed intraoperative mediolateral laxity by manually applying varus–valgus stress across six predefined flexion angles (0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°, and 120°). Measurements of medial and lateral gaps (mm) and varus–valgus alignment (°) were recorded using the ROSA Knee System. Inter-observer differences were analysed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and reliability was assessed using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). The impact of inter-surgeon variability on surgical planning, including bone resection and compartmental space measurement parameters, was also evaluated. Results: No statistically significant inter-observer differences were observed in mediolateral gap measurements or varus–valgus alignment across all flexion angles (p > 0.05). Inter-observer reliability for varus–valgus measurements was good to excellent in extension and early flexion (ICC 0.86–0.91), decreased to moderate at 90° (ICC 0.68–0.74) and was poor for varus assessment at 120° (ICC 0.46, 95% CI 0.29–0.60). For gap measurements, reliability was excellent for the medial gap and good for the lateral gap in extension (ICC 0.93 and 0.89, respectively), and moderate for both gaps at 90° (ICC 0.71–0.74). No significant inter-observer differences were found in cut or space measurements, with excellent agreement for cut parameters (ICC > 0.95). Conclusions: Inter-surgeon assessment of mediolateral joint balance during robot-assisted TKA showed good-to-excellent reproducibility in extension and early flexion, with reduced reproducibility in deep flexion. Statistically significant inter-observer differences were not observed in the resulting cut and space measurements.
