title: Microfoundations of Adaptive Decision‐Making Capability: How Chief Supply Chain Officers Convert Technology‐Enabled Visibility Into Coordinated Action
abstract: ABSTRACT Supply chain leaders increasingly operate with extensive technology‐enabled visibility, yet many firms still struggle to convert shared signals into timely, coordinated action. We frame this tension as the visibility‐to‐action problem in supply chain management (SCM): executives observe more than they can process and often fail to route, prioritize, and execute quickly enough for information to translate into coordinated outcomes. We examine how Chief Supply Chain Officers (CSCOs) close this gap. Drawing on dynamic capabilities and microfoundations research, we adopt a theory‐elaborating qualitative design that pairs a theories‐in‐use approach with the Gioia methodology, analyzing 25 CSCO interviews spanning manufacturing, retail, logistics, and technology sectors. Informants theorize that technology‐enabled advantage depends less on tool acquisition than on the intentional design of interoperable data architectures, conversion routines that filter and route exceptions to accountable owners, and learning stabilizers that preserve reliable adjustment over time. We conceptualize these as the microfoundations of adaptive decision‐making capability (ADMC), a higher‐order managerial capability linking information, judgment, and action into self‐reinforcing learning cycles. As a theorized downstream implication, participants further suggest that ADMC supports the development of adaptive supply chain capability (ASCC), reflected in agility, resilience, alignment, and learning velocity. The study extends microfoundations and dynamic capabilities research by specifying the cognitive, governance, and exception‐management mechanisms through which technology‐enabled visibility becomes coordinated action in data‐intensive SCM settings.
authors: Sreedhar Madhavaram; Kerry T. Manis; Matthew Belford; Robert Glenn Richey Jr

title: Modeling blockchain adoption in the United Kingdom’s banking: an empirical study using technology-organization-environment framework
abstract: Introduction Blockchain technology (BCT) has the ability to significantly change the financial services industry by making transactions faster, cheaper, safer, as well as more transparent. Therefore, the current paper seeks to investigate and empirically validate the variables, which are affecting the adoption of Blockchain in the UK’s banking system. Methods For this purpose the study collected secondary data through reviewing literature for the period January 2015 and June 2025 from well indexed journals, conference proceedings, books, white papers, and industry reports, those are related to blockchain technology and the banking sector. However, primary data for this study were collected from banking and financial services employees in London between the period January 2025 and July 2025 using a structured questionnaire. A non-probability purposive sampling technique was adopted and Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) was used to examine the relationships among the proposed technological, organizational, and environmental determinants of blockchain adoption. The Technology Organizational Environmental framework served as the model for the scale used for measuring BCA enablers. Results Consequently, the study found that perceived Compatibility, relative advantage, learning culture, top management, consumer readiness, and competitive pressure significantly affects the adoption of blockchain, whereas perceived cost limits this adoption process. Additionally, the results reveal that perceived compatibility, relative advantage, learning culture, top management support, customer readiness, and competitive pressure positively influence blockchain adoption, whereas perceived cost negatively affects adoption. Discussion Moreover, the findings indicated that Blockchain might therefore be viewed as an emerging disruptive force in digital technology that is transforming business models and is becoming as an essential element on a global scale.
authors: Mohammad Sami Ali; Sultan Abdullah Alabdullatif; Saleh Mohammed Baqader; Mohammad M. Hariri

title: Motor Evoked Potentials in Preclinical Models of Spinal Cord Injury and Stroke in Rodents: A Systematic Review
abstract: Abstract Motor Evoked Potentials (MEPs) serve as an invaluable tool for assessing corticospinal tract (CST) integrity and motor pathway function in preclinical models of spinal cord injury (SCI) and stroke. Despite their diagnostic and prognostic utility, substantial methodological variability persists across studies, complicating interpretation and cross-study comparisons. This systematic review synthesizes MEP acquisition and interpretation protocols from 83 rodent SCI and stroke studies published since 2015, aiming to outline common practices, identify sources of variability, and highlight methodological gaps. Our analysis reveals a predominance of SCI models and a focus on hindlimb MEPs, employing diverse stimulation protocols including transcranial electrical stimulation (TES), direct cortical stimulation (DCoS), and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). Anesthetic approaches are notably heterogeneous, representing a potentially large source of variability in MEP acquisition. Amplitude and latency, often measured jointly, emerged as the most frequently reported MEP parameters. Critically, MEPs bridge cellular and molecular changes to observable behaviour by reflecting the integrated functionality of neural cell populations and their circuits. However, a lack of standardization in reporting, particularly for secondary electrophysiological features and stimulation intensity, hinders reproducibility. We emphasize the necessity for standardized protocols for stimulation, electrode positioning, and data analysis, particularly the use of comprehensive recruitment curves. Adopting these best practices will enhance the transparency, comparability, and translational potential of MEP methodology in advancing our understanding and treatment strategies for neurological disorders. Graphical abstract Motor evoked potentials (MEPs) in rodent models of spinal cord injury (SCI) and stroke. This review focuses on various brain stimulation techniques (orange) and electromyographic approaches employed to quantify MEPs (green) and factors affecting MEP recording and analysis (blue). Future directions include greater standardization of stimulation, recording-electrode placement, and data-analysis practices; such as the potential use of recruitment curve features and high-density EMG recordings such as Myomatrix. Recruitment curves provide a more comprehensive characterization of evoked responses than single-pulse stimulation. While a single pulse only offers a snapshot of a subject’s motor threshold, recruitment curves yield a dynamic, S-shaped (sigmoidal) function that reflects the net excitability of upper and lower motor pathways across a range of stimulation intensities. This enables better control over sources of variability, such as stimulation and recording electrode placement, anesthetics dose, that can alter amplitude-based features. Because recruitment curves quantify the relationship between stimulus intensity and response rather than relying solely on absolute amplitude, the derived features are less susceptible to these artifacts (e.g., slopes, S50—stimulation intensity to reach half of the maximum amplitude). In addition, high-density recordings make it possible to better characterize the evoked activity of multiple motor units within the same target muscle and to identify the innervation zones of the motor units under study. authors: Rubab Shahid; Dylan F. Cooke; Gustavo Catusso Balbinot

title: Motor cortex pain compensation is modifiable: allostatic load degrades its analgesic efficiency and rehabilitation restores it
abstract: The primary motor cortex is a critical hub for pain control, yet its few identified regulatory mechanisms - intracortical inhibition and oscillatory markers - predict symptoms inconsistently. The prevailing view holds that pain results from reduced inhibition, a fixed deficit, rather than from resistance to inhibition that rehabilitation can reverse. Here we show that motor cortex pain compensation is instead a modifiable state whose analgesic efficiency depends on allostatic load. In a fibromyalgia trial and a knee osteoarthritis cohort assessed with parallel EEG and transcranial magnetic stimulation, a signature combining central theta asymmetry and intracortical inhibition was unrelated or inversely related to symptom burden under low allostatic load but positively related to it under high load in fibromyalgia, and its protective association was attenuated under high load in osteoarthritis - the same signal carrying different clinical meaning. A burden-adjusted index modelled on the homeostatic model assessment of insulin resistance was elevated under high load, predicted improvement after rehabilitation beyond baseline severity, and fell in responders but not in non-responders; in both cohorts the neurophysiological component itself recalibrated with response. Motor cortex compensation is thus degraded by allostatic load and restored by rehabilitation.
authors: Felipe Fregni; Marta Imamura; Lucas Camargo; Kevin Pacheco‐Barrios; Anna Lepesteur Gianlorenco; Linamara Rizzo Battistella; Wolnei Caumo

title: Multi-omics characterization of anoikis-related hub genes and macrophage-centered immune persistence with validation of HAVCR2 in atherosclerosis
abstract: Background Atherosclerosis (AS) is a chronic inflammatory vascular disease characterized by immune dysregulation, metabolic disturbance, and progressive vascular remodeling. Although anoikis resistance has been extensively investigated in cancer biology, its involvement in immune-cell persistence and plaque progression in AS remains poorly understood. Methods We integrated two publicly available bulk transcriptomic datasets (GSE100927 and GSE28829) to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and performed weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) to determine disease-associated gene modules. Anoikis-related candidate genes were obtained by intersecting DEGs, WGCNA-derived module genes, and a curated anoikis-related gene set, and were further prioritized using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression and random forest algorithms. Immune infiltration and cell type–specific expression patterns were evaluated using CIBERSORT and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analyses. The expression of the leading candidate was validated using both in vitro and in vivo experiments. Results We identified eight core anoikis-related hub genes—HAVCR2, CD36, PLAU, TNF, PYCARD, SERPINA1, BLNK, and CHI3L1—that were closely associated with AS. These genes were enriched in inflammatory and metabolic pathways and showed strong diagnostic performance across validation analyses, with AUC values greater than 0.83. Immune deconvolution and single-cell transcriptomic analyses revealed that the anoikis-related signature was predominantly localized to macrophage and T-cell compartments within atherosclerotic lesions. Among the identified candidates, HAVCR2 showed the most consistent disease-associated pattern. HAVCR2 expression was markedly increased in oxLDL-stimulated THP-1-derived macrophages and was enriched in macrophage-rich atherosclerotic lesions in high-fat diet–fed ApoE −/− mice, supporting its association with lipid-induced macrophage activation and vascular inflammation. Conclusion This study defines a macrophage-centered anoikis-related immune signature in atherosclerosis and identifies HAVCR2, together with CD36, PLAU, TNF, PYCARD, SERPINA1, BLNK, and CHI3L1, as potential biomarkers and candidate targets for future diagnostic and therapeutic investigation.
authors: Qiang Shen; Zhengfeng Fan; Jincheng Hou; Fei Li; Yixuan Wang; Zongtao Liu; Chen Jiang; Nianguo Dong

title: Multimodal data-driven intelligent diagnosis in traditional Chinese medicine: Current status and future perspectives
abstract: With advances in artificial intelligence, traditional Chinese medicine diagnosis is gradually becoming more intelligent. This review departs from the conventional framework that categorizes the four diagnostic methods in isolation. Instead, it starts from five heterogeneous data modalities, namely vision, audition, olfaction, textual, and tactile, and systematically reconstructs the digital mapping relationships of traditional Chinese medicine diagnostic information, thereby directly aligning traditional Chinese medicine diagnostic problems with the input paradigms of artificial intelligence. This study comprehensively examines the current state of research on multimodal acquisition technologies, fusion methods, and clinical applications, and analyzes the core challenges and future directions in this field. This study aims to provide a theoretical foundation for achieving truly intelligent integration of the four diagnostic methods.
authors: Jiaqi Sun; Zheng Yu; 高俊虹

title: NESTApp: A GUI-Based MATLAB Application for Auditable TMS-EEG Preprocessing with EEGLAB
abstract: Abstract Electroencephalography (EEG) preprocessing determines signal quality and interpretation, particularly for transcranial magnetic stimulation combined with EEG (TMS-EEG), where recordings are affected by large and complex stimulation-related artifacts. Several preprocessing approaches have been developed, but substantial variability remains in how pipelines are implemented, documented, and evaluated across recordings, limiting reproducibility and comparability across studies. We developed NESTApp, a MATLAB-based graphical interface built on EEGLAB, to provide an accessible and reproducible framework for implementing and evaluating TMS-EEG preprocessing pipelines. Rather than prescribing a specific pipeline, NESTApp allows users to construct and consistently apply customisable workflows incorporating established EEGLAB and TMS-EEG processing tools, while automatically documenting processing decisions and parameters. Integrated quality-control procedures track data removal and flag recordings based on user-defined criteria, facilitating systematic evaluation across participants. The application also supports group-level visualisation and export of processed TMS-EEG measures for subsequent analyses. Applied to 29 recordings from 16 participants, NESTApp processed 27 and identified those requiring further inspection. By integrating pipeline implementation, documentation, quality control, and group-level evaluation within a single interface, NESTApp provides a transparent framework for TMS-EEG preprocessing that may improve reproducibility, facilitate consistent processing across cohorts, and lower technical barriers to the implementation of established preprocessing approaches.

title: Network-targeted neurophysiological biomarkers of dysconnectivity and cognitive decline in Alzheimer’s disease
abstract: Abstract Background Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is marked by progressive network disconnection that begins decades before symptoms emerge, yet detecting early functional disruptions remains a key challenge. Transcranial magnetic stimulation combined with electroencephalography (TMS–EEG) provides a direct, non-invasive probe of cortical dynamics and may yield biomarkers that index cortical network dysfunction, track progression, and inform personalized neuromodulation strategies. Methods We enrolled 86 participants: 28 HC (mean age 69.7 ± 6.0, 15 female), 27 MCI (73.1 ± 5.2, 16 female), and 31 ADD (75.8 ± 4.9, 17 female). TMS–EEG targeted individualized default mode (DMN) and executive control (ECN) network nodes identified via resting-state fMRI. Using a data-driven strategy, we extracted early TMS-evoked potential (TEP) components within 50 ms. We assessed group differences, associations with hippocampal volume, white matter integrity, and cognition, and prediction of cognitive decline over ~ 1.5 years ( n = 55). Results After left DMN stimulation, the contralateral frontal N20F peak was increased in both MCI (P-adj. = 0.0001, Δ = 1.89 µV) and ADD (P-adj. = 0.0003, Δ = 1.76 µV) relative to HC, achieving an AUC of 0.82 for HC-versus-MCI classification. In the ECN, N20C amplitude showed a diagnosis-by-hemisphere interaction: reduced in MCI after left stimulation (P-adj. = 0.036, Δ = −13.64 µV) but increased in MCI and ADD after right stimulation (P-adj. = 0.028, Δ = 14.59 µV and P-adj. = 0.048, Δ = 10.30 µV). Left DMN N20C amplitude correlated with superior longitudinal fasciculus integrity ( P = 0.009, β = 37.15). TEPs were selectively linked to executive function: in ADD, larger left ECN N20F predicted worse Trail Making Test scores (P-adj. = 0.0003, β = −24.35). Longitudinally, lower left DMN N20C predicted steeper global cognitive decline (β = 0.74, P = 0.014), and right ECN N20C predicted executive decline in MCI (β = −35.15, P = 0.0004). Conclusions Early network-targeted TEPs capture functional alterations linked to AD progression. Limitations include the moderate sample size, clinical rather than biomarker-confirmed diagnosis, and single-site design. These network-specific, hemisphere-sensitive measures may serve as biomarkers for diagnosis, tracking, and prognosis of cognitive decline, and could inform personalized network-targeted neuromodulation in AD. Trial registration Not applicable (observational study).

title: Neuroimaging-Guided Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation for Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
abstract: Rates of response to repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) in obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) vary widely. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated whether neuroimaging-guided targeting personalization, from fixed-coordinate neuronavigation to individually connectivity-personalized targeting, moderates clinical response, safety, and neural mechanisms in OCD. Following PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) 2020 guidelines, PubMed, the Cochrane Library, and ScienceDirect were searched through July 2026 for randomized and non-randomized studies of neuroimaging-guided transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) in OCD. Risk of bias (RoB) was assessed using Cochrane RoB2 for RCTs (randomized controlled trials) and ROBINS-I (Risk of Bias in Non-randomized Studies of Interventions) for non-randomized studies. Random-effects inverse-variance and risk-ratio models pooled Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) scores and responder rates; non-poolable data were synthesized narratively. Nine study cohorts across eight publications met inclusion criteria (five RCTs and four open-label/single-arm). Pooled analysis of four sham-controlled RCTs showed no significant benefit of neuroimaging-guided TMS on Y-BOCS total score (MD = −0.64, 95% CI = −3.60, 2.32) or responder rate (RR = 1.46, 95% CI = 0.68, 3.15), with moderate heterogeneity. However, trials using individually connectivity-personalized pre-supplementary motor area (pre-SMA) targeting consistently trended toward benefit, while fixed-coordinate neuronavigated trials trended toward null or sham-favoring results. A narrative synthesis of non-poolable and non-randomized studies showed larger, mostly positive within-group reductions in Y-BOCS scores (25%-48%), particularly among patients with moderate disease severity, alongside mechanistic evidence linking individualized connectivity-based targets to symptom improvement. TMS was well tolerated overall, with mild, transient headache being the most common adverse event and no serious safety concerns identified. Overall, neuroimaging-guided TMS showed no pooled benefit in OCD; however, individually connectivity-personalized targeting may be more beneficial than fixed-coordinate approaches, warranting adequately powered trials that directly compare targeting-personalization strategies.
authors: Maria Alejandra Rodriguez Gaviria; Paula Andrea Cuenca Cuevas; Rodrigo Nava Muñoz; Angie Coraline Moreno Báez; Andrés Felipe Cardenas Gamboa; Natalia Vanegas Arias; Christopher Alejandro Jiménez Beltrán; Leidy Catherine Guerrero Pasijojoa

title: Neuromodulatory interventions for Alzheimer’s disease
abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) represent an escalating global public health challenge with major socioeconomic consequences. Although anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies have introduced disease-modifying treatment options for early symptomatic AD, their benefits remain modest and must be balanced against cost, monitoring burden, and safety risks. Neuromodulatory interventions have therefore emerged as promising investigational strategies that may complement existing therapeutic approaches. This narrative review evaluates current clinical and neurophysiological evidence for seven major neuromodulation approaches: 40 Hz gamma rhythm sensory stimulation, also known as gamma entrainment using sensory stimulation (GENUS), transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS), transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), focused ultrasound (FUS), deep brain stimulation (DBS), and transcranial photobiomodulation (tPBM). Integrating clinical findings with mechanistic evidence, we examine synaptic plasticity, neuroinflammation, glymphatic clearance, oscillatory entrainment, and cholinergic signaling as candidate therapeutic mechanisms. A comparative matrix summarizes target specificity, invasiveness, stimulation parameters, and translational status. Finally, we discuss key barriers, including biological heterogeneity, protocol standardization, durability of benefit, caregiver burden, and the uncertain implications of continuous network stimulation for future personalized and closed-loop interventions.
authors: Ruofan Wang; Botao Zhu; Qingda Guo; Jun Steed Huang; Wandong Zhang

title: Neurophysiological and neuromuscular responses associated with the repeated bout effect following eccentric exercise in healthy adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Muscle damage severity decreases after repeated eccentric exercise bouts (the repeated bout effect [RBE]), but whether accompanying neural and neuromuscular changes contribute to protection or arise secondary to reduced damage remains unclear. This systematic review and meta-analysis compared neurophysiological and neuromuscular responses between initial and repeated eccentric bouts in healthy adults. Eight databases were searched from November 1990 to January 2025, and Hedges' g was calculated where outcomes were comparable. Given the small number of contributing studies, all pooled analyses were considered exploratory. Twelve studies met the inclusion criteria. Twitch/evoked force showed recovery-compatible point estimates at 24 h (g = 1.02, 95% CI -0.03-2.06) and 48 h (g = 0.50, 95% CI 0.08-0.92). Voluntary activation findings were mixed. TMS-derived voluntary activation produced positive single-study estimates at 24 h (g = 1.10, 95% CI 0.29-1.92) and 48 h (g = 1.06, 95% CI 0.26-1.87), whereas pooled ITT-derived estimates were imprecise at 24 h (g = 0.36, 95% CI -0.92-1.63) and recovery-compatible but based on only two studies at 48 h (g = 0.44, 95% CI 0.03-0.85). M-wave/Mmax showed no consistent between-bout pattern. Corticospinal, intracortical, spinal, reticulospinal, motor-unit and EMG findings were limited, inconsistent or directionally unclear. Neural and neuromuscular changes accompany the RBE, but whether they contribute to protection or reflect reduced damage remains unresolved. Peripheral contractile outcomes showed the most consistent recovery-compatible pattern, whereas evidence concerning central activation and motor-unit behaviour remained limited or inconsistent.
authors: Oliver Hayman; Abdulrahman T Alsowail; Benjamin Griffiths; Stuart R. Gray; Glyn Howatson; Ken Nosaka; Stuart Goodall; Ashlyn K. Frazer; Dawson J. Kidgell

title: Neurorehabilitation for cognitive and motor recovery: mechanisms, interventions, and translational advances
abstract: This narrative review synthesizes recent advances in neurorehabilitation, focusing on mechanisms of neural plasticity, glial cell function, and interventions for cognitive and motor recovery. We explore multidisciplinary approaches, including cognitive training, motor rehabilitation, neurostimulation, and regenerative therapies, highlighting their translational potential. Special attention is given to clinically relevant rehabilitation modifiers and complications, including spasticity, frailty, and post-stroke epilepsy, alongside strategies for enhancing quality of life and social reintegration. Emerging technologies such as brain-computer interfaces, virtual reality, and robotics are discussed for their role in personalized rehabilitation. This review emphasizes evidence-based, patient-centered interventions to enhance functional recovery and quality of life, identifying future directions for personalized neurorehabilitation across stroke survivors, elderly, and frail populations.
authors: Yingchao Guan; Yanan Gao

title: Neurostimulation in the treatment of psychiatric disorders: Underlying mechanisms and critical analysis of circuit-based interventions
abstract: Neurostimulation of targeted brain regions has emerged as a novel therapeutic approach to induce remission in patients with various psychiatric disorders. This strategy encompasses several modalities, including transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), deep brain stimulation (DBS), and transcranial focused ultrasound neurostimulation (tFUS), all of which aim to modulate dysfunctional neural circuits and restore activity toward physiological ranges. While the clinical efficacy of these techniques is increasingly documented, the mechanisms underlying their effects-beyond immediate changes in regional excitability-remain incompletely understood. Further, neurostimulation represents not only a technical advance, but also a conceptual shift in psychiatry, moving from interventions aimed at modulating neurotransmission or cognition toward circuit-based models of mental illness. This review surveys the current literature to clarify the mechanisms of action of neurostimulation across multiple levels of biological integration, ranging from large-scale neural circuits to cellular and subcellular processes. Subsequently, it explores innovative targets and emerging modalities that expand the scope of circuit-based interventions beyond traditional approaches. Finally, it engages in a critical epistemological reflection, addressing the conceptual challenges that accompany the translation of circuit-based models from neuroscience to clinical psychiatry.
authors: Francis Rodriguez Bambico; Antonine Nicoglou; J Relente; Alexandre Surget; Catherine Belzung

title: Occupancy Network-Guided Autonomous Robotic Partial Nephrectomy
abstract: Autonomous soft-tissue cancer surgery has been limited to interventions on organ surfaces, because current systems cannot perceive and adapt to anatomy once it deforms or is cut. We introduce the first vision-guided autonomous system capable of performing complete tumor resections for partial nephrectomy. Our system integrates conditional occupancy networks, trained entirely in a physics-based simulation, that infer full 3-D anatomy (tumor, margin tissue, and kidney) from single-view partial point clouds. These occupancy networks maintain intraoperative tracking even as tissue is cut and deformed, enabling adaptive planning and execution. The surgical platform combines a depth camera for capturing surface point clouds, dual robotic arms for electrosurgical cutting and vacuum-based tissue manipulation, and an autonomous control strategy for tumor resection. In patient-derived hydrogel phantoms under an open partial nephrectomy setting, the robot performed eight consecutive autonomous tumor resections comprising 77 electrosurgical cuts, with all cuts achieving negative surgical margins and 1.61 $\pm$ 0.48 mm mean absolute margin error. This work demonstrates, for the first time, a foundation for supervised autonomous closed-loop, imaging-driven, margin-negative tumor removal in phantoms.
authors: Ethan Kilmer; Pit Henrich; Jiawei Ge; Paul Maria Scheikl; Laura Connolly; Soum D. Lokeshwar; Joseph Chen; Justin David Opfermann; Kaitlyn Kumar; Lauren M. Shepard; Ahmed Ghazi; Nirmish Singla; Richard Cha; Kevin Cleary; Franziska Mathis-Ullrich; Axel Krieger

title: Optical Coherence Tomography for Quantitative Point‐of‐Care Ear Imaging
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To determine whether an optical coherence tomography (OCT) otoscope can provide quantitative morphological measurements of the tympanic membrane (TM) that distinguish abnormal ears from normal controls. METHODS: Patients with ear disease and normal volunteers were imaged using an OCT otoscope. Integrated video otoscopy with simultaneous OCT imaging guided probe positioning. OCT volumes (< 5 s each) were acquired and fused to generate wide-field volumetric images of the TM and middle ear (ME). Datasets were analyzed using semi-automated segmentation to quantify TM thickness and surface morphology. RESULTS: Fifty-five subjects (63 ears; 16 normal, 10 retraction pockets, 17 postoperative, 10 perforations, 10 cholesteatomas) were imaged. OCT volumetric imaging consistently distinguished normal, pathologic, and postoperative TMs. Mean TM thickness was significantly greater in all pathologic and postoperative groups compared to controls (p < 0.05). Surface gradient mapping demonstrated a characteristic pattern in normal TMs that was disrupted in disease states, with retraction pockets showing broad regions of low gradient consistent with a flattened contour. Longitudinal imaging demonstrated the ability to track disease progression; in one case, a retraction pocket progressed over 1 year to contact the cochlear promontory with associated focal thickening. CONCLUSIONS: OCT otoscopy enables rapid, noninvasive, point-of-care volumetric imaging of the TM and ME. It provides quantitative metrics that improve diagnostic accuracy and allow objective monitoring of disease progression. OCT otoscopy has the potential to become a valuable tool in routine clinical practice.
authors: Marcela A. Morán; Zihan Yang; Wihan Kim; Wejdan Alsherhri; John S. Oghalai; Brian E. Applegate

title: Optimasi Penjadwalan Proses Produksi Berbasis Laxity dengan Algoritma ELLF untuk SmartEdu Station
abstract: Penjadwalan urutan eksekusi job pada mesin produksi merupakan keputusan operasional krusial yang memengaruhi throughput dan pemenuhan tenggat waktu. Di antara algoritma penjadwalan dinamis, pendekatan berbasis laxity dengan Least Laxity First (LLF) secara teoretis optimal namun mengalami laxity thrashing, yaitu peralihan konteks berlebihan ketika beberapa job memiliki nilai laxity yang sama. Penelitian ini mengimplementasikan Enhanced Least Laxity First (ELLF) sebagai perluasan LLF dengan mekanisme exclusion shield untuk menghilangkan thrashing, yang diadaptasi dari penjadwalan prosesor berskala tick mikrodetik ke skala waktu manufaktur berbasis tick detik. Algoritma diterapkan pada arsitektur IoT empat lapis berbiaya rendah menggunakan Raspberry Pi dengan tumpukan pemantauan InfluxDB dan Grafana, pada studi kasus mesin induction-forging baut. Pengujian mencakup dua skenario beban (underload dan overload) dengan delapan job periodik selama lima kali pengulangan independen. Hasil menunjukkan ELLF mencapai nol preemption pada kondisi overload (penurunan 100% dari 1,28 preemption/job pada LLF), dengan trade-off berupa kenaikan waktu tunggu sekitar 15% dan tardiness rata-rata 232 ms. Arsitektur IoT mendistribusikan telemetri penjadwal ke InfluxDB dengan latensi sub-detik tanpa mengganggu kinerja. Melalui pengujian simulasi perangkat lunak, penelitian ini membuktikan secara empiris bahwa pendekatan berbasis laxity, khususnya ELLF, efektif untuk penjadwalan produksi soft real-time pada arsitektur IoT berbiaya rendah. Sistem penjadwalan ini ditujukan untuk diintegrasikan pada SmartEdu Station.
authors: Noer Fajrin; Yuliadi Erdani; Muhammad Avila Thirafi; Suharyadi Pancono; Cyndi Odilia Sumantri; Natasya Nareswari

title: PROSPECTIVE DOUBLE-BLINDED RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL ON ROBOTIC ARM-ASSISTED VERSUS CONVENTIONAL ONE-STAGE BILATERAL TOTAL KNEE ARTHROPLASTY WITH TWO-YEAR FOLLOW-UP
abstract: Introduction Robotic arm assisted total knee arthroplasty(RA-TKA) has gained popularity. Yet for postoperative pain and patient reported outcomes, high quality evidence is lacking. We hypothesize that RA-TKA would provide better postoperative pain control and patient reported outcomes in Chinese patients. Methods This is a double blinded randomized controlled trial(RCT) with 2-year follow-up in patients undergoing one stage bilateral total knee arthroplasty at a tertiary institution. All patients were randomized to receive one conventional TKA(C-TKA) targeting mechanical alignment while the other received RA-TKA targeting restricted kinematic alignment. Triathlon cruciate retaining cementless TKA were used exclusively. Primary outcome measure was numeric pain score(10). Secondary outcome included patient's preferred side, Oxford knee score(OKS), Knee injury and osteoarthritis outcome score(KOOS), mediolateral laxity, range of motion(ROM), alignment and complications. Measurements were recorded preoperatively, daily during inpatient stay, 6 weeks, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year and 2 years. Results 59 patients(118 TKAs) completed the study. RA-TKA group showed statistically significant better pain score than C-TKA on postop Day 3 (RA-TKA: 4.6, C-TKA: 4.2, p =0.014) up to 6 weeks (RA-TKA: 3, C-TKA: 2.6, p =0.04). There was no difference in patient's preferred side at 6 weeks, 1 year and 2 years with 29% favouring conventional side, 36% favouring robotic side and 35% felt no difference between two sides (p=0.36). Oxford knee scores, KOOS scores were comparable. Operating times were longer for RA-TKA(97 min) compared to C-TKA(81min)(p<0.001). Medial-lateral laxity at both 0° and 90° were significantly more in C-TKA(6° and 6°) compared to RA-TKA(4.1° and 3.7°) respectively(both p<0.001). Postoperative alignment showed significantly more alignment outliers(>3°deviation) with C-TKA(16) compared to RA-TKA(10). Discussion and Conclusion This double blinded RCT demonstrated small but significant reduction in pain for RA-TKA compared with C-TKA before 6 weeks but similar patient reported outcomes. There was no clear preference of robotic or conventional side surgery.
authors: Henry FU; Vincent Wai Kwan Chan; Amy Cheung; Man Hong Cheung; Michelle Hilda Luk; Kwong Yuen Chiu

title: PSYCHIATRY The Case for Starting Over
abstract: AbstractPsychiatry is the only branch of medicine that still diagnoses without reference to the organ it treats. Psychiatry: The Case for Starting Over argues that this is a structural failure rather than a temporary gap. The descriptive nosology inherited from Kraepelin and formalized in the DSM achieved diagnostic reliability at the cost of validity. Its categories were assembled by committee consensus rather than grounded in mechanism, and so it cannot guide the circuit-targeted therapies now reshaping the field.The book traces this problem historically and then builds an alternative from three converging lines of work. The first is computational neural-network modeling of psychopathology, from Hopfield and Hinton through Hoffman's simulations of schizophrenia and the author's own work. The second is systems neuroscience, including large-scale networks, global workspace and integrated information theories, attractor dynamics, and small-world connectivity. The third is Friston's Free Energy Principle and predictive processing.From this synthesis the book introduces Neuroanalysis and its clinical instrument, Clinical Brain Profiling (CBP). CBP treats mental disorders as disturbances of dynamic brain-network organization and organizes them across four timescales of plasticity:•Cognizance plasticity (milliseconds) is centered on the central executive network and linked to psychosis and negative signs.•Reactive plasticity (minutes to hours) is centered on the salience network and linked to anxiety.•Adaptive plasticity (days to weeks) sits at the salience–default mode interface and is linked to depression and mania.•Developmental plasticity (lifetime) is centered on the default mode network and linked to personality disorder patterns.The book reviews the neuromodulation toolkit: ECT, DBS, TMS, tDCS/tACS, psychedelic-assisted therapy, and focused ultrasound. It then proposes an entity-matched "grammar of plasticity" for selecting, combining, and sequencing these interventions. Guiding principles include strengthening prefrontal regulation before driving motivation, opening plasticity windows before directing them, and continuous biomarker monitoring.Throughout, the author separates established science from theoretical proposal and untested hypothesis. He outlines what validation would require: prospective outcome trials, clinically feasible network measures, and a cultural shift from single-label diagnosis to multidimensional profiling. The result is a case for rebuilding psychiatry as a measurement-based, mechanism-guided clinical neuroscience.
authors: Peled A.

title: Penjadwalan Proses Dinamis Berbasis Kombinasi Deadline dan LLF pada MES SmartEdu Station
abstract: Penjadwalan proses pada lingkungan manufaktur dinamis memerlukan mekanisme pengambilan keputusan yang mampu merespons perubahan kondisi produksi secara cepat dan tepat. Penelitian ini bertujuan mengimplementasikan metode Deadline Scheduling dan Least Laxity First (LLF) pada Manufacturing Execution System (MES) SmartEdu Station untuk mendukung penjadwalan proses dinamis pada lingkungan job shop manufacturing. Penelitian dilakukan melalui pengembangan modul penjadwalan yang mengintegrasikan evaluasi deadline dan perhitungan nilai laxity dalam proses penentuan prioritas pekerjaan. Data penelitian berupa beberapa pekerjaan produksi dengan waktu kedatangan, waktu proses, dan batas penyelesaian yang berbeda. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa metode Deadline Scheduling mampu mengidentifikasi kelayakan pekerjaan berdasarkan batas waktu penyelesaian, sedangkan metode LLF mampu menentukan prioritas pekerjaan secara dinamis berdasarkan tingkat urgensi yang direpresentasikan oleh nilai laxity. Implementasi kedua metode menghasilkan mekanisme penjadwalan yang adaptif terhadap perubahan kondisi produksi dan mampu mendukung pengambilan keputusan produksi secara lebih efektif pada MES SmartEdu Station.
authors: Yuliadi Erdani; Setyawan Ajie Sukarno; Muhammad Giri Suhada; Susetyo Bagas Bhaskoro; Ismail Rokhim

title: Personalized rehabilitation in autism spectrum disorder: artificial intelligence technologies for diagnosis, prediction, and adaptive interventions
abstract: Autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) represent a heterogeneous group of neurodevelopmental conditions. Diagnosis and treatment of autism carry high social significance, necessitating the development of effective rehabilitation strategies. Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies offer fundamentally new opportunities to personalize rehabilitation interventions in ASD. This comprehensive review examines key directions for AI integration into clinical practice: enhancing diagnostic objectivity through digital phenotyping, predicting individual developmental trajectories and treatment responses, and designing adaptive therapeutic systems. Particular attention is paid to AI-assisted technologies for developing social communication skills, including virtual reality and social robotics. Meta-analytic data confirm the clinical utility of AI technologies, showing moderate-to-large effects for social communication, emotion recognition, and adaptive skills. Naturalistic developmental behavioral interventions, combined with augmentative and alternative communication technologies have been shown to demonstrate sustained improvements in spontaneous communication in minimally verbal patients. The review discusses prospects for personalizing interventions based on physiological monitoring data and prognostic modeling along with the role of telehealth technologies and intelligent family support systems. Critical challenges of AI system implementation are analyzed, ranging from privacy risks to the translational gap between research and clinical practice. Overall, maximizing the potential of AI in ASD rehabilitation requires a balanced approach combining accurate and explainable algorithms, inclusive user design, and interdisciplinary collaboration with active involvement of autistic individuals and their families at all stages of frontier technology development and implementation.
authors: Igor V. Shirolapov; Mariya Stanislavovna Sergeeva; Alexander Vladimirovich Zakharov

title: Perturbational signature of the somato-cognitive action network in human primary motor cortex
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Functional-MRI evidence recently identified inter-effector regions in the primary motor cortex that show preferential connectivity with the action mode network (AMN), constituting the somato-cognitive action network (SCAN). Direct causal evidence for the functional engagement of these regions remains limited. AIM: Here, we investigated the perturbational neural response of one inter-effector region using transcranial magnetic stimulation combined with electroencephalography (TMS-EEG). METHODS: Sixteen healthy participants underwent recording of transcranial evoked potentials from the first dorsal interosseus, tibialis anterior, and the inter-effector region between them, which was identified with TMS motor mapping. RESULTS: Differences between conditions were assessed using cluster-based permutation testing and general linear modeling. Inter-effector-specific TMS-EEG activity was observed at approximately 42 ms post-stimulation, partially involving regions of the AMN. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION: Our findings provide the first perturbational characterization of inter-effector regions in human M1 and identify TMS-EEG markers that enable probing of SCAN functional organization.
authors: Marco Mancuso; Davide Maccarrone; Giulia Ruocco; Angelo Collura; Stefano Pellegrini; Danny Adrian Spampinato; Daniele Belvisi; Alfredo Berardelli; Antonella Conte; Giorgio Leodori

title: Physical Ergonomics in Robotics
abstract: With the emergence of embodied intelligent systems like collaborative robots (cobots), the landscape of physically demanding work is changing. Indeed, robotic devices can augment human strength, optimize performance, and minimize the physical demands associated with a job or a task. These achievements of human-robot interaction (HRI) surely match the objectives of physical ergonomics: making physical interactions between humans and other elements of a system more efficient, more gratifying, and safer. One of the key goals of physical ergonomics certainly is to prevent work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs). Therefore, a cobot must have insight into the effect of physical stress on the human body. One of the most common ways to provide that is to use the established ergonomics look-up tables that indicate which working configurations and conditions may cause WMSDs based on experience. Another approach is to use musculoskeletal models to get real-time estimates of key internal body parameters, such as joint torques, muscle forces, and muscle fatigue. A cobotic or, in general, robotic system can then use these ergonomic indexes and variables to guide a human co-worker to more favourable configurations and conditions. In this chapter, we examine physical human-robot interactions (pHRIs) to have an introductory overview of possible scenarios and constraints. We then look into the fundamentals of physical ergonomics such as anthropometry, biomechanics, and environmental factors, including important ergonomic assessment tools and innovative indicators developed in robotics. Subsequently, concrete examples of methods that address physical ergonomics with collaborative robotics are examined in terms of design and control methods.
authors: Pauline Maurice; Luka Peternel; WanSoo Kim; Simona Crea; Vineet Vashista; Giacinto Barresi; Alberto Ranavolo; Anna Bucchieri; Giulia A. Albanese; Michael Holmes; Jacopo Zenzeri

title: Physical Twins: Accelerating and Enabling Robot Learning with Phantom Platforms
abstract: Improvements in human-robot physical interaction (pHRI) can have major implications for physical therapy, search and rescue, and telemedicine. However, a major challenge concerns human constraints and safety in human-robot physical experiments. Concerns about human studies also include repeatability, scalability, and participant diversity. To conduct such experiments, an IRB and willing human participants are required. In this work, we present an improved phantom device, a physical twin, that enables real-world RL-type testing for physically interactive algorithms. The new device not only replicates the ball-and-socket motion of the shoulder but also renders scapular and protraction/retraction motions. The experiments showcase the device's ability to render multiple 3D joint limits and demonstrate a Franka Panda arm sensing limits and interacting with the device as an arm for ADLs (activities of daily living) and pHRI tasks.
authors: Elizabeth Peiros; Derek Chen; Lucas Yager; Edward Lee; Kevin Wang; Zoe Samuels; Michael C. Yip

title: Physics-informed neural operators for rapid electric field prediction in transcranial magnetic stimulation of healthy and tumor subjects
abstract: Accurate and rapid prediction of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS)-induced electric fields is essential for personalized clinical applications, from individualized therapy in major depressive disorder to presurgical functional mapping in neuro-oncology. Yet conventional finite element methods are often too computationally expensive for interactive use. Existing deep learning surrogate models partly address this limitation but are largely constrained to fixed voxel-grid representations that cannot naturally accommodate the irregular geometry of subject-specific head meshes. We present the first physics-informed neural operator (PINO) for subject-specific prediction of vector TMS electric fields, built on a mesh-native dual-encoder architecture that jointly encodes head anatomy and coil configuration. By incorporating a curl-based regularization term aligned with the curl-free nature of the TMS secondary field, the PINO model promotes physical consistency as a soft regularizer alongside data-driven supervision. Trained on 75 subjects from the IXI dataset, the framework was evaluated across four independent held-out test datasets, including healthy subjects from two additional MRI cohorts and, for the first time in learning-based TMS electric-field prediction, tumor patients. The resolution-agnostic formulation generalizes across subjects, coil types, and spatial resolutions without retraining, predicting vector electric fields on approximately 300,000 gray matter volume nodes in under 100 ms on a consumer-grade GPU. Across all test datasets within the focality-50% region, the PINO model achieved median center-of-gravity errors of 0.39–0.43 mm, RMSE of 0.12–0.16 V/m, and mean angular deviations of 6.7°–7.3°, with performance within or below the error ranges reported by recent deep-learning approaches. At the selected 5% physics-loss weighting, curl loss decreased by 9.1% relative to the data-only model, while RMSE and MAD increased by only 1.6% and 1.3%, respectively. These results suggest that physics-informed neural operators provide a scalable technical foundation for rapid gray-matter electric-field approximation, supporting future studies on real-time electric-field-guided TMS workflows
authors: Philipp Moser; Fabian Greifeneder; Dominik Freinberger; Gernot Reishofer; Pia Ritter; Louis Frank; Stefan Thumfart; Sascha Freigang; K Mahdy Ali

title: Polarization complete left invariant connections
abstract: Let $(M,\nabla)$ be a real analytic Koszul manifold. An adapted complex structure (ac-structure) on a neighborhood $N$ of the zero section in $TM$ is a complex structure on $N$ such that the leaves of the Levi-Civita foliation are holomorphic curves. More generally, a complex polarization $P$ on $N$ is called an ac-polarization if the leaves of the Levi-Civita foliation are tangential to $P$. The bundle of (1,0) tangent vectors of an ac-structure is an ac-polarization. The connection is called entire (resp. polarization complete or simply $\mathcal P$-complete) if the ac-structure (resp. the ac-polarization) exists on $TM$. Although on a small enough $N$ an ac-structure always exists, entire connections are rear and if a maximal domain of definition $N_{max}$ of an ac-structure exists (different from $TM$), $N_{max}$ is a complicated domain. On the other hand in many cases the associated ac-polarization can be extended to the whole $TM$. The main purpose of the paper is to gain better understanding of this phenomenon using a generalized version of the polar map. As special cases we show that many of those metrics studied by Aslam-Burns-Irvine and Halverscheid-Iannuzzi although are not entire but are $\mathcal P$-complete.
authors: Balázs Forman; Róbert Szőke

title: Posterior cruciate ligament biomechanics in pediatric finite element knee models: Validation against cadaveric posterior tibial translation and coupled rotational loading
abstract: Background Pediatric posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) biomechanics remain poorly characterized, and validated computational models are limited. The purpose of this study was to evaluate whether pediatric knee finite element models could reproduce intact cadaveric posterior tibial translation under PCL-dominant loading. Methods Twenty-two pediatric knee models were generated from computed tomography scans using a previously established juvenile modeling workflow. Model predictions were benchmarked against published intact cadaveric data for two loading conditions: a 134 N posterior tibial load at 30° flexion and a coupled 100 N posterior tibial load with 5 Nm external rotation at 0° of flexion. Posterior tibial translation was compared using Welch's two-sample t -tests and confidence intervals. Findings Under isolated posterior loading at 30°, the models predicted 9.4 ± 1.4 mm of posterior tibial translation compared with 10.8 ± 3.7 mm in the cadaveric benchmark ( p = 0.15). No significant difference was found under the coupled posterior loading with external rotation between the models predicted posterior translations of 6.9 ± 0.6 mm and the experimental translation at 6.5 ± 3.1 ( p = 0.56). Interpretation These findings support the use of specimen-specific pediatric knee models as an externally benchmarked platform for studying PCL biomechanics. Accurate reproduction of cadaveric posterior laxity under clinically relevant loading provides a foundation for future analyses of pediatric injury mechanisms and surgical and rehabilitation strategies.
authors: Alexandria Mallinos; Richard P Steiner; Kerwyn C. Jones

title: Postoperative Quadriceps Symmetry, Knee Laxity, and Single-Leg Hop Performance in Association with 24-Month Ipsilateral Graft Retear After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: A Cohort Study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Ipsilateral graft retear after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) remains a major concern in athletes, while the relationship between postoperative mechanical and functional measures and retear remains uncertain. METHODS: This cohort study included 48 athletes after primary unilateral ACLR with hamstring-tendon autograft. Follow-up was scheduled at 6, 9, and 12 months (184 ± 13, 276 ± 17, and 368 ± 22 days), and the analytic export retained one postoperative value per athlete for GNRB side-to-side laxity at 250 N, concentric isokinetic quadriceps limb symmetry index (LSI) at 60°/s, single-leg hop-for-distance LSI, and patient-reported outcomes, without preserving the originating visit. MRI-confirmed ipsilateral graft retear was recorded within 24 months after clinically suspected reinjury; retear dates were not retained. RESULTS: = 0.011), and each 1-SD higher quadriceps LSI was associated with lower retear odds (OR 0.43, 95% CI 0.21-0.89). In an exploratory threshold analysis, quadriceps LSI < 85% was associated with a higher retear proportion (RR 3.21, 95% CI 1.17-8.82). Associations for knee laxity, hop performance, and patient-reported outcomes were not statistically robust. CONCLUSIONS: Postoperative quadriceps symmetry showed the clearest association with 24-month graft-retear status. However, because the originating measurement visit and retear dates were unavailable, temporal precedence could not be established, and the exploratory <85% LSI finding should not be interpreted as a validated return-to-sport threshold.
authors: Georgios Kakavas; Nikos Malliaropoulos; Florian Forelli

title: Postoperative outcomes after conventional, robotic-arm-assisted, and pressure-sensor-guided cruciate-retaining total knee arthroplasty: a retrospective cohort study
abstract: Conventional cruciate-retaining total knee arthroplasty (CR-TKA) uses manual instrumentation and surgeon-directed soft-tissue assessment, whereas MAKO robotic-arm assistance adds geometry- and gap-distance guidance and Verasense pressure sensing adds compartment-load feedback. Whether these approaches are associated with different clinically relevant postoperative outcomes remains uncertain. To evaluate associations between surgical technique and postoperative pain, range of motion, and function across conventional, MAKO-assisted, and Verasense-guided CR-TKA, and explore whether preoperative severity modified associations with postoperative outcomes. The single-centre cohort included 173 knees in 139 patients (36 Conventional, 92 MAKO, 45 Verasense). Analyses proceeded from post hoc favourable change to principal covariate-adjusted postoperative outcomes, followed by post hoc baseline-severity interactions. Principal models adjusted for baseline value, age, sex, and body mass index. Knee-level outcomes accounted for within-patient clustering; the Knee Society Function Score was analysed once per patient. Holm correction was applied within each stated test family. No outcome showed a Holm-adjusted group difference in favourable improvement or adjusted postoperative status. Verasense versus MAKO showed greater pain improvement (0.769 points; Holm P = 0.2195) and lower adjusted postoperative pain (-0.318 points; Holm P = 0.2546), but neither met the corrected criterion. Postoperative pain was zero in 125 of 149 knees (83.9%). The Knee Society Function Score severity interaction disappeared within the baseline range shared by all groups. We found no robust evidence that conventional instrumentation, geometry-based MAKO assistance, and load-based Verasense guidance were associated with different postoperative outcomes or that preoperative severity showed a reproducible technique-dependent association with outcomes. The Verasense-versus-MAKO pain pattern was hypothesis-generating and established neither superiority nor equivalence.

title: Precision cognitive neurorehabilitation: dose, adaptivity, digital therapeutics and implementation
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Cognitive deficits are determinants of long-term disability and socio-professional reintegration across neurological disorders, including stroke, traumatic brain injury, multiple sclerosis, and neurodegenerative diseases. Despite evidence supporting cognitive neurorehabilitation, its implementation remains heterogeneous, and therapeutic parameters are insufficiently defined. AREAS COVERED: The authors reviewed the published literature from PubMed and Google Scholar from 1 January 2015 to 30 June 2026, supplemented by seminal publications. Clinical trials, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and observational and proof-of-concept studies were prioritized. This brief narrative review examines restorative and compensatory cognitive neurorehabilitation for deficits of attention, executive functions, language and disorders of consciousness in people after stroke and traumatic brain injury (TBI), older adults, and those with neurological and neurodegenerative conditions, including multiple sclerosis, Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease. Emphasis is placed on dose, frequency, adaptivity, personalization, and digital and technology-assisted interventions. Methodological challenges include heterogeneity of protocols, limited use of active control conditions, insufficient long-term follow-up, and the gap between cognitive test improvements and meaningful effects on participation. EXPERT OPINION: Advancing cognitive neurorehabilitation requires precision-driven approaches integrating digital therapeutics with clinical frameworks. Large-scale pragmatic trials, meaningful endpoints, and implementation strategies across the continuum of care will be essential to transform cognitive neurorehabilitation into a component of neurological practice.

title: Predictors of 6-month clinical change in primary progressive aphasia following language therapy and transcranial magnetic stimulation
abstract: Abstract Primary progressive aphasia (PPA) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive language impairment. Available treatments and information on factors associated with clinical change and treatment response remain limited. This study is a post-hoc analysis of a randomized controlled trial and aimed to identify baseline demographic, cognitive, and neuroimaging factors associated with clinical change in a subanalysis of a double-blind, randomized, parallel clinical trial of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and language therapy in PPA. Fifty-seven patients diagnosed with PPA received six months of lexical retrieval treatment, 40 with active TMS and 17 with sham TMS. All participants underwent comprehensive cognitive and language assessments before treatment and were evaluated using the Mini Linguistic State Examination (MLSE), naming task, words per minute, the Interview for Deterioration in Daily Living Activities in Dementia (IDDD), the Neuropsychiatric Inventory (NPI), and fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) scans before and after treatment. Predictors of clinical change were analyzed using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) and Elastic Net regression models, and unsupervised k-means clustering was applied to identify response profiles. Models for MLSE (LASSO: R2=0.52; Elastic Net: R2=0.57), naming (LASSO: R2=0.42; Elastic Net: R2=0.41), IDDD (LASSO: R2=0.46; Elastic Net: R2=0.58), and NPI (LASSO: R2=0.81; Elastic Net: R2=0.77) demonstrated good predictive accuracy. TMS treatment consistently emerged as the strongest predictor of clinical improvement across all outcomes. Higher metabolism in several brain regions (left hippocampus, posterior cingulate, and orbitofrontal cortex) predicted greater clinical improvement. Cluster analysis identified two subgroups: responders and non-responders, with 77.5% of patients receiving active TMS in the responder cluster, and 82.4% of the sham group in the non-responder cluster. Among patients receiving active TMS, a positive effect was associated with the non-fluent and semantic variants and with better cognitive performance in non-language domains. In conclusion, TMS treatment emerged as the main factor associated with clinical improvement on cognitive-linguistic and functional measures. Better cognitive performance and preserved brain metabolism in key regions were linked to more favorable clinical outcomes. These findings underscore the potential of TMS in combination with language therapy, and pave the way for precision medicine approaches in PPA, emphasizing the need to identify individual profiles that predict optimal treatment response.

title: Preoperative coronal phenotype is associated with the initial balance state but only weakly with final balance in robot‐assisted TKA
abstract: Abstract Purpose To determine how preoperative coronal phenotype and structural remodelling relate to initial and final intraoperative balance in robot‐assisted total knee arthroplasty. Methods Initial analyses included 429 knees; final/change analyses included 389. Preoperative phenotype was characterised by hip‐knee‐ankle angle (HKA), arithmetic HKA (aHKA), functional knee phenotype (FKP), and categorical aHKA–joint‐line obliquity (JLO) components. Structural factors included medial and lateral osteophyte burden and coronal tibiofemoral subluxation. Medial and lateral gaps and coronal laxity ranges were recorded in extension and flexion before and after balancing. Signed mediolateral gap difference was defined as lateral minus medial, and change as final minus initial. Initial extension signed gap difference was the primary outcome; corresponding initial flexion, final, and change outcomes were secondary. Compartment‐specific gaps, laxity ranges, and varus–valgus analyses were exploratory. Multivariable linear regression adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index, with patient‐level cluster‐robust standard errors and Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate correction. Results The FKP model incorporating all structural factors yielded adjusted R 2 values of 0.201 for the primary outcome and 0.125 for initial flexion, leaving approximately 80% of primary‐outcome variability unexplained. In the overall cohort, the maximum adjusted R 2 across final outcomes was 0.064. For extension and flexion changes, FKP alone and HKA alone yielded adjusted R 2 values of 0.234 and 0.122, respectively. In exploratory comparisons, valgus knees had greater initial extension and flexion signed gap differences than varus knees (adjusted mean differences, 3.10 mm [95% confidence interval, 2.39–3.81] and 2.98 mm [2.23–3.74], respectively; both false discovery rate‐adjusted p values were < 0.001). Conclusions Preoperative coronal phenotype and structural remodelling explained only modest variability in the initial intraoperative balance state and changes between assessments, and little variability in final balance, particularly in flexion. These findings support direct intraoperative assessment. Level of Evidence Level III, retrospective cohort study.
authors: Yugo Morita; Nikolaos Mylonakis; Jonggu Shin; Mohammed El-Hassan; Ittai Shichman; Eustathios Kenanidis; Eleftherios Tsiridis; Peter Keyes Sculco

title: Prevalence of Bovine Spastic Syndrome in Sweden
abstract: Bovine Spastic Syndrome (BOSS) is a chronic, progressive neuromuscular disorder that affects adult cattle. The disorder causes intermittent episodes of painful cramps in the hindlimbs that impair movement. Little is known about its presence in Sweden. This study aimed to explore the occurrence of clinical signs compatible with BOSS in Swedish cattle herds and to identify herd-level factors associated with farmer-reported cases. An online survey aimed at Swedish cattle owners was conducted between June and September 2025, yielding 201 responses from all 21 counties and a range of production systems. Approximately one-third of respondents reported having observed animals over three years of age showing clinical signs consistent with BOSS. Reports were geographically widespread but varied by county. Observations were substantially more common in dairy herds: 60% of dairy respon-dents had observed signs, and dairy producers accounted for 80% of all positive reports. In contrast, only 6% of beef producers reported observing signs. Although the study relied on self-reported observations and cannot confirm clinical diagnoses, the results indicate that clinical signs compatible with BOSS are present in many parts of Sweden and may be more frequently recognized in dairy systems. These findings highlight the need for improved diagnostic awareness, targeted epidemiological surveillance, and further investigation into risk factors and potential genetic components of the syndrome.

title: Probing the role of left inferior frontal gyrus in vocal motor control: Evidence from TMS and causal inference analysis
abstract: Beyond an established role in speech initiation and planning, the left inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) may contribute to sensorimotor control of speech production. We applied continuous theta burst stimulation (cTBS) over the anterior (aIFG) and posterior (pIFG) regions to investigate their roles in vocal motor control. A causal inference analysis (CIA) framework was developed to characterize source-space network organization. cTBS over both left aIFG and pIFG reduced vocal responses and enhanced P2 responses to pitch feedback perturbations, with no significant differences between two active stimulations. However, global dissimilarity analysis revealed greater P2-related topographic deviation from sham stimulation following aIFG stimulation than following pIFG stimulation. CIA further identified different source-space network patterns associated with aIFG and pIFG stimulation. These findings demonstrate the causal involvement of the left IFG in auditory-vocal integration and highlight the potential of CIA for characterizing distributed network organization underlying vocal motor control.
