title: AI-guided epitope engineering of a SARS-CoV-2 spike antigen for broad sarbecovirus neutralization
abstract: The rapid evolution of SARS-CoV-2 and the ongoing risk of zoonotic spillover highlight the need for vaccines that provide broad protection beyond strain-specific immunity. Here, we present a structure-guided, AI-enabled strategy for rational antigen design that enhances cross-reactive B-cell epitope recognition across betacoronaviruses. By integrating comparative sequence analysis with conformational epitope prediction, we identified conserved epitope hotspots within the Spike receptor-binding domain and introduced targeted motif-level substitutions into a SARS-CoV-2 BA.2 backbone. Engineered Spike immunogens, delivered as mRNA-lipid nanoparticle vaccines, elicited robust antibody responses in mice and demonstrated broad neutralizing activity against antigenically diverse SARS-CoV-2 variants, including BA.5 and XBB.1.5, as well as zoonotic sarbecoviruses. Selected designs reached neutralisation breadth comparable to an Omicron-adapted clinical benchmark for shared SARS-CoV-2 antigens, while extending neutralising activity to divergent zoonotic sarbecoviruses. These findings show that minimal, structure-guided epitope remodeling can enhance the presentation of conserved epitopes and improve antibody breadth, providing a generalizable framework for designing vaccines resilient to viral evolution and future pandemic threats.
authors: Alexandru Odainic; Ioannis Vardaxis; Matheus Ferraz; Katrin E. Wiese; Lisette A. H. M. Cornelissen; Akhilesh Sharma; Richard Stratford; Trevor Clancy; Kaïdre Bendjama

title: AI-mediated data collection and the relocation of values in qualitative health research
abstract: As the prospect of the ‘AI scientist’ moves from speculation to practical research agendas, there is a growing need to understand what happens when stages of qualitative health research that have traditionally depended on human judgement are delegated to artificial intelligence (AI). Using chatbot-mediated data collection as a case study, this paper takes a first step towards understanding this broader development by examining how AI relocates the value-laden judgements inherent in research. Drawing on the philosophy of science debate on the value-ladenness of scientific practices, it argues that using AI in research does not eliminate value-laden judgements but relocates them: from researchers exercising discretion throughout the research process to system designers encoding value decisions in prompts, algorithms and conversational architecture at the outset. The paper develops an analytical framework centred around three key decision points within research projects: (1) prioritisation, which refers to the decision of what to study; (2) operationalisation, which refers to how to define and measure it; and (3) adequacy, which refers to what counts as enough evidence. Across all three decision points, chatbot-mediated research is shown to increase standardisation and in some respects auditability relative to human-driven data collection. At the same time, it can reduce epistemic diversity to the extent that designs draw on a limited number of models, prompt patterns and methodological conventions. The paper concludes that AI-mediated instruments should not be treated as neutral tools. While the analysis focuses on qualitative interviewing, where AI’s adaptive character makes the relocation of values most visible, the questions it raises are likely to grow in importance as AI is integrated into other stages of research. Research design and research ethics must give greater attention to the design assumptions and prompts embedded in AI-mediated systems.
authors: Aurelia Sauerbrei; Angeliki Kerasidou; Federica Lucivero

title: Abstract A123: AI-PACED: A prospective feasibility study of automated risk stratification, AI-augmented serial imaging, and biobanking for early detection of sporadic pancreatic cancer
abstract: Abstract Purpose: Sporadic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA) is diagnosed almost exclusively after symptom onset, often when curative resection is no longer feasible. Glycemically-defined new-onset diabetes (gNOD) with an ENDPAC score ≥3 identifies a population at markedly elevated short-term risk, and radiomics-based AI models have identified sub-visual, pre-diagnostic imaging signatures of PDA that precede symptomatic presentation. Translating these signatures into a prospective early detection pathway requires establishing recruitment yield, imaging and biospecimen adherence, and integration of a radiomics-based AI into real-world workflows. We designed the AI-Augmented Pancreas Cancer Early Detection (AI-PACED) study, a prospective, dual-cohort feasibility trial (NCT07324096) evaluating serial AI-analysis of CT and longitudinal blood biobanking in a gNOD, ENDPAC-enriched high-risk population. Methods: Individuals with gNOD, identified through weekly semi-automated EMR-based risk stratification and confirmed by manual chart review, self-select into Cohort A1 (serial CT and blood biobanking), Cohort A2 (blood biobanking alone), or passive EMR surveillance (Cohort B). Target enrollment is 100 (70 in A1/A2, 30 in Group B). Cohorts A1 and A2 undergo blood collection at baseline, 6, and 12 months. Cohort A1 additionally undergoes paired portal venous phase contrast-enhanced CT, concentrated during the first year after gNOD onset, when PDA risk is highest, to prioritize detection while limiting incremental radiation exposure. All CTs are interpreted by non-study radiologists per standard institutional protocol. The AI analyses is applied post-hoc, firewalled from clinical care. Feasibility endpoints include gNOD identification yield, recruitment, and cohort self-selection among eligible high-risk individuals. The protocol is IRB-approved and open to accrual at Mayo Clinic, Rochester, Minnesota since March 2026. Results: Semi-automated EMR screening identified 253 candidate individuals, of whom manual chart review confirmed 175 (mean age: 66.6 years, range 50-84; 50.9% females) as true gNOD, comprising 16 with ENDPAC ≥3, 139 with ENDPAC <3, and 20 in whom ENDPAC could not be calculated. The remaining 78 were excluded as false positives (e.g., active malignancy, inaccurate glycemic values). This confirmation step distinguishes true, actionable gNOD from EMR artifact prior to outreach. Conclusions: AI-PACED supports the feasibility of a two-stage algorithmic and manual workflow for distinguishing true gNOD from EMR artifact, while quantifying the false-positive burden that will inform refinement of a fully automated pipeline. Recruitment into asymptomatic, imaging-intensive surveillance is likely to remain the principal constraint, particularly because most glycemic elevation is managed outside quaternary centers. These constraints motivate extending enrollment infrastructure beyond a single center to inform a multi-institutional trial evaluating lead-time advantage of an AI-driven strategy for earlier, potentially curative detection of sporadic PDA. title: Alzheimer's Disease Biomarkers Measured by Capillary Blood Collection Versus Venous Plasma and Cerebrospinal Fluid
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Blood biomarkers are increasingly critical for non-invasive Alzheimer's Disease (AD) diagnostics and research but typically require on-site processing. Remote point-of-care collection methods could enhance biomarker testing in clinical and research settings. We evaluated the safety and accuracy of blood collection via venous blood and two capillary blood collection devices (Tasso+ and TAPII) for measurements of amyloid-beta 42/40 ratio (Aβ42/40), phosphorylated-tau-217 (pTau217), neurofilament-light (NfL), and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) from capillary plasma to simultaneously collected venous plasma and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). METHODS: Patients seen at the Johns Hopkins Center for CSF Disorders (N = 192) underwent diagnostic lumbar punctures and venipuncture. Warming packs were held to the skin for 5 min before collecting capillary blood (via TAPII or Tasso+ device) and numeric pain scores. CSF, venous, and capillary plasma were analyzed using Quanterix SIMOA immunoassays. Statistical analysis included Pearson/Spearman correlations, Lasso regression, and quantitative comparisons using Bland-Altman plots. RESULTS: 86 TAPII and 126 Tasso+ plasma samples were collected (77 M, 115 F; mean age 61 ± 18.3 years, range 16-91). Tasso+ devices were 90.3% successful in collecting > 50 μL whole blood, and TAPII devices were 86% successful. Mean pain scores were significantly higher in venous than capillary collections (Venous 2.24/10, TAPII 0.73/10, Tasso+ 0.2/10, p < 0.001). Capillary Aβ42/40, NfL, and GFAP strongly correlated with venous plasma analytes (Tasso+: Aβ42/40 r = 0.75, NfL r = 0.91, GFAP r = 0.80, all p < 0.001; TAPII: Aβ42/40 r = 0.74, NfL r = 0.86, GFAP r = 0.84, all p < 0.001). Tasso+ capillary pTau217 weakly correlated with venous (r = 0.23, p = 0.04). Capillary NfL and GFAP correlated modestly with CSF NfL and GFAP (TAPII NfL r = 0.74, GFAP r = 0.6, all p < 0.0001; Tasso+ NfL r = 0.69, GFAP r = 0.59, all p < 0.0001). Capillary Aβ42/40 and pTau217 did not significantly correlate with CSF measures. Lasso regression identified age and GFAP as significant predictors of AD across capillary and venous samples (Tasso+ AUC = 0.87, TAPII AUC = 0.75, Venous AUC = 0.83). INTERPRETATION: Neurodegeneration biomarkers Aβ42/40, NfL, and GFAP in capillary plasma (Tasso+, TAPII) strongly correlated with venous plasma measures. Capillary and venous pTau217 correlated weakly, indicating further assay refinement is needed. Tasso+ collection was less painful and caused less hemolysis compared to TAPII.

title: Apparentness of Unseen Rejection Episodes Post Lung rLTx Is Reliably Enabled by ddcfDNA Detection
abstract: ddcfDNA emerged as a biomarker for post-transplantation management strategies. Lung retransplant recipients represent a particularly vulnerable patient population with an increased risk of allograft injury. The demand for understanding if ddcfDNA levels differ between primary lung transplant recipients and lung retransplant recipients becomes obvious. Eight lung retransplant recipients and 50 primary lung transplant recipients with comparable HLA Class I and Class II mismatch scores were included in this retrospective study. During post-transplant monitoring, ddcfDNA results were evaluated alongside data on patient humoral immune responses pre- and post-transplantation. Antibody profiles of lung retransplant recipients did not differ significantly from those of their primary transplant comparisons. However, significantly higher ddcfDNA levels were observed in the retransplant cohort (median: 1.463%, IQR: 0.810-2.745) compared with primary transplant cohort (median: 0.550%, IQR: 0.338-0.935), U = 100.50, Z = -2.24, p = 0.012, r = 0.29. We identified that lung retransplant recipients exhibit increased allograft injury not solely attributable to humoral responses. Our study highlights that these patients face a higher immunological risk and supports the need for closer clinical follow-up using a resilient biomarker such as ddcfDNA. Incorporating ddcfDNA as a surrogate marker into post-transplant monitoring would provide early and unambiguous insights into allograft rejection, enabling prompt interventions to prevent unfavourable outcomes in this particularly fragile patient group.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Related Risks in Interventional Pulmonology: An Exploratory Enumeration and Ranking Study Across Five General-Purpose Large Language Models
abstract: Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) is entering interventional pulmonology (IP) faster than its potential risks have been systematically catalogued. We explored whether general-purpose large language models (LLMs), now widely consulted informally by patients and clinicians, could provide a rapid and structured means of enumerating and ranking candidate AI-related risks in IP, potentially contributing to risk awareness and hypothesis generation. Methods: Five LLMs (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek) were each queried once, in independent, memory-free sessions, with one standardised prompt requesting ten ranked AI-related risks with impact and likelihood scores (1–5); an informal repeat administration was performed, but output stability was not formally assessed. The resulting 50 risk statements were inductively coded, by an AI coder with independent human validation by two reviewers, into 15 constructs nested in 8 higher-order domains. Results: Mean self-assigned impact was 3.92 (SD 0.78) and mean likelihood 3.54 (SD 0.68). The eight domains comprised AI technical/perceptual accuracy (diagnostic, detection and navigational error); automation bias and over-reliance; generalisability, algorithmic bias and health equity; model and system reliability over time; erosion of procedural competence; explainability, transparency and accountability; cybersecurity, privacy and data integrity; and cognitive and workflow burden. Five domains were raised by all five models and the remaining three by four of five. Two domains-AI technical/perceptual accuracy and automation bias-together accounted for every model’s two highest-ranked risks, and no risk statement outside these two domains was ranked first or second by any model. Deskilling (erosion of procedural competence), although listed by all five models, was never ranked above third by any model, whereas practising IP specialists in our prior international survey rated it the single highest research priority. Conclusions: These exploratory and hypothesis-generating findings suggest that general-purpose LLMs may have potential as a rapid, low-burden means of enumerating and ranking candidate AI-related risks and broadening awareness of issues that may warrant further investigation in IP. The lower ranking of deskilling by the LLMs than by domain experts indicates that LLM-generated rankings may under-prioritise risks that clinicians consider most important. Although their outputs are not validated measures of clinical risk and do not replace expert appraisal, we believe they may provide a starting point for subsequent human-led risk assessment and prioritization in an area of research that remains largely unexplored yet is highly relevant to patient safety.

title: Artificial intelligence and digital health in bronchoscopy: advances in diagnostic accuracy, real-time navigation and procedural skills training
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and procedure-linked digital health technologies are beginning to transform bronchoscopy across three interconnected domains. In terms of diagnostic accuracy, deep learning models applied to endobronchial ultrasound images and bronchoscopic videos can match or exceed human readers in differentiating benign from malignant lesions, although nearly all evidence remains at the level of test-accuracy metrics rather than clinical outcomes. In real-time navigation, AI-augmented fluoroscopy and tomosynthesis platforms represent the clearest example of clinically deployed AI that improves lesion localisation and diagnostic yield for peripheral pulmonary nodules, while camera-based localisation and shared-control robotic systems remain largely preclinical. In training, multiple randomised controlled trials demonstrate that AI-guided simulators significantly improve performance across experience levels, and that AI-derived metrics can objectively assess competence, although the first attempt to show impact on real-world clinical performance was inconclusive. This review synthesises the current literature across these three domains, distinguishing technologies that are currently used in clinical practice with supportive published evidence from those that remain investigational. It provides practising bronchoscopists and trainees with a balanced appraisal of what AI can realistically offer today, what limitations persist, and what developments are likely over the coming decade.

title: Assessment of breakage resistance of Improvacuter® venous blood collection tubes under standardised drop testing conditions
abstract: Blood collection tubes are integral to diagnostic workflows but are routinely exposed to mechanical stress during handling, transportation, and routine laboratory processing. Structural failure of these tubes may result in specimen loss and pose potential biohazard risks to healthcare personnel. This standards-based verification study evaluated the breakage resistance of six categories of IMPROVACUTER® venous blood collection tubes. A total of 108 tubes from three independent manufacturing lots were filled to their nominal draw volumes and subjected to a standardised 1 m drop test, with three consecutive drops per tube onto a concrete surface. Following testing, tubes were inspected for visible cracks, leakage, breakage, or cap dislodgement. Evaluation criteria were based on ISO 6710:2017 and ISO 2859-1 (AQL 1.5), with a predefined practical acceptance criterion of at least 90% passing per tube category. The overall pass rate was 94.4% (102/108; 95% CI, 88.3%–97.9%). Citrate tubes achieved a 100% pass rate, while Gel & Clot Activator, EDTA K2, Heparin, and Glucose tubes each demonstrated a 94.4% pass rate. Clot Activator tubes showed a pass rate of 88.9%. These findings indicate high breakage resistance under the standardised drop-test conditions evaluated; other performance characteristics were not assessed.

title: Assessment of the antibiotics resistant and biofilm formation of Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolated from Iraqi hospitalized patients
abstract: Background: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a leading cause of hospital acquired infections. It has multidrug resistance and high biofilm production leading to difficult treatment. Objectives: This study aimed to identify P. aeruginosa from clinical samples in Baghdad, Iraq. It also correlated the antibiotic susceptibility to quantitative biofilm production. Materials and Methods: 150 samples were collected from hospitals of Baghdad by a cross-sectional study. The isolates were identified by culture, biochemical tests and Vitek 2 system. The Kirby-Bauer method (CLSI) was used to test 10 antibiotics. The bio-film formation capacity was examined by crystal violet microtiter plate method at an absorbance of 630 nm. Results: one hundred isolates, were identified as P. aeruginosa, Infections were found in both sexes. Males made up 54% of cases while females 46% with non-significant P-value (p=0.236) in different age categories. The majority sites of infection from burns in (29%) and Urine (17%), Sputum and ear swabs each contributed (12%), Wound samples (10%) and Blood (8%) with highly significant (p=0.0001) between sources of infection. The results for antibiotic susceptibility test Trimethoprim showed the highest resistance (95%) followed by gentamicin (58%), ceftazidime (56%), piperacillin (52%), amikacin (52%), and levofloxacin (45%) in highly significant(p=0.0001). While colistin emerged as the most effective antimicrobial agent with 85% of the isolates being sensitive. Favorable sensitivity was also maintained for norfloxacin (58%), meropenem (52%), and imipenem (48%). The differences between resistance categories were all highly significant (p < 0.0001), indicating a severe resistance burden within the studied strains. 62% percent of isolates showed resistant phenotype with an overwhelming majority being the extensively drug resistant (XDR) phenotype (42%), Multi drug resistant (MDR) in 15% and Pan drug resistant in 5% . The One hundred isolates formed biofilm (100%) and moderate biofilm producers were predominant (62%) followed by strong 29%, weak 9% . The distribution of isolates by biofilm formation ability and gender shown highly significant in P-value 0.0001 with ratio 63% in males while 37% in females. Also, the biofilm of isolates increased in age categories 41-60, 21-40 37%, 33% respectively. The results also showed the relationship between Biofilm production and clinical sources, the Burn, urine, sputum, and ear swabs isolates showed highly significant in biofilm formation(0.0001 , 0.0079, 0.0094 and 0.0098) respectively. Across, the results had shown significant P-value in wound and skin swabs (0.0317, 0.0483).While non-significant P-value in Blood, ETT, Palatal tissue, tissue, stool, pus and cystic fibrosis. Several antibiotics also showed a significant link with biofilm strength. Such as piperacillin and colistin, resistance was significantly higher in stronger biofilm producers (p=0.0084, 0.0087), also the results showed that significant ratio in Norfloxacin, Meropenem (P-value 0.0316, 0.0325). and non-significant results in other antibiotics resistance. The multi-drug resistance classification was correlated with the level of biofilm three core tires formation this overall association was highly significant (p = 0.0001). However, the sensitive isolates group (p = 0.0001), the XDR group (p = 0.0001), and the PDR group (p = 0.0497) showed highly significant relationship while the MDR group non-significant (p = 0.2174). In particular, the majority of the XDR isolates (moderate 28, strong 11 and weak 3) (66.7%, 26.2% and 7.1% respectively) were corroborated the association between the highest level of resistance and strong biofilm formation. Conclusion: Clinical Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates showed widespread antibiotic resistance and biofilm formation, highlighting the urgent need for effective antimicrobial stewardship.

title: Association Between COVID-19 Vaccine Doses and Neurosensory Symptoms Among COVID-19-Positive Patients: A Retrospective Cross-Sectional Study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Ageusia and anosmia are common manifestations of COVID-19. This study examined whether their frequency among infected patients was associated with the recorded number of Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine doses; it was not designed to estimate causality or vaccine effectiveness. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cross-sectional analysis of 5,348 COVID-19-positive patients over five years of age followed by the San Miguelito Health Region, Panama, from July 7, 2021, through November 2, 2022. Unvaccinated patients and vaccinated patients whose recorded doses were exclusively Pfizer-BioNTech were included. Separate logistic regression models estimated associations between vaccine dose category (zero, one, two, or three to four doses) and self-reported ageusia and anosmia, with two doses as the reference. A post hoc sensitivity analysis additionally adjusted for swab month. RESULTS: Ageusia was reported by 507 patients (9.48%), and anosmia by 584 patients (10.92%). In the primary adjusted models, compared with two doses, adjusted odds ratios (aORs) for zero, one, and three to four doses were 1.87 (95% confidence interval (CI) 1.48-2.38), 2.68 (95% CI 1.99-3.60), and 0.26 (95% CI 0.18-0.36), respectively, for ageusia, and 1.82 (95% CI 1.46-2.27), 2.53 (95% CI 1.91-3.35), and 0.18 (95% CI 0.12-0.25), respectively, for anosmia. After categorical adjustment for swab month, all six dose-category estimates were attenuated, and none remained statistically significant. CONCLUSIONS: Primary models identified strong associations between recorded vaccine dose category and self-reported ageusia and anosmia among infected patients, but these associations did not persist after adjustment for swab month. The results are compatible with substantial confounding by epidemic period and should not be interpreted as causal effects or estimates of vaccine effectiveness.

title: Association Between Ferritin Levels and Hemoglobin Concentration Among Adolescent Girls in Indonesia
abstract: Background: Anemia remains a critical global public health concern, particularly among adolescent girls who face heightened vulnerability due to rapid physical growth spurts and periodic menstrual blood loss. Iron deficiency is recognized as the leading etiological factor, clinically culminating in iron deficiency anemia (IDA). Standard public health screenings routinely rely on standalone hemoglobin (Hb) measurements; however, a decline in Hb represents a late-stage manifestation of chronic iron depletion, which risks masking individuals suffering from latent iron deficiency. Methods: A cross-sectional school-based study was conducted in April 2026, involving 126 adolescent female students aged 12–18 years in Padang City who met the rigorous inclusion criteria. Whole blood samples were collected via venipuncture; hemoglobin concentrations were determined using an automated hematology analyzer, and serum ferritin levels were quantified via Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA). Statistical evaluations were performed using Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient (r_s) and Fisher's Exact test. Results: The majority of the respondents were non-anemic (84.9%) and presented with normal ferritin levels (77%). Spearman's Rho correlation test revealed a statistically significant, weak positive relationship between serum ferritin and hemoglobin levels (r_s=0.398, p=0.000). The scatter plot model illustrated a non-linear trajectory, characterized by a steep increase in Hb within the lower ferritin range (<30" ng/mL" ) before flattening into a plateau at higher ferritin values. Cross-tabulation indicated a highly significant association between anemia and iron deficiency status (p=0.000), showing that 68.4% of anemic participants were iron deficient. Notably, within the non-anemic cohort, 15% of the adolescent girls had already developed latent iron deficiency. Conclusion: There is a significant positive correlation between serum ferritin and hemoglobin concentrations, governed by a non-linear homeostatic threshold. Relying solely on isolated hemoglobin screenings risks misclassifying and omitting adolescent girls with latent iron deficiency, emphasizing the urgent need for comprehensive, universal preventive iron supplementation strategies.

title: Asymptomatic carriage of Streptococcus pyogenes and other potentially pathogenic microorganisms among children and staff in day-care facilities in Varna municipality
abstract: Introduction: Scarlet fever is an acute infection caused by group A β-hemolytic streptococcus, Streptococcus pyogenes. Childcare settings are an important environment for the circulation of pathogens causing upper respiratory tract infections, with asymptomatic carriage playing a significant role in epidemiological control.Aim: To investigate the asymptomatic carriage of S. pyogenes and other potentially pathogenic microorganisms in nasal and throat swabs among children and staff in two childcare facilities in the municipality of Varna.Materials and Methods: The study was conducted in 2025 in connection with Project No. 23013 funded by the Science Fund of the Medical University of Varna, entitled “Investigation of Group A Streptococcus pyogenes Carriage among Children and Staff in Childcare Facilities in the Varna Region,” and in accordance with the decision of the Research Ethics Committee (REC) at the Medical University of Varna, No. 142/18.04.2024. A total of 131 individuals were included in the study—112 children and 19 staff members. A nasal swab and a throat swab were collected once from each participant. Identification of the isolated microorganisms was performed using the Phoenix 100 automated system (BD). Fisher’s exact test was used for comparative analysis, while Fisher’s exact test with Monte Carlo simulation was applied to analyze nasal carriage by age.Results: S. pyogenes was not isolated from any of the samples examined. Resident microbiota was detected in nasal swabs from 99/131 participants (75.6%). Staphylococcus aureus was isolated in 20 participants (15.3%), Streptococcus pneumoniae in 8 (6.1%), and Moraxella catarrhalis with heavy growth in 3 participants (2.3%); a combination of S. aureus and S. pneumoniae was identified in 1 participant (0.8%). In throat swabs, resident microbiota was detected in 129/131 participants (98.5%), while Staphylococcus aureus was isolated in 2 children (1.5%). No statistically significant difference was found between children and staff with regard to nasal carriage (p = 0.157) or throat carriage (p = 0.987). Among the children, no statistically significant differences were observed according to sex or childcare facility. Analysis of nasal carriage by age showed a trend toward differences, although statistical significance was not reached (p = 0.061).Conclusion: The results provide regional data on the microbial colonization of the upper respiratory tract in the childcare settings studied. The absence of isolated S. pyogenes should be interpreted in the context of the specific study sample and sampling period and does not allow for the conclusion that the pathogen is absent from circulation in the community.

title: B-046 Automated De-Capping Compatibility of V-PRO® Blood Collection Tubes in a Total Laboratory Automation System
abstract: Abstract Background V-PRO® blood collection tubes are designed to meet the operational requirements of Total Laboratory Automation (TLA) systems in medical laboratory. Their precise dimensional specifications, consistent stopper performance, and robust medical-high grade polymer construction facilitate reliable automated de-capping, accurate sample handling, and efficient high-throughput laboratory workflows. Accordingly, this study aimed to confirm the compatibility and operational efficiency of V-PRO® blood collection tubes within a fully automated laboratory environment. Material & Methods A total of 510 V-PRO® blood collection tubes representing different tube types, sizes, and manufacturing batches were evaluated for automated de-capping compatibility within a TLA system. The study was conducted using the GLP System automated de-capping unit (Abbott) under standardized operating conditions. De-capping performance was assessed as a binary outcome (success or failure), and the primary endpoint was the de-capping success rate. Exact binomial analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism software to calculate the success proportion and corresponding 95% confidence intervals. Statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05. Results Automated de-capping was successfully achieved for all 510 V-PRO® blood collection tubes, resulting in a 100% success rate with no observed failures. Exact binomial analysis demonstrated that the observed success rate was 100% (510/510), with a 95% confidence interval ranging from 99.25% to 100%. No de-capping failures were recorded (0/510), corresponding to an estimated failure rate of 0% (95% CI: 0.00%–0.75%). The binomial test showed no statistically significant discrepancy between observed and expected outcomes (p > 0.9999), confirming suitability and reliable performance of V-PRO® tubes within the TLA system. Conclusion V-PRO® blood collection tubes demonstrated excellent compatibility with TLA, achieving a 100% automated de-capping success rate with no observed failures. Exact binomial analysis confirmed a high level of performance reliability, with narrow confidence intervals supporting the robustness and consistency of tube design under automated conditions. These findings indicate that V-PRO® blood collection tubes are well suited for high-throughput automated laboratory workflows and can be reliably integrated into TLA-based pre-analytical processes.

title: B-313 Validation of the MGISP-100 Automation Platform for Pre-Capture NGS Library Preparation in Clinical Workflows
abstract: Abstract Background Automation of next-generation sequencing (NGS) library preparation can improve efficiency, reproducibility, and contamination control by standardizing pipetting-intensive steps and reducing operator-dependent variability. In clinical laboratories, these gains may translate into more predictable turnaround times, reduced hands-on labor, and tighter control of process critical quality attributes (CQAs) that impact downstream sequencing performance. Here, we evaluated the MGISP-100 Automated Sample Preparation System (MGI Tech) for pre-capture library preparation in a routine-like clinical setting, using CQAs and sample-integrity indicators relevant to day-to-day laboratory release criteria. Methods Fifty-three routine-like specimens (29 whole-blood EDTA and 24 oral swabs; 24 males and 29 females) were processed. Genomic DNA was extracted using Maxwell (Promega). Pre-capture library preparation (DNA fragmentation, end-repair/A-tailing, adapter ligation, SPRI-based cleanups, and library PCR amplification) was performed either by an established manual workflow or on the MGISP-100 Automated Sample Preparation System using the xGen DNA Library Prep kit and xGen UDI Primer Plate 1 (Integrated DNA Technologies). Libraries were quantified by Qubit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and sized by TapeStation 4200 (Agilent). Capture/enrichment was held constant (manual, identical conditions in both arms) and was not evaluated as an outcome; analyses focused on pre-capture library preparation. Sequencing was performed on DNBSEQ-G400 (paired-end 300-cycle). A reference control sample was prepared under both conditions for head-to-head variant calling comparison using DRAGEN v4.3.17 (Illumina), summarized by F-measure across SNVs, INDELs, and CNVs. To assess sample integrity and potential mixture/cross-contamination, IDR_BAF (inter-decile range of B-allele frequency across variant sites) was extracted from validation-run samples and compared between workflows. Comparisons were reported overall and stratified by specimen type (whole blood EDTA vs swab). Results No MGISP-100–specific failures occurred, and QC pass rates were consistent across specimen types. Libraries met sequencing QC targets with appropriate fragmentation and yield (mean fragment size: MGISP-100 342.76 ± 13.19 bp vs manual 334.20 ± 20.80 bp; mean concentration: MGISP-100 70.97 ± 12.81 ng/µL vs manual 64.33 ± 13.97 ng/µL). In the control sample, variant calling performance was comparable between workflows (F-measure: SNVs > 0.97, INDELs > 0.77, CNVs > 0.50). IDR_BAF values remained below the laboratory alert threshold (<0.20) in both groups, supporting preserved sample integrity. Overall mean IDR_BAF was higher with MGISP-100 (0.12328 ± 0.01096; n=25) than manual preparation (0.11464 ± 0.00776; n=28) (p=0.00210; 95% CI 0.00332–0.01396), while remaining below the threshold. Conclusion In both whole-blood EDTA and swab specimens, the MGISP-100 Automated Sample Preparation System produced pre-capture libraries with QC metrics and downstream variant calling performance comparable to the manual workflow. The small shift in IDR_BAF observed with MGISP-100—although statistically significant—remained below the established alert threshold and is consistent with minor process effects (e.g., subtle differences in pipetting dynamics, bead mixing, or cleanup stringency) rather than actionable cross-contamination. Overall, MGISP-100 supports standardized, scalable pre-capture library preparation suitable for routine clinical NGS implementation without compromising key QC or sample-integrity indicators.

title: Behavioural and hormonal correlates of virtuality during autobiographical memory retrieval
abstract: Virtual reality (VR) is increasingly permeating medical practice, facilitating new health interventions and diagnostic tools to delay or alleviate cognitive aging. However, it remains unclear whether fully automated virtual memory tasks match the efficacy and physiological safety of traditional interventions administered by human providers. To address this, we evaluated an odour-triggered autobiographical memory task across four discrete conditions. Selected as strategic points along the latent „virtuality continuum”, these conditions model the step-by-step translation of clinical memory tasks—from reality human-facilitated real-world care (VR0), augmented care using multisensory VR (VR1) to fully autonomous, text-guided VR (VR2) and virtual agent-mediated interactions (VR3). Subjective sense of presence was equivalent across all VR environments (VR1–VR3), confirming a controlled baseline of visual immersion. Subjects recalled comparable numbers of autobiographical memories in all conditions, but the virtual social environment (VR3) triggered the longest recall durations. All VR environments elicited memories with more positive emotional valence than real-person delivery. Critically, salivary levels of the social hormone oxytocin were significantly decreased after tasks performed in automated environments (VR2 and VR3) compared to the human-guided VR1. These findings confirm VR’s high potential for memory training while highlighting a possible reduction in physiological social activation when replacing human providers with virtual agents. As virtual agents expand in daily healthcare, our data underscore the importance of assessing physiological social responses, particularly for prolonged interventions.

title: BronchoTop: Bronchoscopy Navigation via RGB-Only Topological Localization
abstract: Accurate localization of the bronchoscope within the bronchial tree is essential for clinicians to be able to reach target lesions, perform biopsies and avoid misidentification of airway segments during diagnostic and therapeutic procedures. However, existing navigation systems typically rely on patient-specific CT scans or additional external sensors, increasing cost, setup time and patient radiation exposure. This work presents BronchoTop, a real-time, RGB-only framework for topological bronchoscopy localization that eliminates the need for patient-specific data. BronchoTop estimates scope location relative to a generic airway model through four modules: lumen detection and tracking, lumen-branch label association, probabilistic scope location estimation, and switch verification. By using only standard bronchoscopy video input, BronchoTop provides practical, real-time navigational assistance to physicians. Evaluation on phantom, simulated and real data demonstrates state-of-the-art accuracy, improving existing approaches performance by over 20% on real bronchoscopy sequences. BronchoTop is the first published framework including both the localization algorithms as well as all the real data used, together with code to generate additional simulations, encouraging and facilitating further developments and benchmarking. The results highlight BronchoTop's potential to enhance procedural safety, efficiency and accessibility in clinical and robotic bronchoscopy.

title: CORPORATE SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY(CSR) PRACTICES IN MAHARATNA COMPANIES: AN ANALYSIS Of CSR ACTIVITIES AND EXPENDITURE
abstract: The foundations of corporate social responsibility (CSR) are based on the premise that, apart from public policy, corporations need to be sufficiently accountable for dealing with social issues. companies are expected to use their profits in areas such as education, poverty, gender equality, hunger alleviation, etc. The research methodology is a qualitative and is grounded on data gathered by already existing sources, including books, reports, research papers, and websites. The main goal of the study is to look at the CSR programs of the six leading Maharatna companies. The data has been compiled regarding the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, and subsequent initiatives are recommended based on the review. The research suggests that meeting the stated CSR objectives requires CSR approaches by the corporation to be identified with core business objectives and to involve strategic investment decisions and include careful measurement and reporting to the public. The paper outlines best practices, implementation challenges, and future opportunities of enhancing the role of corporate social responsibility in aggregate growth and development in India

title: COWFISH2A+ as a versatile and accessible platform for digital bioanalysis
abstract: Digital bioanalysis enables single-molecule detection of biomolecules and holds transformative potential across the life sciences and clinical diagnostics. However, its broader translation remains limited by accessibility and versatility. Here, we present COWFISH2A+, a compact, fully automated device integrating wide-field imaging with a custom dispensing module. Using an open-type microchip, COWFISH2A+ enables diverse assays at low cost through direct liquid deposition. As a proof of concept, we demonstrate two types of digital bioanalysis: a digital enzyme assay and an amplification-free digital genetic assay, SATORI. The digital enzyme assay discriminates alkaline phosphatase, a blood biomarker, at the single-isozyme level with sub-femtomolar sensitivity, while SATORI achieves attomolar-level detection of multiple pathogen-derived genetic targets. Furthermore, to demonstrate the translational potential of SATORI, we directly test 159 clinical specimens, detecting SARS-CoV-2 from nasopharyngeal swabs within ∼20 min with 92% sensitivity and 85% specificity. COWFISH2A+ thus provides an accessible and versatile platform for digital bioanalysis.

title: Capillary self-blood collection for centralized testing – a pan-European cross-sectional pilot study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Self-collection of capillary blood allows study participants to provide samples without in-person healthcare contact and to return them by mail to a central laboratory. We evaluated the feasibility and analytical agreement of internationally mailed self-collected capillary blood in a pan-European setting. METHODS: In this cross-sectional pilot study, adults attending the INFORM EU plenary meeting in Hannover, Germany provided two capillary blood samples: one sample was mailed from their country of residence (capillary mail-in sample, CMS); the other was analyzed within 24 h (capillary comparison sample, CCS). Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), C-reactive protein (CRP), creatinine, and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) were measured. Agreement was assessed with correlation coefficients, Deming and Passing-Bablok regression, and Bland-Altman analysis. RESULTS: Of 66 participants, 49 (74.2%) returned a mailed sample after a median transit of 8 days (Q25-Q75: 5-12). Analytically valid pairs were available for 17 (TSH), 16 (ALT), 16 (creatinine), and 19 (CRP) participants. Agreement was high for CRP (r and CCC = 1.00) and good for TSH (r = 0.90; CCC = 0.88). Creatinine showed a strong correlation but low concordance (r = 0.85; CCC = 0.19) with a proportional bias, and ALT showed the weakest agreement (r = 0.54; CCC = 0.21) and largest bias. Longer transit was associated with higher ALT differences (ρ = 0.57). CONCLUSIONS: International postal return of self-collected capillary blood was achievable, and the main constraint was insufficient plasma volume rather than delivery. CRP, and to a lesser extent TSH, reached acceptable agreement, whereas ALT and creatinine did not. Given the small number of valid samples and healthy study population, these findings need further confirmation. GERMAN CLINICAL TRIALS REGISTER IDENTIFIER: DRKS00033172 on January 30th, 2024.
authors: Dominik Schröder; Louis Kuhnke; Linda Hoffmeister; Christopher Schuchardt; Eva Hummers; Georg M N Behrens; Andrea Stölting; Metodi Stankov; Alexandra Dopfer‐Jablonka; Christine Happle; Frank Müller

title: Capsule biopsy and targeted sampling techniques: current status and future perspectives
abstract: Early screening and definitive diagnosis of gastrointestinal (GI) diseases remain major clinical challenges. Although wireless capsule endoscopy enables patients to undergo minimally invasive imaging of the GI tract, it cannot obtain tissue or fluid samples; therefore, a separate invasive endoscopic procedure is still required when a suspicious lesion is identified. The next logical step is to develop capsule systems capable of both visualizing and sampling lesions during a single swallowable examination. This review summarizes recent advances in smart GI sampling capsules, categorized according to the type of specimen collected (solid tissue vs. luminal fluid or microbiome) and the mode of device control. Miniaturized electromechanical systems (MEMS), stimuli-responsive materials, and magnetic actuation have substantially expanded the technical capabilities of sampling capsules; however, most active tissue-biopsy platforms remain at the preclinical stage. In contrast, several passive or environment-responsive luminal-sampling systems have progressed to early human evaluation. Major barriers to clinical translation include reliable lesion targeting, adequate and reproducible specimen acquisition, prevention of cross-contamination, device miniaturization, and demonstration of procedural safety. Artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted and autonomous targeting remain areas for future investigation rather than established clinical practices.
authors: Yixin Wan; Zichuan Han; Yuan Tian; Long Rong

title: Cerebral Air Embolism After Navigational Bronchoscopy Treated With Aspiration Thrombectomy: A Case Report
abstract: Systemic arterial air embolism is a rare but potentially devastating complication of bronchoscopic lung biopsy.A 68-year-old man with severe emphysema developed abrupt bradycardia, hypotension, and failure to regain consciousness after navigational bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia.Computed tomography demonstrated air within the left middle cerebral artery, and angiography confirmed proximal large-vessel occlusion.Urgent aspiration thrombectomy achieved complete reperfusion after one pass, with retrieved material compatible with thrombus.Despite technically successful reperfusion, major neurological deficits persisted.This case highlights haemodynamic collapse and delayed emergence as warning signs and supports rapid neuroimaging with selective endovascular treatment when an accessible large-vessel occlusion is present.
authors: Matthew Eardley; Anushka Jayakrishnan; Essam Hashem; Darshana Dhaka; Ashvini Menon

title: Clinical Artificial Intelligence in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: From Early Detection and Computational Pathology to Precision Oncology
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is being developed to analyze radiological, histopathological, molecular, and clinical data across the non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) pathway. This narrative review examines representative applications through August 2026, focusing on intended clinical use, validation, and the evidence required to influence care. Studies were selected purposively for clinical relevance and methodological importance. Imaging models support investigation of nodule detection, malignancy estimation, and future lung cancer risk, although predictive performance does not establish the benefit of changing screening or diagnostic pathways. In computational pathology, models classify tissue, quantify morphological features, and estimate selected molecular alterations. Foundation models extend these capabilities, but their evaluation requires attention to pretraining provenance and independence of downstream testing. Histology-based molecular prediction does not currently justify replacing validated molecular assays; prioritization of testing requires prospective workflow evaluation. Models evaluated in immunotherapy-treated cohorts can predict response or survival, but these associations do not establish differential benefit between treatments. The principal limitations include selected retrospective populations, incomplete assessment of calibration and clinically relevant thresholds, uncertain transportability, and limited evaluation of model-guided care. Evidence should therefore be interpreted at the level of the individual system and intended decision. Prospective evaluation, appropriate comparators, explicit failure procedures, and post-deployment monitoring are required before technical performance can be translated into clinical benefit.
authors: Luca Bertolaccini; Matteo Chiari; Sara Degiovanni; Antonio Mazzella; Giorgio Lo Iacono; Juliana Guarize; Monica Casiraghi; Lorenzo Spaggiari

title: Clinical advancements in Pulmonology – from Biological drugs to AI interaction in screening and detection
abstract: Clinical pulmonology has evolved from a pandemic-driven crisis care to a more precise, preventative and data-rich model of respiratory medicine. This chapter reviews the main clinical advances of this period against the background of the continuing global burden of chronic respiratory disease, tuberculosis and lung cancer. Seven approved monoclonal antibodies, including the biannual anti-IL-5 agent depemokimab, have changed the treatment goal to clinical remission in asthma. Real-world evidence from the PASSAGE study and the 2026 CHEST guideline for biologic selection supports this shift. Biologic therapy for eosinophilic, type 2 phenotypes in COPD is now established with mepolizumab and dupilumab, whilst the anti-IL-33 antibody tozorakimab and inhaled dual PDE3/4 inhibitor ensifentrine expand the treatment armamentarium. Nerandomilast, a selective inhibitor of PDE4B, is the first new antifibrotic for idiopathic and progressive pulmonary fibrosis in over a decade. DPP-1 inhibitor brensocatib is the first disease-modifying therapy for non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis. Pulmonary hypertension care is now risk-based, with the oral prostacyclin receptor agonist ralinepag, and tirzepatide is now the first drug therapy for obesity-related obstructive sleep apnea Robotic-assisted bronchoscopy, EBUS, and molecular profiling have improved lung cancer diagnosis, and oscillometry and multiple-breath washout have improved pediatric lung function testing. Today, artificial intelligence enhances CT nodule detection, cough and breath sound analysis, spirometry interpretation, exacerbation prediction, and clinical documentation. Its sensitivity gains, however, are frequently offset by reduced specificity, limited external validation and risk of bias. The chapter also addresses ethical and regulatory issues such as unequal access in low- and middle-income countries, data privacy and accountability. It said future progress should be based on precision, prevention and participation, with clinicians overseeing AI and ensuring effective therapies reach everyone who needs them.
authors: Dr. Ayesha Farheen; Anokhi Panchal; Srijamya Srijamya

title: Clinical evaluation of an intelligent venipuncture robotic system: performance, patient acceptance, and pre-analytical outcomes.
abstract:
Objectives

In high-throughput outpatient settings, manual venipuncture is frequently constrained by extreme time pressure and inherent human operator variability, which collectively exacerbate pre-analytical errors and diminish operational efficiency. To address these clinical challenges, we conducted a retrospective study of an intelligent venipuncture robot using 13,803 clinical encounters collected over 18 months in a high-volume outpatient clinic.

Methods

We analyzed performance metrics and patient feedback across three consecutive phases to evaluate both the system's technical maturation and patient acceptance. Furthermore, we validated its clinical utility by comparing procedural success, failure causes, and specimen rejection rates against historical manual practice records.

Results

The results demonstrated that the robotic success rate increased steadily over time (from 95.02 % to 97.57 %) alongside sustained high patient acceptance (up to 96.70 %). Most crucially, the robotic system demonstrated a remarkable full-period zero specimen rejection advantage, effectively eliminating the pre-analytical sample rejections that typically compromise manual phlebotomy. During the same observation window, the primary cause of failure shifted chronologically from device puncture errors (47.58 % in Phase I) to patient movement (57.14 % in Phase III).

Conclusions

This study provides robust real-world data supporting the integration of intelligent venipuncture robotics. Given the evident shift in failure mechanisms toward human factors, future advancements must prioritize optimizing human-machine interaction design and implementing targeted pre-procedure psychological interventions to mitigate involuntary patient movements.
authors: Wang B, Yao Y, Ye L, Wu D, Zhao H, Zheng M, Xu Y, Zhang M, Xia J, Wang A.

title: Clinical validation of an AI-based computer-aided detection system for risk classification of radiologist-identified prostate MRI lesions
abstract: AI-based tools for MRI demonstrate high sensitivity for clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) detection, yet performance varies across cohorts. We evaluated a commercial AI-based computer-aided detection (AI-CAD) system for csPCa classification in radiologist-identified suspicious lesions in a real-world setting. This retrospective, single-centre study included 113 men with a PI-RADS ≥ 3 index lesion undergoing 3T in-bore MRI-targeted robotic biopsy. Cases were analysed using QP-Prostate ® . Lesion-level diagnostic performance was assessed for csPCa (Gleason ≥ 7) and overall PCa (Gleason ≥ 6) under two positivity thresholds (Moderate + High and High-only). Analyses were stratified by prostate zone; exploratory analyses included PI-RADS 3 lesions and a theoretical simulation of biopsy-sparing. Mean age was 70.1 (SD 7.9) years; csPCa prevalence was 58.4%, and 15.9% of lesions were PI-RADS 3. For csPCa classification, sensitivity and specificity were 0.92 and 0.32 (Moderate + High), and 0.79 and 0.43 (High-only), respectively. Performance was higher in the peripheral zone (PZ) than in the transitional/central zones (TZ + CZ) across both thresholds. For overall PCa, sensitivity and specificity were 0.91 and 0.43 (Moderate + High), and 0.80 and 0.61 (High-only), respectively. In PI-RADS 3 lesions, csPCa sensitivity was 0.33 across thresholds, with specificity improving from 0.60 (Moderate + High) to 0.67 (High-only). In the theoretical biopsy-sparing simulation, 20/113 biopsies (17.7%) would have been withheld with Moderate + High and 34/113 (30.1%) with High-only, with 5/66 (7.6%) and 14/66 (21.2%) csPCa cases missed, respectively. Among patients without csPCa, 15/47 (31.9%) and 20/47 (42.6%) biopsies would have been avoided, respectively. In a challenging cohort of radiologist-identified PI-RADS ≥ 3 lesions, the AI-CAD system maintained high sensitivity for csPCa classification particularly in the PZ, with lower performance in the PI-RADS 3 exploratory subgroup. The theoretical biopsy-sparing simulation showed a threshold-dependent trade-off between potential biopsy withholding and missed csPCa. Prospective validation is required before AI-CAD-informed biopsy avoidance can be considered clinically safe and effective.
authors: Joan Carles Vilanova; Rubén Martínez-Granados; David Bazaga; Encarna Sanchez Bernabe; Almudena Fuster-Matanzo; Claudia Llinares-Monllor; Andrea Lorenzo Polo; Ana Jiménez-Pastor; Ángel Alberich‐Bayarri

title: Clinically Suspected Systemic Arterial Gas Embolism during Robotic-Assisted Bronchoscopy: a Case Report
abstract:
Background: Systemic arterial gas embolism (SAGE) is a rare but potentially catastrophic complication of robotic-assisted bronchoscopy with lung biopsy. During general anesthesia, the earliest manifestations of SAGE may be limited to transient electrocardiographic or hemodynamic abnormalities. The absence of visible intracranial gas on subsequent imaging does not exclude the diagnosis. We report a case of clinically suspected SAGE during robotic-assisted bronchoscopy in which intraoperative sentinel signs preceded delayed emergence and focal neurologic injury. Case presentation: A 78-year-old woman underwent robotic-assisted bronchoscopy under general anesthesia for biopsy of a 4.6-cm right middle lobe ground-glass opacity using transbronchial needle aspiration and cryobiopsy. Significant airway bleeding occurred after sampling. Immediately after biopsy, she developed transient tachycardia, hypertension, bradycardia, and ST-segment elevation in lead V5. Although these abnormalities resolved, she was unresponsive shortly after extubation and developed right gaze deviation, facial twitching, abnormal movements, and absent right upper-extremity withdrawal to pain. Head computed tomography showed no acute abnormality, and brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated left frontal and precentral cortical diffusion restriction without visible intracranial gas. Because SAGE was strongly suspected, she received 100% oxygen, levetiracetam, endotracheal reintubation, and hyperbaric oxygen therapy at 2.8 atmospheres absolute approximately 4 hours after bronchoscopy. High-sensitivity troponin I peaked at 5,116 ng/L and left ventricular ejection fraction improved from 45-50% to 60% the following day. She was extubated on post-procedure day 10 with persistent neurologic deficits. On post-procedure day 18, she experienced hypoxic cardiac arrest associated with bilateral pulmonary emboli and an acute aortic dissection and died the following day after transition to comfort-focused care.

Conclusions:

During bronchoscopic biopsies under general anesthesia, unexplained ST-segment changes, hemodynamic instability, or delayed neurologic recovery should prompt immediate consideration of SAGE, even when initial neuroimaging is negative. Administration of 100% oxygen, airway and hemodynamic support, minimization of airway pressures, and urgent consultation for hyperbaric oxygen therapy should not be delayed while awaiting radiographic confirmation.
authors: Hom BM, Rosenberg B, Xu NY, Szokol JW, McCarthy M.

title: Closed-loop artificial intelligence agents for animal epidemic prediction and decision support in livestock farming: a review
abstract: Animal diseases continuously threaten livestock production and public health, yet current surveillance approaches remain largely passive and fragmented. Conventional artificial intelligence models typically function as open-loop predictors, delivering static outputs that fail to accommodate the dynamic operational needs of veterinarians in real-world farm settings. This review explores an emerging paradigm of AI agents for animal disease monitoring, emphasizing how such agents can transition from passive observation to active intervention through a closed-loop perception-decision-feedback architecture. We first classify multi-scale sensing technologies: at the micro-scale, automated molecular diagnostics and biosensors; at the macro-scale, computer-vision-based phenotyping. These technologies collectively provide the data streams required for continuous surveillance. The review then discusses how multi-modal inputs, time-series forecasting, resource-aware decision-making, and reinforcement learning can be integrated into an agent-based workflow. Importantly, most current veterinary research evidence supports only the individual components of this framework, rather than the deployment of fully autonomous, iteratively evolving closed-loop agents in actual field environments. Translating closed-loop AI from a conceptual framework into a reliable veterinary decision-support tool will therefore require further advances in validation, standardization, governance, and human oversight.
authors: Yuzhi Wang; Yingtong Zhou; Liyu Li; Huiling Xu; Wangze Ni; Xiaoliang Li

title: Comparative Clinical Impact of Transbronchial Cryobiopsy and Forceps Biopsy Utilizing Radial EBUS Guidance for the Diagnosis of Peripheral Pulmonary Lesions
abstract: BACKGROUND: The prevalence of peripheral pulmonary lesions (PPLs) is increasing; however, their diagnosis remains challenging despite the availability of various modalities. Transbronchial cryobiopsy (TBCB) offers an additive benefit in diagnostic yield. Combining radial endobronchial ultrasound (R-EBUS)-guided transbronchial forceps biopsy (TBFB) with cryobiopsy may enhance tissue acquisition. METHODS: This retrospective study reviewed 197 patients with pulmonary lesions who underwent bronchoscopy-guided biopsy between January 1, 2023, and December 31, 2023. Strict diagnostic yield and diagnostic accuracy were calculated according to the predefined definition, and the additive impact of cryobiopsy was further analyzed. RESULTS: The cohort comprised 117 patients in the TBFB group and 80 in the TBCB group. The overall mean age was 68 years and 60% were male; baseline lesion characteristics were comparable across groups, with lesions <20 mm in 45% and 44% of the TBFB and TBCB groups, respectively, and a positive CT bronchus sign in 82% and 85%. Compared with TBFB alone, the TBCB group achieved a higher strict diagnostic yield (76.2% vs. 63.2%) and diagnostic accuracy (86.8% vs. 80.4%), respectively. Among the 33 patients in whom R-EBUS-guided TBFB was followed sequentially by cryobiopsy, the addition of cryobiopsy further increased diagnostic yield and accuracy by 21.6% and 13.5%, respectively. Procedure-related severe bleeding and severe hypoxia occurred in 2.5% and 1.3% of patients in the TBCB group, both significantly higher than the corresponding rates in the TBFB group (p < 0.05). CONCLUSION: R-EBUS-guided TBCB demonstrated efficacy for diagnosing PPLs, offering superior diagnostic yield and accuracy than conventional R-EBUS-guided transbronchial lung biopsy alone.
authors: Rong Lih Ho; Jung Ho Han; So Yeon Kim; Junsu Choe; Sun Hye Shin; Byeong‐Ho Jeong; Sang‐Won Um; Kyungjong Lee

title: Comparative Evaluation of Conventional, Chromogenic, and Automated Methods for Identification of Candida Species
abstract: Background: Accurate identification of Candida species is essential for timely antifungal therapy, particularly in the context of the rising prevalence of Non-Candida albicans species with variable antifungal susceptibility. Advances in diagnostic methods have expanded laboratory options beyond conventional phenotypic techniques, necessitating systematic evaluation of their diagnostic performance. Aim: The present study was therefore undertaken to comparatively assess conventional phenotypic methods, chromogenic media, and automated identification systems for the identification of Candida species isolated from clinical specimens. By evaluating their diagnostic performance in a tertiary care setting, this study aims to provide practical insights to guide laboratory workflows and optimize the diagnosis of Candida infections in diverse healthcare environments. Materials & methods: A prospective laboratory-based comparative study was conducted in a tertiary care teaching hospital in eastern India from November 2013 to September 2015. A total of 400 clinical specimens were processed, yielding 150 Candida isolates. Species identification was performed using conventional phenotypic methods, chromogenic media (CHROMagar Candida), biochemical sugar assimilation tests, and an automated identification system (VITEK). The sensitivity and specificity of Sabouraud’s dextrose agar, CHROMagar Candida, and corn meal agar were calculated using automated identification as the reference standard. Results: Non-Candida albicans species predominated among isolates. CHROMagar Candida demonstrated the highest diagnostic performance, with a sensitivity of 98.6% and specificity of 99%, enabling rapid and reliable presumptive species identification within 24–48 hours. Sabouraud’s dextrose agar showed comparable sensitivity (98%) but lower specificity (97%), while corn meal agar exhibited high specificity (98%) with reduced sensitivity (96.6%). Sugar assimilation tests provided supportive biochemical confirmation but required longer turnaround times. Conventional methods such as germ tube testing remained useful for presumptive identification of Candida albicans but lacked discriminatory power for non-albicans species. Conclusion: CHROMagar Candida offers superior accuracy and speed for routine identification of Candida species and, when integrated with conventional morphology and automated systems, forms an effective tiered diagnostic approach. Adoption of such strategies can enhance laboratory efficiency and support antifungal stewardship, particularly in resource-limited settings. Keywords: Candida species; Chromogenic media; CHROMagar Candida; Automated identification systems; Diagnostic accuracy; Clinical mycology
authors: Ansuman Dash; Dipti Pattnaik; Nirmala Poddar; Dr. Madhushree Mishra

title: Comparative diagnostic performance of robotic, electromagnetic navigation, and fluoroscopy bronchoscopy for lung cancer in peripheral pulmonary lesions: a prospective, multicenter, parallel-controlled trial.
abstract:
Introduction

Peripheral pulmonary lesions (PPLs) are difficult to access bronchoscopically due to their distal location. Although robotic, electromagnetic navigation, and fluoroscopy-guided systems have been developed, inconsistent study designs have limited direct comparison of their diagnostic performance.

Objectives

This study aimed to compare the diagnostic performance and lesion-specific advantages of robotic bronchoscopy system (RBS), electromagnetic navigation bronchoscopy(ENB), and fluoroscopy bronchoscopy(FB) for PPLs.

Methods

In this multicenter, prospective, parallel-controlled trial, consecutive patients with suspected PPLs from 7 centers were assigned to the RBS, ENB or FB groups according to a predefined cyclic sequence for biopsy between 2019 and 2023. Subgroup analyses of diagnostic yield were performed according to lesion characteristics. Machine-learning models and a web-based platform were developed for clinical evaluation.

Results

A total of 270 patients were included, with 90 patients in each group. RBS achieved a higher overall diagnostic yield than ENB and FB (87.8%, 83.3% and 63.3%, respectively; P < 0.001). Strict diagnostic yield was also highest in the RBS group (81.1% vs 61.1% and 47.8%; P < 0.001). In the subgroup analysis, RBS performed better for 15-30 mm lesions and lesions within 15 mm of the pleura (P < 0.005), whereas ENB showed a diagnostic yield comparable to RBS for malignant, larger and solid lesions. Navigation and biopsy success rates in the RBS group were 100%, with more precise trajectories and lower displacement than the other two techniques (P < 0.001). Based on lesion characteristics, internally developed models (all AUC > 0.96) were integrated into a visualization platform to estimate the technique-specific diagnostic success for individualized PPLs.

Conclusion

This multicenter study demonstrates that RBS, ENB and FB have distinct diagnostic advantages across different PPL subgroups. RBS showed better diagnostic performance in selected challenging lesions, whereas ENB achieved comparable performance in malignant, solid, or larger lesions. The image-based prediction platforms may further support individualized selection of transbronchial navigation strategies for PPL or lung cancer diagnosis.

title: Comparing MiniDock MTB, chest radiography, and symptoms for tuberculosis screening: a community-based evaluation in Karachi, Pakistan

title: Comparison of Procedural Safety and Diagnostic Yield Between Robotic-Assisted Bronchoscopy Platforms.
abstract: Robotic-assisted bronchoscopy platforms are becoming ubiquitous to aid in sampling peripheral pulmonary nodules. A head-to-head performance between the 2 widely available platforms (Ion and Monarch) has not been investigated. To explore differences in diagnostic yield and safety parameters of the Ion and Monarch platforms. A secondary objective was to elucidate radiographic features of nodules that predicted procedural success. A retrospective, 2-site cohort study of adult patients scheduled for robotic-assisted bronchoscopy of pulmonary nodules between August 2020 and August 2023. The procedure was performed with either the Ion or Monarch robotic-assisted bronchoscopy platform, depending on the site, with the assistance of standard 2D fluoroscopy. A series of logistic regression models was constructed to explore the effect of platform type on diagnostic yield, after correction of prespecified confounders. We utilized an inferential lasso regression model to explore the predictive properties of nodule radiographic characteristics on yield. A total of 217 cases were analyzed. The median nodule size was 1.4 cm (IQR=1.1 to 2.1), which was similar across both groups. Our parsimonious model suggested no difference in obtaining a positive diagnosis for the Ion platform [OR: 1.5 (0.9-2.7)]. Both nodule size [OR: 1.42 (1.09-1.86)] and presence of a bronchus sign [OR: 2.14 (1.14-4.01)] correlated with diagnostic yield in our inferential model, both in systems and in aggregate. Both platforms offer promise in sampling small peripheral nodules. Neither platform appears to improve procedural yield, although caution is advised regarding the generalizability of this finding. Both nodule size and the presence of the bronchus sign may be helpful in preprocedural patient selection.
authors: Peter C Nauka; S Mehdi Nouraie; John Tepper; Paul Yacono; Matthew Vercauteren; Matthew Schuchert; Rajeev Dhupar; Daniel G Dunlap; Roy Semaan

title: Cotton‐Swab‐Anchored Suspension Technique for Hands‐Free Lower Extremity Limb Sterilization During Surgical Preparation
abstract: Manual limb suspension during surgical preparation is labor-intensive, requires additional personnel, and may increase the risk of musculoskeletal injuries among surgical staff. We describe a cotton-swab-anchored suspension technique that uses a sterile bandage (Kerlix) looped around the ankle, secured with 2 cotton swabs inserted into the knot, and suspended from a heavy-duty intravenous pole. This method enables hands-free limb elevation, allowing efficient preoperative preparation. After completion of preparation, the limb is released by simply removing the cotton swab. This technique eliminates the need for manual limb holding, reduces occupational strain, provides stable mechanical support, and enables quick, controlled limb release without instruments. It is cost-effective, reproducible, and suitable for various lower extremity procedures.
authors: Chen Zhou; 狐周周; Lather Sagar; Shengwu Yang; Zhenhan Deng

title: DNA metabarcoding samples from nest soil and beaks outperform samples from talons and faeces when identifying diversity of white-tailed eagle diet in South Greenland
abstract: Abstract DNA metabarcoding is an emerging approach to study diets across a broad range of species but requires careful optimisation of the sample collection method and substrate used. The suitability of different sample types to identify the diet of the target species remains under investigated. Here, we address these knowledge gaps by collecting four different sample types - faeces, beak swabs, talon swabs, and soil samples - during nest visits of white-tailed eagles ( Haliaeetus albicilla ) during the 2025 breeding season in South Greenland. We further investigated whether some eagle dietary taxa could act as vectors for microplastic pollution. Our analyses revealed a broad diet, with 25 dietary taxa for white-tailed eagles. Lumpfish ( Cyclopterus lumpus ) was the most frequently detected dietary taxon in the diet, which was composed of 75 % fish, 19 % birds, and 7 % mammals. Our findings indicate that diets varied strongly between nesting sites. Although each sample type was efficient in capturing diet, soil and beak swabs were most promising for eagles and gave comparable results. On the other hand, faeces provided a distinct dietary profile with a reduced detection of fish, while requiring an increased sample size, and talon swabs missed rare food items. Finally, we recovered microplastic contamination in 33 % of our samples, but no dietary taxon was associated with microplastic pollution. Taken together our results underline the overlooked value of soil from nests to provide dietary information and highlight the necessity to deepen our knowledge of Arctic food webs and their microplastic contamination.
authors: Mael Perroud; Kay Lucek; Knud Falk; Nicholas Per Huffeldt

title: Data‐Driven and Physics‐Informed Modeling Perspectives for Soft Manipulators: From SINDy to Hybrid Intelligence
abstract: Soft manipulators offer a route to safer, more adaptive and physically intelligent robots, but their compliant bodies remain difficult to model, predict and control. Large deformation, distributed actuation, hysteresis, material variability and contact-rich interaction challenge both classical mechanics-based models and purely data-driven approaches. Here, we examine emerging modeling perspectives for soft manipulators through a conceptual progression from sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics to hybrid intelligence. We discuss how sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics (SINDy), Koopman learning, neural ordinary differential equations, physics-informed neural networks, and hybrid physics machine learning models contribute complementary capabilities, including interpretable reduced-order dynamics, control-ready prediction, continuous-time latent modeling, physics-constrained field reconstruction, and residual correction. We present that no single modeling approach is sufficient for the next generation of soft robotic systems. Instead, progress requires integrated modeling ecosystems that combine mechanical structure, data-driven discovery and task-aware adaptation. Such hybrid-intelligence frameworks can transform models from passive descriptions of deformation into active components of sensing, control, design and decision-making, enabling soft manipulators that are more interpretable, robust and deployable in real-world environments.
authors: Wenbo Hui; Yunyi Wang; Teng Zhang; Yang Chen; Min Pan

title: Designing a Functional Social Robot for Blood Test Procedures in the Emergency Department: A Human-Centered Approach
abstract: Blood tests are a common initial procedure in the emergency department (ED) and are often experienced as highly stressful, particularly in acute care areas. Robots’ social capabilities may help address patients’ emotional needs, yet their integration into such a complex environment requires clear alignment with existing clinical workflows. We present a human-centered design process for a robotic platform intended to support blood test procedures in the acute care area of the ED. A need study indicated two central guidelines: practical assistance with blood test equipment and emotional support for patients and nurses. The informed iterative design process resulted in a robotic platform that provides a mobile work surface for blood test equipment, with a small robotic arm that performs social gestures intended to provide emotional support. An initial field-validation deployment of the robot across four blood test procedures suggested that patients and nurses perceived the robot as a positive assistant capable of supporting emotional needs. We highlight the potential of integrating social features into functional robots in challenging environments such as the acute care ED.
authors: Yuval Rubin Kopelman; Dikla Dahan Shriki; Zohar Fein; Mahmod Hamdan; Rony Ben Ami; Daniel Armoni; Andrey Grishko; Nevo Heimann Saadon; Hadas Erel

title: Detection of Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) in Black-Horned Capuchin Monkeys, Brazil
abstract: We carried out a viral surveillance study on 30 black-horned capuchin monkeys (Sapajus nigritus) in Rio Doce State Park, a protected area in the Brazilian Atlantic Forest. Samples were tested for orthopoxviruses, flaviviruses, coronaviruses, influenza viruses, and a wide range of other respiratory viruses using molecular and serological methods. RT-qPCR detected the respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) genome in oral swabs from two asymptomatic juvenile females sampled in an area with high human interaction. This finding indicates a possible exposure of an population to RSV, a contagious human pathogen, and highlights the importance of increased surveillance at the human-wildlife interface.

title: Detection of Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa among Diabetic Foot Ulcer Patients in Wasit Province
abstract: Diabetic foot ulcer infection is a severe clinical complication that is determined by neuropathy, vascular impairment, tissue injury and successful bacterial invasion. Diabetic foot infections are the most common complication affecting people with diabetes, and bacterial pathogens play a key role. In this study, 90 subjects including 35 patients with diabetic foot ulcer (DFU) as well as 35 diabetic patients without ulcers and 20 healthy controls were enrolled. Methods: Wound swabs from ulcer group were processed through conventional culture, selective media, VITEK 2 identification and PCR. Univariate analysis identified isolation of P. aeruginosa (17/35;48.6%) being the most frequent isolate followed by S.aureus (13/35;37.1%) while other bacteria represented only 14.3%. Molecular confirmation using 16S rRNA, nuc and oprL genes showed complete concordance with phenotypic identification. Identification probabilities of both species on the VITEK 2 were greater than 90%. P. aeruginosa and S. aureus are clinically significant in diabetic foot ulcers due to their persistence, biofilm-forming ability and antimicrobial resistance; study results highlight concurrent use of culture, automated identification and PCR for accurate diagnosis/management
authors: Zaman Sami Kareem; Alaa Ali Matrood

title: Detection of the pqsA Gene and Histological Changes Induced by Pseudomonas aeruginosa
abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa uses quorum-sensing systems to coordinate activities regulated by specific genes, such as metabolic and environmental responses. The pqsA gene is a key component of the pqs pathway (quinolone signaling in Pseudomonas aeruginosa).This study focused on applying a mouse model to some local isolates of P. aeruginosa and identifying those carrying the pqsA gene. The study included isolating 150 samples for analysis, which resulted in confirmation of the presence of 58 isolates of P.aeruginosa. The specimens including wound swabs, burn samples, urine samples, middle ear swabs, and sputum were collected from different hospitals. The presence of the pqsA gene was confirmed molecularly using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) on 19 selected isolates, all of which showed positive amplification (448 bp). The experimental mouse model consisted of Swiss albino mice, divided into a control group and two treatment groups with low (1×10⁴ CFU) and high (1×10⁸ CFU) concentration of bacteria. We evaluated body weight before and after exposure and also performed histological examinations of the liver and lung tissue. The results showed that increased bacterial concentrations led to increased weight loss and extensive histological changes. In contrast, low concentrations produced only minor tissue changes. Statistical analysis (results are presented as means ± SE calculated using one-way ANOVA) confirmed these findings as statistically significant (p ≤ 0.05). Based on the above information, it can be concluded that the pqsA gene is highly conserved in local isolates of P. aeruginosa and that the presence of this gene leads to significant effects in host tissue in controlled in vivo studies. Therefore, this research contributes to understanding of the bacterial quorum sensing mechanism, the pathogenicity of bacterial species and their ability to interact with host bacteria in in vivo studies
